Haitian mayor says 30 people killed in violent weekend attacks
Attacks occurred late Sunday, mayor of Kenscoff area says
A powerful gang coalition attacked a once-peaceful farming community nestled in the hills above Haiti's capital, killing multiple people, an official told The Associated Press on Monday.
Jean Massillon, mayor of Kenscoff, said armed men raided the community late on Sunday, setting fire to homes and killing residents.
"It is still impossible to establish a definitive death toll due to access difficulties and communication problems," he told the Associated Press.
Massillon, speaking separately to Reuters, said at least 30 people had been killed.
'Sowed chaos'
Wails filled the air in Kenscoff as survivors found the bodies of friends and family strewn on the streets early Monday.
Farmer Mathurin Pierre, 41, told The Associated Press that he lost 14 loved ones and that an unknown number remain missing.
Massillon blamed the attack on members of Viv Ansanm, which the U.S. government designated as a foreign terrorist organization last year.
"They sowed chaos," Massillon said.
He said gang members targeted a church and homes, including those owned by Dr. Jean (Bill) Pape. He is a renowned doctor who runs a non-governmental organization in Haiti that helps patients, including those with HIV and tuberculosis.
No further details about the attack were available. A spokesperson for the U.N.-backed gang suppression force did not immediately return a message seeking comment.
Gangs control an estimated 70 per cent of Port-au-Prince, the capital, with Viv Ansanm repeatedly targeting nearby Kenscoff.
Gang violence has displaced a record 1.5 million people across Haiti, where more than 3,100 people were reported killed from January to June and another 1,189 injured, according to UN statistics.
The attack comes less than a week after the U.S. government deported more than 160 people to the troubled Caribbean country for the first time since the Trump administration won a legal battle to end temporary protected status (TPS) for some 350,000 Haitians.
Haiti's government has said some of the deportees included TPS holders working legally in the U.S. and even some who were Haitian in origin but not born in Haiti. The U.S. Department of Homeland Security said in a statement to the AP on Monday that those deported on Friday included several gang members with criminal records ranging from assault to drug trafficking.
Haiti is scheduled to hold general elections for the first time in more than a decade on Dec. 13, and it has been registering voters in Port-au-Prince and beyond. Experts have warned it's currently too dangerous to hold elections.
With files from Reuters

Tiranga Yatra at 13000 Feet- National Pride Celebrated in Tawang’s Border Villages
The spirit of patriotism reached the high frontiers of Arunachal Pradesh as the Chuna and Mago Sector Vibrant Villages in Tawang district hosted a Tiranga Yatra at an altitude of nearly 13,000 feet. The event brought together local communities, the civil administration, Panchayati Raj representatives, and security forces in a celebration of national unity and pride.
The program was organized as part of the Har Ghar Tiranga campaign and commemorated 150 years of Vande Mataram, connecting the national celebration with the people living in one of India’s most remote border regions.
A Community Celebration at the Frontier
The Tiranga Yatra was organised by the Jang Sub-Divisional Administration in collaboration with the Indian Army, Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP), BJP Mandal 3-Mukto, and residents of Chuna and Mago.
The yatra was flagged off by the Zilla Parishad Chairperson, in the presence of the Additional Deputy Commissioner, Assistant Commissioner, Panchayat representatives, Heads of Offices, senior personnel of the Indian Army and ITBP, and local residents.
The participation of people from different sections of the community reflected the spirit of collective responsibility and the strong bond between frontier communities, the administration, and the forces serving in the region.
A 300-Meter Tricolour Across the Mountains
The highlight of the celebration was the carrying of a 300-meter-long National Tricolour from Chuna to Mago village.
Against the backdrop of the Eastern Himalayas, the Tricolour made its way through the high-altitude terrain, turning the yatra into a memorable expression of national pride. The event was further enriched by a band performance by students of Higher Secondary School Jang, whose participation brought the enthusiasm of the younger generation to the celebrations.
Honouring India’s Frontier Communities
Events such as the Tiranga Yatra also highlight the important role of Arunachal Pradesh’s border communities in the country’s frontier landscape. Villages such as Chuna and Mago are located in challenging high-altitude terrain, where communities continue to live, work, and contribute to the social and economic life of the region.
The participation of villagers alongside the Indian Army, ITBP, civil administration, and Panchayati Raj representatives demonstrated the importance of community participation in strengthening the social fabric of the border areas.
The event also complemented the broader objective of the Vibrant Villages Programme, which seeks to improve infrastructure, connectivity, livelihoods, and public services in strategically located border villages while strengthening their connection with the rest of the country.
The Tricolour at the High Frontiers
The Tiranga Yatra at Chuna and Mago was more than a ceremonial event. It brought the national spirit directly to communities living at one of India’s highest and most remote frontiers.
The sight of a 300-meter Tricolour moving through the Himalayan landscape served as a powerful reminder of the unity that connects every part of the country, from its cities and towns to its most distant border villages.
At nearly 13,000 feet, the celebration reflected the resilience of Arunachal Pradesh’s frontier communities and the enduring spirit of national unity.

Would Marmoush joining Tottenham be a masterstroke or risk?
- Published
Tottenham are looking to sign Manchester City forward Omar Marmoush, with talks between the clubs progressing.
No agreement has yet been reached, but the Egypt international could become the latest addition to Roberto De Zerbi's squad, with the north London club's summer spending looking set to exceed £300m.
Spurs have already spent £229.5m on centre-back Jan Paul van Hecke and midfielders Sandro Tonali and Mateus Fernandes.
And on Friday it was announced that they have agreed a £75m deal to sign Manchester City winger Savinho as they look to strengthen their attack.
Spurs forward Dominic Solanke has endured injury problems over the past 18 months, while team-mate Richarlison has entered the final year of his contract.
Marmoush's influence at City has diminished but the numbers suggest Tottenham would be getting a forward whose skillset differs considerably from their existing options.
- Spurs in talks to sign Man City's Savinho and Marmoush 
  - Published23 hours ago
From Frankfurt sensation to City understudy
Joining Eintracht Frankfurt in May 2023 on a free transfer from Wolfsburg, the then 24-year-old Marmoush found form in his first season with the German side scoring 17 times across all competitions.
He then scored 15 Bundesliga goals from 8.9 expected goals (xG) during the first half of 2024-25, while registering nine assists in 17 league appearances. Across all competitions before leaving Germany, he had 20 goals and 13 assists in 26 games.
Set-pieces were another notable part of his game. Marmoush became the first player in Europe's top five leagues since Lionel Messi in 2019 to score directly from a free-kick in three consecutive competitive matches. Manchester City then paid £59m for him in January 2025.
The early signs were encouraging. Marmoush scored his first career hat-trick against Newcastle, struck the winner in City's FA Cup quarter-final at Bournemouth and then scored from long range against the same opponents in the Premier League. It was judged to be the goal of the season.
But there were difficult moments too.
With City trailing Crystal Palace in the 2025 FA Cup final, Erling Haaland handed Marmoush the ball for a penalty. His effort was saved by Dean Henderson as City went on to lose at Wembley.
Former Manchester City defender Nedum Onuoha does not believe that moment should define Marmoush's spell at the club.
"When I see Marmoush, I don't see the penalty miss," Onuoha told BBC Sport. "I see the strength he has with some of the runs he makes in behind."
Why did his role shrink?
Marmoush has scored 16 goals in 62 appearances in all competitions for City since arriving from Frankfurt.
Eight of those came in 36 appearances in 2025-26, but his Premier League involvement fell considerably.
He started only eight league games and played around 700 minutes, fewer than he managed after joining midway through the prior campaign.
His league return was three goals and three assists, with his 3.53 expected goals figure close to his actual scoring output. The issue was therefore not simply finishing.
Marmoush found himself competing for minutes in a side built around Haaland, while City further strengthened their attacking options.
"All the positions Marmoush could play are being filled by people who are specialists in those roles," said Onuoha. "Haaland is essentially always going to be the number nine, while City also regularly play with number 10s and Guardiola likes his wingers to stay wide."
What would Marmoush give Spurs?
Marmoush is primarily a number nine, but he has rarely been confined to one role across the front line.
At Frankfurt he was used predominantly through the middle but also appeared as a second striker and from the left. City have followed a similar pattern, using him mainly as a central attacker while also deploying him from the flank and just behind another forward.
That flexibility could suit De Zerbi. His teams have often relied on forwards changing positions, dropping towards the ball and then attacking the space created when opponents are drawn out. Marmoush is comfortable doing both.
Onuoha sees the Egyptian as most dangerous when he is able to threaten the space beyond the defence.
"As much as he is good dropping towards the ball, I think he is better when he plays on the shoulder," he said. "He needs to be in a team that will constantly play balls in behind and force the opposition to run back towards their own goal. That's when you see a better version of Marmoush."
Opta's Premier League numbers from last season show he averaged 11.46 runs in behind per 90 minutes, almost identical to Solanke's 11.61 and ahead of Richarlison's 10.03. But he also offered considerably more with the ball.
Marmoush averaged 5.67 progressive carries per 90 minutes, compared with 3.24 for Solanke and 2.48 for Richarlison.
He also led both Tottenham forwards for shots, chances created, successful take-ons and touches in the opposition penalty area.
He had 3.86 shots per 90 minutes compared with 2.81 for Richarlison and 1.80 for Solanke, while Marmoush created 1.55 chances against 0.92 and 0.54 respectively.
He also produced 0.77 goals and assists per game, ahead of Richarlison's 0.69 and Solanke's 0.27.
The sample is smaller because of his limited league minutes, but the profile is clear.
Marmoush is more inclined to take opponents on and manufacture shooting opportunities for himself than Spurs' existing central forwards.
That could make him particularly useful when opponents sit deep and deny Tottenham the space to attack directly. Onuoha feels De Zerbi's style could suit him better.
"Sometimes the fit can simply be better," he said. "Marmoush's ability to run in behind and link the play could be huge assets for Spurs. They won't be shy about playing those passes into him and forcing opponents on to the back foot."
Alongside Solanke rather than instead of him?
Marmoush would not necessarily have to replace Solanke.
His experience playing off another attacker creates the possibility of using the pair together, with Solanke occupying central defenders while Marmoush moves into wider areas or drops between the lines.
That may be particularly attractive to De Zerbi because Marmoush can also accelerate into the spaces opened when Tottenham play through an opposition press.
"Solanke is different to Marmoush. He's got more of a physical presence," said Onuoha. "I could see the goalkeeper playing a flat ball into Solanke, Marmoush coming underneath him to receive it, and that becoming the start of the attack.
"The two of them could complement each other. Playing in a front two might bring out more of Marmoush's strengths."

The Hatred That Broke American Politics
Race is the wound America sees. Anti-Semitism is the one it doesn’t.
“If you want to defend the South and Western civilization from the Jew and his dark-skinned allies, be at Charlottesville on 12 August.” Nine years ago, that message spread across the internet. The call was answered by several hundred white supremacists, who marched through the University of Virginia. The rage-filled men carried torches, chanting, “Jews will not replace us.” They swarmed around the historic rotunda, arriving at a statue of the school’s founder, Thomas Jefferson. There they met a tiny band of student counterprotesters who responded with their own chant: “Black lives matter.” That evening turned violent, the first act in a deadly weekend. Most Americans remember the torches, the rage, the death. But those clashing chants also revealed a gap between the targets of hatred and the words available to name it.
Race is the wound America sees. Anti-Semitism is the one it doesn’t. Jews have frequently been imagined as a colorless minority whose great persecution took place elsewhere, or as a group whose Christian-adjacent faith flourished with the religious freedom they found in the United States. But their in-betweenness has always been part of the danger: Jews have never fit neatly into America’s frameworks of identity, and that failure to fit has marked them as suspect, out of place, or impossible to categorize. Depending on the audience, Jews are dismissed as beneficiaries of white privilege or treated as not quite white at all—too assimilated and not assimilated enough, too powerful and too marginal. That ambiguity has placed them, again and again, at the center of America’s battles over free speech and equal protection. When hatred does not fit existing categories, we tend either to ignore it or to overcorrect—both responses that distort the boundaries of free expression.
Our failure to reckon with the anti-Semitism of Charlottesville—on the right and the left—was not merely a missed opportunity. It helped create the opening into which illiberalism has since rushed.
August 2017 marked a turning point, not just for racial populism but for American democracy. That crisis seeded a surge in anti-Semitism. It also helped produce a government campaign against such bigotry that has become a tool for undermining freedom, championed by the Trump administration only when it serves the White House’s purposes. Meanwhile, the progressive left has struggled to sustain its critique of Israel’s war with Palestine—and of American responsibility for a moral catastrophe—without letting that critique curdle into conspiracism.
Americans appear to face an impossible choice between protecting free speech and safeguarding equal rights. But that is a false dichotomy. Honoring both will, however, require de-exceptionalizing anti-Semitism. And that, in turn, necessitates returning to Charlottesville, and reckoning with how both the left and the right failed in its aftermath.
Over the course of 2017, three separate racist rallies took place in Charlottesville. In May, the alt-right provocateur Richard Spencer led a small rally in downtown Charlottesville to protest a city-council decision to remove two century-old Confederate monuments. A University of Virginia alum with a passion for Wagnerian opera, Spencer dressed old hatred in new clothes. He spoke grandly of restoring white supremacy, and of defeating liberal conspiracies to change America beyond recognition. President Trump’s election gave him cause for hope that Black Lives Matter and antifa would be crushed. “We will not be replaced from this world,” Spencer screamed as plumes of green and gray smoke from flares rose into the sky. “Whites have a future! We have a future of power!”
Two months later, the Ku Klux Klan paraded through town. Although they had come to protest the removal of a statue of Robert E. Lee, they held banners denouncing Jewish communism and the satanic Talmud. They were met with a massive, raucous counterprotest, inspired in part by a newly formed Black Lives Matter chapter in town, staged by citizens determined to oppose the hatred.
August brought round three: Spencer returned to town, accompanied by a who’s who of the far right, answering the call to join what they labeled the “Battle of Charlottesville.”
Officially, Unite the Right was a free-speech march in defense of the monument. But several organizers had ties to violent extremist groups and online they made their intentions clear. “Next stop: Charlottesville, VA. Final stop: Auschwitz,” wrote Andrew Anglin of The Daily Stormer. The planners fantasized about mowing down protesters with cars, and repeating the Holocaust—even as they denied it happened. They wrapped retrograde hatred in constitutional pretense. Free speech became both shield and sword.
The weekend brought mayhem: dozens of injuries, the murder of Heather Heyer, the death of two state troopers. Yet it also exposed the entanglement of race and religion in the racist imagination, which conceived of Jews as invisible power brokers, racial chameleons, white imposters, and anti-Christian infidels.
Charlottesville shocked the country. Yet in its aftermath, America had no vocabulary for describing anti-Semitism in relation to other hatreds—let alone for responding to it. Then–UVA President Teresa Sullivan denounced the violence and “racist, anti-immigrant, homophobic and misogynistic chants,” but made no mention of Jews. The great majority of other statements issued by Virginia-college presidents repeated the same failure. The local school superintendent discarded her back-to-school speech and instead spoke of the need to name “the hate that had visited our city,” which had targeted “our Latino, Muslim, bisexual, transgender, Christian, and Black students.” Jews, again, went unmentioned.
These educators were not anti-Semites. They were well-meaning liberals for whom other forms of hatred eclipsed anti-Semitism; anti-Black racism, for one, loomed larger. But anti-Semitism was hardly new to Charlottesville. The poet Karl Shapiro wrote of his time at UVA in the 1930s: “To hurt the Negro and avoid the Jew is the curriculum.” The dean once tracked applicants in three categories: “Virginians, non-Virginians, and Hebrews.”
And that was not true of just Virginia. Americans have long been accustomed to seeing Jews as a model minority whose success proved their belonging, and to dismissing anti-Jewish hatred as something that happened elsewhere. Without having reckoned with their nation’s own long history of anti-Semitism, Americans met it in 2017 with confusion and silence.
The centrist liberal response constituted a form of occlusion. White supremacy was understood strictly in racial terms, and anti-Semitism was blocked from view. The chants in Charlottesville fixated on Jews. The response did not.
What liberals failed to see, the populist right first denied, then exploited. Trump could not condemn the marchers without asserting there were “very fine people on both sides.” For two years, his administration shrugged off any serious response.
Then the strategy shifted. Trump seized on anti-Semitism—but only anti-Semitism from the left. A 2019 executive order focused on college campuses, targeting anti-Zionist expression while lifting anti-Semitism out of the broader landscape of hatred for special treatment. This marked the first moment in which Trump threatened to defund American universities without even a proper investigation. Anti-Semitism became a cudgel for the administration to wield against political enemies and liberal institutions, not a hatred to be fought on equal, consistent terms.
The same pattern played out in Virginia. Glenn Youngkin tried to ignore Charlottesville entirely while running for governor in 2021. On his first day in office, he issued several executive orders. One of them banned “inherently divisive concepts” such as critical race theory from classrooms in the name of free speech. Another announced a commission on anti-Semitism whose final report reduced Charlottesville to two paragraphs out of 13,000 words.
Many Republican politicians chose to attack civil-rights protections for most minorities while selectively championing them in the Jewish case. Genuine anti-Semitism was met with a sledgehammer instead of a scalpel, violating other rights in the process. UVA faced a wholesale attack as part of the wave of disproportionate punishments inflicted on institutions of higher education in the aftermath of October 7, 2023. But the institution’s vulnerability had deeper roots. The progressive left had its own failure to reckon with—one that played out on campus and left universities unable to articulate a coherent defense when the attacks came.
The progressive left failed by exclusion. After the weekend of terror in 2017, UVA’s Jewish Leadership Council worked with the Minority Rights Coalition on repair and renewal. Yet when they applied to join as a member organization, they were rejected on account of their pro-Israel affiliate group. Remove that Zionist organization, they were told, and they could join. After objections that Jews had been prime victims, a compromise was floated: Jewish students could join as an honorary minority group without voting rights. Jewish student leaders, among them a young woman who had fled fearing her life on August 11, denounced the moral myopia.
As this conflict escalated in spring 2018, pro-Palestinian protesters stormed a Hillel event featuring Israeli Druze and Jewish reserve soldiers. Shouting slogans through a megaphone, they denounced Zionists as fascists and refused “dialogue with racists.” Their heckler’s veto muddled their critique of Israeli military propaganda. Jewish students claimed the rhetoric threatened them; protesters said the soldiers’ presence did the same to Palestinian students.
Everyone claimed the mantle of free speech while denouncing the other side as perpetrators of hate speech. The progressive left, for all of its commitment to confronting hatred, rarely turned that lens inward. The question of where anti-Zionism ended and anti-Semitism began was dismissed, not deliberated.
That moment was a rehearsal for every debate we’ve lived through since. How do you balance free speech and equal rights when competing groups on campus have political and personal ties to a live conflict? Where does legitimate critique end and hatred begin? All of it was there, seven years ago, before October 7, before the campus protests of 2024. When war erupted again, Americans were unprepared. Each side had made its cause exceptional—anti-Semitism a unique hatred, Zionism a unique evil—and that rhetorical brinksmanship left no room for the harder work of ensuring uniform equality and pluralism for all. From silence to chaos, we found ourselves without a coherent language to combat hatred.
The past several years have illustrated an old Yiddish saying: Lekh mikh nisht, un lakh mikh nisht. Literally: “Don’t beat me, and don’t lick me.” But in effect: Don’t demonize us, but don’t fetishize us, either. Since Charlottesville, Jews have been both demonized and tokenized across the political spectrum. Building a way forward requires de-exceptionalizing anti-Semitism—not erasing its distinct features, but treating it as one hatred among others, deserving the same protections, no more and no less.
This wisdom extends beyond Jews. Every group deserves protection from hatred without becoming a political football. Every group deserves to be seen clearly—neither as villain nor as mascot. That includes Palestinian Americans, who have watched their own dehumanization dismissed while anti-Semitism is used against their speech.
This is why we need a new model—one that treats no group’s claim to protection as special, one that recognizes free speech and equal protection as complementary values enabling all citizens to participate fully in democratic life. Building that model will require Jewish communal leaders to resist the politicization of Jewish fear—and progressive coalitions to make room for Jewish particularity without imposing a litmus test on Jews alone.
What would this look like in practice? Rejecting the warping of anti-Semitism for partisan ends. Acknowledging anti-Semitism from all directions rather than only the versions that serve our politics. Building democratic coalitions across differences rather than demanding ideological purity as the price of admission.
Nine years after Charlottesville, we have seen the stumbles and overcorrections, the cynicism and despair. What we haven’t done is imagine a better future in which fighting anti-Semitism strengthens civil rights for all.
That work begins with honesty about how we got here. The bigots who marched in Charlottesville were real. So is our capacity to build something better. In 2017, two chants collided in the dark. We can still answer them together.

Stocks stagger and oil rises as traders eye Iran threat, Nvidia results
HONG KONG: Asian stocks fluctuated on Tuesday (Aug 25) while oil edged up as investors assess a US plan for the "economic asphyxiation" of Iran, while tech firms struggled following another down day on Wall Street and ahead of earnings from chip titan Nvidia.
With the war against Tehran now in its sixth month, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the White House was declaring an "economic D-Day" on the Islamic republic and threatened to hit countries that trade with it.
The threat comes with talks to reopen the Strait of Hormuz stalled and neither side showing any sign of backing down - pushing oil prices up for most of August, which has in turn fanned long-term inflation fears and put pressure on bond markets.
"Around the globe, our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone," Bessent told journalists Monday.
"We are going to hold everyone accountable, and this is economic asphyxiation of this regime," he said, adding that countries not joining US sanctions would "share" in Iran's isolation.
President Donald Trump was making phone calls to world leaders with requests to stop interactions with Tehran, Bessent said.
The Treasury Department said Iran's digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping sectors would be targeted for sanctions.
Both main contracts fell more than two per cent Monday as Bessent's comments appeared to suggest the US will hold off military action, but they ticked higher in early Asian trade.
His "increasingly aggressive economic campaign against Iran is designed to squeeze Tehran's access to the global financial system while keeping the pressure economic rather than allowing the market to immediately price another military escalation", wrote Stephen Innes, global strategist at Quintex Intel.
"For now, oil appears to have heard the message that way, which is doing Washington the considerable favour of taking some inflation pressure out of the system."
Still, equities struggled as tech firms once again bore the brunt of selling, tracking a retreat in their counterparts on Wall Street.
Tech-rich Seoul sank more than two per cent at one point as chipmakers SK hynix and Samsung retreated, while Hong Kong, Shanghai, Taipei and Manila were also off.
There were gains in Tokyo, Sydney, Singapore and Wellington.
The tepid performance comes ahead of much-anticipated earnings from Nvidia, which has become something of a bellwether for the AI boom.
With vast sums lavished on artificial intelligence investment over the past two years, markets are growing increasingly nervous about whether firms can deliver results to match.
And analysts have warned that even forecast-beating figures can sometimes not be enough.
Charu Chanana at Saxo Markets said: "Investors are not simply asking whether Nvidia can deliver another strong quarter. They are asking whether it can deliver enough upside to justify already-high expectations, especially with bond yields elevated."
Eyes will also be on other tech names' releases, including Salesforce and Marvell.
Also in focus is this week's annual gathering of central bankers, economists and finance chiefs in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, where the Federal Reserve's boss Kevin Warsh is due to speak.
His comments will be parsed for clues about monetary policy with inflation still stubbornly high and after Bessent said the Treasury would buy back more of its own bonds to push down borrowing costs after the 30-year yield surged to a 19-year high.
The Canadian dollar edged slightly higher after retreating against the US dollar Monday as Trump vowed to double tariffs on vehicles from its neighbour, fanning a trade war.
The US president's threat comes after the two failed Friday to reach a deal to avert new 50-per cent US tariffs on select Canadian goods. The duties took effect Saturday, and Ottawa laid out plans for retaliation.

French tourist dies in Death Valley after car gets stuck in mud
- Published
A French tourist has died in California's Death Valley after becoming stranded on the side of the road during 46.6C (116F) heat.
Police found 68-year-old Pierre Michel Formosa recently following a brief search, with the National Park service saying he died while trying to seek help in the blistering heat when his car got stuck in mud.
"This is a heartbreaking reminder of how quickly conditions here can turn dangerous," Death Valley National Park Superintendent Mike Reynolds said in a statement.
Soaring temperatures across the United States have caused millions of people to sweat through record heatwaves, leading to dozens of heat-related deaths.
Formosa was driving through Death Valley with his French travelling companion last Monday when their vehicle became stuck in mud on West Side Road.
The pair sought help by walking across the salt flats, before severe heat prevented the 68-year-old from continuing after 1.3 miles, according to the Death Valley National Park.
The travelling companion managed to hail down a nearby driver, before rangers and police found Formosa later that afternoon where he was pronounced dead.
"Death Valley is an extraordinary place, but its heat, distances, and remoteness can be dangerous, regardless of experience," Reynolds said.
"We're grateful to everyone who took part in the search, and our thoughts are with his loved ones."
Coroners would determine the cause and manner of his death, the national park said.
An extreme heat warning is currently in effect across Death Valley, which brands itself as the "hottest place on Earth", according to its official website, having recorded a global high of 57C (134F) in 1913.
Forecasters at the National Weather Service expected Southern California would experience its "hottest week of summer so far", the bureau said in a recent statement.
Record heatwaves have endangered tourists visiting US landmarks throughout the summer.
At least four hikers died in June while trekking through the Grand Canyon, state authorities reported in Arizona.

Grealish back for Man City - but for how long?
- Published
Jack Grealish is back in the fold at Manchester City... for now.
The 30-year-old is into the final year of his reported £300,000-a-week contract at Etihad Stadium and was discarded by Pep Guardiola in the Spaniard's final season in charge, being allowed to join Everton on a season-long loan deal.
That spell on Merseyside was cut short in January by an Achilles tendon injury, but the Englishman has returned to full fitness and featured in both of City's games so far this season.
Grealish came on during the Community Shield defeat by Arsenal and played the final eight minutes of City's late comeback win over Bournemouth in Sunday's Premier League opener.
The winger appeared to be in good spirits while sitting on the bench against the Cherries and thanked City fans on social media afterwards for a "nice welcome" on his home return.
Though he has been handed a new lease of life under Guardiola's successor Enzo Maresca, no guarantees are being offered that Grealish will remain a City player come transfer deadline day on Tuesday, 1 September.

Options open as Maresca waits 'to see what happens'
Grealish was spotted in training when the City players reported for pre-season in mid-July. He was supposed to join his team-mates on the tour of the Far East but was ruled out after suffering an injury setback.
The former Aston Villa skipper has seen Guardiola's departure as a fresh start and impressed in training to such an extent he has earned a place back in the squad.
Heading into the final week of the transfer window, clubs sources have left all options open for Grealish's future - staying at the club, going out on loan again or leaving permanently.
Maresca has not ruled out a move either, saying after Sunday's game: "He is here and it is my duty to coach Jack and to try to get the best.
"Then it is one more week to go and we will see what happens. Not only with Jack but also other players."
Everton have 'remained in contact'
Grealish looked to be getting back to his best during his loan at Everton, contributing two goals and six assists in 20 appearances before his injury.
Such was his form at the beginning of last season, he claimed the Premier League's Player of the Month award for August and quickly became a fans' favourite.
City sources say there have been no concrete offers for Grealish so far this summer, with a return to Hill Dickinson Stadium looking the most viable option, should he move away.
Everton are yet to make an approach and try to agree a deal, but he remains of interest to the Toffees.
"He is a player we have remained in contact with," Everton chief executive Angus Kinnear told BBC Radio Merseyside.
"It was no secret he decided to have his injury rehabilitation done here for the remainder of last season - he didn't have to do that as he could have gone back to Manchester City.
"He is a player who has fallen in love with the right shade of blue, but ultimately he is a City player and we have to respect that. What I do know is that the supporters and the team embraced him and treated him as one of our own. That gave us a good platform to have a longer term conversation with him.
"The most important thing is that he is back fit after he had a serious injury, so I was delighted to see him get some minutes in the Community Shield."

I Tested the Best Mattress Toppers for a Good Night’s Sleep
Featured in this article
My hunt for the best mattress toppers has taught me how transformative they can be. It started years before now, when I was throwing my back out nightly on a thin futon mattress in my fresh-out-of-college days. I tried a few cheap sheets of foam that barely helped with my back pain. I gave up for a while and instead switched to a too-soft mattress (equally problematic), until finally finding the right combo: a firm, supportive mattress with a nice mattress topper on top to support my problem areas and side-sleeper shoulder pain.
These toppers can alleviate your aches, sink you into insanely comfortable memory foam, and even pack supportive coils like a mattress. My favorite toppers range from soft wool layers and memory foam to firm and even hybrid toppers (yes, you can get mattress toppers with springs in them) to find the best option for you and your mattress.
Curious what you should get? Read on to find my best mattress toppers for everything from back pain issues, college students, and more. All prices below are for queen-size toppers.
Updated August 2026: The Layla Memory Foam Mattress Topper and Nectar Firmer Mattress Topper are new picks, and I've added a new section about mattress protectors and ensured up-to-date links and prices.
Honorable Mentions
Not everything we test makes the cut as a pick, but that doesn't mean it's a bad mattress topper. Here are a few that our testers slept on and got a good night's sleep with but didn't love as much as the picks above.
Avocado Alpaca Topper for $1,240: If you're looking for a mattress topper that's extra soft, WIRED reviewer Scott Gilbertson recommends the Avocado Alpaca Mattress Topper. He says it's one of the softest things he's ever slept on, and that it's like sleeping in a cocoon of fluffiness. While it's only 2 inches thick, it still has that cozy sinking sensation of deeper mattress toppers. There are two options: medium-firm or plush, with the first using organic wool and the second using what Avocado calls “baby alpaca” fiber. Luckily that's a reference to how soft it is, not the age of the alpaca itself. It's certainly a luxury purchase, but a great pick of you want something super soft. Right now only the twin and twin XL sizes are in stock.
Avocado Eco Organic Mattress Topper for $339: This is another good organic mattress topper, made from latex foam. It's got a pleasant bouncy feel to it thanks to the latex, rather than a sinking feeling you'll get from memory foam. It's softer than our main organic pick, which might be more your preference, but I really prefer this to memory foam if I'm not sleeping on the Birch topper.
Brooklyn Bedding 3-Inch Latex Mattress Topper for $629: This latex mattress topper was fine, with a nice spring to it and a good softness without being too soft. But the Avocado Eco was more comfortable and nearly half the price.
Helix Dual Comfort Mattress Topper for $372: If you and your partner have different sleep surface needs—specifically, one of you loves a firm surface while the other wants a softer one—Helix has made a mattress topper with you in mind. The Helix Dual Comfort Topper has a softer side and a firmer side, so each person can get their ideal mattress feel without needing to splurge on a split king bed. The softer side uses memory foam infused with copper gel, which promises the “Luxury Plush” feel that has a gentle sinking sensation, while the firmer side uses high-density foam that kept my back-sleeper husband's spine nice and straight as he likes. Plus, it has a cooling cover wrapping it up into one cohesive topper.
Helix Premium Memory Foam Mattress Topper with GlacioTex for $372: This memory foam topper doesn't have as much of a sinking sensation as the Company Store or Tempur-Pedic toppers, for better or worse—my hips felt a little lower than the rest of my body, and I noticed more motion transfer than with the aforementioned foams. But this Helix topper is a good option if you don't want that super-sinking feeling. There's no heat retention whatsoever due to the hypoallergenic GlacioTex cover, and it has handy straps that attach to each corner of the mattress. Helix also has a trial period and limited lifetime warranty, so you can give this one a try and change your mind, unlike Tempur-Pedic, which has no return policy. —Kat Merck
Nest Soft Latex Topper for $644: Nest's latex-based topper looks and feels like an incredibly soft pillow top has been added to your mattress. It's one of the softest toppers I've ever tried, and it had a memory foam-adjacent feel of sinking into the topper, but with a little more spring and pillowy feel to it. It's one of the most expensive ones we've tested, though, and isn't hugely better, nor does it offer the most support.
Nolah Mattress Topper for $292: If you're looking for that new-bed feel, Nolah's topper adds a fresh layer of a semi-dense proprietary foam inside an organic cotton cover to the top of any mattress. It's just 2 inches thick, and the firm version softened WIRED reviewer Martin Cizmar's bed, offering some pressure relief and a plush new-bed feel.
PlushBeds Natural Latex Mattress Topper for $316: If you love something firm but want a thicker option than 2 inches, Scott recommends PlushBeds’ topper instead. It has five firmness levels, and he's a big fan of the extra-firm option. It's also a nice range if you want to pick a really specific level of firmness, as most other toppers only offer one or two options.
Saatva’s Graphite Memory Foam Topper for $305: This topper's three inches of foam are infused with graphite, which draws in and dissipates heat. Memory foam is notorious for running hot, but WIRED reviewer Kat Merck and her husband both thought the graphite worked pretty well in cutting down on some (though not all) of the body-heat absorption, and the thickness of the CertiPUR-US-certified foam worked to virtually eliminate motion transfer. Former WIRED reviewer Julia Forbes similarly found the cooling properties to be more neutral than truly cooling, but that can still be a big help. Saatva offers a long trial of 180 days, so you can easily try it out and see if it works for you.
Tempur-Pedic Tempur-Adapt Mattress Topper for $359: According to WIRED reviewer Kat Merck, our resident memory foam fan and reviewer, this is a top-of-the-line memory foam topper for softening a too-firm mattress, and it works very well to prevent motion transfer. It doesn't have her favorite iteration of Tempur-Pedic's memory foam, but it still works well. It also has a washable cover that zips off, and corner straps keep the topper securely in place, plus a 10-year warranty (but no trial or returns).
Tempur-Pedic Tempur-Cloud Topper for $164: I like a soft bed. In fact, if you had asked me before I tried the Tempur-Cloud topper if a bed could be too soft, I’d have said no. But I have changed my mind. There actually exists a mattress topper that might be too soft. I’m a stomach sleeper, and this memory foam is so plush and so deep that during my week of testing I found myself having to practically fling my body if I needed to move at any point during the night. It also has a tendency to sleep hot, and because a user sinks so deep, there’s a potential for neck pain if they normally sleep with an overstuffed pillow. But aside from that, the Tempur-Cloud topper is basically the last word for soft-bed fans who want to completely eliminate both motion transfer and any trace of a hard mattress. —Kat Merck
Turmerry Latex Mattress Topper for $199: If you want something organic on a budget, this 2-inch latex topper is a good price and our favorite organic topper on a budget. You'll have to buy the cover separately, but you don't need it if you want to save the money. Turmerry uses a five-zone design to make the topper firmer in some areas, like your head, and softer around others, like your shoulders.
Toppers We’d Skip
Leesa Mattress Topper for $224: This mattress topper didn't have great construction. We found it didn't fit neatly on the bed, had weird spots on the edges, and was too soft.
Brooklyn Bedding 4 lb. Memory Foam Topper for $290: Neither my husband nor I could get a good night's sleep when this mattress topper was on our bed. It also doesn't offer the same benefits as other memory foam toppers we've tested.
What About Mattress Protectors?
If you looked up mattress toppers when you really meant mattress protectors, which are a thin, water-resistant covers to keep your mattress safe from spills and stain, then fear not: We have a few options for you. You might even want to buy one of these to protect your mattress topper, especially if it doesn't have a washable cover. Here are a few mattress protectors we've tried and liked.
Bear Waterproof Mattress Protector for $72: I love this waterproof mattress protector. It's on my son's bed, and I'm incredibly jealous of how easy it is to get on and off the bed; my bed has an irritating design that needs to go underneath the mattress and get zipped on and off. This Bear one is similar to a bedsheet with elastic sides to go over the mattress. The sides of the cover aren't waterproof, but the long middle section is and is easy to spot with its quilted topping. You'll want to line up the cover to make sure you cover as much of your mattress as possible. While it's lightweight and thin, it's kept everything from nighttime accidents to surprise throw-up sessions off the mattress, and has walked away from it stain-free after a quick wash. I need one for every bed in the house in this era of my life with young children. The protective top layer is made of cotton and polyester. Bear also promises that it's breathable and won't hinder the Celliant cooling factor of its mattresses or similar ones thanks to HeiQ technology built into the protector.
Sijo TempTune Cooling Mattress Pad for $175: I’d personally consider this model from Sijo as a mattress protector more than a pad, since it functions more as a protective cover to help the bed stay cool rather than adding much padding. It’s made from moisture-wicking mica nylon (mica is a naturally heat-resistant and thermally conductive mineral) and Tencel (synthetic fiber made from eucalyptus wood pulp), which combine to help create a cooling fabric that regulates surface temperature. It also has a cotton lining underside that's infused with Sijo Clima microcapsules that Sijo claims adapt to your body to stay at optimal temperatures throughout different seasons. The surface is also waterproof, which I consider more water-resistant, as it didn’t soak up liquid entirely, but when I dumped half a glass of water on the surface, it stayed on top for over thirty seconds before I started to feel the liquid seep below. I also appreciated the 16-inch deep sides that helped it stay on top of my mattress, unlike some others I tested. Plus, it’s Oeko-Tex certified and has a 30-night trial, and free shipping on orders over $100. Although this cover is more water-resistant rather than -proof, it stayed on without bunching throughout the night. It added another layer of protection; just don’t expect it to add cushioning like a true pad would. —Molly Higgins
Sijo AiryWeight Eucalyptus Mattress Protector for $80: I like eucalyptus bedding because it’s breathable—good for hot sleepers like me—and it has a silky, soft feel. The eucalyptus fibers naturally wick away moisture, and this protector from Sijo is OEKO-TEX certified, hypoallergenic, and asthma-friendly. It’s composed of soft lyocell—semisynthetic fiber made from wood pulp—on top, with recycled polyester, and enhanced double TPU backing for waterproof protection. Because of the softer lyocell, this water-resistant cover isn’t crinkly or noisy like similar models claiming to be waterproof. However, the elastic sides tended to bunch and pull up on the sides, and it didn’t stay perfectly in place nightly. Overall, I’d say this protector is more water-resistant than waterproof. During testing, I poured small amounts of water, which didn’t leak through to the mattress underneath, but any more than half a cup slowly leaked to the side underneath and needed to be dried/aired out. If you’re looking for a lightweight, cooling natural eucalyptus cover that will resist small amounts of moisture, this works, but don’t expect to be able to have complete protection against accidents or major spills. —Molly Higgins
Quince Organic Waterproof Mattress Protector for $82: If you’re looking for an inexpensive water-resistant mattress protector that’s more heavy-duty and also organic, this is the pick for you. Although it’s not as “crunchy” and stiff as older waterproof mattress cover models of yesteryear, it definitely feels more natural and utilitarian than other models I’ve tested. It has a slightly rough feel because it’s made from undyed organic jersey cotton. Its underside is a waterproof polyurethane nonwoven material. Of all of the mattress protectors and covers I tested, this one kept the mattress drier for longer, although after over a minute and a half of a knocked-over glass of water, there was some seepage. My mattress underneath still stayed a lot drier than other models tested. I appreciated that this model is naturally hypoallergenic and doesn’t include harmful chemicals like phthalates or latex, and was deep enough with stretchy elastic that it stayed on my bed without slipping. Although it is a little rougher to the touch because of the woven natural fibers, it’s an affordable price point for a high-quality, water-resistant, organic mattress cover. —Molly Higgins
FAQs
What Is a Mattress Topper?
A mattress topper is a sheet of supportive materials—options include memory foam, latex foam, cotton, or even coils—that you add to the top of your mattress to change the feel without replacing the entire mattress. It's a good option to soften up a mattress that's too firm or to add some targeted support to a mattress you already like. Some toppers can make a mattress more firm, too, like our favorite organic topper pick.
How Do You Know if You Need a Mattress Topper?
It's a great thing to add if you need a surface change without needing to replace your entire mattress. A mattress topper won't fix an old or unsupportive mattress (check out our guide to the Best Mattresses to fix that!), but it can take a good mattress and make it into a perfect one with the right makeup.
I struggle with back pain and am a side sleeper, so I gravitate toward toppers that are soft for my shoulders but aren't so soft that my back isn't supported. My editor Kat Merck has a too-firm mattress to which she likes to add a memory foam topper to achieve her ideal level of softness. What you want in a topper will depend on your sleeping preferences and what changes you want in the mattress you already have. But a lot of folks can benefit from a good topper.
What Are the Types of Mattress Toppers?
Wool: Wool mattress toppers are usually filled with wool batting or stuffing—think the stuff you fill a quilt or upholstered chair with—and wrapped in cotton. It's soft, but not as extremely soft as memory foam and not as springy as latex is, either. Wool is a good temperature regulator, so it's a nice choice for hot sleepers.
Pillow Top: Pillow top mattress toppers are designed to have the fluffy feel of a pillow on top of your mattress. The insides of a pillow top can vary: Some add a pillow top design over layers of foam, while others are simply a pillowy layer of down feathers between you and your mattress. Our favorite pillow top uses latex but still has a fluffy, slightly sinking feeling of lying down on a pillow.
Latex: Latex is a manufactured substance, made from rubber trees. That rubber base gives it a nice bounce and spring compared to memory foam. Even though it's not labeled as foam, a latex topper usually has a foamlike sheet similar to memory foam as its base. It's also sometimes referred to as man-made organic, since its base is a natural substance, but it does have to be processed in order to become the latex you'd sleep on or use in other products. You'll get less sinkage with latex compared to memory foam, and less heat retention.
Memory Foam: Memory foam is actually polyurethane (a plastic polymer) foam, created by adding other compounds—the exact combination of compounds varies by company—to the polyurethane to create the memory foam itself. It's also known as “viscoelastic” polyurethane foam, or low-resistance polyurethane foam (LRPu). It's designed to conform to your body but return to its original shape afterward; the “memory” name comes from remembering its original shape. Memory foam tends to be one of the softest toppers, and it has a lot of sinkage (which you might love, might hate) and tends to retain more heat. Some companies add extra ingredients, like cooling gel or graphite, to help make the memory foam cooling.
Serene Foam: Serene foam is a newer trademarked material created by Carpenter Co., the parent company of Casper Sleep. It's made of billions of polyurethane bubbles like memory foam, but also consists of microscopic air capsules. It's designed to address some of the downsides of traditional memory foam, including heat retention and variable firmness levels, while maintaining the same plush, pressure-relieving feel. A quick warning if you love a heating pad: polyurethane Serene foam is not recommended for use with heated devices like electric blankets or heating pads.
Hybrid: Hybrid mattress toppers use multiple fillings that can be found on their own. These combinations can vary; our favorite hybrid topper from Helix uses coils and foam, while ViscoSoft's hybrid topper uses a mix of memory foam and soft fiber for a pillow top feel. If you're feeling like a single type of topper isn't suiting your needs—whether it's too soft or not soft enough—a hybrid option might be best for you.
How Thick Should a Mattress Topper Be?
Mattress toppers are usually available in 2- or 3-inch heights, and some even come in a whopping four inches. The inches aren't necessarily an indicator of how good a topper will be for your sleeping needs, but if you know you want a super soft experience, you might want a thicker topper to get a softer feel.

Williams was already a well-known radio star when she launched “The Wendy Williams Show” on TV in 2008. The series ended in June 2022, although the host had taken a leave of absence starting in 2021 due to medical issues related to lymphedema and Graves’ disease.
The star entered a court-appointed guardianship in 2022, and in 2024, her team disclosed that she had been diagnosed with aphasia (affects language and communication abilities) and frontotemporal dementia, a disorder that impacts behavior and cognitive functions.
Williams has been vocal about her objections to the guardianships, and her attempts to be removed from it. Just last week, a paparazzi took a video of Williams in New York, where according to the New York Post, she said, “I want out!” as she entered a building. Last year, she called into ABC’s “The View” and told her guardian Sabrina Morrissey and the judge who declared her “legally incapacitated” to “get off my neck,” declaring, “I need a new guardian.” Also last year, she told “The Breakfast Club” radio show that “I feel I’m in a prison” and “I am not cognitively impaired.”
While past documentaries on Williams have focused on her health crises and guardianship, “Clap If You Care” appears to be more focused on the star’s career prior to the end of her show. The doc, according to Peacock, “celebrates the outrageous fun, cultural impact and meteoric rise of ‘The Wendy Williams Show.’”
Here’s the full logline: “Skyrocketing from unlikely beginnings as a radio host to her impact on entertainment culture, Williams redefined the daytime talk genre with her outrageous on-screen fun on the long-running, Daytime Emmy-nominated talk show. While praising Williams’ TV reign, the documentary also sheds light on the complicated truths about the cost of fame and answers long-lingering questions surrounding the infamous exit from her own show. Over 20 former staffers from the talk show will share their behind-the-scenes experiences and memories of the pop culture icon.”
Williams was an executive producer on Lifetime’s two-part docuseries “Where Is Wendy Williams?,” which chronicled her decline via footage shot between August 2022 and April 2023. It was a sequel of sorts to Lifetime’s 2021 documentary “Wendy Williams: What A Mess,” which looked at her public divorce and other public mishaps.

WNBA star Natasha Cloud confronts Enes Kanter Freedom over anti-trans shirt at Fever-Sky game
Former NBA centre was ejected from WNBA game after confrontation
Former NBA centre Enes Kanter Freedom was ejected from Sunday night’s Indiana-Chicago WNBA game after he was confronted by Sky guard Natasha Cloud late in the third quarter.
Freedom was sitting along the baseline. He had on a black shirt that read “WOMAN noun. adult human female.”
The Fever called for a timeout after Cloud scored inside with 1:22 left in the third. Cloud then did a chest bump with teammate Aicha Coulibaly before turning around and walking in Kanter’s direction.
Cloud, 34, started yelling and pointing at Kanter, also 34, as she approached him. A standing Kanter held his arms out and took one step on the court as security and a handful of Sky players moved in between the two.
“There was just a fan incident and the security handled it, and we’re just going to focus on the game,” Chicago forward Azura Stevens said after the Sky’s 113-90 loss.
Chicago coach Tyler Marsh said Cloud was concerned about being a distraction for the team.
“I told her she wasn’t,” Marsh said. “I told her that we all embrace her as someone that protects our team and protects people that need to be protected, and so Tash is always going to stand on that, and we stand for Tash.”
Freedom stopped near the basket to plead his case to security as he was escorted from the court area. He spun around while holding his shirt out and encouraged the crowd to respond as he walked toward the front lobby.

He had a conversation with a group of police officers before departing Wintrust Arena.
“I didn’t see it, we were talking about the next play in our huddle,” Indiana star Caitlin Clark said, “so I think that’s probably a question for Chicago.”
Cloud met with team and league security after the game. She did not speak with the media.
WNBA subject of debate on transgender women
The WNBA has been the subject of recent debates on whether transgender women — people assigned male at birth who transition to align with their gender identity — should be allowed to participate in the league. There has never been a trans player in the WNBA.
Although the league’s collective bargaining agreement says the WNBA is restricted to women, it contains no more specific language about gender identity or sex assigned at birth.
In an ESPN profile published last month, Fever guard Sophie Cunningham said she was opposed to transgender girls and women competing in girls’ and women’s sports.
Freedom and Royce White, another former NBA player, have mockingly declared themselves eligible for the WNBA draft, saying they now identify as women.
Kanter joined a small rally in support of Cunningham outside the arena before the game.
Asked if he had a message for Kanter, Marsh praised the league and its players.
“If you come to a game, you should probably come to enjoy the basketball,” he said. “That seems pretty simple to me. I think these players deserve that and have earned that. Being a former basketball player, you should probably understand and feel that, too.”

President Trump’s pledge to make pricey weight loss drugs widely available for low-income Americans is not panning out as planned, Politico explains. Last year, Trump promised Medicaid would provide access to GLP-1 drugs if states signed on with his administration to negotiate prices directly with manufacturers. But only Indiana has publicly done so. Some states stopped covering the drugs for Medicaid patients who need them for weight loss. Others are considering ending coverage. States opting out of coverage cited budget constraints and concerns about the long-term financial sustainability of Trump’s model.
The Trump administration plans to use a new approach to deny Medicaid coverage of drugs for gender-affirming care, STAT tells us. The precedent it sets could also be used to avoid paying for other drugs, upending an expectation that Medicaid covers the vast majority of prescription medicines. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services issued a final rule this month barring use of federal Medicaid and CHIP funding to pay for pediatric gender-affirming medications and surgery. The rule, set to go into effect Oct. 13, attracted attention because it is the latest development in the administration’s campaign to halt transgender health care for young people.

Ukraine-Russia war latest: Putin passes law to seize retail warehouses if they face Ukrainian drone attack
Kyiv has increasingly targeted online retail logistics centres, accusing them of providing support to the Russian armed forces
Russian president Vladimir Putin has issued a presidential decree to allow the Russian state to take control of private critical infrastructure if they are not protected from Ukrainian drone attacks.
Putin’s order covers online retail warehouses that have increasingly been targeted by Kyiv, as well as energy, industrial and transport facilities deemed critical to the stability of the nation.
It comes as Ukraine has expanded its aerial assault on Russian infrastructure, repeatedly targeting logistics centres belonging to shopping websites Wildberries and now Ozon. Ukraine has accused these facilities of providing support to Russia’s armed forces.
Earlier, Britain and France pledged to provide Ukraine with access to classified technology and faster deliveries of air defence missiles during a meeting of allies to mark Kyiv's Independence Day celebrations.
Andy Burnham offered Ukraine the UK’s unwavering support “despite Russia’s outrageous threats to my country”.
“This is the moment to keep up the pressure on Russia. The moment to squeeze their ability to fund this illegal war," Burnham said, calling for further economic sanctions.
Ukraine eyes local production of Anglo-French missile
European leaders brought pledges of further military and financial support as they met Volodymyr Zelensky in Kyiv yesterday for Ukraine’s Independence Day celebrations.
PM Andy Burnham announced his government has agreed to allow defence company MBDA to release classified information relating to British components used in the SCALP long-range missile.
That paves the way for France and Ukraine to advance plans for the weapon's production in Ukraine.
SCALP is the French version of the UK’s Storm Shadow missile, with both systems incorporating shared technology.
“Ukraine has been Europe’s protector, not a drain on our security, but the front line of keeping Europe safe,” Burnham said, adding that Kyiv and its partners “must keep up the pressure on Moscow.”
Ukraine has leaned heavily on Nato countries for help fighting Russia’s bigger army, although relations with the United States have been cooler under president Donald Trump.
Russia, meanwhile, is getting help from North Korea and China.
First British national killed fighting for Putin in Ukraine ‘dies in drone attack’
A British man has died fighting for Russia after being killed in a drone attack in Ukraine, according to a report.
Bradley Townsend, 33, from Barnsley in South Yorkshire, is reported to be the first UK national killed fighting for President Vladimir Putin.
According to LBC, the former fisherman travelled to Moscow in April where he met other British pro-Russian fighters Aiden Minnis and Ben Stimson who are thought to have recruited him online.
He was killed in a “storm operation” on 10 June, according to a Russia-linked social media account seen by LBC.
Townsend was described as a “warrior in a holy war” who had “sacrificed his life for the cause” by the account.
First British national killed fighting for Putin in Ukraine ‘dies in drone attack’
Ukraine targets Ozon in widening attacks on Russian online retailers
Ukraine has targeted four logistics hubs owned by Russia's second-largest online retailer Ozon, widening a campaign of drone strikes on Russian e-commerce companies intended to inflict more damage on the war-battered economy.
Ozon's shares tumbled after it reported the strikes in southern Russia, which brought to six the number of its facilities targeted in the last three days.
Kyiv had until last week focused on Ozon's rival, Wildberries, in attacks on the e-commerce sector — one of the fastest-growing parts of the Russian economy.
Ozon said in a statement that a logistics hub in Makhachkala in Dagestan was on fire and had halted operations after a drone attack, adding: “According to preliminary information, several people were injured.”
A fire also broke out at an Ozon logistics hub in the town of Enem on the outskirts of the city of Krasnodar, and workers were evacuated from warehouses in Adygeysk, in the Adygeya region, and in Nevinnomyssk in the Stavropol region although neither facility was damaged, it said.
North Korea deploys drone unit among 8,500 troops fighting Ukraine war, says Kyiv
North Korea has sent at least 8,500 troops to Russia, including a drone attack unit to survey and hit targets inside Ukraine, according to Ukrainian intelligence.
The deputy head of Ukraine’s defence intelligence, Major General Vadym Skibitskiy, said that the North Korean forces are mostly spread in Russia’s Kursk region and around a thousand of them are engineers and deminers.
At least 400 more are believed to be drone operators, marking the first time North Korea has deployed an official drone warfare unit in the Ukraine war on behalf of Russia, the official said. Many of them have received direct or indirect experience from previous North Korean deployments.
Mr Skibitskiy said Russian president Vladimir Putin could ask his North Korean ally Kim Jong Un to deploy another 50,000 forces if they meet in September as part of Moscow and Pyongyang’s continuing military cooperation.
Putin allows Russia to take control of infrastructure deemed vulnerable to drone attacks
Russian president Vladimir Putin has handed the Russian state the power to take control of critically important infrastructure if it is deemed to be poorly protected from Ukrainian drone attacks and other threats.
The special powers, set out in a presidential decree, will allow the state to take over temporary administration of such facilities at a time when Ukraine has stepped up drone attacks on oil refineries and retail warehouses.
The state will be able to take control of physical and financial assets and formal ownership rights if entities responsible for such facilities are judged to have failed in their duty to protect them and are too slow to repair them after any attack, according to the decree.
It applies to fuel, energy, industrial, communications, transport and logistics facilities and other objects regarded as critically-important for ensuring the security and economic stability of the state and the population.
First deputy prime minister Denis Manturov said the measure should not be viewed as a precursor to nationalisation and would not be used on a broad scale.
Russia's Afipsky oil refinery afire after drone attack
The Afipsky oil refinery in Russia's southern Krasnodar region was on fire following a drone attack, regional governor Veniamin Kondratyev said this morning.
He added that two people were killed and two others were injured due to falling drone debris in the area.
Britain and France pledge stronger support on Ukraine's Independence Day
Leaders of Britain and France pledged to provide Ukraine with stronger military support — including access to classified technology and faster deliveries of air defence missiles — at a meeting of allies to mark Kyiv's Independence Day celebrations.
PM Andy Burnham, in Kyiv on his first foreign visit since taking office last month, urged the gathering of the "Coalition of the Willing" to "do everything we can" to bolster Ukraine's defences against Russian air strikes.
“This is the moment to keep up the pressure on Russia. The moment to squeeze their ability to fund this illegal war,” Burnham said, calling for further economic sanctions.
Britain announced on Monday it would allow Kyiv access to classified technology to start its own production of Storm Shadow long-range cruise missiles, capable of carrying out strikes deep within Russia. France has already given its assent to license the technology for the European missile.
French president Emmanuel Macron, co-chairing the coalition meeting via video link, said that a string of deadly attacks on Ukrainian cities in recent weeks had shown that allies needed to step up the deliveries of interceptors and France would do its part.
“I think it's very important that all of us accelerate in terms of delivery,” Macron told the meeting, urging countries not to back down in the face of Russian intimidation.
“The bottom line is, for me, very clear: keep calm and carry on.”
Zelensky told the meeting that Ukraine's war effort was complicated by a $27bn defence funding gap this year and appealed for additional financial support.
He suggested that Russia's frozen overseas assets could be used to finance the deficit.
PM Burnham will head to US to lobby Trump on Ukraine needs next month – report
Prime minister Andy Burnham is planning to head to the US next month to speak with US president Donald Trump about Ukraine's needs, reported Bloomberg.
“I am looking forward to going to New York in September,” the PM said, referring to the UN General Assembly gathering.
While the details are not “fully confirmed”, Burnham said it is “likely” he will go.
“Leaving today, I'm quite clear what I need to do in the next few weeks," he said as he wrapped up his first official visit to Ukraine, where he vowed to use pressure on Russia to end the war.
The White House is yet to issue a comment on a likely meeting between Trump and Burnham.

AI models trained on Ukrainian battlefield data will be used to stop protesters and foreign states targeting UK defence sites, railways and energy plants under a deal struck between London and Kyiv.
Private companies will also be given access to the vast trove of data from Ukraine’s Avengers AI lab to help build new systems, the first agreement of its kind in the UK.
The scheme will be piloted at a UK defence site, building a model to identify protesters or a hostile-state attack. It uses AI-optimised sensors in buried fibre-optic cables to detect different kinds of movement.
The government has suggested the technology, if proven workable, could be used at airports, prisons, railways and energy infrastructure.
The controversial proscription of the activist group Palestine Action was sparked after the group breached RAF Brize Norton on scooters last June, a highly embarrassing security lapse as a result of which the group was able to deface two military aircraft with spray paint before escaping the site without being detained.
Palestine Action said at the time that it had targeted RAF Voyager aircraft used for transport and refuelling, and that “activists have interrupted Britain’s direct participation in the commission of genocide and war crimes across the Middle East”.
Private companies will be able to access the data once approved by the MoD on a secure platform, though the data sharing is likely to raise alarm among privacy campaigners.
Pilot projects have already been approved with three British AI companies – Sintela, Mind Foundry and Skyral. Sintela, a Bristol-based company that specialises in fibre-optic sensors, recently struck a $35m (£26m) deal with the Trump administration to provide surveillance on the US-Mexico border.
The partnership with the Ukrainian AI lab means new UK security systems can be trained on operational drone datasets, strike mission footage and flight profiles, likely to include Russian sabotage attempts against critical Ukrainian infrastructure.
The cache of four years’ worth of military data contains a far deeper picture than models outside Ukraine have previously been trained on, which had been mostly restricted to open-source data.
The government eventually hopes to use the AI models to predict quickly when infrastructure such as railways, the power grid or military bases might be coming under threat or stress from hostile actors.
That would primarily come from the laying of fibre-optic cables that are able to identify unique movements of people or vehicles around sensitive sites. Ministry of Defence sources said that would specifically include when a site might be targeted by protesters – not just hostile states.
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said it would be an opportunity for British companies to combine their AI expertise with Ukraine’s battlefield data, which would “accelerate the development of capabilities that not only strengthen our national security but better protect our critical infrastructure and growth in every postcode here at home”.
Other potential projects could include new AI chips to power drones, robotics and automated weapons systems.
Steven Murdoch, a professor of computer science at University College London, said technologies to detect movement from sensors in fibre-optic cables had been around for decades and that it was unclear if data from Ukraine would refine their capabilities.
“I haven’t heard anything that is very convincing, but there is a plausible scenario where they could see something that could be predicted easily and isn’t in any publicly known dataset,” he said.
Ukraine, however, has a lot of other data that may be valuable, especially related to new threats that countries in western Europe might face in the short to medium term.
“What’s valuable is something we’re seeing today which other countries will be worrying about in the future,” Murdoch said. “Anything to do with drones, for example.”
The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said Ukraine was “pushing the frontier of defence innovation as they bravely resist Putin’s illegal invasion”.
“By combining the UK’s world-leading scientists, engineers and tech companies with Ukraine’s unique battlefield experience and data, we will strengthen both of our nations’ defence and security,” he said.
