The Trump Comedians Are Tired
The president’s first administration was a boon for satirists. Today, many of them are sick of the shtick.
In 2017, as Donald Trump was getting used to the White House furniture, Alec Baldwin was feeling exultant. His impersonation of the new president on Saturday Night Live had made him momentarily inescapable and given the comedy show its highest ratings in years. To capitalize on the momentum, Baldwin co-authored a book-length satirical memoir written from Trump’s perspective. Baldwin’s autobiography—which also came out that year and was excerpted as a cover story for Vanity Fair—noted that his take on the president “seemed to delight nearly everyone in the People’s Republic of Manhattan.” When he accepted an Emmy for his performance in the fall, he addressed Trump directly: “At long last, Mr. President, here is your Emmy.”
It was disorienting, then, to hear Baldwin declare, when I spoke with him earlier this summer, that this sort of comedy has become stale, boring, and useless. “None of it’s funny. I don’t find it funny anymore,” he told me. “There’s nothing left to say about Trump.”
Clearly, something has changed—and not just for Baldwin, who effectively retired from the role back in 2020. The first Trump administration was a boon for comedians and for television. A cottage industry of new, politically inflected clip shows offered satirical commentary on the new president to a mostly liberal audience. Late-night comedy adopted Jon Stewart’s old playbook, trading quippy gags for more full-throated (and sometimes outright defiant) critiques of government. Ambiguity was out; everyone knew whose side these commentators were on, and other impersonators began vying for Baldwin’s crown. But the bubble collapsed right around the moment of Joe Biden’s ascension, and Trump’s return to power hasn’t inspired the same volume of riffs. Today, some of the comedians who rode the initial wave have come to feel a little like Baldwin does. They’re sick of the shtick—and they’re skeptical about the function of political comedy in a world that’s arguably beyond parody.
Part of what once made Trump such a rich vein for comedic send-ups was that, at the start of his political career, he seemed straightforwardly ridiculous. Hadn’t this guy been shilling for Omaha Steaks with Gary Busey and Lil Jon? How would he spin the Oreo commercial he’d done with Peyton and Eli Manning, in which he’d challenged the brothers to a “lick race”? The jokes practically wrote themselves. Anthony Atamanuik, a Trump impersonator whose parody series, The President Show, ran for one season on Comedy Central in 2017, told me that at its best, the political comedy of that era also had a kind of diagnostic power: “I wanted my show to continue mostly because I saw each episode as an essay on an issue in American life, and the albatross I had was Trump.” His hope was that, for a liberal audience still reeling from the shock of his election, skewering the president could be a way to crystalize what had happened to the country.
That initial burst of left-leaning satire didn’t last. Studios gave the former Daily Show correspondents Michelle Wolf, Larry Wilmore, Hasan Minhaj, and Wyatt Cenac their own shows, only to cancel them before the end of the president’s first term. A 2020 New York Times Magazine story on this “boom and bust” suggested that some comedians—and some audiences—were tiring of the material even before it became clear that Trump would lose the election. Network late-night shows continued to treat the president as a punching bag, but the novelty had worn off.
Overexposure is one explanation for that decline. Another is that these liberal viewers started to expect something different from comedy as the reality of MAGA’s ascendance set in. More than over-the-top impersonators and Daily Show correspondents ridiculing the news, people seemed to be craving simple palliatives. By 2020, the most visible Trump satirist was the comedian Sarah Cooper, who filmed herself mouthing along to the president’s public statements while mimicking his facial expressions. Her work was almost post-comedic: Rather than writing her own material, she was giving people permission to laugh at the strangeness of his mannerisms. She eventually parlayed viral fame into a guest-hosting gig on Jimmy Kimmel Live and a Netflix special directed by Natasha Lyonne.
Trump’s return to office in 2025 could have been an opportunity for any of these comedians to stage comebacks, or for new shows to emerge. But although the president remains a target in liberal comedy circles, the market for this brand of humor has shrunk considerably. It remains most evident in today’s late-night lineup: The Daily Show, one of the progenitors of the form, remains on the air. (Its original host, Jon Stewart, returned in 2024.) Last Week Tonight With John Oliver—which once cautioned viewers against voting for Trump by reminding them of his family’s historical surname, Drumpf—is still going too, and in a recent episode covered Trump’s efforts to reshape the Department of Justice. Jimmy Kimmel and Seth Meyers have consistently pursued Trump since his rise; even Jimmy Fallon, who was once reluctant to get political, will now occasionally take a shot.
Some new impersonators have risen to take Baldwin’s place: James Austin Johnson and Shane Gillis have both played the president with some success in recent years. But in this cohort, things aren’t quite the same as they were. Johnson’s impression hasn’t created the kind of splash that Baldwin’s once did; his version of Trump is reminiscent of the de rigueur presidential impressions of SNL seasons past. (That’s no judgment of comedic value—Johnson’s version is as accurate as it gets.) And last year, when CBS decided to end its long-running program The Late Show With Stephen Colbert, late-night TV lost one of its most prominent and consistent critics.
The administration’s attempts to chill dissenting speech elsewhere, although disturbing, don’t appear to have suppressed this sort of comedy’s prevalence in American culture. And in one case, such attempts had the opposite effect: In September, ABC suspended Kimmel’s show after Federal Communications Committee Chairman Brendan Carr demanded that it do so; a few days later, in response to a public outcry, the network reversed course. The fracas turned out to be good for ratings—Kimmel’s first show back was its most-watched in more than a decade.
Still, the old guard doesn’t totally see the point. “All the majors that continue to just throttle him and carry on about him—move on to other people!” Baldwin told me. “It’s not gonna make any difference.” Atamanuik told me that by fixating on Trump, comedians risk missing the bigger issues, and that young people especially have “an anger at the entire system.” (The top-three late-night talk shows have been fighting for viewers in the coveted 18–49 age demographic for more than a decade.) “They know that Trump is just a product of something else,” he said. Meanwhile, Cooper said a few years ago that she has “no desire” to revisit her lip-syncs, and that “there’s nothing left to really do with it.”
Brent Terhune, another veteran of the short-form-video scene that flourished during the coronavirus pandemic, is less gloomy about the future of Trump-inflected comedy. This is partially because he’s not interested in taking on the president directly. Instead, he makes videos in the persona of a Trump fan. The character he’s played for nearly a decade, “Alpha Male,” is a sort of disgruntled MAGA vlogger—“a reaction and a reflection of people that are Trump die-hards,” Terhune told me. Part of what distinguishes the performance is that it’s at least somewhat empathetic; he said he’s always being told that Alpha Male reminds people of their brothers, dads, and uncles. His view is that because the Alpha Male character isn’t just about skewering Trump, it could potentially outlast his administration.
Terhune’s enthusiasm has certainly outlasted that of many of his peers, so maybe on-screen political comedy is just in need of new subjects. Although Atamanuik no longer consistently plays Trump, he has lately been impersonating Robert F. Kennedy Jr.—and Baldwin suggested that House Speaker Mike Johnson and former Acting Director of National Intelligence Bill Pulte could be deserving targets.
Or maybe you can make the same joke only so many times before you start wondering what it is you’re really doing. In 1962, when the impressionist Vaughn Meader released his landmark comedy album, The First Family, which poked fun at the Kennedys, the anthropologist Margaret Mead remarked that its very existence illuminated something about American society. “This making fun of people in authority is very healthy,” she told Life magazine. “It is the difference between democracy and tyranny.” The impressionists I spoke with might hesitate to agree with that assessment. But beyond the easy laugh of a presidential impersonation, humor can still be a potent force in defending a free society against tyranny—that is, if comedians are willing to keep finding new angles rather than repeat old gags.

In a parallel universe, this week is Harry Brook's first as England's new Test captain.
There are numerous reasons why it will be Joe Root, rather than Brook, leading England into a new era against Pakistan at Headingley: the timing of Ben Stokes' retirement, Brook's workload as white-ball captain and Root's surprise willingness to resume the job among them.
Inescapably, there is also what happened during the winter, when Brook was punched by a nightclub bouncer in Wellington on the eve of a one-day international against New Zealand.
In June, Brook said it would be an "honour" to be asked to succeed Stokes. Almost two months later, he does not know if the Wellington incident has cost him the top job, at least for now.
"I dunno," he tells BBC Sport. "I honestly don't know. I don't really look at it like that.
"The decision to make Rooty captain is the right one. I'm actually really excited to see what he can do. He's definitely the right man to take over that job. I'm really looking forward to working alongside him."
For some, Brook became the poster boy of everything they disliked about the Bazball era, both for what happened off the field and for the way he plays the game on it.
At this point, it's probably worth noting that no man has scored more international runs across formats since Brook made his Test debut in 2022. Of all players to have batted at least 20 times in Test cricket for England in the past 60 years, no one has a higher average than Brook's 53.04.
Brook has occasionally done himself no favours, but there is also something uncomfortable about the narrative that surrounds the 27-year-old, especially in a sport that struggles with elitism.
He often speaks about how he is living his dream - his parents have told him he has been talking about playing for England since he uttered his first words.
But not everything about playing for England is a dream. Scrutiny, criticism and the court of public opinion. Brook had the lot after the Wellington misdemeanour became public knowledge.
"It was a tough period, especially when I was at home, getting ready to face the media," he says.
"I feel like the character that I showed throughout that period to go out there and still perform and lead the white-ball side fairly well - I was proud of myself and the team.
"I don't want to say it's helped me, but it's made me realise how big it is to be England captain. It's not just the leadership on the field. It makes a massive difference if you can lead with responsibility off the field."
Amid the Wellington fallout, Brook led England to important ODI and T20 series wins in Sri Lanka, as well as the semi-finals of the World Cup that followed. His own form was superb. In the maelstrom, he drew on an experience from three years earlier.
In 2023, his only season in the pressure cooker of the Indian Premier League (IPL), Brook struggled. After his one significant score for Sunrisers Hyderabad - admittedly an unbeaten century - he said he was glad to "shut up" supporters that had been "slagging me off".
"I got into a little bit of a rabbit hole with scrutiny and social media when I was at the IPL," says Brook.
"It didn't help me as a person on the field or off the field. I decided to, not stay away from social media, but also not go out of my way to look at it.
"On the other hand, I actually feel it's a little bit of a compliment if people are giving me scrutiny and have an opinion about my game.
"I know it's not a nice thing to see people slagging you off, but it means people care and people think I can put in a better performance than I have done that day."
There are comparisons that can be drawn between Brook and Stokes. Maverick players from working-class backgrounds, often finding themselves outnumbered by the well-to-do members of the dressing room.
But, like Stokes, Brook is authentic in the way he plays and speaks, even if that can get him into trouble. One example would be Brook's "who cares" line about batters being caught in the deep after an ODI against Australia two years ago.
"I would say that I'm an extremely honest person," says Brook. "I'm honest with myself and honest with my game.
"A lot of people say honesty is the best policy. I probably have got into trouble a few times being too honest."
Authenticity bleeds into Brook's batting, for better and worse. He is probably the most thrilling batter to wear an England shirt since Kevin Pietersen and no batter with at least 3,000 Test runs has scored more quickly than Brook, whose strike rate is almost 87 runs per 100 balls.
But Brook can delight and frustrate in equal measure, nowhere more so than on an Ashes tour when an average just under 40 was a disservice to his ability.
Costly crimes included his drive at Scott Boland in the calamitous second-innings collapse in the first Test and trying to hit Mitchell Starc for six over extra cover in the first innings of the second Test. "Shocking shots" were how Brook described them in Australia.
"If supporters get frustrated, imagine how frustrated I get," says Brook.
"It's something I've been really trying to work on, trying to assess conditions quicker, and read the surface better. To go out there knowing what shots are going to be hard and what is going to be easier.
"I practise every single shot and have done since the age of eight. In the nets, I'd do a 360 challenge with my dad. He'd throw balls and I'd have to try to hit it to a certain place: that corner, then that corner.
"I have the ability to hit it everywhere, I just have to figure it out quicker in games."
At the end of that Ashes, Stokes pulled Brook aside to tell him his Test average could be as high as 65 or 70.
Though Brook says it's "not that easy", Stokes' point is only a select few have Brook's talent, and he might not be making the most of it.
"Yeah, maybe," says Brook. "I'm definitely not the finished article and maybe never will be."
And, when Brook says he knows what it is like to be a disappointed supporter, he pulls out his own example from when he was 16 years old, one that goes some way to explaining why he has grown so close to Brendon McCullum.
"I remember as a kid going to watch Baz play at Headingley for Warwickshire and Matthew Fisher got him out in his first over. I was absolutely devastated. I'd only gone to watch him," says Brook.
"After he got out I said to my dad, 'Can we just go home'. I kind of understand it as a fan of cricket."
Brook grew up at Burley-in-Wharfdale Cricket Club, where his entire family is part of the furniture.
Brook's father David recently had his 50th birthday party at the club, while Harry still nets there and gets along to watch while he can.
A scholarship to Sedbergh School - "posh", in Brook's words - was where he honed his game, with 6.20am nets run by former Kent player Martin Speight. Speight remains one of Brook's closest advisors.
Challenged to improve his conditioning as a teenager, Brook has worked hard on his fitness as a professional.
He used the time when he missed England's tour of India in early 2024 - his grandmother Pauline died in March that year - to get back on track after he had "slipped on the wrong path".
"I wasn't as good an athlete as I could have been," says Brook. "I went on meal plans, I went to the gym and ran, with schedules from the strength and conditioning coach.
"When I came back, I felt like I was seeing the ball a hell of a lot easier. The pace of a delivery felt slower. It helped to bat for longer periods of time and run twos better.
"It made a massive difference to my fielding as well. I just think it was a vital area of my career so far that I've improved on and it's made a massive difference."
When he was named as England white-ball captain last year, Brook pulled out of the IPL and remains banned from the competition as a result.
"Not really," says Brook, on suggestions of regrets over his exile from cricket's most lucrative tournament.
Club cricket, school, fitness and no franchise gigs apart from The Hundred are all parts of what Brook has put into his England career.
He may not be Test captain now, though he knows there is a good chance the job will come. When it does, Brook will have a better understanding of what it means to be captain because of his experiences of the past year.
"There are little things you learn throughout your career," he says. "Obviously, the past few months have been on quite a high scale.
"Having that responsibility now has made a massive difference for me. There is the potential I could be captain, but at this moment in time all I'm focusing on is trying to win a few games of cricket. I will be 1,000% behind Rooty and I'm really looking forward to what this Test side can do."
And, in the tough moments, Brook's England career never stopped being his dream.
"I'm an extremely upbeat person. I'm always happy," he says. "Even when things are bad, I think there's no point dwelling on things. You've got to be happy.
"I'm in a very privileged position to be able to say I do something I love as a job. I refuse to call it a job, but I'm doing something I love for work. That is a dream come true.
"Every time I step over the white line, it's always a phenomenal feeling to be able to say, 'This is my life.'"

Throughout 2026, a claim circulated online that U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said, "Republicans are trying to rig elections by only allowing U.S. citizens to vote." Social media users who shared the alleged quote did not say when the New York Democrat supposedly said this or in what context.
For example, in August, the manager of a popular Facebook account shared the rumor (archived), adding, in part: "According to AOC, requiring voters to actually be U.S. citizens is somehow 'rigging' elections. This isn't a slip of the tongue — it's the Democratic Party's blueprint laid bare."
Other examples of the claim were posted on X and TikTok in April, Threads in June, and elsewhere on Facebook in July.
Snopes readers have repeatedly searched our site and emailed us asking whether the New York lawmaker authentically said the remark.
In short, Ocasio-Cortez never produced these words. Therefore, we've rated this quote as being incorrectly attributed to her.
Google searches for Ocasio-Cortez's name and portions of the purported quote did not reveal any credible news reports, videos or news releases documenting her saying those words. If she had truly made that statement, reputable news media outlets likely would have covered it.
When asked by email whether Ocasio-Cortez said the quote or anything similar, Karla Santillan, the New York representative's press secretary, said, "She did not say that."
In February 2023, Ocasio-Cortez argued on the House floor against a Republican-led effort to prevent the D.C. Council from passing a law allowing noncitizens to vote in local elections in the nation's capital. While the House of Representatives passed a bill designed to block the law, the Senate did not. As a result, Washington, D.C., became one of a handful of municipalities around the country to allow noncitizens to vote in local elections.
During the House debate over the measure, Ocasio-Cortez argued for D.C.'s right to pass its own laws without meddling from Congress. She did not argue that it was necessary for noncitizens to vote, or that laws allowing only citizens to vote were "rigging" elections. What she said in full was:
It is so rich to hear the other side discuss the sacred right of voting, discuss what our veterans and our service members fought for, and the sacred right of voting while defending and continuing to defend the disenfranchisement of American citizens in D.C. for their right to vote.
They don't believe in statehood. They don't believe in the actual enfranchisement and voting rights for D.C. residents who are U.S. citizens.
Yet, they have the audacity and the gall to not just continue in that position and claim they believe in the sacred right to vote while denying that right to vote to an overwhelmingly Black city, but then expanding their position — expanding their position — so that, in direct contradiction of their "conservative" values of small government and defending freedom, they have decided to expand the jurisdiction of this body to meddle into the business of D.C. residents.
The D.C. Council has the right to determine its policies for D.C. residents. If any member of this body does not like that, they can feel free to change their registration, resign their post and run for D.C. Council.
For those who are residents here of Washington, D.C., they could have gone, as the ranking member state, to any of the many hearings on this issue.
I understand that there may be disagreement. I understand that Republicans may not be happy with what the D.C. Council is doing, but when cities in Vermont pass the same provisions, when San Francisco, when nine Maryland cities brought up this provision, did the Republican Party corral all of Congress and bring this issue down to the floor for a vote?
No, they did not.
They are singling out the residents of the District of Columbia and expanding in the history of disenfranchisement that goes all the way back to the legacy of slavery, and they are bringing it right here to this floor. Because why? They don't have any real bills to debate. We are not here to talk about health care; we are not here to talk about abortion; we are not here to talk about voting rights. We are here to talk about the expansion and the continued subjugation and disenfranchisement of the people of the District of Columbia. Let them govern themselves.
Ocasio-Cortez is frequently the target of many claims regarding what she has done or said. We've previously fact-checked a number of these rumors.
Snopes previously fact-checked this claim in April 2026. We're fact-checking it again due to the continued spread of the rumor and renewed reader interest.

Nothing gives a better idea of what Madras was like 80 years ago than scenes from the film En Manaivi, released in 1942. Indian medicine specialist Vembu Iyer, played by the late T.R. Sarangapani, tells his friend and patient that he moved from Pattanam (Mylapore) to the village of Kodambakkam to prevent his wife from visiting her relatives regularly.
The film begins with the arrival of a train at Kodambakkam railway station, surrounded by trees, waterbodies, and houses set amid paddy fields. In 84 years, Kodambakkam — or Kollywood, the heart of Tamil cinema — has changed beyond recognition. So has the Tamil film world.
The film was produced by A.V. Meiyappan, who established the AVM studio in Vadapalani on 10 acres of land that once housed a tannery. He bought the land for ₹37,500, a princely sum in those days.
He constantly experimented with filmmaking and was among the first to achieve post-synchronisation when the required technology was not available. In the film Sri Valli, when the heroine, Kumari Rukmini, could not match the pitch of the hero, T.R. Mahalingam, Meiyappan recorded the songs in the voice of playback singer Periyanayaki.
In his memoir, Enadhu Vaazhkai Anubhavangal, he writes that his experiment was a phenomenal success, and that the film — produced on a budget of ₹2 lakh in 1945 — earned a tenfold profit. He introduced the latest technology and imported the U.S.-made Mitchell 35 mm camera, which is preserved at the AVM Heritage Museum, offering a glimpse into the sweeping changes embraced by the film world.
Who would have thought that cinemas that once ran with a single projector — with four breaks as there was no second projector to keep the entire film ready for screening — would adapt to IMAX, even though they have fallen on hard times with the advent of exclusive film channels and OTT platforms?
Even filmmaking has undergone great changes — from shooting thousands of feet of film to embracing digital technology. Writer Ashokamitran, in My Years with Boss at Gemini Studios, recalls how thousands of feet of film shot for Avvaiyar were trimmed to create the final product. “Vasan (the boss) sat down to select from the miles of footage — only in films can the footage be in miles. He sat for hours viewing the projection of all that had already been shot, while his editors stood by with scissors and splicers. Every time he closed his eyes, a thousand feet were cut. He streamlined the multi-styled rendering, freshly shot, and inserted connecting links from scene to scene, gave a truly poetic beginning to the film, and ended it with a spectacular ‘ascent to the heavens’ finale,” he writes.
But Meiyappan dispensed with the practice of shooting 20,000 feet of film and inserting over 50 songs, and began making shorter films. When he released Naam Iruvar, S.S. Vasan congratulated him on making a good film in a small town without sophisticated equipment.
Cinematographer-turned-actor M. Ilavarasu said the primitive Mitchell camera, due to its pull-down claw and pin registration, could shoot only up to 24 frames per second (fps), both forward and reverse. It gave way to the German Arriflex 2C and 2BV, which, designed with pressure pad registration, could shoot up to 48 fps. But this was not suitable for masking double action shots. Later came Mitchell high-speed cameras with 144 fps, but they were not popular in India, he said.
“In the early days, the Mitchell camera was the non-reflex type, with a rack-over viewfinder; camerapersons could start shooting only after plenty of rehearsals as they could not see through the viewfinder while filming. The Arriflex 2C and 2C BV are high-speed cameras capable of shooting 48 fps, but with a fixed viewfinder,” he, who worked with Stills Ravi and cinematographer Kannan, the cinematographer of Bharathiraja, before working as a cinematographer for 11 films between 1991 and 2005, said. Subsequently, filmmakers imported Arriflex 3C and Arri 3 with rotating viewfinders, and much later, the Arri 435, whose viewfinder could be shifted to the other side for left-eyed camerapersons, he added.
The film reels, stored in boxes (petti), were transported across the State to cinema halls for release/screening in the past. “Potti vanthuruchu, potti vanthuruchu,” the chorus in the film Aan Paavam after the arrival of the reels in a box, recalls the years when films were made on the expensive celluloid.
Writer Perumal Murugan, in his memoir Nizhal Mutrathu Ninaivugal, recorded how multiple theatres would screen the same film by quickly dispatching the reels to another after a screening. Any delay would anger the audience, who would be eagerly waiting to watch the next part of the film.
“My Vaathiyar (mentor) Balu Mahendra used to tell me how careful he had to be while using film for shooting. He recalled the days when he worked as a cinematographer on the film Chattakari (1974), directed by K.S. Sethumadhavan, who would touch his shoulder while saying ‘cut’,” recalled writer and director Suka.
But today, digital technology has revolutionised filmmaking, and cinematographers and directors can experiment with any number of takes until they are completely satisfied.
“Digital cameras allow 120 fps and come with an additional monitor that lets a third person supervise the production while the cameraperson focuses on the viewfinder,” Mr. Ilavarasu said. Nowadays, films are sent in the file format for screening, with amazing sound effects.
Theatres have survived all odds to become one-stop destinations — they sell everything and allow online ticket booking, making the rush to buy tickets and the beeline to the canteen for a cup of tea, goli soda, a thattu murukku or a bun, things of the past.

The Atlantic announces Jessica Goldstein as SVP of events
Goldstein joins after leading events at NPR and the Skoll Foundation
The Atlantic has hired Jessica Goldstein as senior vice president of events, who will work in partnership with managing director for events Evan Smith to lead and produce the magazine’s robust live programs nationwide. She begins with The Atlantic in early September.
Jessica has spent her career telling stories through reporting and creating live experiences that resonate far beyond the stage. She spent eight years creating and leading NPR’s live cultural programming, including creating the Tiny Desk Contest, NPR’s annual search for new musical talent, and the How I Built This Summit. She most recently led the Skoll Foundation’s global convenings strategy and directed the Skoll World Forum.
At The Atlantic, she will work with Evan to lead one of the most influential and long-running events practices in media. The Atlantic convenes dozens of annual in-person and virtual events that reach thousands of people every year, anchored by its flagship event, The Atlantic Festival, which returns to New York City September 17–19, after being held for nearly two decades in Washington, D.C. The Atlantic is also under way with a new 50-state tour, The Atlantic Across America, that has already held events in 10 states, addressing some of the most complex issues of our time.
Below is Evan Smith’s announcement to staff:
I’m excited to let you know that we’ve hired the amazing Jessica Goldstein as our new senior vice president of events. As the second-in-command on our growing team, she’ll oversee the operations, planning, and execution of our robust public programs, working closely with our sales, marketing, design, and CSG colleagues to grow The Atlantic’s audience and revenue; shine a great, big light on our brand; and—most crucially—bring our journalists and our journalism to stages from coast to coast through The Atlantic Festival, The Atlantic Across America, The Atlantic Summits, and so much more.
Jessica comes to us most recently from the Skoll Foundation, where she was managing director of convenings, leading the organization’s global events strategy and directing the Skoll World Forum, a weeklong gathering of heads of state, social entrepreneurs, and civil-society partners. But it’s her reputation at NPR that really precedes her—and makes her the ideal hire in this moment. As senior director and executive producer of Events & Experiential, she spent eight years creating and leading NPR’s live programming, including the Tiny Desk Contest and the How I Built This Summit. Previously she was a senior supervising producer for NPR Music, a senior producer on the science desk, and a producer of audio documentaries known as NPR Radio Expeditions. A native of New York, Jessica is a graduate of the University of Wisconsin at Madison.
Jessica believes in the power of storytelling, of sharing ideas and sparking inspiration, which is precisely how we think about our work in the events space. There is no loftier task before us than getting people from divergent backgrounds—great minds who don’t think alike—in a room to listen and talk and continue the conversation after we’re gone. She will bring to bear her decades of experience, her imagination, her creativity, her calm, and her charisma as we expand the ambitious work of the Live team.

The ongoing Ebola outbreak is now the second-most lethal on record and the deadliest in the history of Democratic Republic of Congo. Only the epidemic in West Africa in 2014-16 killed more people.
The grim milestone was reached on Sunday when government data showed that confirmed deaths topped the toll for Congo's 2018-2020 Ebola outbreak, previously the worst the country had seen. Delayed detection, overwhelmed surveillance teams, armed conflict and a lack of vaccines and treatments for the species of the virus involved have allowed Ebola to outrun containment efforts this time.
How fast is it spreading?
Health officials say the current outbreak is spreading five times faster than previous outbreaks did in Congo at this stage. There are now 4,945 cases confirmed, including 2,325 deaths, according to the latest data published on Sunday.
The 2018-2020 outbreak in Congo ended with 3,481 cases and 2,299 deaths recorded over two years.
It took more than 10 months to hit 2,000 confirmed cases in that outbreak. The current outbreak reached that figure in roughly two months.
In the West Africa epidemic, the World Health Organization recorded more than 28,000 cases and 11,000 deaths across Liberia, Guinea and Sierra Leone.
A head start for the virus
The rare Bundibugyo species of the virus spread undetected for months before the outbreak was declared in May. Reuters reported that early cases were missed, some being diagnosed as peritonitis. Local funeral practices helped the virus spread before any alarm was raised, and continue to undermine the response. Health workers initially relied on tests for the wrong species of Ebola and samples sent to Kinshasa were mishandled. A July report published in Science, a peer-reviewed academic journal, concluded that the outbreak had begun at least as early as January on the outskirts of the mining town of Mongbwalu.
Surveillance teams unable to catchup
World Health Organization officials estimated in July that around 80% of new infections emerged outside known transmission chains, suggesting most cases are identified only after the virus has spread rapidly through communities. Health surveillance teams are overstretched, but undetected transmission can lead to even more cases.
The growing proportion of confirmed Ebola patients dying after an infection is an indication of persistent shortcomings in the response, experts say. The case fatality rate, as this figure is known, has risen from about 20% in early June to 47%, according to government data.
The trend does not indicate the virus has become more lethal. The early figure was likely underestimated, while its increase highlights the fact that many cases are still being detected late, experts say.
Aid cuts and unpaid salaries
Aid cuts have hampered surveillance efforts.
USAID was awarding a five-year contract in 2025 to carry out health surveillance in Congo when the agency was abruptly shuttered, Tom Van Boven, the global health security team lead, told Reuters. Reuters reported in June that key parts of the Ebola response were facing funding and staffing shortfalls. As of mid-July, WHO had received less than half the funding needed to fight the eastern Congo outbreak. Health workers have also protested over unpaid salaries.
No vaccine and no proven treatment
Unlike the more common Zaire species behind the 2018-2020 outbreak, for which vaccines and treatments exist, there is no licensed vaccine or proven treatment for the Bundibugyo species.
Most vaccines developed over the past decade focused on the Zaire species. A small number of experimental vaccines and therapies are being evaluated, while global health authorities assess whether existing Ebola treatments could offer protection. Evidence so far is limited to animal studies.
Conflict and mistrust
The outbreak is concentrated in eastern Congo, a region affected by violence for decades, where conflict has delayedaccess to communities, disrupted the movement of personnel and supplies, and made contact tracing more difficult. Attacks on hospitals and health teams continue and have put response workers at risk.
Eastern Congo sits along major trade and migration routes, with people travelling between towns, displacement camps and neighbouring countries. Reuters reported in June on dozens of suspected Ebola-linked deaths at a displacement camp, raising concerns about transmission among hard-to-monitor, mobile populations.

Simple to set up. Streams content perfectly in multiple scenarios. Useful streamer remote. Lets you control a computer from another room.
TIRED
USB ports for a keyboard and mouse on the receiver unit seem unnecessary. Both the transmitter and receiver run a little hot.
Cable clutter is more than just annoying—it’s been shown to raise stress levels. A famous 2010 study from UCLA found an association between household clutter and elevated cortisol levels. One peek behind my own TV stand raises mine. The Nyrius Phoenix Home True 4K60 is one attempt to solve this problem.
The Phoenix Home is designed to transmit an HDMI source—think an Xbox Series X or a Google TV Streamer—across your room without needing to connect it directly to your television or monitor. directly to physical cables. The kit includes both a transmitter (for the source video) and a receiver (that you connect to your TV or projector), and transmits high-speed, lossless radio frequency signal between the two.
I tested the Phoenix Home True 4K60 over several months and found it to be a highly capable $250 kit that made cable management much easier.
Start Me Up
Setting up the Phoenix Home is remarkably easy. For the transmitter, you screw the two antennas into place, connect an HDMI cable to your source (like an Xbox or streamer), and plug in the power cord. The receiver is a similar story, only you connect it to your screen of choice. When I tried a Google TV Streamer, it worked right off the bat, connecting after only a few seconds.
The Phoenix Home transmitter only has one HDMI input for the source video and the receiver only has one HDMI out for connecting to a TV or projector. This was never an issue for me and kept things simple.
The transmission quality is frankly amazing. The Phoenix transmits in 4K resolution at up to 60 frames per second (fps) and supports Dolby Atmos, DTS, and 7.1 channel surround sound. It can transmit up to 500 feet away in clear areas with no obstacles, and 75 feet through walls, floors, and ceilings. That’s a better range than the more expensive options like the $450 SIIG 4K HDMI Wireless Extender Kit, for example.
The Phoenix Home transmitter also has a USB-C port that you might think is for connecting more devices, but it’s actually for controlling a computer wirelessly. You can connect a laptop over USB-C to the transmitter, then connect a mouse and keyboard to the receiver, and control the laptop remotely. I had to adjust the mouse speed, but it generally worked without any issues, allowing me to control a laptop that was physically in a totally different room. I imagine the USB ports would be helpful for school teachers, allowing them to control a slideshow or other apps. But for those who just want to stream video, it’s a bit unnecessary.
The transmitter and receiver also both have a port for an IR extender, which can be used for controlling a remote. An HDMI out lets you see whatever you are transmitting by connecting a TV or computer monitor, but I found that capability was entirely optional.
With everything connected—including the IR extenders, a keyboard, and a mouse—I was ready to start testing how it all performed for HDMI wireless transmission.
Testing Through Walls
Photograph: John Brandon
I used three scenarios to test the Phoenix Home True 4K. I started by playing games on my Xbox Series X and didn't noticed any lag or slowdowns. I completed a couple of chapters of Crimson Desert over several hours, and every controller nudge felt instantaneous to me. (The brand says there is a system latency of up to 88 milliseconds, but I never noticed it.)
I also used the Xbox Series X as a Blu-ray player to watch Blade Runner 2049. The signal stayed perfectly clear, never pausing or stuttering during the film. I found the device could transmit easily within the 75-foot range in my house.
For sound, I used a Klipsch Flexus Core 300 soundbar with my television for surround sound and watched Unbroken and Masters of the Air. Surround sound emanated around the room cleanly, whether I was using the Xbox Series X, Google TV streamer, or a laptop. To my ears, it all sounded as if it were connected directly to the source—no transmitter at all.
In terms of range, I had no trouble transmitting in the same room, to a side room where I tested a projector, and to my office to control a gaming laptop. The only glitch I experienced was that the Google TV streamer emitted a strange noise when I tested it with a very old Sony Bravia television. (A Nyrius representative said the HDMI handshake likely didn’t work with the old TV.)
My only gripe—and a minor one at that—was that both the transmitter and the receiver felt a bit hot after a full day of use.
Wireless clarity
Using the Phoenix Home True 4K60 was like I had run a really long HDMI cable from one room to another, which is probably the best thing I can say about how well it works. I never noticed any stuttering or lag in my three scenarios (video games, streaming, and a laptop). For anyone who hates cable clutter on movie night or wants to connect a video game console or laptop far away from a TV, the Phoenix Home True 4K earned my recommendation.

A landslide at a huge waste dump in Guinea’s capital has killed 30 people, the government said on Sunday, after heavy rains overnight prompted it to collapse, engulfing nearby tents and shacks.
The incident occurred less than a week after the government announced plans to close the site and relocate the waste because of the threat it posed, especially during the rainy season, which causes landslides and fatal flash floods each year in crowded, underdeveloped cities across parts of West Africa.
The landslide took place at about 2am (3am UK time) in the Gbessia commune of Conakry, according to a government statement.
The death toll was 30, with six people seriously injured and 16 more lightly injured, the statement said.
Rescue workers were using excavators and other tools to clear the site of the landslide, which witnesses said was large enough to bury an apartment building along with more precarious dwellings.
One woman, Cire Diallo, told reporters at the scene that her five children were killed. “I have lost all my children. All I can do is put my trust in God,” she said.
Guinea holds the world’s largest bauxite reserves and richest untapped iron ore deposit at Simandou, where a massive mining project was launched in November. But the west African country has poor infrastructure and widespread poverty, with 3.7 million of its 15.1 million people living on less than $4.20 a day, according to a World Bank report published in April.
On Thursday Guinea’s minister of territorial administration, Djénabou Touré Camara, announced that the government was closing the landfill because it was unsafe and said the waste was to be relocated outside Conakry.
The prime minister, Amadou Oury Bah, visited the landfill on Sunday to assess the damage and supervise the response, the government statement said, adding that people should “remain calm, show solidarity, and strictly follow the instructions of rescue services and the competent authorities”.

Chhattisgarh CM urges workers' children to dream big, work hard
Raipur, Chief Minister Vishnu Deo Sai on Monday said providing quality education and equal opportunities to children of workers was essential to realising the vision of a developed Chhattisgarh and a developed India.
Addressing a felicitation ceremony of the Atal Utkrisht Shiksha Yojana at Pandit Deendayal Upadhyay Auditorium here, Sai said workers formed the foundation of development and ensuring their children's education, security and prosperity was a priority of his government.
During the programme, the CM felicitated students who excelled in academics, sports, arts and co-curricular activities. More than ₹39.67 crore in assistance under various labour welfare schemes was also transferred through direct benefit transfer to the bank accounts of 1,45,841 workers, officials said.
Sai said he was happy to see children from workers' families confidently communicating in English and excelling in different fields.
"Their achievements show that when children get the right opportunities and quality education, circumstances cannot stop talent from progressing," he said.
The Atal Utkrisht Shiksha Yojana, launched last year with 100 students, has now been expanded to 200 pupils, Sai noted.
Under the scheme, talented children selected from all 33 districts are provided free education from Classes 6 to 12 at residential institutions, including Rajkumar College, Delhi Public School and Rungta Public School .
The chief minister said the scheme was not limited to admission in good schools, but aimed at providing children with a conducive educational environment, confidence and equal opportunities to pursue their aspirations.
He said financial constraints should not prevent talented children of workers from receiving quality education.
Highlighting the contribution of workers to the state's development, Sai said their labour was behind roads, bridges, buildings and other infrastructure projects.
He said 67 welfare schemes were being implemented through three boards of the Labour Department, covering education, healthcare, maternity assistance, support for persons with disabilities, pensions, skill development, employment and housing.
Benefits under these schemes were being transferred directly into beneficiaries' bank accounts, he maintained.
Interacting with students, Sai shared experiences from his life and encouraged them to dream big, work hard and remain disciplined. He said they could aspire to become doctors, engineers, scientists, administrative officers, entrepreneurs or serve society through other professions, but education remained the foundation for achieving their goals.
Chhattisgarh now has premier institutions such as IIT, IIM and AIIMS, while provisions were also being made for higher education loans and assistance to children of workers pursuing studies abroad, he said.
The chief minister said new educational opportunities were being created in remote and formerly Naxal-affected areas, including Education Cities at Orchha and Jagargunda in Bastar.
Speaking on the occasion, Labour Minister Lakhan Lal Dewangan said more than ₹774 crore had been transferred to workers through DBT under various welfare schemes over the past two-and-a-half years.
The government was working on initiatives to support workers in emerging occupations, including assistance to parcel-delivery workers for purchasing vehicles and financial support for livestock herders, he said.
Revenue Minister Tank Ram Verma said the Atal Utkrisht Shiksha Yojana was providing children of workers with an opportunity to pursue their aspirations through quality education.
Students also shared their experiences of the scheme. Atish from Bijapur, studying at DPS, Rajnandgaon, said he aspired to become an IAS officer, while Ishika Dahre from Kabirdham, studying at RPS, said the scheme had significantly improved her confidence in speaking English.
The chief minister later had a meal with the students and interacted with them informally. The students asked him about his childhood, education, favourite food and experiences.
Sai urged them to remain curious, disciplined and committed to learning and said their success would bring pride to their families and the state.

The Gun Lobby’s Most Cynical Move Yet
New data show how pro-gun groups target their political spending after fatal school shootings.
As a newspaper reporter, I covered my first school shooting in 2007 at Virginia Tech, where 32 students and faculty were murdered and 17 others were wounded. In one story, I recounted how Emily, a 19-year-old sophomore, was lying partially behind a desk on the floor of her French class while the shooter gunned down her teacher and nearly every student around her before shooting himself in the head. I can’t forget the image of Emily, shot twice herself, who pretended to be dead but surreptitiously grabbed a cellphone on the floor that another student had used to call 911 before he was shot. I listened many weeks later to a recording of the call. At first, she was too terrified to speak. All the police dispatcher could hear was the sound of her breath and the loud pop pop pop of gunfire all around her.
“I can’t talk,” she whispered, gasping for breath. “Please hurry.”
After the Virginia Tech massacre, I reported on many other school shootings, including Sandy Hook in 2012, when twenty 6- and 7-year-olds were shot to death in their first-grade classrooms and six staff members were killed. Attorney General Eric Holder, whom I covered at the time as The Washington Post’s Justice Department reporter, told me that walking through the bullet-riddled classrooms still caked with blood was the most difficult day of his professional life. He later cried openly when he saw the crime-scene photos of the children lying dead in their classrooms.
I wrote about so many school massacres that I lost count. After each one, I reached out to the National Rifle Association, the National Shooting Sports Foundation (the gun industry’s trade association), and other organizations that the nation’s gun lobby comprises for their response. They rarely commented beyond a statement offering thoughts and prayers to the victims and their families. I twice attended the world’s largest firearms trade show, held annually in Las Vegas for tens of thousands of gun makers, sellers, and other professionals but closed to the general public. There, too, leaders of the NRA, other advocates, and representatives of the multibillion-dollar gun industry would not comment on school shootings, except to reiterate their support for armed guards in schools and a government registry of mentally ill people, and to resist calls to strengthen background checks and restrict access to semi-automatic rifles such as the AR-15.
But the gun lobby had another response to school shootings behind the scenes—one I didn’t know about at the time. A study by Stanford University researchers this year found that after fatal school shootings, pro-gun political-action committees dramatically increased their contributions to their preferred U.S. House candidates in the districts where the shootings occurred, when those races were competitive. These shifts in spending were not observed after other incidents of mass gun violence or after nonfatal school shootings—only when children were killed in schools. Over the many years that I reported on gun violence, the gun lobby’s enormous campaign spending was no secret. But the Stanford study reveals how these groups targeted their money, raising their aggressive tactics to a new level.
In the first study of its kind, the authors analyzed 25 years of data, linking campaign-finance records to every fatal K–12 school shooting from 2000 to 2024. They then compared campaign contributions between the districts that did and did not have a school shooting. After school shootings where children died, pro-gun contributions to candidates in competitive congressional districts increased on average by more than 30 percent. And when the shooting occurred within two months of an election, contributions surged by 2,820 percent. “The data shows that the gun lobby saves its political firepower for the moments when public grief is greatest and lawmakers are under the most pressure to act,” Eric A. Baldwin, one of the authors, told me.
In November 2021, for example, a 15-year-old killed four students and injured seven other people at Oxford High School, in Michigan. The pro-gun PACs contributed $50,650 during the 2021–22 election cycle in the district where the high school was located, a 434 percent increase from the previous cycle and a 591 percent increase from an average of the previous five cycles, according to the Stanford researchers. In December 2013, a 17-year-old senior was killed at Arapahoe High School, in a suburb of Denver. Before the shooting, the pro-gun PAC contribution had been $1,000. Afterward, it soared to $49,470.
Gun-safety PACs also increased their spending in competitive districts after school shootings. But the pro-gun groups were by far the dominant spenders until 2018, the year of the Parkland shooting, which left 17 students and faculty dead at a high school in Florida; at that point, gun-safety groups began to significantly increase their spending, sometimes equaling or even surpassing the spending of the pro-gun groups.
The Stanford researchers did not find that increased spending by either side after fatal school shootings measurably affected which party actually won a competitive House election. (The districts that the study looked at represent only a subset of the gun lobby’s overall election spending.) Nevertheless, the study shows how pro-gun PACs work to undermine anti-gun feelings in communities suffering from the trauma of children being killed in schools.
In poll after poll for more than a decade, the majority of Americans have favored stricter gun laws. Most Americans specifically want a ban on weapons such as AR-15s, and also favor stricter background checks. That sentiment is particularly acute after a school shooting, when “public demand for reform is especially high,” according to the Stanford researchers. But, they write, the pro-gun spending surge means that “instead of yielding to constituent pressure, candidates are fortified to resist it and are empowered to reframe their opposition to reform as principled rather than unresponsive.”
Although the NRA’s power has been waning in recent years, it still spent $10 million in the 2024 election. Other pro-gun groups have emerged and are influencing national policy; together with the NRA, they spend about $14 million a year on lobbying. In response to lawsuits from a number of pro-gun entities, including Gun Owners of America, a federal judge in Texas recently found unconstitutional a 1934 federal law that placed strict requirements on anyone purchasing silencers, short-barreled rifles, and shotguns, among other firearms. The Justice Department did not immediately appeal the ruling.
In recent months, the Trump administration has announced new actions to make it easier for gun purchasers to avoid background checks when obtaining firearms. In April, then–Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche and other Justice Department officials announced the rollback of gun regulations alongside leaders from the NRA, the National Shooting Sports Foundation, the National Association for Guns Rights, and Gun Owners of America. And House Republicans proposed a bill to cut nearly $300 million from the budget of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives, the agency that enforces the nation’s gun laws.
The killing of America’s children and teenagers in their classrooms has become normalized. From a young age, our children and grandchildren are being taught vocabulary and math alongside lessons in how to hide when an “active shooter” storms their classrooms. The Stanford study is a compelling reminder of how far the gun lobby will go to block any efforts to protect our children.

Prime Video’s God of War video game adaptation has not gone on without some bumps in the road, but development on the show continues.
First eyed for a TV series adaptation by the producing studios in March 2022, the casting for the show gained momentum at the beginning of January 2026 after some creative shuffling.
For everything we know about Prime Video’s God of War adaptation, read on.
When will Prime Video’s God of War show come out?
Watch on Deadline
A date has not yet been set for the show’s release.
Is Prime Video’s God of War in production?
Yes, though the shoot had some complications when Ryan Hurst sustained a serious injury four months into shooting. Pre-production began at the end of 2025. The plan remains to film two seasons back to back.
Who is in the cast of Prime Video’s God of War show?
Ryan Hurst was originally cast as Kratos, the titular character of the video game. Kratos is a Spartan by birth and a god by nature, raised in martial culture. After rising in the ranks and commanding armies to protect his homeland, he made a fateful deal with the Greek God of War, Ares, exchanging his soul for being victorious in battle.
Following Hurst’s tearing a bicep while performing a stunt during production in June, as first reported by TMZ, Deadline reported that the role of Kratos was being recast. Sony Pictures Television and Amazon MGM reached out to Dave Bautista to initiate talks shortly after they made the decision to recast the role.
RELATED: ‘God Of War’ To Recast Lead Kratos After Ryan Hurst Suffers Injury On Set Of Prime Video Series
Bautista, who is known for portraying Drax in the Guardians of the Galaxy film trilogy and for more recently voicing Tagah in Avatar Aang: The Last Airbender, closed his deal to take on the role in late August after reports that he was in talks started circulating at the beginning of the month.
Following Hurst’s casting as Kratos, Deadline broke the news that Teresa Palmer (A Discovery of Witches, Warm Bodies) was cast as Phoebe/Sif, wife of Thor and goddess of family.
Max Parker (Boots), will star as Heimdall, the Watchman of Asgard and one of Odin’s sons. Heimdall is a god in his own right, and he has the ability to anticipate what might happen in any moment. He’s constantly looking fore ways to improve his status and position in the hierarchy because he feels unappreciated by his father. Heimdall first appears in the second God of War game, God of War Ragnarök.
Ólafur Darri Ólafsson will portray Thor in the mythology-themed video game adaptation, as Deadline first reported. The God of Thunder is haunted by the price he paid in a war he fought long ago, making him a shadow of his former self who resorts to alcohol to escape what haunts him. He was once loyal to Asgard and his father’s right-hand man. He keeps his wife and children at arm’s length, further isolating himself, but his power lurks beneath the surface.
Ed Skrein (Jurassic World Rebirth) will portray Baldur, Odin’s youngest son and most dangerous weapon. Baldur was cursed as a boy, and the curse took away his ability to feel physical sensation and pleasure.
Deadline first reported Mandy Patinkin’s (Homeland, The Princess Bride) casting as Odin. Odin is the All-Father, or patriarch and most powerful Aesir god. He constantly seeks knowledge to prevent the prophecy of Ragnarök, or the Norse end of the world. He also presents an antagonist for Kratos.
Callum Vinson (Chucky, Long Bright River) will portray Atreus, the 10-year-old son of Kratos. Raised almost entirely by his mother Faye, Atreus grew up in a remote cabin, where he honed his archery skills and developed an affinity for animals. Things change, though, when he is left with his distant father, who he barely knows, after the death of his mother.
At the end of January 2026, Alastair Duncan (God of War, God of War Ragnarök) became the first voice actor from the video games to reprise their role in the Amazon MGM and Sony Pictures Television TV series. Duncan will portray cheery and chatty Mimir from Celtic lands. Jeff Gulka (The X-Files, Stargate SG-1) and Danny Woodburn (The Witcher, Bookie) are set to play brothers, Sindri and Brok, in recurring roles.
Sonya Walger (For All Mankind) will portray Freya, Vamir goddess and princess who wields ancient and powerful magic. She is Odin’s ex-wife and former queen of the Valkyries in Asgard, a title she gained on her wedding day. Her unhappy marriage to Odin resulted in her exile as well as being cut off from her family and native land, Vanaheim. She has lived alone in Midgard for a century, and she is called the Witch of the Woods.
Louis Cunningham, Ben Chapple, Evelyn Miller and Island Austin will play recurring roles of Modi, Magni, Gna and Thrud, respectively. Modi, Magni and Thrud are children of Thor and Sif, with Magni being the eldest son, Modi the middle child, and Thrud, their youngest. Gna is Odin’s Valkyrie commander.
What will Prime Video’s God of War show be about?
Based on the popular PlayStation video game, God of War follows father and son, Kratos and 10-year-old Atreus, as they embark on a journey to spread the ashes of their late wife and mother, Faye. Through their adventures, Kratos tries to teach his son to be a better god, while Atreus tries to teach his father how to be a better human.
Will there be multiple seasons of Prime Video’s God of War show?
Yes, the adaptation was officially greenlit in December 2022, and then, when Emmy-winning director E.O. Toye (Shōgun, The Boys) came aboard, the show received a two-season order.
Who else is behind Prime Video’s God of War TV show?
At first, Rafe Judkins, Hawk Ostby and Mark Fergus were attached to the project with Judkins in the showrunner role as well as an executive producer alongside Ostby and Fergus. The trio left the project in October 2024 after completing multiple scripts for the first season.
Ronald D. Moore came aboard as showrunner shortly after Deadline broke the news of creative changes. Toye, who will direct the first two episodes of the action-adventure series, joined the creative team Dec. 1, 2025. God of War is co-produced by Sony Pictures Television and Amazon MGM Studios in association with PlayStation Productions and Moore’s Tall Ship Productions.
The video game was created by David Jaffe, who also created Twisted Metal which received a series adaptation on Peacock. Jaffe made some comments about the series’ first-look image, released at the end of February 2026. This was before Bautista had taken over as Kratos, though.

West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari on Monday (August 24, 2026) said that 23,000 certificates under the Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA), 2019 have been distributed out of the 2.30 lakh applications that have been made.
“Through the district magistrates, we will complete the hearings and grant the certificates. Now it is up to us to give certificates,” Mr. Adhikari said. The Chief Minister said that about 2.07 lakh applications are pending with the State government. He also urged people who have to come to India after facing religious persecution to apply to the State government for CAA certificates.
A few days ago, the Union Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) transferred the processing of pending citizenship applications under the Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA), 2019, from Empowered Committees to District Collectors in eight States and Union Territories.
During the campaign for the West Bengal Assembly elections 2026 Prime Minister Narendra Modi promised to fast-track and accelerate the implementation of the Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA) to grant legal citizenship rights to refugee communities like the Matuas and Namasudras.
Speaking to media persons at the State Secretariat, the Chief Minister said that the State’s Governor, R.N. Ravi, has given his nod for the new Act enabling the arrest of those attacking police, cost recovery for public property damage, and a notification was issued in this regard during the day.
Mr. Adhikari was referring to the West Bengal Maintenance of Public Order (Amendment) Bill, 2026, which imposes a payment of compensation on persons committing offences such as causing damage to public or private property. Another Bill passed by the State Assembly, the West Bengal Public Safety and Control of Anti-Social Activities Bill, 2026, which empowers the government to detain a person for 12 months is awaiting the nod of the President.

The hotel booking mix-up that could free mushroom murderer
- Published
Last July, hundreds descended on Australia's Gippsland region from around the country for the most exciting event on the annual table tennis calendar.
But as elite players vied for medals at the national championships, one of the biggest criminal cases in the nation's history - that of mushroom murderer Erin Patterson - was unfolding just a few kilometres away.
This tournament inadvertently became part of a perfect storm which the triple killer's lawyers are now arguing "fatally undermined" the fairness of her trial.
The jury which condemned Patterson to prison were supposed to be isolated - sheltered from the frenzy surrounding the case while they deliberated.
But accommodation shortages in the region, exacerbated by the table tennis competition, meant they shared a hotel with members of the prosecution, a key police witness, and journalists.
Now Patterson's legal team is trying to overturn her convictions on appeal.
"The only proper remedy is... the order for a re-trial," Patterson's barrister Richard Edney said.
Towns overwhelmed by frenzy
When Patterson served her estranged husband's relatives a poisonous mushroom-laced lunch in 2023, killing three and gravely injuring another, she thrust the sleepy Gippsland region into the global spotlight.
The community of Korumburra, where the victims were beloved figures, became shrouded in grief. Leongatha, where Patterson lived, was gripped by shock. And Morwell, host of the lengthy trial, was overwhelmed by journalists, lawyers and spectators - as were towns nearby.
You couldn't walk down the main street without spotting some of the courtroom's stars, or grab a coffee without overhearing chatter about the case.
It was this frenzy from which the jury of 12 needed protection, the trial judge decided.
Jurors are required to consider only the evidence presented to them in court, and must only talk about the case among themselves. In Australia, these rules are so strict that discussion with outsiders is forbidden even after a trial wraps up.
To reduce the risk of contamination and the temptation of gossip, Justice Christopher Beale decided the jury should be sequestered once deliberations began - a relatively rare move which meant they would stay in supervised accommodation with little to no contact with the outside world until they reached a decision.
But finding the jury, and the jury keepers watching them, somewhere to sleep became something of a logistical nightmare.
As the trial dragged on, stays became longer than anyone anticipated and accommodation became a constant scramble.
And the week the table tennis tournament came to town - which by a stroke of bad luck was the one in which the jury finally retired - turned the accommodation drought into a famine.
Early morning email revelations
At 08:28 on Monday 7 July, an email from the judge's chambers popped into the inboxes of the lawyers in the case.
It revealed that the lead detective who investigated the murders - a key trial witness - and two prosecution solicitors had been staying at the same hotel as the sequestered jury.
The jurors had exclusive use of a separate floor of the hotel, the email said, and had eaten their meals in a conference room, away from all other guests.
Common areas like the lobby were used by everyone, but the jury keeper who reported the issue said there had been no interaction between his charges and anyone from the prosecution case.
"I understand that there is a shortage of accommodation in the district, but it is obviously undesirable," Justice Beale wrote.
About two hours later, the prosecution responded, admitting they had been aware of the situation for days.
The detective "took steps to avoid common areas from the point that he became aware that [the jurors] were there", their email read.
Upon learning their team would cross over with the jury for a single night, the prosecution had done its best to find other hotels for staff. But they couldn't get alternative rooms for two solicitors, though the email stressed the pair also took steps to avoid any "incidental contact".
However, another missive from the judge's chambers quickly overshadowed the hotel snafu that same afternoon: the jury had reached their verdicts.
They had found Patterson guilty on all counts.
'Most critical week of trial'
Patterson's lawyers are now arguing the hotel mix-up amounted to a "fundamental irregularity" which "fatally undermined" the integrity of the verdicts.
"We would describe... it as catastrophic," Patterson's appeal counsel, Edney, told Victoria's Court of Appeal this week.
"What occurred here was an inexplicable and perhaps still unexplained failure in the process."
The defence - which Edney pointed out had been kept in the dark several days longer than anyone else - didn't immediately move for a mistrial last July.
Instead, it twice asked the state's juries commissioner to investigate in the weeks following the verdicts. Both requests were rejected, the barrister said, and the reasons have not been made public.
A year on, there remains a "vacuum of evidence" around what occurred during "the most critical week" of the entire trial, Edney argued.
There is no CCTV from the hotel; no sworn statements from those who were sharing it with the jury - a group which also includes an unknown number of journalists; and nothing to say what happened except the two brief emails sent last July.
There was also at least one media report at the time - raised by Edney this week but rubbished by the prosecution lawyers as "unverified" and "seemingly inaccurate" - that the mix-up had led to "people hiding in doorways to avoid contact" and "skipping breakfast".
"My question is... so what?" Justice Peter Kidd bit back.
In any criminal trial, jurors see other parties all the time - in corridors, or even nearby cafes - but they're under the constant supervision of jury keepers who have sworn to ensure there's no improper communication, he said.
Edney conceded there was "no evidence" that the jurors had communicated with anyone else, but said innocent contact - even just seeing the detective or solicitors - could have resulted in "subconscious influence".
"This was a hotel with windows," Edney said several times - a likely thing for it to have, someone from the judge's bench countered.
Patterson's team cited two cases to support their argument: one in which jurors were discharged when one was offered a throat lozenge by a defendant's relative during a coughing fit, and another in which a retrial was ordered after jurors caught a taxi without being escorted by a jury keeper.
The prosecution's response was simple.
"The system worked as it was intended to work," Director of Public Prosecutions Brendan Kissane KC said.
The jury was constantly supervised, and when a potential problem was identified, steps were immediately taken to prevent it becoming an actual issue.
The jury keeper, the lead detective, and the prosecution all say there was no contact.
"The evidence in this case is that there was no interaction between any other person and the jury," he said.
Other cases the defence pointed to in which jury errors resulted in retrials all had evidence of actual contact, he noted.
"That's not the situation here."
Patterson has seven appeal grounds - the others relating to rulings on evidence and alleged unfairness by the prosecution - but this one, by the defence's own admission, is unprecedented.
Just as important as actual interference is the perception of interference, said Edney, quoting the trial judge's own speech as he selected jury members on the very first day of the trial.
"Justice must not only be done, it must be seen to be done."
The trio of judges are now deliberating on Patterson's appeal, as well as an argument by the prosecution that her parole period should be scrapped.
They will announce their decisions at a later date.

On World Humanitarian Day, observed on August 19, we honour the people who provide care in crises and the communities who endure them. Often when we look at health crises, we look at large-scale disasters such as disease outbreaks, armed conflict or extreme weather events. But, on this day, let us push the envelope a little further and talk about the kind of crisis that does not show up at our doorstep overnight. This is the kind of health and humanitarian crisis that brews over years, decades, feeding off inefficient policies and profit-driven systems.
In South Asia, this crisis is especially urgent. The region is home to proven medical talent, pharmaceutical capacity, public health experience, and community resilience. Yet it also carries a heavy burden of preventable illness, malnutrition, infectious diseases, climate-related health risks, and out-of-pocket expenditure. For millions here, a health crisis begins not when an ambulance arrives, but when a treatable condition becomes unaffordable, diagnosis comes too late, or when a family must choose between food, rent, education, medicines, and a day’s pay.
World Humanitarian Day should therefore prompt a harder question: why do so many people need humanitarian assistance in the first place?
Personal crisis
For Médecins Sans Frontières/Doctors Without Borders, these questions are not theoretical. Across our medical interventions in South Asia, we repeatedly see people reaching free care only after they have exhausted their savings, sold assets, borrowed money or spent heavily in private health facilities. And by then, the illness has often evolved into a personal crisis — monetary and social.
The warning signs are visible across the region. Out-of-pocket expenditure remains a major barrier to care. When illness pushes families into poverty, the cost is not only personal. It is also social and economic. A region that hopes to benefit from its demographic dividend cannot afford to have large numbers of people sick, untreated, indebted or forced out of work because healthcare is inaccessible.
Over five years from 2018-19 to 2022-23, the per-capita out-of-pocket expenditure(OOPE) in India rose 28.4%. In the same period, though India’s public share of total health expenditure grew to around 48%, it still stands far below that of China, Brazil and many OECD countries. Meanwhile, medical costs continue to rise sharply. One corporate health report placed medical inflation in India at 14%, while also finding that 71% of workers paid for healthcare out of pocket and only 15% had employer-supported insurance.
Of course, insurance does play a role, but it cannot replace public investment. A health card is not the same as a functioning primary healthcare network. A reimbursement package is not the same as a staffed clinic with doctors and nurses who are not burnt out, a reliable laboratory, affordable medicines, counselling, nutrition support or community follow-up. If public foundations are weak, purchasing care from private providers will not automatically create equity. It will simply move public money into private systems without ensuring long-term care for those most in need.
Investing in public healthcare is, therefore, not a welfare expense to be minimised. It is an investment in productivity, resilience, and human dignity. Healthy children learn better. Healthy adults work, care, innovate and contribute. Families protected from catastrophic health costs are more likely to invest in education, livelihoods and long-term wellbeing. Public health systems do not only treat disease; they protect the future capacity of societies.
South Asia also has lessons within its own borders. Sri Lanka, despite resource constraints and economic pressures, has been recognised for stronger public-sector health delivery and impressive progress on key health indicators, including maternal and child health, immunisation and life expectancy. Its experience shows that health outcomes are not determined only by national wealth. They are also shaped by political choices: sustained investment in public services, accessible primary care, trained health workers, and a commitment to care that is not dependent on a person’s ability to pay.
Multiple challenges
This matters because South Asia’s health challenges do not stop at borders. Outbreaks, antimicrobial resistance, climate shocks, displacement, conflict and access to medicines are regional issues. A weak surveillance system in one place can affect communities elsewhere. A climate disaster can displace people across districts and borders. Drug-resistant infections do not respect national boundaries. In such a context, investing in public health is also an act of regional preparedness. Preparedness therefore cannot begin when disaster strikes. It must be built into everyday public health systems. Humanitarian response can save lives in moments of crisis, but it cannot substitute for sustained public investment.
The region also needs to strengthen the public character of medical education, research and health workforce planning. Expanding medical seats is important, but numbers alone are not enough. Public medical colleges need adequate funding, training quality must be protected, and research capacity must be strengthened. South Asia needs doctors, nurses, laboratory staff, public health professionals, counsellors, and community health workers prepared to serve in diverse and difficult settings, not only in profitable urban markets.
India, as the region’s largest country and a major producer of medicines and health technologies, has a particularly important role to play. Its choices influence not only its own population but also wider regional access to medicines, diagnostics, research, manufacturing and public health cooperation. But the core message is larger than any single country: South Asia’s future health security depends on whether governments treat health as a shared public good.
On World Humanitarian Day, we should recognise those who respond when systems fail, and the most authentic tribute to them would be to acknowledge and act on the urgent need to build systems that fail fewer people in the first place. The measure of our health systems should not be how much profit they can generate, but whether a person with the least power can receive timely, affordable, respectful care.
South Asia does not need health systems that treat illness as a market opportunity. It needs systems that treat health as a shared public good — and build from the last person first.
Parthesarathy Rajendran is Executive Director, MSF South Asia
