Trump Is Losing Touch With the Public
As the president spends less time with his base at rallies, his populist instincts are failing him.
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.
One of the few issues that unites voters and politicians of both parties right now is data centers. Three-quarters of Americans would oppose a data center being built near where they live, according to a new poll released last week by Heatmap Pro and Embold Research. The two leading lights of the left, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Senator Bernie Sanders, have sponsored a bill in Congress to create a temporary moratorium on new centers. They have an unlikely ally in archconservative Governor Greg Abbott of Texas, who said yesterday on ABC’s This Week that data-center companies “basically dug their own grave” and “got the backlash they deserve.”
Standing against this consensus is Donald Trump. The president remains a big booster of data centers. “Communities that don’t take a data center—they’re making a mistake,” he said Thursday during an interview with his on-again, off-again lackey Michael Cohen. “Data centers throw off tremendous amounts of jobs and money.”
This was no one-off. Trump had made several similar comments recently. “If I were the mayor of a town or the governor of a state and I had a chance to get a big plant in, an AI plant or a data center, I would absolutely want it, because the jobs are enormous and the money paid, the taxes paid, are just enormous,” Trump said last week—although he allowed that the sector could use “a little public-relations help.”
This puts Trump, the most successful demagogue in American political history, in the unusual position of misreading, and opposing, a populist groundswell. During his 2016 presidential campaign, Trump took many stands that were unpopular among establishment politicians. Some of these positions put him at odds not only with Democrats but also with most Republican elected officials. Trump broke with Republicans in claiming that he would protect social-welfare programs such as Medicare and Social Security, and he broke a bipartisan consensus by attacking free-trade agreements and promising protectionism. On these matters (as well as on his willingness to encourage and participate in gutter racism), Trump demonstrated that a big constituency existed for views that other politicians had deemed electoral liabilities.
Data centers’ political arc has been different. Initially, many officials seemed to back the centers, following exactly Trump’s logic: They offered jobs and tax benefits. But as public opinion turned—driven by a mix of backlash to AI in general, environmental concerns, worries about energy prices, and old-fashioned NIMBYism—politicians changed their view as well.
Why has Trump missed the shift? Presumably one reason is that he is surrounded by advisers and tech executives such as David Sacks and Larry Ellison, who are major boosters of and players in the industry. Tech companies invested heavily in Trump at the start of his second administration, lavishing him with gifts, including a gold-plated bauble and donations to projects such as his inauguration and his ballroom, and Trump has reciprocated by taking policy stances that benefit them. Trump may also be personally profiting from the AI boom; his financial disclosures show he’s become more of a tech investor.
Trump has always tended to adopt the latest thing he’s heard, no matter what it is. He has been willing to alienate corporate interests in the past—when he saw some political upside. But he is not hearing from voters who might alert him to how unpopular data centers are. Trump’s rallies and speeches once created a feedback loop in which he conveyed his message to voters and—crucially—they conveyed their thoughts to him. Now, as his energy sinks, his travel schedule gets lighter, and security makes events more challenging, Trump is getting out less.
Though his stump speeches dragged on for hours, Trump was carefully attuned to audience attention and what did and didn’t work. “You know, if it gets a little boring, if I see people starting to sort of, maybe thinking about leaving, I can sort of tell the audience, I just say, ‘We will build the wall!’ and they go nuts,” he told The New York Times in 2016. I think often about a speech Trump delivered in July 2022. It was billed as the launch of a new policy agenda, but as he read it, both Trump and his audience seemed bored. Then he ad-libbed a riff about trans athletes and the crowd came alive. Trump picked up on the shift and emphasized it; trans issues would become a central talking point for his 2024 campaign.
The president has always been susceptible to fake news and bad at filtering information, but rallies provided a gut check about his base, if not about the broader national reality. Now Trump isn’t even receiving that kind of information. One of his major conduits for information is Natalie Harp, a sycophantic aide who isn’t interested in exposing Trump to criticism. He could read public-opinion data, but as his own approval sinks, he has taken to saying (and may well believe) that polls are fake.
As his world shrinks, Trump’s populist touch has faded. Despite being elected twice on an antiwar platform, he’s launched attacks on Venezuela and Iran. As the Iran war has gotten bogged down, he’s been incapable of reading the public mood. He has dismissed voter frustration over rising fuel costs, saying “I don’t even think about” gas; he previously called affordability a “hoax.” In response to reports that American sailors aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln were struggling with a long deployment, Trump said they hadn’t been deployed “nearly long enough.” And the collapse of trade talks with Canada on Friday threaten Republican prospects in border states including Michigan and Ohio.
Each of these cases represents a growing gap between Trump and his base, but none is as ironic as Trump’s stance on data centers. The AI facilities store terabytes of data, but the president can’t get access to the information about them that he needs.

The Trump Comedians Are Tired
By Will Gottsegen
In 2017, as Donald Trump was getting used to the White House furniture, Alec Baldwin was feeling exultant. His impersonation of the new president on Saturday Night Live had made him momentarily inescapable and given the comedy show its highest ratings in years. To capitalize on the momentum, Baldwin co-authored a book-length satirical memoir written from Trump’s perspective. Baldwin’s autobiography—which also came out that year and was excerpted as a cover story for Vanity Fair—noted that his take on the president “seemed to delight nearly everyone in the People’s Republic of Manhattan.” When he accepted an Emmy for his performance in the fall, he addressed Trump directly: “At long last, Mr. President, here is your Emmy.”
It was disorienting, then, to hear Baldwin declare, when I spoke with him earlier this summer, that this sort of comedy has become stale, boring, and useless. “None of it’s funny. I don’t find it funny anymore,” he told me. “There’s nothing left to say about Trump.”

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Kingdom of the Netherlands have renewed their strategic partnership in addressing the growing impacts of climate change on global health.
The Netherlands is providing a new allocation of €500 000 for 2024 to WHO, reinforcing its commitment to climate resilience and sustainable healthcare systems worldwide. This allocation supports WHO’s ongoing efforts to strengthen the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health Secretariat and advance climate change and health programmes globally.
This contribution builds on the partnership established in 2023 between the Netherlands and WHO to collaborate on climate change and health. Together, they have supported African, Asian and Eastern Mediterranean countries in advancing the implementation of integrated climate and health surveillance and early warning systems, enhancing capacity to deliver on COP26 health commitments, helping harmonize early warning systems for health-related climate risks, and empowering countries to advance climate-resilient health system readiness.
This partnership along with the support from other organizations is pivotal in assisting Member States in developing climate-resilient and low-carbon health systems. Engaging with relevant partners, including civil society, Multilateral Development Banks, UN Agencies, and health professionals in concerted action on climate change and health, is also a core activity.
The Netherlands has been at the forefront of advocating climate action in health, aligned with the Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030 which emphasizes the intersection of climate change and health. In addition, the Netherlands, together with Peru, led the adoption in 2024 of the World Health Assembly 77 Resolution on Climate Change and Health at the to renew the current one from 2008. Recognizing the increasing urgency and the need for accelerated efforts, the resolution calls for a WHO global action plan, increased national efforts and mainstreaming of climate change and health in WHO’s new Fourteenth General Programme of Work.
The partnership’s renewal brings the total support from the Netherlands to WHO activities on climate change and health to over €1.1 Million since 2023 and comes at a crucial time as countries face increasing health challenges from climate change and as the global health community gears up for discussions on climate change and health at COP29 in Azerbaijan in 2024. Climate change will continue to be a key priority area in the new GPW, and where WHO’s work in collaboration with Member States and partners will result in 7.5 million lives saved in the next four years, as estimated in WHO’s latest Investment case.
The Netherlands and WHO will continue to leverage their partnership to ensure that health remains central to climate negotiations and actions. A focus on building resilience in vulnerable regions and empowering countries to implement sustainable, low-carbon healthcare solutions remains central.

Filmmakers have always used certain symbols, motifs, and signifiers to represent ideas, concepts, and places. Over the many years, popular city landmarks, including the hotel Taj Mahal Palace in Mumbai and the Cubbon Park in Bengaluru, have been used as establishing shots to depict the city in which a film is set. For Chennai, it has always been a toss-up between Marina/Elliot’s Beach, Central Station, Anna Flyover, Spencer Plaza, and LIC Building.
While one could argue that the LIC Building established the “big city” vibe and that Spencer Plaza represented Chennai’s “modern and capitalist” aspects, the beach has always been used to represent love and life.
Remember the song, Enna Paarvai, Undhan Paarvai, from Kadhalikka Neramillai, a popular 60s film that many, swear to be the unmatched “evergreen romantic” comedy. The song showcases a young couple — Muthuraman and Kanchana — shaking a leg to a melodious song at the beach, unrecognisable with manicured lawns and the absence of cars. Similarly, in Mani Ratnam’s Alaipayudhey, staying true to the perception of the beach as a sanctuary for those in love, the lead-in to the song, Snehithane, shows the hero waiting for the heroine at the beach.
The iconic Ilaiyaraaja song Idhu Oru Pon Malai Pozhudhu from the film Nizhalgal showcases the beach as a place where college students go to smoke weed after bunking classes and build grandiose dreams about their future.
Filmmaker Venkat Prabhu’s debut film, Chennai 600028, captured another aspect of the beach — its popularity as a space for playing sports, until the police began imposing restrictions. While the Gen Z crowd may not be aware, the black tar road on the beach used to be where hundreds of tennis ball cricket matches took place in the evenings, while the fiercely contested football and volleyball games happened on the beach sands. The final “match” with the school kids at the beach reflected its popularity as a space for playing sports, until the police began imposing restrictions.
Filmmaker Vetrimaaran’s Vada Chennai portrayed the lives of those who live near the coast and depend on the Kasimedu Fishing Harbour for their livelihood. While the film itself is about Chennai’s underworld, it focuses on the trials and tribulations of those living near the beach through various points in recent history. Not just the beach, but its people, their politics and economic conditions were the focus of the critically-acclaimed film.
In actor Sivakarthikeyan’s Marina, the beach becomes a place of refuge for those running away from home.
In a way, the Marina, the Elliots Beach, and the sandy beaches along the East Coast Road evoke different perceptions. While the Marina has maintained its position as the city’s major landmark for tourists, the Elliots’ Beach and those further down the East Coast Road have slowly transformed themselves to attract the hip and fashionable youngsters of Chennai.
With the city growing at a rapid pace, there may be more “landmarks” or cultural markers that the filmmakers will be interested in, but one thing is for sure, the beaches in Chennai will continue to fascinate the storytellers for many years to come.

US to rescind 200,000 business and travel visas from those seeking asylum: report
The move would amount to the largest mass revocation of visas in American history
The Trump administration is reportedly planning to rescind up to 200,000 business and tourism visas, the Associated Press reports.
The alleged plan could amount to the largest mass cancelation of visas in U.S. history.
“We are coordinating with [the Department of Homeland Security] to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently,” State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott told The Independent in a statement. “These types of visas are issued with the clear understanding that they are for those who intend to return home. Obtaining a visa in order to seek asylum is fraud — which is grounds for visa revocation.”
The mass cancelation would apply to individuals who applied for B1 and B2 visas between 2016 and 2026 then sought asylum, according to the AP.
The visas, respectively, cover business trips and voyages for other common reasons such as tourism, family visits and medical care.
The visa plan would likely face strong challenges in court, as have many of the Trump administration’s immigration efforts.
Last week, a federal judge struck down a Trump administration policy that suspended visa processing for nationals from 75 countries whose citizens were deemed likely to need public assistance upon coming to the U.S.
The Trump administration has moved aggressively to tighten immigration requirements, halt refugee resettlement and cancel scores of existing visas.
Since Trump took office, his administration has revoked more than 175,000 visas from foreign nationals, according to the State Department.
That’s quadruple the pace of the final year of the Biden administration, an analysis by The Guardian found.
The White House is pushing to permanently impose a $100,000 fee on businesses seeking H-1B visas for high-skill workers, despite a federal judge previously striking down a similar plan.
This is a breaking news story and will be updated with new information.

India has reiterated its developmental and health-related commitments to the state of Palestine and emphasised the need for a ‘two-state solution’ to the Israel-Palestinian conflict. India’s message was conveyed during the ongoing visit of Secretary of the Ministry of External Affairs, Sripriya Ranganathan, to Ramallah, the administrative headquarters of the Palestinian Authority (PA).
Ms. Ranganathan, the highest-ranking Indian diplomat to visit the West Bank since Hamas’s October 7, 2023, attack, discussed a range of Indian initiatives with Palestinian officials, including the deployment of an Indian field hospital in the Gaza Strip, said the Indian Representative Office in Palestine.
On Wednesday (August 19, 2026), the Indian and Palestinian teams launched the construction work of a super-speciality hospital in Jenin, West Bank.
“She highlighted India’s expanding support to the Palestinian health sector, including essential medicines and anti-cancer drugs, an Artificial Limb Fitment Camp, and the deployment of an Indian field hospital in Gaza. During the engagement, the Secretary also handed over a consignment of medicines from the Government of India to the Palestinian Ministry of Health, reaffirming India’s continued support to Palestinian healthcare services,” the Indian mission in Ramallah said in a statement.
Watch: Israel-Palestine conflict: What’s the two-state solution?
Ms. Ranganathan met Dr. Majed Abu Ramadan, the Minister of Health of the State of Palestine and Dr. Varsen Aghabekian Shahin, the Minister of Foreign Affairs, and reiterated India’s support for a “two-State solution” and pitched for addressing the “humanitarian situation in Gaza”. Ms. Ranganathan called on Dr. Mohammad Mustafa, Prime Minister of Palestine, on Wednesday (August 19, 2026). “Discussions focused on further strengthening the longstanding India-Palestine partnership and advancing bilateral cooperation across key areas of mutual interest,” the Indian mission said.
On Wednesday (August 19, 2026), the Indian and Palestinian teams jointly carried out the groundbreaking ceremony for the 200-seat super-speciality hospital that will be built in the Arrabeh city in Jenin Governorate in the northern West Bank.
Palestinian ambassador calls for an end to illegal Jewish settlements in West Bank
Ms. Ranganathan’s visit to the West Bank coincided with a press conference on Wednesday (August 19, 2026) that was held at the Palestine embassy by the Ambassador of Palestine, Abdullah M. Abu Shawesh.
“The international community must not wait until the Israeli election is over to ask what happened to Palestinian communities in the meantime. It must act now to halt settlement expansion, forced displacement and de facto annexation, demand accountability for extremist Israeli settler terror and protect the Palestinian people’s fundamental right to exist,” said Ambassador Abu Shawesh in his remarks. The envoy cautioned against the influence of the “hard-right, fanatical and messianic” sections over politics in Israel that will go into election in October this year.
“What is happening right now in the Occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, must be called by its name: terror carried out by extremist, racist Israeli settlers,” said Mr. Abu Shawesh.

The new leader of Iran’s top security body has warned its neighbours against joining new US efforts to squeeze Tehran’s economy, and threatened US commercial interests in the region, as Donald Trump doubled down on his fanciful view that the strait of Hormuz was a new US territory.
Mohsen Rezaei, the hardline new leader of Iran’s supreme national security council, told state television that Iran would target oil-shipping routes out the Gulf – alternatives to the strait of Hormuz – if its neighbours joined what he called the “economic war” waged by the US. Those neighbours would be “considered an enemy” and “we will target their interests”, he said.
Rezaei was a commander-in-chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) for most of the 1980-88 war with Iraq and was named this month in a series of senior appointments widely seen as hardening Tehran’s political and military stance.
His interview with broadcaster IRIB is his most extensive public statement since his appointment.
Rezaei also claimed the Islamic republic had more cards to play in the war, saying “we have not yet attacked any American economic interests”.
“So far, we have only targeted military bases, but if they want to impose economic sanctions on us, the United States has oil and economic companies around Iran and elsewhere, and we will strike them,” Rezai said in the interview, broadcast on Saturday.
Last week, Trump announced a new campaign to isolate Iran’s economy, threatening “tremendous economic consequences” on any country that helps or does business with Tehran, as the US president’s unpopular war drags toward the six-month mark without any significant sign of resolution.
Trump’s efforts to finish the war he started along with Israel on 28 February have foundered after a ceasefire agreement signed in June collapsed – leaving Iran in control of the strait of Hormuz, a waterway that was the conduit for one-fifth of the world’s oil supplies before the conflict.
Washington has called on other governments to join its efforts to isolate the Iranian economy, notably China, among Iran’s top strategic partners. However Beijing has criticised the initiative, arguing that US sanctions would not resolve the conflict in the Middle East.
One of Iran’s major trading partners, the United Arab Emirates, announced on Tuesday last week that it was suspending all trade and financial transactions with Tehran until further notice.
The US treasury has for months been carrying out Operation Economic Fury, aiming to cut off Iran’s funding with targeted sanctions, while a naval blockade in the strait of Hormuz has sought to block Iranian ports from exporting oil vital to keeping the country’s economy afloat.
The US president has in recent days repeatedly raised the concept of declaring the strait a US territory. “We control it with the blockade, and I like the idea of declaring it a territory,” he told reporters on Monday when asked about that comment.
On Friday, the US president told a crowd in South Carolina: “We don’t even know if we won, because I view the strait of Hormuz as an American territory right now.”
On Saturday night, Trump again shared on his social media platform a map graphic showing the Gulf and describing the strait of Hormuz as a “new US territory”.
Rezaei said in his interview that discussions continued with cross-strait neighbour Oman over management of the waterway, and said fees would be imposed.
French president Emmanuel Macron and Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman are expected to discuss plans to develop alternative routes to the strait of Hormuz during the Saudi leader’s two-day visit to Paris that starts on Sunday, according to officials in the presidency who weren’t authorised to speak publicly.
Proposals include increasing trade through Omani ports outside the Gulf, expanding or doubling pipelines in Saudi Arabia and elsewhere, and developing new rail links, the officials said.
France and Saudi Arabia have formed a taskforce on energy and logistics connections between the Middle East and Europe that is scheduled to meet at the ministerial level on Monday. The officials said the work would focus on identifying the most strategic projects, securing financing and establishing roles for French companies.

17-year-old gangraped in MP’s Pachmarhi; 3 arrested: Police
According to police, the incident occurred on August 19, but the survivor lodged a complaint on Sunday night
Three people were arrested on Monday in connection with alleged rape of a 17-year-old girl in Madhya Pradesh’s Pachmarhi, police said.
Police identified the accused as Hariom, Gypsy driver, and two hotel staff Pawan Bansal and Abhishek Vanshkar.
According to police, the incident occurred on August 19, but the survivor lodged a complaint on Sunday night.
Narmadapuram additional superintendent of police Abhishek Rajan said, “The victim, a school student in Pachmarhi, was standing at the bus stand with a friend on August 19 afternoon. The accused offered them a lift in a Gypsy and took them to a forest near the South Scout Guide Centre.”
According to police, the accused gangraped her and her friend to the vehicle when he resisted.
“After the rape, they dropped both students back at the bus stand and threatened them with death if they revealed the incident. The girl stopped attending school, and her health deteriorated. Her sister noticed unusual behaviour and after counselling, learned of the ordeal. The family then approached the police late Sunday night,” said the ASP.
A medical examination of the survivor has been conducted, police said.
Police said that the accused confessed to the crime during interrogation. They have been booked under sections 70(2) (gang rape), 115(2) (voluntarily causing hurt), 351(3) (criminal intimidation), and 3(5) (common intention) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, along with provisions of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act.

New Zealand prime minister Christopher Luxon has said his party will introduce a bill in parliament that seeks to ban children under 16 from using social media, proposing fines of up to 10% of a platform’s global revenue for non-compliance.
The bill would require social media platforms to take reasonable steps to verify users’ ages, including by utilising existing account information, facial technology and digital identity documents.
“We simply cannot accept the harm being done to a generation of New Zealand children,” Luxon said in a statement on Monday.
“Social media is exposing them to harmful content, addictive technology and pressures they are not equipped to deal with and it’s affecting their family life, mental health, sleep and education.”
It was not immediately clear if the bill would garner sufficient support to pass through parliament, with one of Luxon’s coalition partners – the New Zealand First party – saying it would not support it.
“We have been concerned with the proposed legislation and the direction and slippery slope that legislation like this will inevitably take our country,” New Zealand First’s leader, Winston Peters, who is also the country’s foreign minister, said on X.
In December, Australia became the world’s first country to ban social media for children under 16, blocking them from platforms including TikTok, Alphabet’s YouTube and Meta’s Instagram and Facebook.
That legislation had been a “colossal failure”, Peters said, adding that keeping children off social media should be the responsibility of parents.
“I won’t pretend that it will be simple or that it will be perfect,” Luxon said at an event.
“We won’t get every single child off social media. Some will always find ways around it, but frankly, it’s just way too important not to at least try.“

The federal government does not control property taxes, which are levied at the state and local levels.
In August 2026, a rumor spread online that U.S. President Donald Trump proposed eliminating property taxes for people age 65 and older who have paid off their mortgages.
People shared the claim on Instagram and Facebook. An X user claimed Trump had already announced such a measure, which would affect "HOMEOWNERS 65+ WHO OWN THEIR HOMES OUTRIGHT" (archived):
Meanwhile, Snopes readers emailed us to confirm the veracity of the rumor.
The claim was false. We found no evidence Trump ever proposed lifting property taxes for seniors who have paid off their mortgages. Furthermore, the federal government does not control property taxes, which are levied at the state and local levels. In other words, Trump does not have the power to lower property taxes for seniors.
A White House spokesperson told Snopes via email that Trump "has not stated this."
To investigate the rumor's legitimacy, we first used search engines such as DuckDuckGo, Google and Bing. If Trump had made such a proposal, reputable news outlets, such as The Associated Press or Reuters, would have widely reported on it, and those search inquiries would have uncovered such evidence. This was not the case.
Instead, it appears people online may have confused federal tax relief measures Trump proposed with ideas for property tax reform.
For example, in 2025, Trump's signature legislation, known as the One Big Beautiful Bill, sought to create a "$6,000 bonus deduction for taxpayers 65 and older."
The OBBB also raised the federal itemized deduction cap for certain state and local taxes from $10,000 to $40,000.
Also, on Feb. 10, 2026, California's government announced an initiative to exempt certain homeowners age 60 and older from paying property taxes on their principal residence if they have lived in it for at least five years, or in California for at least 10 years.
Further, Trump was reportedly considering a tax break on capital gains on the sale of property. This claim has not been confirmed as of this writing.
Lawmakers in several states have also proposed slashing property taxes amid steep increases in property values.
However, none of these proposals or measures amount to Trump eliminating property taxes for seniors.

The inside story of how Trabzonspor pulled off Salah deal
- Published
As Mohamed Salah signed his two-year deal in front of tens of thousands of fans inside Trabzonspor's Papara Park stadium, the man putting his signature to the contract next to the Egyptian was struggling to keep the smile off his face.
The reaction of supporters over the previous few days had already convinced club president Ertugrul Dogan he had pulled off a transfer coup.
"He's the biggest Muslim footballer in the world. He's an influential role model," he told BBC Sport Africa and BBC Turkish.
"We held Salah's signing ceremony in front of 35,000 people.
"It was clear from everything he did that he felt that love, and he told us as much too. He thanked us."
So how did Dogan persuade one of football's megastars to join a club without Champions League football and which has won the Turkish title only once since its heyday in the 1970s and early 1980s?
'Why should I choose Trabzonspor?'
Located on the Black Sea coast, the city of Trabzon sits near the border with Georgia in the north-east corner of Turkey.
With a population of around 800,000 people, it is not even in the top 20 when it comes to the country's largest urban centres.
But Dogan claims it has something special.
"I always say this about Trabzonspor and the city - we're the biggest one-club city in the world.
"Salah asked us something like, 'Why should I choose Trabzonspor now?'
"We told him about the city and said: 'You can be sure you will meet a group of supporters unlike any you have experienced before. You'll feel the genuine love those people have inside them'."
Born in January 1977, Dogan is himself a son of Trabzon.
The businessman made his money through a series of different ventures, including real estate and hazelnuts, before moving into the energy sector and specialising in biofuels.
He became Trabzonspor president in 2023, shortly after the club's most successful season in recent memory - having won the league title in 2021-22.
Under Dogan's watch, the Black Sea Storm, as the club is known, have finished third, seventh and third in the Super Lig.
Last season they won the Turkish Cup under coach Fatih Tekke, who is now looking to guide his team into the Europa League, despite a 1-0 home defeat in the first leg of their play-off tie against Hungary's Ferencvaros.
"We are working to make Trabzonspor and Trabzon itself a destination for talented young players from all over the world," said Dogan.
"We want to take them to the next level, to move on to bigger European clubs. Those young players… [combined with] star players… a star in every way, with their lifestyle, their professionalism, their smile, their positive energy.
"Mohamed Salah is a really great example in this respect."

- Why has Salah chosen to join Trabzonspor? 
  - Published6 August
Attention 'cannot be given financial value'
During the off-season, Trabzonspor sold 20-year-old Ivorian midfielder Christ Inao Oulai to Fiorentina and Brazilian forward Felipe Augusto, 22, to Zenit St Petersburg - both for large profits after only one season at the club.
Young players from Albania, Belgium, Cape Verde and Portugal have arrived to replace them, but Dogan wants to continue balancing those talents with experienced names.
Cameroon goalkeeper Andre Onana has returned for a second season on loan from Manchester United, but the deal for Salah is the potential gamechanger.
"The attention it has generated and the level of engagement it has created around the world cannot easily be given a direct financial value," explained Dogan, who has openly admitted that Salah will be earning €17m per year (£14.6m, $19.9m), as well as 20% of any merchandise with his name on.
"Purely from a financial perspective, this transfer has no direct return as such.
"We put up our season tickets this year. We had to make another increase. I told our fans, 'Look, I'm bringing you Salah, one of the biggest stars in the world'."
Dogan says nearly 70% of Salah's salary this year was covered by season ticket sales made within the first four or five days after the announcement of his arrival.
The initial target was 25,000 season ticket sales, but the club now expects to exceed 30,000, while major companies have been calling the president, looking to get involved in Salah-mania.
"We're having important discussions in Turkey, Europe and the Arab world as well."
'The whole city lives for football'
The news that Trabzonspor had won the race for Salah's signature after nine stellar seasons at Liverpool raised a few eyebrows.
Many had expected the man who sits fourth on the all-time list of Premier League goalscorers to sign a huge contract with a club in the Saudi Pro League like Cristiano Ronaldo or join Lionel Messi in the United States.
But while there was competition, Dogan says the deal happened quickly once negotiations really got going.
"Once we started talking, both sides genuinely approached each other very sincerely," he said.
"We'd actually been pursuing him since the World Cup, but we knew at the start he was also talking to other clubs."
This meant Trabzonspor initially had to bide their time, given Dogan says there is an unwritten rule in Turkey that if one club is holding talks then the others will wait.
"Yes, there were clubs in Turkey who were interested," he confirmed.
"After they said, 'We've pulled out of this transfer', we started talks. I think it took about five or six days to conclude.
"We had the first meeting over Zoom. At that point it was really just the two sides getting to know each other. Then Salah was on holiday - he was in Mykonos - and after that the talks continued again via Zoom."
Trabzonspor finally brought Salah to Turkey for his medical in Istanbul.
Dogan says they decided to hold it there to show the 34-year-old the kind of reception he would get across Turkey, not just in Trabzon.
Thousands of fans were at the airport to greet Salah when he arrived, even though it was in the middle of a working day.
Trabzonspor's new star also made his debut in Istanbul, entering the fray as a second-half substitute in a 1-1 draw against Kasimpasa on the opening day of the new league season last weekend.
He is expected to make his home league debut in Trabzon on Sunday.
"The whole city lives for football," said Dogan.
"Everywhere you go, on every corner, the city gives that player that energy and that happiness."
Thanks to Mohamed Salah, Trabzonspor's president could be smiling for a while yet.

Former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan was transferred back to jail early on Friday (August 21, 2026), hours after being taken to a hospital for court-ordered medical checks, the government said.
Also Read | Pakistan government to challenge court on moving Imran Khan to private hospital
The Supreme Court ordered on Tuesday (August 18) that Mr. Khan, Pakistan’s most popular politician, be taken to the private Shifa International Hospital in the capital Islamabad within 48 hours for treatment, after his lawyers petitioned the court over concerns that his health was poor.
The ex-cricket captain and his wife Bushra Bibi, who is also his spiritual guide, were both sentenced late last year to 17 years in prison.
Information Minister Attaullah Tarar wrote on X that Mr. Khan was instead taken to the public hospital Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) in Islamabad, blaming the “security situation” caused by Mr. Khan’s supporters at the private clinic.
“A team of qualified doctors, including an ophthalmologist, a cardiologist, and a physician, conducted a detailed examination of him and declared him medically fit,” Mr. Tarar said.
“After the completion of this entire process, he was transferred back to Adiala Jail,” he said.
Mr. Tarar also said that Mr. Khan’s sister, Uzma Khan, who is a medical doctor, was present during the examination
Hundreds of police, some wielding sticks, were deployed near Shifa International Hospital late on Thursday (August 20), with roads leading to the clinic cordoned off ahead of the transfer.
Dozens of the 73-year-old’s supporters had waited outside the hospital.
The former prime minister received eye treatment at PIMS earlier this year, with his family and lawyer saying at the time that he had lost most of the vision in his right eye.
The court had warned against public gatherings on the hospital grounds or the use of information about Mr. Khan’s health for political gain, cautioning that any breaches could lead to the order being reversed.
The next court hearing was set for September 16.
Mr. Khan was prime minister from 2018 to 2022 before being removed in a no-confidence vote during a political crisis over tensions between his government and the powerful military establishment
He has since faced multiple legal cases on corruption and other charges, which Mr. Khan and his Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party maintain are politically motivated.
His arrest triggered nationwide protests in May 2023, some of which turned violent and led to hundreds of arrests.
Ending decades of political dominance by dynastic parties, Mr. Khan was voted in by millions of Pakistanis who grew up watching him play cricket, where he excelled as an all-rounder and led the nation to a World Cup victory in 1992.
But PTI made little headway improving the country’s finances, with galloping inflation, crippling debt and a feeble rupee undermining economic reform.

Denmark's PM blasts plastic surgeon for his unsolicited offer to 'fix' spot on her nose
Mette Frederiksen, who had just returned from a trip to Ukraine, posted the note on Instagram
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen is fed up with getting unsolicited beauty advice.
The 48-year-old wrote on Instagram Monday that she had just returned back home from a trip to Ukraine, where she was exposed to air raid sirens amid the ongoing war, only to find a message from a plastic surgeon offering to "fix that little spot on your nose."
"I've lost count of how many messages I've received over the years about my appearance," Frederiksen wrote. "Especially that I have ugly teeth and thin hair. That I have an ugly 'wart' on my nose and well-meaning advice to get some Botox."
She posted a screenshot of the plastic surgeon's offer without identifying him.
She also posted her response: "Oh no. I'm happy with my body — I really don't need a male plastic surgeon to have an opinion about it!"

Frederiksen, a Social Democrat and Denmark 's second female prime minister, is now in her third term, making her one of Europe's longest-serving and most experienced leaders. She has led the European Union and NATO member country since mid-2019.
She has pledged to maintain a firm stance against U.S. President Donald Trump's ambitions for Greenland, the kingdom's semiautonomous territory, and continue supporting Ukraine against Russia's war of aggression.
On Instagram, Frederiksen stressed that she does not interfere with other people's appearance and wrote: "I'm perfectly fine with my body — as it is when you're a woman approaching 50."
She added that "if you're going to write to me (and you're more than welcome to), I hope you'll use your time to talk about something more meaningful. Not my nose."
The prime minister also said that those unsolicited beauty tips and suggestions made her feel "indignant" and that "today, I'm sending an extra loving thought to all of you who have to put up with the 'perfect imperfections' we all walk around with every day."

Last week I revealed the sneaky physics behind the “joule thief,” an electrical circuit that lets you squeeze more energy out of seemingly dead batteries. The key, it turned out, was a clever pairing of a transformer and a transistor. But the transistor deserves its own headline, because it's maybe only the most important invention of the 20th century.
Life would be completely different without transistors. For starters, there would be no personal computers or cell phones, so no Amazon, no video games, no dating apps, no messaging, no streaming, no social media, no Apple Pay or Google Maps, and no AI (hmm). Cars contain billions of transistors. They're really everywhere. So what is a transistor?
The best way to understand this pivotal technology is to follow the evolutionary trail, all the way back to the electric relays used in telegraphs in the 1800s.
Electric Relays
Telegraph lines were basically long electrical circuits. And you probably never thought about it before, but they ran on batteries—primitive, low-voltage batteries that filled an entire closet at the telegraph station—because there was no electrical grid back then.
The electric relay, invented in 1835, was a key component in these systems. Basically, it was a switch that turned an electrical current on and off—sort of like the wall switch that you use to turn a light on. But lacking fingers, the relay used a second electric current to flip the switch. Why would you use a current to turn on a current? That's a good question.
Suppose you wanted to turn on a light in another town 50 miles away. Well, you’d string real long wires on utility poles. Then you could toggle the light on and off, and even use a code with dots and dashes to send text messages. But there was a problem: The longer the wire, the more resistance it had, so not enough current would get through to deliver an intelligible signal.
The solution? Split the circuit into two 25-mile lengths and connect them with a relay. When you closed the switch on the first circuit, it operated the relay, sending the same pattern of current from a second battery through the next circuit and turning on the light. Here's a diagram:
Of course, the telegraph used a buzzer instead of a light, but same idea. Anyway, relays are still widely used today, and the idea of using a current to turn on another current opened up all kinds of possibilities. In cars, for example, it lets you use low-power dashboard controls to switch on high-power circuits that operate things like starters, headlights, or air conditioners.
How does the relay work? Basically, it's just an electromagnet. Here's a simple diagram, along with a real-life example:
Inside there's a coil of wire wrapped around an iron core. When a current flows through this control wire, it creates a magnetic field. This pulls down the metal switch on top, which contacts the output wire. You've heard relays. When your oven’s thermostat turns the heating element on and off, it's what makes that audible click.
Although relays are cool and useful, they are basic on/off switches. We have something else that’s sort of like a variable relay—the vacuum tube, invented around 1905, which made possible old-time radios.
Vacuum Tube
You can think of a vacuum tube as a modified light bulb. An incandescent light is just a thin wire that gets super hot when current runs through it, so that it glows. That filament is put inside a glass container, and the air is pumped out so the filament doesn't burn. (That's the whole purpose of the bulb—to keep out oxygen.)
But there's something else that happens, which you can't see: When the filament gets super hot, electrons are ejected from it. Since a flow of electrons is an electric current, you can use these thermal electrons in a way that's similar to a relay. Here's a diagram of a rudimentary vacuum tube:
Electrons travel across the bulb to a collector plate, which creates the output current. Now, it might seem like a silly way to do that. But if we add another wire (a grid) between the filament and the collector, we can control this output current. A negative voltage on the control will push the electrons back away from the collector to reduce the output current. Putting a positive voltage on the grid increases the flow of output current.
So this is again a current switch, and just like the relay, it's controlled by a different wire. But there are two big differences: First, there's no mechanical contact, which means the output current can change much faster. Second, the output current is not just on or off; it can vary with the strength of the control voltage.
This is what made the first audio amplifiers possible. If you had a weak signal from a distant radio station, it would not produce enough current to drive a speaker so that you could hear anything. But if you fed that signal into the control voltage in a vacuum tube, you could get an output that's much stronger yet maintains the same pattern (like music) as the original signal.
But wait! There's something else you could do with vacuum tubes—you could build a computer. Yes, early computers were just a bunch of vacuum tubes controlled by other vacuum tubes, creating logic gates. You used an input signal that is either 1 volt or 0 volts. An AND gate had two signal inputs and one output. If both inputs are 1 volt, it output 1 volt. Otherwise it gave 0 volts. An OR gate would output 1 volt if either of the inputs was 1 volt.
Actually, you could have built a computer with electric relays. But relays are much slower than vacuum tubes, and all that clicking and clacking would have been maddening. Vacuum tubes were silent, purely electronic components, with no moving parts, and that was a game changer.
Transistor
Still, there were three problems with vacuum tubes. They used a lot of power, so early computers ran hot, required massive cooling systems, and were insanely expensive to operate. Second, the tubes were fragile and easily burned out, so the computers required constant maintenance. (Literally, like full-time crews that spent their days locating and replacing dead tubes.) Finally, the tubes were just big. Those early computers, like ENIAC in 1945, filled entire rooms.
The transistor, invented at Bell Labs in 1947, fixed all that by using semiconductors. That's a word you hear all the time, but what is a semiconductor? Well, you know how some materials (like copper) conduct electricity, while others (like rubber) are insulators? Well, a semiconductor (like silicon) can switch between being one or the other.
There are two types of semiconductor: If you add extra electrons to silicon, you get an n-type semiconductor; take away electrons and you get a p-type. Electrons, of course, have negative charges, so the missing electrons act like positive charges, and we call those “electron holes.”
A transistor is created by combining different types of semiconductors. Here’s an example called an NPN transistor:
The two n-type semiconductors are separated by a p-type. This prevents electrons from moving from the input region (the “source”) to the output region (the “drain”). However, if a voltage is applied to the control, or gate, then electrons can move to the output. Yes, once again, it's basically a switch, where one current turns on a second current—but now with much finer control.
Best of all, they could be miniaturized—and boy oh boy oh boy, were they ever. Floor-standing radio consoles were replaced by “transistor radios,” carried everywhere by teens in the 1950s and ’60s. They contained six to 10 transistors. Today, the iPhone 17 Pro contains up to 30 billion transistors. That is crazy, but it's what makes our computer-based world run.

A post by an X user named Sonali (@Sonalimumbai1), who describes herself as a BJP leader and is followed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the platform, went viral last week. The post carries a somewhat blurred black and white image of a group of women dancing atop a table in what seems to be hotel. Sonali implied that one of these women is Congress leader Sonia Gandhi.
The image, posted on August 14, has more than 353,800 views till date. (Archive)
बारबाले चे मूत्र पिणारे असंच बोलणार. pic.twitter.com/C0jpHXHXMa
— 🚩 सोनाली 🚩🇮🇳 (@Sonalimumbai1) August 14, 2026
The post came shortly after Congress leader and Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi on August 14 mocked at the BJP government’s foreign policy and took a jibe at PM Modi’s customary hugs with international leaders.
The remarks triggered immediate backlash from the BJP and its supporters. As a part of that, X user Sonali, posted a video of Indira Gandhi hugging former President of Cuba Fidel Castro. The caption read, (translated from Marathi), “Whenever Rahul talks nonsense, all the misdeeds of his family come out in the open. Now watch this video. In this, Indira Gandhi is hugging Fidel Castro of Cuba. I don’t think anything there is wrong with it. What will the son of a bar dancer say about this? Now what do the sycophants of Congress have to say about this?”
राहुल्या जेव्हा कधी तोंडाने हागतो त्याच्या खानदानाची सगळी कर्म रस्त्यावर येतात.
आता हा व्हिडिओ बघा.
याच्यामध्ये इंदिरा गांधी Cuba च्या Fidel Castro यांच्याशी गळाभेट घेत आहेत.
I don’t think anything wrong with it.
बारबालेचा पुत्र याच्यावर काय बोलणार…??
आता यावर… pic.twitter.com/FVz3c1USL6
— 🚩 सोनाली 🚩🇮🇳 (@Sonalimumbai1) August 14, 2026
After an X user responded to Sonali’s post with derogatory comments, she countered it with the aforementioned image with the caption: “That’s what people who drink bar dancer’s urine would say.”
Fact Check
To verify the authenticity of the image, which was bearing the watermark of Getty Images, we ran a reverse image search on Google. This search led us to the archive of Getty Images, where a clearer version of the same image is available. The caption of this image reads: “Go Go dancing girls help break the beer drought on Rawson Hotel in Auburn on 21 November 1967.”
The image comprises three dancing women. If one zooms in on the image, it becomes clear that none of these women is Sonia Gandhi.
Upon further investigation, we came across a Facebook page named ‘I Grew Up in Mortdale 2223’. On November 17, 2025, the page posted the same image with the caption: “#OnThisDay 17 November 1967, a strike by more than 2000 brewery workers in Sydney led to what was to be known as the “Draught Beer Drought”. When, after 14 days of negotiations, the workers voted to return to work, a group of go-go dancers helped patrons to celebrate at the Rawson Hotel in Auburn. [Photo by Vic Sumner » Fairfax Archives]
This news was also featured on the November 15, 1967, edition of The Canberra Times of Australia.
According to publicly available information, Sonia Gandhi studied at Bell Education Trust, Cambridge, United Kingdom in 1964, where she met and married Rajiv Gandhi in 1968. During her studies, she worked as a part time server at a local restaurant in Cambridge. There is no official record mentioning that she moved to Australia in that time period.
Thus, it can be conclusively stated that an image from 1967 of go-go dancers in Australia was shared by X user Sonali to falsely claim that one of those women was Sonia Gandhi.
Sharing unrelated images to attack the Congress leader is not a new trend. Alt News published a fact-check on March 25, 2019, debunking a similar claim. At the time, BJP supporters circulated an image of actress Ursula Andress from the James Bond film Dr No, falsely claiming that it showed Sonia Gandhi in an “inappropriate” dress.

Mexico ‘optimistic’ on US trade deal after Canada talks collapse
President Claudia Sheinbaum’s top trade negotiator is in Washington, seeking to lower 50 per cent US tariffs on Mexican steel and aluminium
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum expressed optimism she can reach a trade deal with US President Donald Trump as her chief negotiator leads talks in Washington, just after negotiations between the US and Canada collapsed.
“As President Trump said, we hope to reach an agreement with the US,” she told reporters on Monday after being asked about the escalating US-Canada impasse. “I’m optimistic an agreement can be reached.”
Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard, Sheinbaum’s top trade negotiator, will remain in Washington for several days as he seeks to lower 50 per cent US tariffs on Mexican steel and aluminium, and 25 per cent duties on cars.

The breakdown also triggered a 50 per cent US levy on about US$20 billion of Canadian goods, while Prime Minister Mark Carney announced retaliatory tariffs to take effect on September 8.

If there’s one thing young moviegoers seem to fear these days, it’s the idea of the in-between. The term liminal horror has gone from niche internet speak to Hollywood trend, thanks to the acclaimed TV show Severance and the recent smash-hit movie Backrooms. Stories like these mine the unsettling feeling of nondescript office corridors and basement halls that seem to self-replicate into infinity; this spring also saw the U.S. release of the excellent Japanese film Exit 8, a video-game adaptation about someone getting trapped in a subway station with seemingly no way out. Now there’s It Ends, a low-budget bit of creepy cleverness with a punchy pitch: What if you got lost driving down a road that never ends?
That this type of premise has grown more commonplace makes sense. Such a film typically needs only one set (for example, a long, lonely road, flanked by trees), a small cast of characters, and a spare, intentionally circular script. It Ends uses that scrappy charm to its advantage, the lack of frills dialing up a sense of realism. The film, written and directed by the newcomer Alexander Ullom, follows James (played by Phinehas Yoon), Day (Akira Jackson), Fisher (Noah Toth), and Tyler (Mitchell Cole), four friends who are headed on a celebratory graduation road trip. Their drive is occupied by the sort of nonsensical, wandering conversations young people love to have; there’s no real sign of anything being wrong until Tyler notices that he’s missed his turn.
The horror builds gradually, spikes, then slows to an existentially brutal crawl. The group realizes that there’s no way off the road, but when they get out of the car to look around, swarms of people emerge from the woods and fight to enter their vehicle. As the friends continue on in search of safety, they notice that the gas tank never goes empty, they never feel hungry, and nobody needs to sleep. They’re in a sort of limbo, condemned to keep moving despite having no destination. It’s essentially a Gen Z take on Sartre’s No Exit, a gentle riff on hell being other people, with a few jump scares tossed in for fun.
But while prior small-scale horror movies such as The Blair Witch Project and Paranormal Activity had an unseen villain guiding the scares, It Ends thrives on an utter lack of information about what is happening and why. The terror of liminality is how effortlessly it evokes the creepiness of a bad dream, the kind that begins in the middle of the story and seems just off. There’s no monster around the corner, no demonic puzzle to be solved. The characters of It Ends initially debate what’s going on, keeping track of patterns occurring around them in search of some explanation. While James keeps doing so as a way of staying sane, the others start to accept their frozen existence; the strangers in the woods, it seems, are also confined to the road’s environs.
That Ullom manages to squeeze a feature-length movie out of such a mundane premise is impressive; it helps that his cast is charming enough to carry it off. As the film plods on, it starts to skip further and further ahead in time, warping the viewer’s sense of chronology. It Ends is more aggressively aimless than other recent entries in the genre: Exit 8 sees its heroes try to figure a way out of their infinite subway station (it was based on a video game, so some resolution is built into the plot); the protagonists of Backrooms discovered a world of non-Euclidean corridors and lobbies in a basement, then found out that opportunistic corporate villains were plundering it; such a revelation hints at sequels that could expand its lore.
The simplicity of It Ends, by comparison, is wonderful and jarring, as is the total inability for future properties to spill out of it. Part of the dread that liminal horror mines is the drudgery of the never-ending scroll, a familiar feeling for anyone who’s been on social media; no matter how much you look, you’ll never hit bottom, only summon more of whatever the algorithm wants to serve you. It Ends is set entirely outdoors but captures that same fear of being stuck without any touchstones to distinguish simulation from reality.

Lanterns episode 2, “Trust Fall,” sees John Stewart (Aaron Pierre) attempt to escape alien captors on the highway while maintaining custody of Hal’s (Kyle Chandler) lantern and trying to keep his conjured bird alive.
The dynamic sequence, which features a close quarters fight in the back of a moving van and a chase into oncoming traffic, is the HBO Max original’s first high stakes action scene and it was choreographed by stunt coordinator and second unit director Justin Riemer.
I caught up with Riemer to delve into the challenge of orchestrating the standout moment around a bird and giving the audience our first real look at who John is as a fighter.
Justin Riemer On The Bird In ‘Lanterns’ Episode 2 Highway Fight
Riemer shared that conceptually Lanterns creators Chris Mundy and Damon Lindelof “had a pretty clear idea of where we started and where we needed to end in the sequence,” his job was to figure out how the scene gets there.
He described incorporating John’s bird as a “unique challenge” which led to a lot of discussions about how to convincingly pull it off. For a sequence as propulsive as episode 2’s highway chase, it’s not as simple as knowing a bird is present. They had to consider “how big it would be, how it would move, [and] how it would react to John and the environment.”
That last point encompassed not only the van where the bird starts off cradled in the hands of one of John’s captors but also outside as it flies past and through cars caught in the wreckage piling up as John tries to escape and chase it down.
Riemer said, “The goal was to make the interaction feel as seamless and natural as possible.” But, of course, choreographing the scene meant taking into account a living creature that’s not physically there.
“The physicality of the fight and the sequence stays the same,” he explained. “But you’re constantly thinking ahead for when the bird actually becomes part of the scene.” The answer for Lanterns was immediately.
As soon as John wakes up in a moving van with his hands zip-tied, he locates his bird and then uses it to his advantage. The bird serves as a distraction, first for the man watching John and then for the driver as John fights to free his hands and take down his captor.
It’s the first time viewers see John square off with someone and the team wanted the audience “to understand from the beginning that John is extremely capable.” The choreography drew from three facts about him—he’s “an ex-Marine, and a boxer, he’s someone who has trained for this his entire life.”
For John, it’s not a question of if he’s able to handle the situation. It’s how. That’s why he’s showcased as being “incredibly powerful, but at the same time, very technical and controlled in the way he fights.”
However, this is also a two-person dance. The man John fights factors into the choreography’s storytelling as well. Riemer said, “With the captor, hopefully the audience picks up that there’s something just a little different about him and his capabilities,” even with the subtle choices that were made.
This is in reference to the building suspicion during the fight that John’s captors aren’t human. It starts with the gentle way the man in the back of the van holds his bird and continues through the close quarters clash into the chase down the highway as the man hops from car to car.
The reveal that the beings who captured John are aliens doesn’t happen until after the highway chase, but the action sequence sets it up well.
Bearing the bird in mind also helped the Lanterns team figure out the logistics of getting John out of the van and onto the highway without sacrificing momentum. Riemer said they treated the fight in the van and the chase on the highway as two separate scenes and the bird was the connective tissue between them.
He shared, “Inside the van, It’s about John versus the captor. It’s close, physical, and contained. Once we hit the highway, the dynamic shifts to John and the bird. The objective remains the same, John has to catch the bird.”
John’s doing this while keeping up with Hal’s lantern and trying to put distance between him and his captor. But the road isn’t empty, it’s not that simple. The highway presents its own challenges as it’s broad delight and traffic is not exactly light. Riemer described this new element as a change of obstacles.
He said, “The cars and traffic essentially replace the captor, creating new obstacles and danger,” which becomes part of the choreography that John has to navigate to reach his objective.
“Even though the captor is still there,” Riemer continued. “He almost becomes secondary to John’s pursuit of the bird.”
As the audience, we see that clearest when John dives over a car to catch his bird and is so preoccupied with having protected it—while taking note of his captor still chasing him—that he neglects to account for the cars still heading toward him. The scene ends with John knocked out by a van that swerves in order to not hit him dead on.
Riemer couldn’t tease much about what viewers can expect to see regarding John’s fight sequences as we move further into the season. However, he did say, “John is extremely capable with or without the ring,” emphasizing that the DC icon is adept at using what he has on hand to protect himself whether that be his own body or what he’s willed into being.

A post is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) claiming that US President Donald Trump said he had spoken with Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and that the US was in talks to adopt India’s EVM system for the 2028 election. It further claims that Trump praised India’s EVMs as secure and called for an end to mail-in voting. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: Donald Trump said the US is in talks with India to bring its EVM system to America for the 2028 election.
Fact: The viral post is fabricated. In his original post, Trump mentioned CEC Gyanesh Kumar’s interaction with the US administration and praised India’s voter ID system while urging Congress to pass the SAVE America Act. However, he did not say that the US was in talks to bring India’s EVM system to America for the 2028 election. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
To verify the claim, we conducted a Google search using relevant keywords but found no credible reports or official information confirming that US President Donald Trump said the US is in talks with India to bring its EVM system to America for the 2028 election.
We then reviewed the social media accounts (here, here, and here) of US President Donald Trump to check whether he had made the statement mentioned in the viral post. However, we found no post from Trump stating that the US is in talks with India to bring its EVM system to America for the 2028 election.
During this process, we found a Truth Social post (archived) by Trump dated 18 August 2026. In the post, Trump stated that earlier that month, India’s Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar had asked his administration how the US could conduct elections without valid photo ID. Trump also referred to India’s last election, which had 646 million voters, noting that less than 1% voted by mail and that every voter had to provide a valid photo identity document. He concluded by calling for the passage of the SAVE America Act.
The post was also reposted (archived) by US Ambassador to India and Special Envoy to South and Central Asia Sergio Gor on the same day, stating, “President Donald J. Trump is absolutely correct! 646 MILLION voters, every single one, required an ID in India’s last election. Congress should pass THE SAVE AMERICA ACT.” This further confirms that the viral post claiming Trump discussed bringing India’s EVMs to the US is fabricated.
We also found multiple media reports (here, here, and here) about Trump’s post, in which the US President praised India’s election system and called for the passage of the SAVE America Act, referring to the conversation with CEC Gyanesh Kumar. However, none of these reports mentioned that the US is in talks with India to bring its EVM system to America for the 2028 election.
The SAVE America Act (H.R. 7296), or the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility Act, is a proposed US federal law that would require people registering to vote in federal elections to provide documentary proof of US citizenship and require voters to present an eligible photo ID when voting. The bill was introduced in the US House of Representatives on 30 January 2026 and referred to the House Committee on House Administration. As of 20 August 2026, it has not (here, here) become law. The legislation concerns voter eligibility and identification and has no provisions related to adopting or importing India’s EVM system.
To sum up, this viral post alleging that President Donald Trump said the US plans to bring India’s EVMs for the 2028 election is fabricated.

Shigellosis has surfaced again in Keralam, with a three-year-old child from Kottukal in Thiruvananthapuram district admitted to SAT Hospital with the infection.
Following this, health officials have renewed public health warnings, urging people to be cautious about the food and beverages they consume outside their homes, especially during the festival season.
According to reports, the child had travelled with her family to Nagercoil on August 12. On the way, they reportedly consumed cold drinks from a wayside vendor. The child developed diarrhoea and vomiting the following day and was later admitted to SAT hospital, where she is now recuperating in one of the paediatric wards. The case was confirmed on Tuesday (August 18, 2026).
One more case of shigellosis was also reported from Vizhinjam in Thiruvananthapuram on Tuesday; and three scattered cases from Pazhayannur in Thrissur; Kattipara in Kozhikode and Noolpuzha in Wayanad.
Shigellosis (bacillary dysentery) is a highly contagious bacterial diarrhoeal infection caused by shigella, which is contracted through contaminated food or water. The disease can present with mild symptoms or as severe cases of diarrhoea.
Health officials point out that cases of shigellosis are reported sporadically throughout the year from all districts in Keralam, with some cases triggering small local outbreaks.
The infection spreads through contaminated water, food and contact from infected surfaces.
While shigellosis is self-limiting in healthy adults, it can be fatal for children under five years, in whom the highest mortality is reported. The elderly and immunocompromised individuals are also highly vulnerable.
Symptoms usually appear within one to two days of infection and include fever, diarrhoea, vomiting, nausea, blood in stools, and painful, frequent urges to use the washroom.
The Health department has advised that affected persons use solutions of oral rehydration salts so that dehydration is avoided and that they seek treatment if there is no respite in diarrhoea.
It was in June this year (2026) that Keralam reported major Shigellosis outbreaks, with over 225 cases and six deaths reported from Kozhikode, Malappuram, and Wayanad districts. Outbreaks were officially declared in Kozhikode (77 cases), Wayanad (27), Malappuram (37), Thrissur (15), and Alappuzha (5). Cases were also reported from Thiruvananthapuram (20), Kollam (15), Kannur (14), Palakkad (6), Ernakulam (4), Idukki (3), and Pathanamthitta (1) during June and July.
As of August 18 this year, as many as 441 confirmed cases, 106 probable cases and eight deaths due to Shigellosis have been reported in the State. Last year, a total of 133 cases were reported, with zero deaths.

Gurugram rain chaos: School buses stranded for hours with kids, ambulances stuck; WFH, online classes advised
Gurugram experienced significant disruption from rain-induced waterlogging, affecting traffic and stranding vehicles.
Heavy rain brought Gurugram to a standstill on Monday, with school buses and ambulances getting stuck in waterlogged roads and traffic slowing across several parts of the city. The administration has advised offices to allow work from home and ordered schools to conduct online classes on Tuesday.
The district administration said Gurugram received 70 mm of rainfall by 1.30 pm. Waterlogging was reported from Narsinghpur, Hero Honda Chowk, Rajiv Chowk, IFFCO Chowk and several parts of old Gurugram, while vehicles were stuck around Rajiv Chowk. School buses and ambulances were also caught in waterlogging on Sohna Road.
The rain affected several major roads, including Rajiv Chowk, IFFCO Chowk, Railway Road, Sector 5, Old Delhi Road, Mehrauli Road and Basai Road. The Naharpur underpass was also waterlogged. Traffic remained slow on several roads, with commuters seen wading through flooded streets.
School buses stranded
Deep Dive
School buses carrying children home bore the brunt of the waterlogging, with several stranded for hours at Rail Vihar in Sector 47 and Subash Chowk.
The administration subsequently ordered all government and private schools and educational institutions in the district to conduct classes online on Tuesday. The decision was taken citing the safety of students and staff and the likelihood of traffic congestion due to waterlogging.
Offices advised work from home
Deputy Commissioner Uttam Singh, who is also chairperson of the District Disaster Management Authority, said the work-from-home advisory for corporate and private offices would remain in effect on August 25.
The decision was aimed at reducing traffic congestion and facilitating repair and maintenance work on roads and drains by civic agencies, according to an official statement.
The rain also brought traffic movement in parts of old Gurugram to a standstill. Sadar Bazar, Gurdwara Road and Old Delhi Road were among the areas where waterlogging led to traffic jams that continued into the afternoon.
A senior traffic police officer said vehicular movement was choked near the Sirhaul border, Rajiv Chowk, Narsinghpur and some other locations. Traffic police personnel were deployed to manage the situation.
Expressway submerged
A large section of the Delhi-Gurugram Expressway near Cyber Hub, opposite Gateway Tower Metro station, was submerged, disrupting traffic on the major thoroughfare.
Sheetla Mata Road, which has emerged as one of Gurugram's flood-prone locations this monsoon, was also among the worst-affected areas.
Gurugram Traffic Police deployed drones to monitor waterlogged areas and major roads during the rainfall. Officials said the aerial surveillance helped assess traffic conditions, identify sensitive locations and issue directions to personnel deployed on the ground.
Municipal Corporation officials remained on the ground as the rain affected several parts of the city.
Municipal Commissioner Pradeep Dahiya and Additional Municipal Commissioner Yash Jaluka inspected waterlogging-prone areas along with officials from the Gurugram Metropolitan Development Authority and the National Highways Authority of India.
They inspected areas including Jhar Sa Chowk, Rajiv Chowk, Medanta Underpass, Tau Devilal Stadium, Sohna Road and Elante Mall.
Dahiya directed officials to keep pumping arrangements active in waterlogged areas and ensure that teams reached locations immediately after receiving reports of waterlogging and drained accumulated water. He also directed officials to ensure swift drainage and continuous monitoring.
