Three reasons Chelsea could challenge for title - and one they may not
- Published
If football is won in both boxes, it seems as though Chelsea have one far better covered than the other.
Xabi Alonso began his Stamford Bridge reign with an entertaining 3-2 Premier League win at west London rivals Fulham on Monday - and their new-look front three stole the show.
Morgan Rogers, making his debut after his club record £117m summer move from Aston Villa, combined with Cole Palmer and Joao Pedro to produce a devastating attacking display.
All three scored, with Palmer in particular looking back to his best after a difficult year hampered by injuries, culminating in his omission from England's World Cup squad.
At the other end, though, questions remain over goalkeeper Robert Sanchez after two errors contributed to Fulham's goals from Josh King and Gonzalo Garcia.
Alonso said his front three needed to "lead the rest" so that the "other ones will follow".
But Sanchez has some catching up to do - and when asked about his mistakes, Alonso could only stress the collective responsibility of the team.
"We need to accept and learn from them [the mistakes]," said the Spaniard. "This is going to be a process.
"All the lines, from the strikers, the midfielders, the defence, the goalkeepers, we want to do better in everything."
After the match, ex-Liverpool defender Jamie Carragher - a former team-mate of Alonso - said on Sky Sports that Palmer, Rogers and Joao Pedro are "as good as anything in the Premier League right now".
He also said they would they "will never win the league with Sanchez in goal".
Will that come to pass?
'Sensational' Palmer 'hungry' again
It took Joao Pedro just 31 seconds to open the scoring, latching on to a pass from Palmer and lifting his shot over Fulham goalkeeper Bernd Leno for Chelsea's fastest goal since October 2016.
After King had equalised, Rogers then marked his debut with a goal before half-time by tapping in from close range.
But it was Palmer - scorer of Chelsea's third - who stood out most.
He has endured a frustrating 18 months since a niggling groin problem disrupted his sensational start to life at Stamford Bridge, highlighted by the fact he matched last season's Premier League assist tally by setting up Joao Pedro.
His trickery and creativity was on display throughout against Fulham, along with an impressive work-rate. This was more like the Palmer we saw during his first season at Stamford Bridge - and like the one who tore Paris St-Germain apart during last year's Club World Cup final.
"Over the summer I rested, I recharged and, yeah, I'm ready and I'm hungry," Palmer, who is now just two goals away from 50 in the Premier League, told Sky Sports.
He certainly looks refreshed.
During Chelsea's pre-season tour of Australia, he spoke of having a point to prove and admitted a lengthy summer break felt unusual after featuring in major tournaments in each of the previous three years.
"Cole Palmer was sensational," said former Manchester United defender Gary Neville on Sky Sports. "Him and Morgan Rogers were electric with Joao Pedro - the front three were brilliant.
"That tonight was the old Cole Palmer. It was unbelievable to watch. One of the best things I've seen this weekend."
How two best mates and Joao Pedro linked up
While Palmer and Joao Pedro have generally carried Chelsea's biggest attacking threat in recent times, they have now been joined by the impressive Rogers too.
His arrival reunites him with Palmer, an ex-Manchester City team-mate and someone he described after the win at Craven Cottage as his "best friend in football".
"He had a difficult season with injuries and stuff last year - and you could see it in his eyes in pre-season and training that he's ready this year and ready to prove people wrong," added Rogers when asked about Palmer's display.
"You saw that with that performance. He was the best player on the pitch by a mile and that's what he does. It's good to have him on our side."
Indeed, it was also encouraging how Rogers, whose pre-season was shortened by his involvement in England's run to third place at the World Cup, looked so fit and powerful.
Rogers is the first Chelsea player to score on his Premier League debut since Christopher Nkunku in 2023 - and the first to create five chances in his first league appearance since records began in 2003-04.
It was also the first time Chelsea supporters sang the new Rogers chant in the away end.
Like Palmer, Joao Pedro missed out on the World Cup - as a high-profile omission from Brazil's squad - but returned in pre-season with eight goals in seven games.
It was no surprise to see him on the scoresheet so early in the Premier League campaign, having inherited the number nine shirt from Liam Delap, who was left out of the squad on Monday, following the contract extension the Brazilian signed this weekend.
"Great combination, great quality," Alonso told BBC Match of the Day when asked about his front three.
"We know if we reach them [Joao Pedro, Morgan Rogers and Cole Palmer] in good positions, they have this talent to create special things and I am very happy the three forwards have scored.
"We need to put them in the best situations. I am happy for the three of them. They played for the team."
'Sanchez will undermine everything they do'
Yet questions remain over Sanchez, who allowed King's low strike to go straight through him for Fulham's equaliser and then tamely parried Timothy Castagne's shot into a dangerous area for Garcia to head in from close range to set up a nervy finish.
"They have strengthened in every position of the pitch but you cannot take a chance on goalkeepers," said Neville.
"I've said before it's the most difficult position on the pitch, it's the one that carries the most scrutiny and if you have got a goalkeeper who's making mistakes and is anxious, it will undermine everything you're trying to do.
"It's a problem. You've got to say it's a problem."
There was nowhere to hide for Sanchez.
King's equaliser in the 23rd minute had an expected goals on target (xGoT) value of just 0.05, making it the lowest-rated shot to result in a goal during the opening weekend of the Premier League season.
In other words, Sanchez really should have saved it.
He did make a number of other saves, but he also conceded a corner after failing to clear the ball before it ran out of play and was later unconvincing when coming off his line to deal with a long ball, with Antonee Robinson missing the target to let him off the hook.
While Alonso defended his goalkeeper after the game, in his pre-match news conference on Thursday, he said: "The pitch is the boss of everything. I don't decide. The players need to show me."
That message applied to his goalkeepers - Sanchez and number two Mike Penders, 21, who is waiting to make his debut after returning from a successful loan spell at Strasbourg.
With the transfer window still open, many Chelsea fans will be asking whether the club need a new first-choice goalkeeper.
As Carragher said: "They have to sort the goalkeeping issue out because it's going to come back and haunt them again this season as it did tonight."

Where Do America’s Colleges Go From Here?
The Trump administration has a new series of questions for colleges about affordability, curriculum, and “national service”—how will they respond? And: W. E. B. Du Bois and Booker T. Washington in a dubious battle over education, from the Atlantic archives.
Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts
On August 3, Education Secretary Linda McMahon sent a letter to states and higher-education leaders with instructions to, as McMahon put it, “describe to the American public your commitments to rigorous teaching, pathbreaking research, and national service—commitments that make our universities a bedrock institution of the American republic.”
A request like that would be simple enough if not for the history between the Trump administration and higher education—a relationship that can fairly be described as antagonistic. Case in point: last year’s “Compact for Academic Excellence in Higher Education,” which critics from across the political spectrum argued effectively asked colleges to compromise academic freedom in exchange for privileged, if vague, access to federal funds. There’s also the suite of federal investigations targeting diversity programs on college campuses.
Questioning colleges is normal. There are outstanding concerns about the experience, the education, and the enterprise of higher education: How much does it cost, and is that more than families can pay? Who gets in, and why? Are faculty members treated with dignity? What is college even for? So, although college leaders argue that a few of the concerns voiced in the document are legitimate, they also see within it the bane of Ilium.
Read: A deal that would end universities’ independence
On this week’s Radio Atlantic, I’m joined by Jack Stripling, the host of the College Matters podcast at The Chronicle of Higher Education, to consider higher education in the Trump era, and the purpose of college itself.
I also go back into the Atlantic archives to look at a debate between W. E. B. Du Bois and Booker T. Washington over their theories of advancement for Black people, and how it should inform our thinking about colleges today.

Now, I was always a big fan of the first day of school. In grade school, I’d pick out my clothes the night before, have them sitting and ready next to my bed. My bag was packed with everything I could possibly need, and some things I definitely didn’t. In college, every new year meant new books, new ideas, and new challenges.
But over the last several years, there has been a battle raging for the soul of higher education in America that’s divorced from those idyllic memories—a battle that has many asking what college is supposed to be and whom it is supposed to serve. Earlier this month, Education Secretary Linda McMahon sent a letter to colleges asking them to respond to a series of questions. Questions about their institutions, their programs, and how they contribute to the American project. The letter gives college leaders one more thing to consider in an era marked by funding woes, by fears of enrollment stagnation and decline, technological advancements, and political pressures.
How will it all play out? And what will school leaders be thinking about throughout the next year?
Jack Stripling is the host of the College Matters podcast at The Chronicle of Higher Education and my former colleague. And he joins me now to discuss.

They’re already working on these things. And you mentioned that other institutions are concerned about these things. Are they also working on those things? Like, how much of this is the rest of higher education already doing?
Stripling: Well, I think that we’re having a national conversation around things like the SAT, for example. Some colleges went test optional, or even test blind. And even, you know, the liberal state of California is starting to grapple with this question. Did doing away with the SAT mean that we got students here who weren’t prepared for the level of work they were going to get at a University of California campus? So that conversation is happening in states red and blue, and it’s something the Trump administration emphasizes and cares deeply about.
It’s part of this larger merit conversation.
Harris: And of the things that are in the actual call to action, how much of it are colleges already doing? I thought that was a really interesting critique, was that these questions are things that we’ve already outlined; they’re things we’re already trying to address. So how much of it are the colleges actually already doing?
Stripling: Well, your mileage may vary on whether they’re doing enough to control cost, whether they’re doing enough to address ideological capture within their own departments.
Cost you can’t argue with; we now have from the highly selective institutions that are charging over $100,000 to other privates that are much lower but still very much out of reach for most American families. Very hard to argue with that.
Then you have recent reports from Yale and one commissioned by the chancellors at Vanderbilt and Wash U that have both said there’s some credence to this idea that politicization has become a problem in our academic departments. So those voices are coming from within. Clearly there has been some recognition within higher education that some of these critiques have some merit.
Harris: To that point though, one of the administration’s plans, goals, is to address the high cost of going to college. But how much control do institutions actually have over the cost of education?
Jack Stripling: Well, Adam, you’ll know from our days working together at The Chronicle, which were the best of my life, I should say—2017 was a great year for me.
Harris: Incredible. I enjoyed it so much.
Stripling: But in any case, you’ll remember it was the same story that we were hearing then, which was that a lot of the drivers of cost have to do with personnel; they have to do with structural issues within higher education; they have to do with students wanting more amenities—that was kind of an old sall. And I think you’re hearing a lot of the same things, but the fact is they can’t get away from the reality that people are losing confidence in higher education as an institution.
If you look at the latest polling on this, I think it’s, like, four in 10 Americans that say they have high confidence or a lot of confidence in higher education now. And even Democrats who have historically supported higher education more than Republicans are starting to lose their affection for the institution.
So I think there’s a recognition that it’s a real problem, and I really do think that the money is the big factor. We keep talking about the politics, but when people are saying I don’t know if college is worth it, they’re usually saying I don’t know if it’s worth the money, not I don’t know if it’s worth risking meeting a liberal person.
Harris: I do want to talk more about the purpose of higher education, but I wanted to ask first about the pressures for ideological change from the administration and state lawmakers. You’re in Florida, and that’s a good example of the changes in terms of curriculum, institutional culture. So are you noticing any effects?
Stripling: I think it kind of remains to be seen, Adam. I still—and again, this is really more gut than data—but I still do think cost is the major thing families are worried about.
I will say that, to your point, I do live in Florida and, you know, this is famously the place where woke goes to die, as Ron DeSantis said. And a lot of action has been taken on the ideological front that is also connected to this question of What is college for?
So if you think about the core curriculum, the courses that colleges are saying everybody should take, there’s usually some menu of sorts. A lot of institutions over time—there’s been a lot of bloat there. There’s been a lot of things that we might not consider essential that have come into the core curriculum. So some of these ostensibly sort of ideological attacks resonate to some degree with faculty who say, Actually we have gotten a little out of control in what’s in this core.
But what you’re pointing to, Adam, is the key distinction, which is, is higher education about vocation or does it have some sort of more aspirational mission? And this is an old problem. Are you there to learn about how to prepare for your first job, or is it about preparing you for a life of greater intellectual enrichment? And I think that that’s at the heart of a lot of the conversations we’re having, even if they are politically coded. What is college for? continues to be something that, you know, sort of divides people.
What’s interesting is that parents and even students will tell you, I really want to go to college and be able to get a good job. And I want to be able to leave here with a credential that matters and that is seen as authentic, even though I use ChatGPT for half my classes.
But students also say they want more. If you look at the studies around mental health that places like the Harvard Grad School of Education have done, they are desperate for something real. And so when they come to an institution that seems like it’s all about pleasing the next corporate overlord, they chafe. That’s why they’re booing at commencement ceremonies when people praise AI, right? So students actually do want something more than something to punch up their résumé.
Harris: So, Jack, we’re in August, whole school year ahead of us. What will you be keeping your eye on the most as this year develops?
Stripling: I go back to what I said before, which is this collective sense of Is the Trump administration done with us?
I think that that is something that I’m starting to hear people in higher education ask. Like, Was this Act 1, or is this letter in and of itself a form of surrender, a sort of concession? They’re looking for a symbolic win. Using the DOJ and these other arms of the government to try to exact concessions or revenge is very expensive. It’s very time consuming, and they’ve lost in court in some big ways. Now these cases are still unfolding, but that’s the reality.
What I will be paying attention to is this question of purpose, though. And I know this is going to sound weird, Adam, but have you read Stoner?
Harris: Yes, I have.
Stripling: Okay. So for folks who don’t know, this is a 1965 novel by John Williams. We just talked about it on my podcast, College Matters. We had sort of a reading club.
And it’s the story about this professor at Mizzou, who’s this farm boy who goes to the University of Missouri thinking that he’s going to major in some kind of agricultural sciences. He’s going to come back and work on the family farm, and life’s gonna be happy for him and his parents. What ends up happening instead is that he goes into this class and he’s exposed to his first Shakespearean sonnet, and it immediately changes his world. He can’t explain why, but the way he sees people, the way he sees worlds, the way he interacts with the universe changes in some profound way. And the frustration of the novel is that he can’t really explain it to anyone. It’s just something he feels.
And that’s the problem with this product that we call “higher education.” When it works as it should, it’s transformational. It changes you in profound ways. But it’s nearly impossible to explain how.
And that makes it really hard to charge $100,000 for. And so what higher education is going to have to do this year, like it has every other previous year I’ve been covering it, is explain that transformational experience in a way that resonates with every constituency, whether it’s the Trump administration, the student who doesn’t have enough money to go to college, the parents who are skeptical about the the job return, the people who care about AI and how that’s changing credentials. Somehow they’re going to have to make that case, and maybe reading Stoner is a good start. But that’s what I’m always thinking about.
Harris: Well, Jack, as always, it is fantastic to see you, to talk to you, and you’ve given us a lot to think about as we head into this new school year. It’s great to have you on.
Stripling: Thank you, Adam. Let’s do it again. I really appreciate it.
Harris: We’re back in the archives this week with a look at a question that has troubled some of the greatest minds throughout history. It’s a question that Booker T. Washington and W. E. B. Du Bois tried to answer in The Atlantic between 1896 and 1903: Are colleges designed only to train people to work for their own improvement, or are they designed to train people to create a better society?
Booker T. Washington was the most powerful Black man of the late 19th and early 20th century in America. He was born on a tobacco plantation in 1856, and he was emancipated from slavery at the end of the Civil War. He was 9 years old then. Education changed his life.
Writing about his upbringing in the September 1896 issue of The Atlantic, Washington said: “After the close of the war, while working in the coal-mines of West Virginia for the support of my mother, I heard in some accidental way of the Hampton Institute.”
Hampton Normal and Agricultural Institute, near the Chesapeake Bay in Virginia, had opened its doors in 1868. It had a simple mission: “to train selected Negro youth who should go out and teach and lead their people first by example.” The students from Hampton were expected to get land and homes, to work for their money with knowledge of why they were doing the work—or, as the institution’s founder put it, “to replace stupid drudgery with skilled hands.”
Washington would later write in the pages of The Atlantic in 1896 the education he received at Hampton changed him, it “caused me for the first time to realize what it meant to be a man instead of a piece of property.”
He was ready to proselytize, to spread the word on this industrial, practical education that wasn’t just a mirror of what was popular. It wasn’t just teaching French for the sake of saying that it did or the piano while expecting nothing but a future of poverty in return for its graduates. It was a functional education, which would help Black people less than a generation removed from slavery learn the skills they needed to advance.
In 1881, Washington went to the Deep South, to the Black Belt in Alabama, to establish a school in Tuskegee. The school opened with one teacher, 30 students, and not a lick of property to speak of save a shanty and a church. But Washington was a savvy dealer; he coaxed donations from wealthy people in both the North and the South by preaching a philosophy of self-reliance. The students worked to build buildings on campus while they received an industrial education. And by the time he was writing in The Atlantic in 1896, that little college in Tuskegee had grown to 800 students, taught by 79 faculty members, spread across 1,400 acres of land which housed 30 buildings.
Washington’s reputation grew alongside the institution, not least because of what he was willing to set aside to achieve his goal.
His philosophy would have allowed—at least in the short term—the continuation of Black Americans’ second-class citizenship.
Black people, Washington argued in his Atlantic essay, were to find their dignity through their industrial labors and the financial gains it brought them. He wrote that “it is through the dairy farm, the truck garden, the trades, and commercial life, largely, that the negro is to find his way to the enjoyment of all his rights.”
Now, despite the critique that Washington’s school only taught Black people to do the same jobs that they did during slavery, even his critics were forced to admire his brilliance and thrift and ability to make a tangible difference in the lives of Black people in the Black Belt.
Perhaps most prominent among those critics was W. E. B. Du Bois, who argued that the training students received at Tuskegee was necessary but insufficient on its own. Sure, it might lead to the economic advancement for some of its students; it might make them self-sufficient, able to eat and clothe themselves. But Du Bois argued that there was more to life than food and clothing.
Du Bois thought a true college education—a liberal education of the kind taught at Fisk, Atlanta University, Wilberforce, Howard, and Lincoln, among others—was the foundation of advancement. In the September 1902 issue of The Atlantic, Du Bois argued that there needed to be teachers for would-be students. Those colleges like Fisk that were training Black people to go back and teach their kin were of the highest importance. Du Bois wrote: “In a single generation they put thirty thousand black teachers in the South; they wiped out the illiteracy of the majority of the black people of the land, and they made Tuskegee possible.”
The schools Du Bois praised developed not only workers but full men. They produced people capable of critical thought. The Bible says that man shall not live by bread alone; Du Bois had his own version. “We shall hardly induce black men to believe that if their bellies be full it matters little about their brains.”
The reality that both men acknowledged is that both forms of teaching—the one that begins with the theoretical and the other with the practical—are necessary to improve the situation for Black people in America, to unwind the damage done by generations of laws which banned Black education.
Washington thought enough of his critics to respond, which he did in the October 1903 issue of The Atlantic, where he wrote: “I cannot understand how any reasonable person can object to such education for a large part of a people who are in the poverty-stricken condition that is true of a large element of my race, especially when such hand training is combined, as it should be, with the best education of the head and heart.”
But the issue was that Washington’s idea of a practical education which would disregard social equality was weaponized: It was treated as the only way rather than a way.
As Du Bois noted in his 1902 essay, “I sit with Shakespeare and he winces not. Across the color line I move arm in arm with Balzac and Dumas, where smiling men and welcoming women glide in gilded halls.” Reading the classics gave him a sense of the ties that bind humanity; they welcomed him to the great brotherhood of mankind.
The question animating the debate between Washington and Du Bois is as relevant as ever: Is college meant to train people for the workforce of today or to produce graduates capable of building a better tomorrow? It’s a question that we should all be considering.
That’s all for today’s show.

“The Traitors” has won more Emmys in three years than “Survivor” has won in 25.
It’s not close, either. Since arriving on Peacock, Alan Cumming’s Scottish castle whodunit has banked eight total Emmys — a casting win before it ever cracked the marquee race, back-to-back reality competition trophies in 2024 and 2025, two hosting wins for Cumming and a Creative Arts sweep in 2025 that added cinematography, directing and picture editing in a single cycle. CBS’ long-running “Survivor,” the show that made all of this possible, owns five. That includes Jeff Probst’s four consecutive hosting Emmys from 2008 to 2011 and a 2010 cinematography win. The trophy that matters most, however — outstanding reality-competition program — has eluded it since the Television Academy created the category.
And let’s be clear about why the category exists at all.
Popular on Variety
When “Survivor” premiered in the summer of 2000, it drew 51 million viewers to its season finale, which crowned Richard Hatch the first-ever Sole Survivor. The Academy created the reality competition program Emmy in 2003, in direct response to the boom “Survivor” ignited. Then it handed the inaugural trophy to its CBS sister series “The Amazing Race.” “Survivor” lost to “The Amazing Race” four straight times from 2003 to 2006, before it did something stranger than losing: It completely disappeared.
For 16 consecutive years, the biggest brand in the genre couldn’t even get nominated — from 2007 through 2022. That stretch included the “Cook Islands” and first Fiji seasons (Seasons 13 and 14), which crowned Yul Kwon — in the first season to feature a final three instead of a final two, a format that coincidentally included Season 50 contestant Ozzy Lusth — and Earl Cole, who became the first unanimous winner in the show’s history.
During that drought, “The Amazing Race,” “The Voice” and “RuPaul’s Drag Race” took turns building dynasties. When the new-era “Survivor” finally clawed back into the field in 2023, it lost to “RuPaul’s Drag Race.” It took another year off before returning in 2025, only to lose to “The Traitors.”
An interesting note is the reality-competition Emmy has gone to a Mark Burnett production four times — all for “The Voice.” The category has spent two decades rewarding the man who helped define the genre while conspicuously never rewarding the show that made him.
So here we are again, coming off a celebratory 50th season — “In the Hands of the Fans” — that crowned Aubry Bracco over runners-up Jonathan Young and Joe Hunter in an 8-3-0 jury vote and awarded a record-setting $2 million grand prize.
“The Amazing Race,” a nominee in every eligible year of the category’s existence except the pandemic-scrambled 2020 ceremony, missed the cut entirely for only the second time ever. ABC’s “Dancing with the Stars,” riding its viral resurgence, is back in the race after an 11-year absence, chasing its own 0-for-10 correction.
The case for “The Traitors” is that it has become the category’s auteur piece.
Last year’s Creative Arts haul — directing, editing and cinematography — was the TV Academy telling us it doesn’t just enjoy the show; it admires the filmmaking. A third straight win would put it on the most exclusive shelf in reality television, joining “The Amazing Race,” “The Voice” and “RuPaul’s Drag Race” as the only shows to three-peat.
Cumming, meanwhile, is chasing a hosting three-peat of his own, and the man he’d have to beat — for the third year running — is Probst. There’s a whole column in that proxy war alone: the tuxedoed theater lifer with two Tonys against the dimpled adventure guide who won this category’s hosting award the first four times it existed.
The case for “Survivor” is the one the Emmys sometimes secretly love, and that’s the “overdue” correction.
This is the Martin Scorsese- “The Departed” scenario — the institution that should have been honored in its prime, finally embraced late, with a milestone providing cover. “Survivor” hit Season 50 this spring, a fan-voted celebration of a quarter-century on CBS, exactly the kind of legacy moment that lets a voter feel like they’re honoring history rather than simply a season of television.
Probst has spent the year as the genre’s beloved elder statesman. If there was ever a cycle for sentiment to beat momentum, it’s a 50th-season cycle.
But sentiment has to overcome a structural problem: This category does not do lifetime achievement. It does dynasties.
In 23 previous ceremonies, it has crowned exactly seven different shows. And once it falls for something, it falls hard — seven straight for “The Amazing Race,” four in five years for “The Voice,” four straight for “RuPaul’s Drag Race.” Television Academy voters — and this is a category voted on by the entire membership, rather than a specific peer group — aren’t correctors; they’re serial monogamists.
Right now, they’re in love with a castle in the Scottish Highlands.
Did enough of the all-stars fighting it out on the islands of Fiji build enough goodwill to get “Survivor” across the finish line?
“Survivor” has outlasted every rival, every trend and every obituary written for network television. The one thing it has never figured out how to outlast is Emmy voters’ attraction to the newest game in town — a lesson it has now been taught by three different shows across three different decades.
The torch, as Probst would say, represents life in the game. “Survivor” has kept its lit for 25 years — and will light a new one again this fall.
On Sept. 14, we find out whether the Academy finally notices — or whether the castle drawbridge stays up for one more year. Voting closes Aug. 26 at 10 p.m. PT.

In a three-day strategic dialogue, Belgium and WHO reviewed progress in their longstanding partnership, and agreed to further boost their collaboration on universal health coverage, health-systems strengthening and equitable access to essential vaccines, medicines and health technologies.
The Belgian delegation – headed by H.E. Christophe Payot, Ambassador of Belgium to the United Nations and other international organizations in Geneva – discussed issues of strategic importance, exchanged views on how to smoothly align WHO strategic directions and Belgium's development cooperation priorities in the context of an evolving global health landscape.
The partners exchanged updates on Belgium's support to global health areas brought in the spotlight during the Belgian presidency of Council of the European Union in 2024. WHO was represented by leadership and technical experts from Headquarters and from the Regional Offices for Africa and for Europe.
"After listening to the leaders and experts of WHO we now better understand how they are navigating these challenging times", said Mr Koen Van Acoleyen, Minister Counselor at the Permanent Representation of Belgium to the UN. "We are honoured that we can walk this road together."
Accelerating equitable access to vaccines, medicines and health technologies
The partners reviewed the current status and the most noticeable results achieved by the Access to Medicines programme funded by Belgium. WHO illustrated its work and challenges with an example of country-level implementation in Senegal. It also explained WHO's policies and work on equitable access and local production. Both parties recognized a shared goal for sustainability of the Access to Medicines initiative, as market shaping is key to ensure long-term success.
Health emergencies and pandemic prevention, preparedness and response
Discussions covered WHO's role in strengthening the global architecture for health emergency prevention, preparedness, response and resilience, including the pandemic agreement negotiations and the One Health approach. WHO's crucial field work on health emergency response was demonstrated by presenting the activities in Gaza. The debate also touched upon threats posed by acceleration of biological risks and zoonoses, along with WHO engagement, in particular, risk mitigation.
Universal Health Coverage (UHC)
Elaborating on progress made on UHC-Partnership, the participants reviewed results achieved by WHO with Belgium support in the period 2021-2024, specifically in Belgium's partner countries. They discussed the way forward, exploring the potential for enhanced collaboration at country level, including eventual alignment between WHO country office programmes and Belgium's country level bilateral cooperation. Examples included a summary of the work and challenges at country level from the Democratic Republic of Congo. The visitors listened to a recap of WHO's policies and work on mental health in the context of primary health care.
The partners also reviewed progress in other areas of collaboration on WHO programmes supported by Belgium, such as Neglected Tropical Diseases and Sexual, Reproductive Health and Rights. The review underpinned the importance of an evidence-based approach in these areas.
WHO appreciates Belgium's commitment and engagement, displayed by the participation of representatives of the country's Federal government as well as the Flemish and Walloon governments. "We thank you for your support, honesty, and strong engagement for global health", said Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General, External Relations and Governing Bodies. "Your efforts in supporting our work in Mozambique and Senegal are clear examples of the crucial work we accomplish together".
Looking into the future
The partners discussed ways forward for the Belgium-WHO collaboration framework and multi-year agreement, including progress towards a renewed WHO-Belgium Country Cooperation Strategy.
The enhanced collaboration between Belgium and WHO will support a strong global health agenda under the WHO 14th General Programme of Work (GPW14). There was a shared vision that UHC and health systems strengthening being at the heart of GPW14 ambitions will be taken as essential scope in WHO's ongoing prioritization work.
"We recognize WHO as a trustworthy partner in global health. We felt proud hearing how crucial our support is to the Organization and how it is having a positive impact at country, regional, and global levels", said Mr Dirk Brems, Director of Thematic and Multilateral Cooperation, Directorate-General Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Aid. "It's important we continue these discussions as we tread uncharted territories, and we look forward to working together for strong and sustained multilateralism".

The biggest downsides to using a digital car key
You can use your phone to access your car -- but should you?
Digital car keys are so convenient. You can lock and unlock your vehicle from your phone instead of fumbling with a physical key or even a key fob. But like every technology advancement that touts convenience, they also come with risks. In many cases, these risks can be mitigated once you have a better understanding of how digital keys work and take the proper precautions.
Digital car keys are available for Android and iOS phones; Samsung even has its own digital key technology that works with select vehicles. With compatible Android and iPhone devices and vehicles, you can use Google Wallet or Apple Wallet, respectively, to not only lock and unlock the vehicle but, with some cars, start it as well. The technology is built around criteria set by the Car Connectivity Consortium, which devised the standard for digital keys way back in 2018.
There's no denying how easy digital car keys are to use and even share with others. But there are concerns. For example, what if your phone dies, malfunctions or is lost? Can you still get into and start your vehicle? It's important to understand these concerns around digital car keys.
What to consider when using a digital car key
Digital car keys are not at risk for relay attacks like key fobs, whereby a thief amplifies the fob's signal to unlock the car without even having the fob in their possession. Instead, digital keys use ultra-wideband (UWB) or near-field communication (NFC) to communicate with your vehicle, so the car won't unlock unless your phone is actually nearby. But they aren't completely immune to attacks. If your phone is stolen and someone gets hold of it, this means they might be able to gain access to your vehicle. That said, most car makers include additional levels of authorization to help prevent thieves or even your underage kids from being able to access the car.
The best defense against this is to keep your phone as secure as possible with two-factor authentication, secure passwords and remote wiping capability in the event of loss or theft. There may also be an option to use a second device to suspend the digital key until you locate your phone. With iPhone, for example, all you need to do is mark your device as lost, and Apple CarKey will automatically lock down the app.
Another common concern is that scary scenario when your phone dies. It's bad enough not to be able to hail an Uber or call home, but what if this means you can't even get into your car? Thankfully, that isn't the case. Just as most key fobs have a hidden physical key or a secondary option to start your car if the battery dies, digital keys have failsafe options. With both Apple and Android, many keys and cards can work up to five hours after your device battery dies, using reserve power via NFC. There are concerns as well that Bluetooth or NFC technology might not be working, but it's unlikely. It's slightly more probable that the app could crash, freeze or require an update at the worst possible time. The company's cloud server could also go offline, though most big companies have backup servers just in case. None of these scenarios are common, but it's good to know what's possible.
Digital keys are the future
Just as so many other technologies are going digital, from wallets to door locks, digital car keys are the future. That said, it's always a good idea to have a backup. Keep the key fob with you anyway, or safely at home so someone can get it to you in the event of an emergency.
But provided you keep your phone sufficiently charged and the app updated, using digital keys should be easy as pie. Sure, things can always go wrong with digital technology. But with the right precautions and a backup plan in place, you'll be able to use your digital car keys daily without issue.

Anyone waiting for municipal approval of a building plan may wonder why a local body should regulate construction on private land. In the Madras Presidency, such powers were formalised under the Madras City Municipal Corporation Act, 1919. After Independence, the first Conference of State Ministers on Town and Country Planning in 1960 gave impetus to master plans, planning legislation and similar regulatory systems across India. Behind these powers lay a public health purpose: ensuring proper drainage, sewage disposal, and healthier settlements. That rationale had been powerfully reinforced decades earlier by the work of a British doctor in India, who showed how environmental neglect could enable a tiny member of the animal world to transmit a deadly disease killing millions.
On August 20, 1897, inside a modest laboratory in Secunderabad, a British medical officer named Ronald Ross bent over his microscope and examined the stomach of this creature. What he saw that afternoon would help change the course of medicine. Within the stomach wall there were small and pigmented bodies. Ross had allowed the creature to feed on a patient with malaria several days earlier. The structures he was seeing provided crucial evidence that the malaria parasite did not merely pass through that creature by accident, but developed inside it. That was the point at which the role of that creature in the malaria lifecycle began to become scientifically visible. That creature is none other than a mosquito, and World Mosquito Day on August 20 was to commemorate this discovery in India.
The hidden enemy
For centuries, people suffered from malaria without knowing what caused it. The disease was particularly common around marshes and stagnant water. Since people living near such places frequently developed fever, chills and weakness, the illness came to be associated with unhealthy air. The very word ‘malaria’ comes from the Italian mala aria, meaning ‘bad air’. The association with stagnant water was not entirely wrong. What people could not see was that the water provided breeding sites for mosquitoes.
An important breakthrough came in 1880, when the French physician Alphonse Laveran examined the blood of patients with malaria and identified the parasite responsible for the disease. For the first time, scientists could actually see the organism causing malaria. But solving one mystery created another. If the parasite lived in human blood, how did it move from one person to the next? It could not simply appear in another person’s bloodstream. Some mechanism had to carry it. This missing link became one of the great medical questions of the late nineteenth century.
The mosquito idea
Patrick Manson, a physician who had studied tropical diseases, had already shown that mosquitoes played a role in the lifecycle of filarial parasites. He began to suspect that mosquitoes might also be involved in malaria. Ronald Ross, an officer of the Indian Medical Service, met Manson in England in 1894 and became interested in testing this hypothesis. Ross returned to India and began a painstaking series of experiments. He allowed mosquitoes to feed on people with malaria. He later dissected the insects under a microscope and proved with evidence that the parasite had entered and developed inside them.
The complete story did not emerge in a single experiment. Ross continued his work, particularly using malaria parasites of birds, and demonstrated further stages of the parasite inside mosquitoes, including its movement towards the salivary glands. Scientists in Italy subsequently established the transmission cycle of human malaria through Anopheles mosquitoes. Science had finally connected the pieces. A mosquito bites a person carrying malaria parasites. The parasites undergo further development inside the insect. When the infected mosquito later bites another person, the parasite can enter the new host and begin another infection. Ross received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1902 for his work on malaria.
Health revolution
This discovery did more than solve a biological mystery. It completely changed malaria control. If mosquitoes transmitted malaria, preventing mosquito bites and reducing mosquito populations could prevent the disease. Drainage of stagnant water, environmental sanitation, mosquito nets, screening of houses and later, insecticides became important public health tools.
Disease prevention was no longer directed against an invisible ‘bad air’. Public health had acquired a clearly identifiable target. Its danger lay not in physical strength, but in what it carried from one human being to another. Though the mosquito appears to be an unlikely killer, it is considered the world’s deadliest member of the animal world because different species transmit malaria, dengue, chikungunya, yellow fever, Zika, Japanese encephalitis, lymphatic filariasis, and other infections. This distinction also explains why mosquito control cannot rely on a single strategy.
India’s long battle
India occupies a distinctive place in the history of malaria. It was in India that Ross carried out much of the work that clarified the relationship between mosquitoes and malaria. The country has also lived with the enormous health and economic consequences of mosquito-borne diseases for generations. India has made substantial progress in reducing malaria and has set the goal of malaria elimination by 2030. Yet dengue, chikungunya and other vector-borne diseases continue to remind us that success against one mosquito-borne infection does not automatically eliminate the larger mosquito problem. Surveillance, early diagnosis, prompt treatment, vector control and environmental management must therefore work together.
The tools available today would have been unimaginable to Ross. Modern laboratories can identify pathogens using molecular methods. Genomic surveillance can track changes in parasites and mosquito populations. Insecticide-treated nets protect millions of people. Yet, mosquitoes remain remarkably successful because they adapt to human environments and exploit the conditions we create.
In 2025, India recorded 233,917 malaria cases but only 76 deaths. The low fatality reflects the success of diagnosis and treatment; the continuing caseload shows that prevention remains unfinished. Planning authorities were empowered to regulate buildings, drainage, and sewage, in part to prevent environmental hazards, including stagnant water where mosquitoes breed. Yet stagnant water pools remain in and around buildings, providing mosquitoes with their breeding grounds. Public-health authorities are then left to control what should partly have been prevented, while battling insecticide resistance, increasing human and animal movement, urbanisation, and fragmented coordination with planners.While the discovery of mosquito’s role in the spread of disease was made in India, we are still battling to govern the environment in which it breeds.
(Dr. C. Aravinda is an academic and public health physician. The views expressed are personal. aravindaaiimsjr10@hotmail.com)

America’s US$40tr debt gamble is getting harder to ignore, economists say after ‘grow’ goal
Analysts warn that high spending, rising interest costs and tax cuts could impede Washington’s efforts to ‘grow our way out of’ record-high national debt
With Washington claiming that the United States can “grow” out of its mounting fiscal burdens, some economists are sceptical that growth alone could absorb the country’s mountain of national debt, which just surpassed US$40 trillion.
The milestone, reached last week, has amplified concerns about the long-term sustainability of maintaining such a massive debt pile – one that has doubled in size from a decade ago.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent defended the trajectory last week, telling CNBC that much of the spending had gone towards investments in factories and equipment, and that the country would “grow our way out of” that debt level.
However, some analysts remain doubtful, pointing to elevated government spending, growing debt-servicing costs, and tax cuts as structural barriers that economic growth alone cannot overcome.
“The US has no chance of growing out of its debt problem through growth only,” said Alicia Garcia-Herrero, chief economist for the Asia-Pacific region at French investment bank Natixis.
Despite high nominal growth rates – boosted by inflation – in recent years, the US has continued accumulating debt, adding US$10 trillion since 2022, as public expenditure remained high, she noted.

Questions remain over Vieira deal amid Senegal uncertainty
- Published
The arrival of Patrick Vieira as the new coach of Senegal comes at a particularly difficult time for the national team - so much so that there is the possibility the former France captain may not even take charge of the Teranga Lions.
The 50-year-old's appointment has been announced despite him not having signed a contract, and the date of his official presentation remains unknown.
Senegal's football federation (FSF), which is currently riven by off-field issues, said discussions regarding the "administrative and contractual arrangements" for Vieira are continuing between the two parties.
The ex-Arsenal and Inter Milan midfielder was unanimously approved as the man to succeed Pape Thiaw at an FSF meeting on Monday, with former Netherlands international Patrick Kluivert among the other names considered.
However, uncertainty surrounding the termination of Thiaw's deal remains.
Vieira's predecessor was sacked following the dramatic last-32 exit to Belgium at the Fifa World Cup without Senegal's government, which funds the national team, formally endorsing the decision.
He is demanding the payment of several months' worth of outstanding wages as well as various bonuses, with the total reportedly amounting to almost $815,000 (£600,000).
Meanwhile, a ruling on the election of the current FSF leadership - which has been contested for the past year - is expected from the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) by Friday.
With the FSF leadership increasingly isolated, without the backing of the government or the general public's support, and constrained by the impending Cas ruling, it nevertheless had little choice but to act quickly to fill the Teranga Lions hotseat.
The calendar will not wait, with Senegal back in action in the qualifiers for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) on 23 September when they travel to Mozambique in their Group J opener. A meeting with Ethiopia follows days later.
The Cas ruling in Lausanne could call into question the legitimacy of the FSF hierarchy and potentially even the choice of Vieira as head coach.
Moreover, for all his achievements as one of the greatest footballers of the modern era Vieira's record in management has been less impressive.
A long-awaited homecoming
Beyond all of that, Vieira's connection with Senegal carries a deeply symbolic significance.
Born in Dakar in June 1976 to a Cape Verdean mother and a Gabonese father, Vieira began kicking a football around the sandy streets of the capital until the age of eight.
His family moved to France and his life went in a different direction, becoming a Premier League icon during his time with Arsenal, amassing over a century of France caps, and helping Les Blues to the World Cup in 1998 and the European Championship in 2000.
He faced Senegal only once as a player, in the opening game of the 2002 World Cup when France suffered a shock 1-0 defeat against a generation led by Aliou Cisse and including Thiaw - the two men whose coaching legacy he is now following.
But Vieira never truly severed ties with the country of his birth.
Indeed, one of his most significant contributions came towards the end of his playing career when he made a major investment in the creation of the Diambars Institute.
It would go on to become one of Africa's leading football academies and, less than two decades later, one of the foundations of Senegal's recent success.
Diambars has produced players including Idrissa Gana Gueye, Bamba Dieng and Abdoulaye Seck, all of whom have played a part in Senegal's story since 2018.
Crowned champions of Africa for the first time in February 2022 at the delayed 2021 Afcon, the Teranga Lions secured a second title with a 1-0 win after extra time in January's Afcon final. However, the ultimate destination of the trophy will be settled by Cas after Thiaw called his side off the pitch following a controversial penalty awarded to hosts Morocco in stoppage time.
The challenge facing Vieira is the rebuild of a team attempting to look towards the future after one of the most successful chapters in its history.
There is plenty of promising young talent coming through but those players will have to carry the weight of a formidable legacy left by the old guard of Sadio Mane, Edouard Mendy, Kalidou Koulibaly and Gana Gueye.
The shortlist for the new coach included Kluivert, Vieira's compatriot Patrice Carteron and two former Senegal internationals in Habib Beye and Oumar Daf.
The Frenchman dropped a series of hints that he was in the running to take charge, most notably during the unusually high-profile coverage of his recent holiday in Senegal.
Vieira's mixed coaching record
Vieira amassed a glittering list of honours as a player but has found similar success hard to come by as a manager.
He began his coaching career with New York City FC in 2016, leading them into the play-offs in both of his two seasons at the helm, only to see his team lose twice in MLS conference semi-finals, including a 7-0 aggregate hammering by Toronto FC.
He then guided Nice to creditable seventh- and fifth-placed finishes in Ligue 1 before being sacked in December 2020 and joining Crystal Palace in July 2021.
Vieira earned praise for an attacking style as he led the Eagles to a 12th-placed finish in the Premier League and the FA Cup semi-finals in 2021-22, but was dismissed in March 2023 when Palace were three points above the relegation zone following an 11-match winless run in the league.
Then-chairman Steve Parish said the decision was taken with "enormous regret" but in order to keep the Selhurst Park side in the top flight.
Then came a year at Strasbourg and another mid-table finish in Ligue 1. The Frenchman's most recent job was at Italian side Genoa, whom he departed by mutual consent last November with the team winless and bottom of Serie A.
International management presents its own challenges and, with defeated candidate Mady Toure contesting last August's election of FSF president Abdoulaye Fall, Vieira may find his long-awaited return to Senegal far more dramatic than he intended.

WHO and Netherlands Strategic Dialogue in The Hague, Netherlands 10 April 2024. Credit: Michel Mees Photography
The WHO and the Netherlands convened in The Hague on 10 April 2024, to discuss joint priorities and alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and WHO’s key strategic goals, marking a new milestone in their longstanding partnership.
Rooted in the Netherlands' unwavering commitment to global health, human rights, and universal access to comprehensive health services, the collaboration between the WHO and the Netherlands is instrumental in addressing global health challenges and fostering health and well-being, worldwide and in the country.
Against the backdrop of ongoing conflicts, disasters, and the escalating impact of climate change, and the interconnectedness of the Dutch public health landscape in the Netherlands with global health challenges, this year’s Strategic Dialogue emerged as a critical platform for reflecting on this partnership’s long-term vision.
“In this Strategic Dialogue, throughout all sessions, WHO and the Netherlands showed a commitment to cooperation and to deepening their partnership based on the strong alignment between their respective priorities and objectives”, said Ms Marjolijn Sonnema, Director General for Public Health at the Netherlands’ Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport.
A key outcome of the Strategic Dialogue was the recognition of the alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and the WHO's forthcoming 14th General Programme of Work, paving the way for synergies in areas such as health system strengthening, pandemic preparedness, climate change and health, anti-microbial resistance (AMR) and mental health support.
"At a time when inequity in health and in access to essential health services and financial protection is increasing, disproportionately impacting the poor and most vulnerable, the Netherlands stands as a global health leader and trusted WHO partner. With shared priorities and commitment to sexual and reproductive rights, gender equity, health systems, security, climate resilience, and mental health, we look forward to strengthening our partnership to enhance the health and well-being of all, globally and in the Netherlands", said Dr Bruce Aylward, WHO Assistant Director-General, Universal Health Coverage, Life Course.
WHO acknowledged the Netherlands' global leadership as a flexible donor, with an agreement around the imperative to ensure WHO's financing is more sustainable, through the inaugural WHO Investment Round. This WHO initiative aims to mobilize predictable, sustainable and flexible resources essential for the WHO to respond swiftly and effectively to global health challenges and improve health outcomes, particularly for vulnerable populations.
Addressing contemporary challenges such as geopolitical tensions while seizing opportunities for advancing global health objectives were also on the table during the dialogue. Both parties stressed the importance of sustained collaboration to address pressing health issues comprehensively.
Taking stock of the joint achievements since the previous strategic dialogue in 2022
In 2022, the Strategic Dialogue between the Netherlands and WHO called on both partners to enhance synergies between WHO priorities and the new Dutch Global Health Strategy. Implementing this approach, the Netherlands and WHO:
- Expanded their cooperation to new areas of joint interest, e.g., climate change and health;
- Renewed their longstanding cooperation on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene and Mental Health and Psychosocial Support in health emergencies and humanitarian settings;
- Improved the flexibility and predictability of the Netherlands’ financial support through renewed General Arrangements with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (2022-2025) and the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport (2024–2028) demonstrating the Netherlands’ commitment to WHO’s sustainable financing;
- Hosted together the 2nd World Local Production Forum in the Netherlands;
- Continued and deepened their technical cooperation through secondments, Junior Professional Officers and the Collaborative Centres.
The outcomes of the 2024 dialogue will inform future collaboration between the Netherlands and the WHO, so that efforts are aligned, and the optimal use of resources is helps achieve improved health outcomes worldwide. The enduring partnership between the Netherlands and the WHO stands as a cornerstone in the global health landscape, reflecting a shared commitment to advancing health and well-being globally.
-----------------
The Netherlands is a key supporter and strategic partner of the WHO.
In 2022- 2023, the Netherlands was one of the top five flexible WHO contributors with nearly US$ 19 million in core voluntary contributions. Overall, the Netherlands contributed more than US$ 106 million to the WHO in 2022 - 2023, of which US$ 93 million, nearly 90%, was voluntary funding.
The Netherlands also supports the WHO's technical expertise through secondments of staff and helps boost young people's careers in public health via the WHO's Junior Professional Officer Programme.
This demonstrates the Netherlands' commitment through its Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport to the WHO’s central role in the global health architecture.
Through this support, the Netherlands contributes to crucial activities in the areas of sexual and reproductive health, water and sanitation, mental health in emergencies, emergency preparedness, tuberculosis, One Health, primary health care, antimicrobial resistance, while facilitating cooperation with top Dutch institutions.

U.S.-Canada trade talks collapsed last night. Punitive Trump tariffs will now go into effect. Canada will reciprocate with retaliatory tariffs of its own.
The story may not be over. Donald Trump is notorious for issuing threats, then reversing them. Wars are on, off, on again, off again, then on a third time—but only as a “little detour.” This is not an administration that thinks even one move ahead. But without a supersized Trump TACO, the U.S.-Canada impasse likely won’t resolve soon.
The Trump administration has one big idea about Canada: The U.S. is larger, stronger, and richer than Canada, so Canada must sooner or later surrender to Trump’s demands. That one big idea is wrong.
Yes, Trump can hurt Canada more than Canada can hurt Trump. That part of Trump’s thinking is true. But wars are not decided only by the question Who can inflict more pain? Wars are also decided by the question Who can endure more pain? Trump’s failure to accept this truth is why he lost the Iran war—and why he is losing his trade wars.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has much more political permission to accept pain from a U.S.-Canadian trade war than Trump does.
To read current Canadian polling is to see a country united under its political leadership—and energized by its dislike and distrust of Trump’s United States. A majority of Canadians view Trump’s America as a more immediate threat to their security than Russia or China. Two-thirds favor the government taking a hard line in trade talks; fewer than one-quarter regard the United States as trustworthy. Meanwhile, Carney is backed by the Canadian public, polling at about 60 percent approval, a remarkable figure in a multiparty political system.
The Canadian economy has definitely suffered because of Trump’s hostility. Exports were down last year, and growth slowed. But this year, Canada got an unexpected bailout: Trump’s Iran war and Trump’s inflation have boosted prices for Canadian oil, gas, minerals, and food products. Canadian incomes are rising again. Meanwhile, Canada’s low levels of public debt have kept inflation low. Whereas the U.S. government must pay 5.3 percent to borrow money for 30 years, Canada pays 4.2 percent.
By contrast, Trump is facing an omnishamble. “Trump’s Economic Challenge: $40tn Debt, 6.7% Mortgages and $5 Diesel.” That’s a headline in today’s Financial Times. The paper could have added one more: 33 percent job approval, and falling fast.
Trump’s tariffs are costing the typical American household $1,100 a year in both direct collections and indirectly in higher prices, according to the Yale Budget Lab. Although teasing out Canada-specific costs is tricky, one indicator is the price of aluminum. In 2024, about one-fourth of the aluminum consumed by Americans came from Canada, the U.S.’s single largest source of imported aluminum. Result: Whereas European and Japanese consumers now pay about $3,000 a ton for aluminum, Americans pay almost $5,000, driving up the cost of everything from a can of beer to the construction of a new hospital.
Although Canada’s economy is much smaller than the U.S.’s, Canada’s government has a more rational and intelligent leadership—and can therefore target its retaliation in ways that better serve national ends. U.S. alcohol exports to Canada have collapsed by 80 percent as Canadian provincial liquor stores ban U.S. wine and spirits. Canada’s booze boycott hurts more than one might expect given the comparatively small size of the Canadian market. Alcohol exporters to Canada prepare special labels for their products to meet Canadian legal requirements. More than 1 million bottles of wine intended for Canadian markets now slumber in U.S. warehouses, unsellable anywhere else without costly repackaging.
More than 30 percent of Ohio’s exports go to Canada, and almost 40 percent of Michigan’s. Both states will this year elect a U.S. senator and fill open governor’s seats. Not only is Trump putting at risk his party’s position in purple Michigan, but suddenly the races in beet-red Ohio look in jeopardy too. With these states, may turn control of the Senate—and Trump’s chances of facing meaningful accountability next year for his law-breaking and corruption.
Trump’s theory of his trade war, like his theory of his Iran war, is that the bigger bully always wins. Size counts for a lot, but not for everything.
As Trump has declared over and over again, his ultimate goal in this trade war is to add Canada as a 51st state. Why? To make the United States look bigger on the map. For that goal, which excites ultra-MAGA crackpots, Trump is hazarding not only America’s most important trading relationships, but very possibly every other political equity he holds, including avoiding investigations and accountability by a Democratic House and Senate after January 2027.
Against Canada, Trump is fighting a trade war that very few Americans support, under leadership that most Americans reject, to achieve results that virtually all Americans would dismiss as pointless if not crazy.
Against Trump, Canadians are fighting a trade war that the great majority support, under leadership that commands broad assent, to defend their independence and self-respect. That’s a war that even the weaker side can win, especially if it needs to hold on only a few months longer to survive.

Heavy showers in many parts of north India on Monday (August 24, 2026) triggered flight diversions, waterlogging and massive traffic disruption, especially in the the Delhi-NCR region, which received the bulk of the rainfall.
Parts of Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh and Himachal Pradesh received rains during the day as well.
Traffic snarls were the worst in Gurugram where parents carrying children on their shoulders were seen wading through flooded roads to get to school buses and vehicles were seen stuck on waterlogged roads.
The downpour caused waterlogging in Narsinghpur, Hero Honda Chowk, Rajiv Chowk, IFFCO Chowk and several areas of old Gurugram. Vehicles were stuck in water around Rajiv Chowk, while school buses and ambulances were also caught in waterlogging on Sohna Road.
The district administration said Gurugram received 70 mm of rainfall by 1.30 p.m. Key areas including Rajiv Chowk, IFFCO Chowk, Railway Road, Sector 5, Old Delhi Road, Mehrauli Road and Basai Road were heavily affected. The Naharpur underpass was also waterlogged.
In Delhi too several key stretches, including parts of Lutyens' Delhi, Mathura Road, Connaught Place, Bhairon Marg, ITO and the Zakhira underpass, were waterlogged.
Waist-deep water, bumper-to-bumper traffic marked the day's heavy downpour, as gusty winds and showers lashed the national capital, with a few areas recording almost 67 mm of rain.
Videos shared on social media showed at least a dozen students waded through waist-deep water in Sangam Vihar. Residents in Sadar Bazar were also forced to wade through waist-deep water after rainwater accumulated in the Old Delhi area.
At least 15 flights were diverted at the Delhi airport due to inclement weather conditions. Scores of flights were delayed and some were cancelled at the Indira Gandhi International Airport (IGIA) in the national capital due to the bad weather. An official said 12 flights were diverted to Jaipur, two to Chandigarh and one to Lucknow.
Many parts of Uttar Pradesh witnessed light to moderate showers and isolated heavy downpours, disrupting normal life in urban pockets, the meteorological department said.
Monsoon remained normal across Uttar Pradesh over the past 24 hours, it said.
In Ghaziabad, heavy spells led to severe waterlogging across major roads and low-lying residential sectors, causing massive traffic congestion.
Autorickshaw overturns
In a mishap captured on cameras, an autorickshaw overturned after hitting a pothole on a waterlogged stretch and passersby rushed to rescue the passengers, who escaped with minor injuries.
According to the local MeT office, thunderstorm activity was recorded at a few places over East Uttar Pradesh and at isolated locations in West Uttar Pradesh during the last 24 hours (ending at 8:30 a.m.).
Heavy rains lashed Jaipur and other parts of eastern Rajasthan, disrupting traffic and causing waterlogging in many places.
Kherthal-Tijara in Alwar district that comes under the National Capital Region (NCR) received heavy rainfall and many areas got flooded with water.
Markets, roads, residential colonies and low-lying areas in Kishangarhbas town were also inundated due to rain.
Jaipur, Alwar, Dholpur, Karauli, Bharatpur, Sawai Madhopur, Dausa and Kherthal-Tijara districts received rains. Cars and two-wheelers were seen wading through the Moti Dungri Road in Jaipur which was completely submerged under water.
Light to moderate rain prevailed in parts of Himachal Pradesh, blocking 98 roads for vehicular traffic in the State.
As many as 98 roads were closed for vehicular traffic, while 21 power transformers and 21 drinking water supply schemes were also disrupted, the State Emergency Operation Centre (SEOC) said.
Mandi reported the highest number of road blockages at 49, followed by Kullu (28), Kangra (8), Shimla, Sirmaur, and Una (4 each), and Lahaul Spiti (1).
Light to moderate rains lashed parts of the State in the past 24 hours since Sunday evening.
Heavy rainfall, triggered by a low-pressure system, lashed most parts of Odisha, with eight places receiving more than 100-mm downpour during the past 24 hours, the IMD said.
Four places in the State recorded heavy to very heavy rainfall, while 47 places received heavy rainfall during the period till 8.30 am on Monday, it said.
The maximum rainfall of 169.4 mm was recorded at Joda in Keonjhar district, followed by Papadahandi in Nabarangpur (158.8 mm) and Paikmal in Bargarh (120 mm), the IMD said in a bulletin.
Other places that received over 100-mm rainfall include Kusumi and Jashipur in Mayurbhanj district, Jharigaon in Nabarangpur, and Telkoi and Champua in Keonjhar.
The low pressure area lay over Gangetic West Bengal and adjoining areas of Jharkhand and north Odisha in the morning, the bulletin stated.
Thunderstorms accompanied by lightning are likely over Gangetic West Bengal till Wednesday morning due to a low pressure area over the region, the IMD added.

U.S.-Canada trade talks collapse just before deadline for tariffs
Trade negotiations between the United States and Canada fell apart on Friday night, shortly before a midnight deadline for 50% tariffs to take effect on $20 billion worth of Canadian products.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a statement, shared on social media late Friday, that "Canada will match those tariffs dollar for dollar to protect our workers and businesses."
Carney said important progress had been made in recent weeks toward "improving Canada's position as having the best deal in the world with the U.S." That progress, however, did not meet Canada's objectives, he said, adding: "As a result, this evening, I have decided to suspend trade negotiations with the U.S. and have directed negotiators to return to Ottawa."
The prime minister blamed the U.S. for the collapse in negotiations. "Last-minute changes in the U.S. proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal," Carney said, concluding, "Canada has what the world wants. And we will not allow any nation to determine our future."
Shortly after midnight, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer responded to Carney with a statement posted on social media saying Canada had "declined to finalize the trade deal under the terms agreed earlier this week."
"Despite the U.S. offer to Canada to receive the best treatment of any major exporter to our market, new demands and walk backs of other commitments by Canada have upended the careful balance reached in the past days," Greer said.
He added that earlier this week "the United States agreed to provide even better treatment to Canada, offering significant tariff reductions on steel, aluminum, autos, and lumber."
"The offer would have led to supply chain coordination on aerospace, complementary actions to address unfair trade practices, critical minerals cooperation, increased enforcement against imports produced with forced labor, and the announcement of formal U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) negotiations," Greer said in his statement.
