After a pause of more than two months, the US military announced Monday that it once again carried out a strike on a vessel in the eastern Pacific Ocean, killing two people accused of trafficking drugs.
It brings the overall death toll to 223 people killed in 67 strikes during the nearly year-long US campaign of bombing alleged drug boats off Latin America’s Caribbean coast and in the eastern Pacific Ocean. US Southern Command says the campaign has resulted in the destruction of 64 speedboats, three “low-profile” ships and a semisubmersible craft.
The command said on social media early Monday that forces “executed a lethal kinetic strike on a low-profile vessel operating along established narcotrafficking routes in the Eastern Pacific”. The military said the strike occurred Sunday, and it marked the first since powerful back-to-back 24 June earthquakes in Venezuela killed thousands of people.
As with most of the military’s statements, Southern Command did not provide evidence that the vessel was ferrying drugs.
“We are committed to imposing total systemic friction on narco-terrorists – disrupting their operations, dismantling their leadership, and eliminating cartel terror across the region,” said Gen Francis Donovan, who leads US Southern Command.
The latest strike comes as the Trump administration pursues deals with allied nations to extend its offensive to land across multiple Latin American countries. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said during a visit to Panama this month that Colombia, Guatemala and Honduras had agreed to allow the US to carry out joint military operations against criminal groups on their soil. Guatemala denied reaching such a deal.
Ecuador launched similar missions with the US in March.
The Trump administration’s boat bombing campaign began in early September and has left numerous survivors, but most of them have never been recovered.
US Southern Command said in a separate statement on Monday that there have been more than 20 search and rescue efforts overall, almost all of which were unsuccessful.
According to data compiled from the command’s social media posts, the strikes have generated 28 survivors with only three people ever being rescued – one person during a strike in March who was transferred to the Costa Rican Coast Guard, and two wounded people who were later repatriated to their home countries of Ecuador and Colombia.
The very first strike in September 2025 left two survivors who were killed in a second, follow-up strike. When that became public, it drew concern from some lawmakers and those who study military law. The White House insisted it was done “in self-defense” to ensure the boat was destroyed and in accordance with armed conflict laws.
But some legal scholars said a second strike killing survivors would have been illegal under any circumstance, armed conflict or not.
Donald Trump has said the US is in “armed conflict” with cartels in Latin America and has justified the attacks as a necessary escalation to stem the flow of drugs into the United States and fatal overdoses claiming American lives. But his administration has offered little evidence to support its claims of killing “narcoterrorists”.
Critics have questioned the overall legality of the boat strikes as well as their effectiveness, in part because the fentanyl behind many fatal overdoses is typically trafficked to the US over land from Mexico, where it is produced with chemicals imported from China and India.
The Pentagon’s watchdog said in May that it plans to look into whether the US military followed an established targeting framework when carrying out the strikes. However, the evaluation is focused specifically on what’s known as the six-phase Joint Targeting Cycle and not on the legality of the strikes, the inspector general’s office said.

I Was a Bicentennial Baby
Behind the moniker, in 1976, was a kind of hope. As I turn 50 and the nation reaches 250, the mood feels distinctly different.
Thirteen seconds after midnight on July 4, 1976, Karen Steele was born in Montclair, New Jersey, and was anointed the first “bicentennial baby.” Newspaper articles followed. President Gerald Ford and his wife, Betty, sent a note to the family. And then it kind of became a thing. Any baby born that year was treated like they had emerged playing the fife and drums. In Mobile, Alabama, new mothers received a commemorative blanket. In Covington, Louisiana, a hospital handed out (for $2.50) special “bicentennial baby” certificates on faux parchment, a “memento that can be framed and cherished as a family heirloom for endless generations.”
This was a year of jaw-dropping kitsch, an explosion of red, white, and blue everything—toilet paper, lollipops, even condoms (pleading: One Time for Old Glory). Branding newborns this way became part of the general patriotic fun. And although the tchotchkes surely ended up moldering in a red, white, and blue landfill somewhere, the label stuck. I know: I was one of those babies, born in August 1976.
Being a bicentennial baby was not anything I ever thought about all that much. In fact, it was really only when meeting another person born in 1976 that it came up at all. Oh, you’re a bicentennial baby too, one of us would say to the other, smiling dumbly. This was a secret handshake that opened zero doors. But unlike other indelible parts of my identity that felt small in their particularity—like being the child of immigrants or being nearsighted—having my birth hitched somehow to the history of the country, to its forward motion, felt big whenever I was reminded of it.
Beyond the horror of realizing that five of my current lifespans stacked up is all that separates me now from Benjamin Franklin, I’ve been thinking about this cohort of which I’m a part. Expounding on the significance of one’s own generation can lead rapidly to wild generalization, self-absorption, and some misplaced nostalgia. I know this. But I’m convinced that my fellow bicentennial babies and I have been through something unique. We’ve followed a distinct arc over the past 50 years: one of disillusionment. Better than most, we understand the disjunctions of our present because they happened at crucial inflection points alongside the timeline of our lives.
We were born during a period of palate-cleansing. The Vietnam War was over. President Richard Nixon had, in 1974, resigned after Watergate, a redemptive scandal that renewed people’s faith in self-government. Journalists—yes, journalists—were sex symbols. Robert Redford played Bob Woodward in All the President’s Men. And the peanut farmer Jimmy Carter, a man who campaigned teeth-first, would be elected president in the fall, having promised a new era of idealism.
I don’t remember any of this, of course, but babies like me were launched into an atmosphere of reawakened good vibes. When Time magazine commissioned the polling firm Yankelovich, Skelly & White to gauge the country’s temperature from June to September of 1976, the company found a 10 percent jump in positivity on its “state of the nation index” between those months, the most rapid increase it had seen since it began tracking the metric. The following years were also a time of crime and stagflation and the Iran hostage crisis, but at least by the indicators used by pollsters to determine collective mood, things continued to get generally sunnier into the ’80s. “The Zeitgeist has turned zesty,” Kurt Andersen wrote in a 1984 assessment of that year’s numbers. “The U.S. is at peace, and between rising employment and fading inflation, the economy is aglow. Americans are feeling more sanguine and comfortable about their country than they have felt in two decades. A rebirth of the American spirit, as Carter dearly hoped five summers ago? It sure feels like it.”
I remember this optimism and confidence. On November 9, 1989, I sat watching television with my grandfather—a Holocaust survivor who that day, and most days, had his shirt off and a captain’s hat on his head. The Berlin Wall was coming down. This happened when we bicentennial babies were 13 and highly impressionable. Look at them, my grandfather said, his voice breaking, as people pick-axed their way out of East Germany. I recall the total elation on their faces when they finally broke through, and then the bracing thought that they were trying to get to the side where I already lived.
For many young Americans in those years, a feeling of transcendence was possible. You had a sense that good fortune had placed you somewhere that everyone in the world wished they could be. At the same time, that wider world, with its crumbling empires and ethnic cleansing and genocides, seemed very far away. Even the Gulf War of the early ’90s appeared, to those of us safe at home, as a ghostly green video game playing on CNN, transmitted from somewhere hard to recognize as real.
You may not believe me when I tell you that I read Francis Fukuyama’s The End of History and the Last Man at 19, for fun, when I was a junior and living abroad in France. But I did, and then after college I went into the Peace Corps and lived in a village in Cameroon for two years. Although many of the people there thought that I was working for the CIA (I was not), I felt I was doing something uncomplicatedly wholesome, even a little patriotic.
We were 25 when 9/11 happened. I moved to New York City in October of that year, like a salmon swimming upstream—or like a salmon following a girl. Everywhere were posters of missing people. During my first days of couch surfing, New Yorkers were further terrorized by anthrax spores sent through the mail, addressed to political and media targets. That terrible fall was a hinge moment for all Americans but maybe especially for us young adults, who were also at a hinge moment in our lives, suddenly vulnerable and less innocent in new ways, feeling silly for having believed that history could have an end.
I haven’t mentioned the internet yet, but it also came around for us as adulthood hit. I got my first email address in college and accessed my inbox in the library basement at a computer lab that perpetually smelled like Doritos. It was all so new that you could forget to send a paper to a professor and then offer the excuse that the email probably just got lost. I spent a lot of time outside that library, chatting, with nothing in my hands besides a cigarette. I think I knew someone who had a beeper. We got flip phones in our 20s. We were in our early 30s when the first iPhone arrived and Facebook showed up. We were told that these were revolutionary tools. Maybe we believed this more than other people did, still being relatively young and feeling like we were being handed powerful megaphones in our prime—a chance to make change, to connect. Then the tools congealed into yet more products that would waste our hours and make us feel terrible about ourselves and our fellow citizens.
We made lives against the backdrop of distant wars, unceasing notifications popping up on our phones. The year we turned 40, Donald Trump was elected president. Four years later came COVID. Just as we were balancing more and more—perhaps children, a challenging job, ailing parents—the world seemed to conspire to keep our heads spinning. In these past few years, before we and the country hit our big milestones, we were assaulted by panicked warnings about the state of American democracy—and the future of the entire human race. What has AI been up to over the past few days? Creating new viruses and independently cyberhacking, it appears. We are less naive, though more exhausted. It has not been lost on us that the people warning that AI could lead to our extinction are the same people who invented it. This is a pattern we’re familiar with now: Technology gives us something with one hand while robbing us of something else with the other.
I’m leaving out a lot. We also had private joys and tragedies totally impervious to what America writ large was up to. But I can distinguish a progression toward an increased sense of emergency, toward alienation, toward a mournfulness that makes me read the newspaper through my fingers most days. I don’t think this is the birthday blues talking—or, if I’m honest, maybe not just the birthday blues. It’s also the metrics: about loneliness and economic stagnation and political polarization and the whole insane technological surround sound of our lives. My point is that bicentennial babies, regardless of their individual circumstances, have all been strapped into the first row of this ride.
Someone born on America’s centennial, in 1876, could well have argued that they had witnessed much more consequential change by their 50th birthday. They might have gushed about the expansion of railroads and telegraphs, about seeing the first airplanes, telephones, and radios, and then explained what it was like to face the reality that as many as 20 million people could be killed in a single war. I wouldn’t want to go head-to-head with them. Every generation has its story. But we bicentennial babies have lived through a major rupture. For all else that might be good in our lives—and I’m lucky to have a lot that’s good—this is not such an exuberant place to find ourselves at 50.
Can we imagine anyone proudly calling the babies born this year—what? semiquincentennial sprouts? A mouthful, granted. But that’s not what makes it sound strange. Behind the “bicentennial babies” moniker was a kind of hope. We would be the Americans of the future. And we would be moving toward that future not with dread but with anticipation. Whatever one’s political affiliation, people do not have much enthusiasm these days when they picture where we’re headed.
When the Pew Research Center surveyed Americans just before this year’s semiquincentennial, 59 percent of respondents said that the country’s best years were behind it. Asked to imagine the United States 50 years from now, 44 percent were pessimistic and only 28 percent were optimistic. Perhaps most telling, 27 percent chose neither option; they just felt blah. Recently, Conan O’Brian, speaking on the podcast The Rest Is History, talked about the “undiluted joy” he remembers feeling as a preteen experiencing the bicentennial. Now: “It’s very hard for some people, maybe, to just say, I’m really excited about our 250th when our current state is so divided.”
I can’t conceive of myself being around for the tricentennial—and if I did suggest living to 100, my mother might faint from all the spitting she’d have to do to ward off the evil eye. But if I do make it there, I will have lived through a third of the country’s existence. I’ll have a lot more data to work with. Will 2026 appear in retrospect as another hinge, or simply as a snapshot of us—mouths open and eyes closed, as in an amusement-park photograph—mid–free fall? Will there be self-correction or a piling-on of bad decisions? Disintegration or newfound connection? No one can really tell. Though I do know what I would like on my 50th birthday and the country’s 250th: something for us to look forward to.

The amount of gas-fired power in development for data centers in the US has nearly doubled in less than a year, new research released Tuesday shows. The findings illustrate just how heavily tech companies are relying on building private fossil fuel plants to power data centers—and how fast artificial intelligence’s energy demand has grown.
Global Energy Monitor, a research firm, has been tracking gas-powered projects that have been announced, are in development, or are under construction in the US. In January, the group found that there were 97 gigawatts of gas projects in development exclusively for data centers at the end of 2025, a massive increase from just 4 gigawatts tracked in early 2024. Now, in an update to the research released Tuesday, the group says that as of mid-2026, that demand pipeline has jumped to more than 189 gigawatts. (A gigawatt can power roughly a million homes.)
“Increasingly, the US gas power buildout is getting tied directly to the data center buildout—you can’t talk about one without the other,” says Jenny Martos, a research analyst at Global Energy Monitor who worked on the report.
Over the past two years, data center builders have increasingly turned to private power facilities, known as behind-the-meter plants, to bypass lengthy grid connection times. This approach can also potentially help avoid saddling ratepayers with higher bills, an issue that’s become a flashpoint as data center opposition mounts around the country. The Trump administration has encouraged tech companies to bring their own power, introducing a voluntary pledge that’s been signed by the likes of Microsoft, Meta, Google, and OpenAI, as well as several Republican governors and some of the country’s biggest utilities.
Adding that much natural gas power comes with a hefty climate cost, particularly because many of the facilities are being built with inefficient turbines, which can increase emissions. As WIRED has reported, some of these gas plants are permitted to emit more greenhouse gases each year than many small- and medium-sized countries.
Global Energy Monitor also tracks energy projects in countries around the world, including China, the world’s largest importer of natural gas. Much of that gas is used for producing products like fertilizer and plastic.
But the country does have a modest fleet of natural gas plants, and it’s seen a surge in gas-fired facilities under development in recent years. In the early 2020s, it even outpaced the US in gas plant construction. The data center boom means that the US has again surpassed China as the country with the most gas projects in the pipeline, according to Global Energy Monitor.
The shift illustrates how China, which the Trump administration has repeatedly emphasized as the US’s rival in the AI race, is relying less on gas fueled-sources in its data center buildout.
“Overall, the data center boom in China is really oriented around renewables,” especially solar and hydropower, says Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution. Many data centers being built in China are being sited in rural areas that have an excess of renewable energy production. Chan says that while there have been a few attempts to develop private power for data centers, they’re “smaller projects.”
He adds that the Chinese buildout of renewables on the grid is a deliberate choice by the government to ensure energy independence.
The US building gas power for data centers “in the near term might make sense economically, and especially if you want to power these data centers fast, and you don't have access to the same kind of cheap renewable energy that you might be able to have in China,” he says. “But over the long term, you pay a price for that—obviously, in terms of emissions, but also, I think in terms of not investing in your own clean energy sector.”
Not all of the projects that Global Energy Monitor tracked will get built, Martos notes. Many of the projects the group has tracked haven’t yet begun construction. “There's a lot of uncertainty: financing, your local opposition, data, your moratoriums, the turbine constraints to supply equipment—there's so many factors,” she says.
Still, “if all of these get built, you're locking in emissions for decades,” she says.

Amid growing concerns over a government-ordered Instagram censorship drive in India, political parties and leaders are now reporting restrictions on their posts, with Meta citing “legal requirements” but providing little information about the basis for the action. Content linked to the Cockroach Janta Party protests, political parties and creators has all been caught up in the restrictions.
Over the past few days, several social media posts and accounts have been geo-blocked in India. On Instagram, users’ posts are either removed citing legal requirements or restricted from being viewed in India. Several opposition organisations and leaders have also faced such restrictions, with their posts suddenly being taken down.

Clicking on a removed post shows a notice stating that it has been restricted by Meta’s automated systems in India, in accordance with legal requirements under India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules.
Opposition Leaders’ Posts Restricted Earlier as well
This is not the first time that posts by political entities have been restricted under these rules. Earlier, posts by Congress and TVK leaders related to Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay had also been removed from Instagram and Facebook, citing the same provisions.
On May 11, Goa Congress president Girish Chodankar posted on X, asking whether Prime Minister Modi was so afraid of a Congress-TVK alliance that even a video of the chief minister’s swearing-in ceremony was being blocked. Similarly, TVK leader Aravind shared a screenshot on social media showing that his Facebook post related to Tamil Nadu chief minister Vijay had been removed.

— Aravind TVK (@Aravind8282) May 11, 2026
Around the same time, Meta blocked a reel featuring Rahul Gandhi and C Joseph Vijay, citing the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules. Following widespread criticism, Meta restored the reel.
The Union ministry of electronics and information technology said at the time that the action was the result of an internal error by Meta and had nothing to do with the ministry.
More recently, Meta itself restricted a video of Prime Minister Narendra Modi addressing students for a few hours. Meta later apologised, calling it a technical glitch. However, the incident too lacked transparency, as Meta did not publicly explain the nature of the technical glitch that had led to the restriction.
What is the Legal Provision?
The legal framework behind these restrictions is Section 79(3)(b) of India’s Information Technology Act. The provision was originally intended to determine when platforms could lose their “safe harbour” protection, or immunity from liability.
Put simply, if online platforms and social media intermediaries fail to expeditiously remove material flagged by the government after receiving notice, they may lose their legal immunity for third-party user content. This could make the social media intermediary directly liable for the material.
However, digital rights activists argue that the government is using this provision as the legal basis for a content-blocking mechanism while bypassing Section 69A, which involves greater procedural safeguards and requires written and reasoned orders.
Lack of Transparency
A serious flaw in this process is the lack of transparency. When the government sends a request flagging a post, users are not told who made the complaint or on what basis the order was issued. Instead, they see a generic notice stating that the content has been restricted in accordance with legal requirements.
Users are neither provided a copy of the order nor a case number. They are also not told which official or authority sent the takedown request.
ALSO READ: Content creators decry Instagram censorship, call restrictions a ‘digital emergency’
An even bigger problem is that ordinary users have no concrete and reliable mechanism to challenge such action. Digital rights organisations such as SFLC and IFF have been assisting some users, but the large-scale removal of posts has exposed the absence of an effective redressal mechanism.
At its core, the mechanism is unbalanced. Content is removed first, without users being given a clear reason or an opportunity to be heard. The entire burden of seeking an explanation or having the post restored is then placed on the user.
According to a recent report by The Indian Express, the government issued around 195,000 blocking orders between March and July 2026. Of these, nearly 100,000 were sent to Instagram and around 80,000 to Facebook. In addition, around 15,000 blocking orders were sent to YouTube.
A senior government official told The Indian Express that a significant share of the blocking orders — particularly those involving Instagram — were issued during a period when protests were gathering momentum.
The report also stated that Meta has integrated its API (Application Programming Interface) with the Sahyog portal. As a result, content marked on the system under government directions can be removed from Meta’s platforms automatically, without separate human review by the company. This automation leaves Meta with no meaningful opportunity to independently review or object to the directions before acting on them.
On August 20, the Press Information Bureau (PIB), the government’s nodal agency, shared details about the matter. It said that the Sahyog portal’s API was integrated in 2025 at the request of Meta, Facebook and Instagram’s parent company. This enables state governments and central ministries to notify IT intermediaries about allegedly unlawful content.
According to the PIB, around 298,000 URLs were sent for takedown between March and July 2026. Of these, 244,000 URLs, or 82%, were sent by state governments. This included 51,000 URLs sent by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) in connection with cyber, infrastructure and stock-investment scams.
How does Meta’s ‘Automated System’ Actually Work?
The most confusing and opaque aspect of this entire process is Meta’s “automated system”. Notices on restricted posts state that Meta acted under an automated system, but users are not told what criteria this system uses.
Does it automatically restrict content flagged through the Sahyog portal? Or does it operate on the basis of certain keywords, images, non-compliance with AI-labelling requirements, or other factors? There is little transparency around these questions.
During the recent students’ protests in Delhi against alleged irregularities in NEET-UG, reels posted by journalists, media outlets and student activists showing police action were also restricted. Posts by creators producing content related to the CJP protests were subsequently restricted as well. Alt News has published detailed reports on both instances.
More recently, an Alt News post that mentioned “Burhan Wani” was repeatedly removed by Instagram. In another instance, an Alt News fact-check was restricted for using the word “Khalistani”. we later discovered that searches on Instagram with ‘Burhan Wani’ or ‘Monu Manesar’ do not yield any result. We wrote to Meta asking whether there is a list of words that are not allowed on the platform or whether there is a government order to that effect, but we are yet to receive a response.

During a recent shift in the emergency department, I helped care for a woman facing a suspected oncologic emergency. She had come to the hospital expecting a routine evaluation, but suddenly found herself confronting conversations about diagnoses that could fundamentally change her life.
When I first entered the room, she was visibly nervous. Her family, gathered around the hospital bed, looked equally concerned. I introduced myself and shook her hand. I then shook the hands of the family members standing beside her.
Soon afterward, the medical evaluation intensified. Like many patients in the emergency department, she was surrounded by unfamiliar faces moving quickly in and out of the room. Nurses entered to draw blood, while my senior resident, attending physician, and I asked questions, explained our concerns, and outlined the immediate medical plan. In the background, monitor alarms sounded intermittently. Within a short period of time, the patient had become the center of a complex medical evaluation that she had little time to process.
Shaking her hand was an extremely simple gesture, but it appeared to ease some of the tension in the room. She smiled, and her family appeared more at ease. Before discussing the initial laboratory results, our diagnostic concerns, and what would happen next, we had a brief moment of connection that felt distinctly human.
The handshake did not change her diagnosis. It did not make the medical uncertainty disappear. But it seemed to remind her (and me) that she was not merely the patient in the room with the concerning test results. She was a person experiencing one of the most frightening days of her life.
The first few moments of a patient encounter shape everything that follows. Before we as clinicians ask about symptoms, perform a physical examination, or explain a treatment plan, patients are already deciding whether they trust us and whether they feel comfortable sharing what is wrong. Shaking the patient’s hand is one small way to begin building trust and fostering a sense of human connection.
This is especially relevant in emergency medicine, where trust has to be built quickly. Emergency physicians do not have years to develop relationships with patients. Right after meeting someone, we have to ask them about substance use, sexual history, violence at home, psychiatric symptoms, housing insecurity, or the worst pain they have ever experienced. We ask patients to let us examine their bodies, call their families, admit them to the hospital, or make decisions that may change the course of their lives. In that context, a gesture of human acknowledgment is part of the foundation on which the rest of the encounter is built.
Research suggests that many patients value the traditional handshake. In a study published in JAMA Internal Medicine, researchers surveyed 415 adults about how they preferred to be greeted by physicians. More than 78% said they wanted their physician to shake their hand. The researchers also reviewed recordings of 123 outpatient visits and concluded that physicians should be encouraged to shake hands while remaining attentive to nonverbal cues indicating whether a patient is comfortable with it.
Other research suggests that similarly small gestures can meaningfully shape the patient experience. A 2023 study found that simply placing a chair near the bedside made physicians more likely to sit during patient encounters and improved patient satisfaction and communication scores without increasing time spent in the room.
A handshake alone will not create a strong patient-clinician relationship. However, it can help establish the conditions for one.
Unfortunately, this simple practice can easily disappear in modern medicine. Clinicians face growing demands from the electronic medical record, increasing patient volumes, frequent interruptions, and pressure to make decisions quickly. In the emergency department, these pressures are particularly evident. We often meet patients during moments of tremendous fear while simultaneously managing several other critically ill patients.
The result is that an encounter can begin with our eyes directed toward a computer rather than the person in front of us. A patient may be asked to repeat their story to several members of the medical team without knowing who is ultimately responsible for their care. It is possible to order the right tests, make the correct diagnosis, and provide appropriate treatment while still leaving a patient feeling unseen.
The Covid-19 pandemic created an additional barrier. Physical distancing, personal protective equipment, and necessary concern about disease transmission changed how health care professionals interacted with patients. Handshakes largely disappeared from hospitals and clinics. In many places, the handshake never fully returned.
There are legitimate concerns about infection. Hands can transmit pathogens, creating a potential risk of infection in the hospital. However, the answer should not be to eliminate human contact indiscriminately. The answer is appropriate hand hygiene and clinical judgment. Health care workers should sanitize their hands before and after patient contact regardless of whether that contact involves a handshake, a physical examination, or a procedure. A handshake is obviously inappropriate when isolation precautions are in place, when a patient is significantly immunocompromised, or when either person may have a transmissible illness.
We must also recognize that not every patient wants to shake hands. Cultural and religious traditions, physical limitations, pain, and personal preferences all matter. Clinicians should never force a handshake or assume that a handshake will be welcomed. A warm verbal greeting, a hand placed over one’s own chest, or another culturally appropriate gesture can communicate the same respect. The goal here is not the handshake itself — it’s deliberate human connection.
This responsibility extends beyond physicians. Every member of the care team shapes how patients experience the health care system. Each introduction is an opportunity to make an unfamiliar environment feel slightly less impersonal.
Medicine is becoming increasingly technologically advanced. Artificial intelligence, remote monitoring, and increasingly sophisticated diagnostic tools will continue to change how we practice. These developments have the potential to improve patient care tremendously.
However, the more technologically advanced medicine becomes, the more intentional we must be about preserving its human elements.
Zain Khawaja, M.D., is an emergency medicine resident physician at Northwestern University whose work focuses on the intersection of health policy and health care economics. His research and writing have appeared in U.S. government publications, The Hill, and MedPage Today.

Vieira named new Senegal head coach
- Published
Former Arsenal and France captain Patrick Vieira has been appointed as the new head coach of the Senegal men's national team.
The 50‑year‑old replaces Pape Thiaw, who was sacked in the wake of the country's last‑32 exit at the 2026 Fifa World Cup.
Born in Senegal's capital Dakar, Vieira will now manage the country of his birth, having moved to France aged eight before later winning over 100 caps for Les Bleus and lifting the World Cup in 1998 and the European Championship in 2000.
Senegal's football federation (FSF) said the appointment reflects its "desire to strengthen its high-level technical staff" and is "perfectly aligned" with the nation's sporting ambitions.
Details of Vieria's contract and his starting date in the role are still being discussed.
His first matches in charge of the Teranga Lions are expected to come next month in qualifiers for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon).
Vieira joins the West Africans after he left his role as Genoa head coach by mutual consent last November, with the team bottom of Serie A.
He won eight and drew nine of his 26 games during the 2024-25 season to guide the Italian club to safety and a 13th-place finish.
However, he left the club after managing just two wins in 25-26, with both of those victories coming in the Coppa Italia.
During his playing career, midfielder Vieira won three Premier League titles and four FA Cups at Arsenal, as well as silverware with AC Milan, Inter Milan and Manchester City.
He retired in 2011 and became the manager of New York City in 2016 before returning to Europe with Nice and leading them to seventh in Ligue 1 in his first season.
Vieira was sacked in December 2020 and became Crystal Palace manager the following year, guiding the Eagles to 12th in the Premier League and the FA Cup semi-finals in 2021-22.
He was dismissed in March 2023 after a 12-game winless run, before joining RC Strasbourg as their first appointment following a takeover by BlueCo, the company which owns Chelsea. He left Strasbourg by mutual consent in July 2024.
His predecessor Thiaw was at the centre of controversy in January when he ushered his Senegal team off the field when Morocco were awarded a stoppage-time penalty in the 2025 Afcon final.
The players eventually returned after a delay of about 17 minutes before Brahim Diaz's penalty was saved and Pape Gueye scored an extra-time winner.
However, Morocco were declared the winners of the tournament in March when the a Confederation of African Football appeals board overturned the result of the final following Senegal's walk-off.
Senegal have lodged an appeal against that decision with the Court of Arbitration for Sport - with the case due to be heard on 8 October.

How to Unlock the Sakura Incubator in Steal an Egg
The Sakura Incubator is located at the back of the Cherry Blossom zone. It is the final biome in Steal an Egg. You cannot use it immediately because you must first offer a Crane to unlock the machine. Here are the full steps to unlock it:
Get a Crane in Steal an Egg
Crane is an Epic Pet that can be obtained from eggs in the Cherry Blossom Zone. You need at least 3.5B speed to successfully steal eggs from this zone. So, make sure you increase speed in Steal an Egg before going to this area. Once you obtain a Crane, keep it in your inventory.
Give the Crane to the Incubator
Interact with the Sakura Incubator while you have the Crane in hand. Submit the pet to activate the machine. It doesn’t matter the size or mutations of the Crane, so use the smallest one from your inventory. You permanently unlock the Sakura Incubator after completing this step. However, you will lose the Crane.
What Is Steal an Egg The Great Bloom Event?
Once you unlock the Sakura Incubator in Steal an Egg, The Great Bloom unlocks. The Great Bloom Event takes place in the Cherry Blossom Zone and repeats every 30 minutes.
You receive an on-screen message when the Great Bloom Event begins. After unlocking the Sakura Incubator, you can also use the timer above the machine to see when the next event is scheduled.
You can simply use the baseball bat from your inventory and smash the cherry blossom trees during the Great Bloom event to get the crystals in Steal an Egg.
Each event lasts for about 3 minutes, giving you a short window to collect as many Sakura Crystals as possible. These Sakura Crystals are used to improve your chances of getting Bloom and Spirit Bloom mutations on an egg in the Sakura Incubator.
How to Get Bloom and Spirit Bloom Mutations in Steal an Egg
You can get the Bloom mutation by putting any egg from your inventory into the unlocked Sakura Incubator and charging it to at least 100% with Sakura Crystals in Steal an Egg. Once the egg is processed, it has a 97.5% chance of receiving Bloom.
Spirit Bloom is the rare Steal an Egg mutation available from the Sakura Incubator. Every egg charged to at least 100% has a 2.5% chance of receiving Spirit Bloom instead of Bloom. It is always better to charge it up to 150% (max) to have a better chance of getting it.
| Mutation | Multiplier | Chances |

| Bloom | 1.5x | 97.5% | 
| Spirit Bloom | 3x | 2.5% |

How to Farm More Sakura Crystals in Steal an Egg
The best strategy is to stay in the Cherry Blossom Zone before the event begins. When the event notification appears, immediately equip your baseball bat and start hitting the Sakura trees.

‘Reagan would be throwing up:’ Ontario premier unloads on Trump and threatens to cut electricity to US as trade dispute escalates
Ford warned that ‘everything is on the table’ should the dispute deteriorate, including shutting off electricity exports and critical mineral shipments from Ontario
Ontario Premier Doug Ford said that Ronald Reagan would be "throwing up" over President Donald Trump’s trade policy as he threatened to cut off electricity and critical minerals to the U.S. as a trade dispute escalates.
Ford said Monday that Trump has miscalculated Canadians’ willingness to endure economic pain rather than give in to U.S. pressure.
"He underestimates Canada. We’re all in," Ford said. "Up here, we’re at a fever pitch, everyone’s in for an economic war. They know they’re going to have to sacrifice."
Ford said Trump has "declared war, economic war against his closest friend and ally" then turned his attention to Reagan and his classic opposition to tariffs.
Ford highlighted that Trump keeps a portrait of Reagan near his desk and stated, "He’d be throwing up on him from the picture if he knew what was going on, spinning around in his grave right now."
"He should maybe take that picture off the wall and move it somewhere else,” Ford continued. “Because right now, Ronald Reagan would be disgusted with President Trump."
The Premier’s remarks followed Prime Minister Mark Carney’s decision to exit trade talks with the Trump administration late Friday, citing excessive demands from Washington in exchange for duty relief. The U.S. enacted 50% tariffs Saturday on roughly $20 billion worth of Canadian goods, prompting Carney to announce matching dollar-for-dollar counter-tariffs starting Sept. 8.
Trump intensified the conflict further on Monday, threatening a 50% tariff on Canadian automobiles, car parts, and steel starting next year.
"Canada has been ripping off the United States of America for years," Trump wrote on social media Monday morning. Criticizing what he called Canada’s "ridiculously high tariffs" on American farmers, Trump added: "Not sustainable, and NOT ANYMORE!"
Ford threatens critical minerals and electricity
Ford warned that "everything is on the table" should the dispute deteriorate, including shutting off electricity exports and critical mineral shipments from Ontario. He also urged Canada to consider using oil and potash as leverage.
"I’ll cut them off," Ford said of critical minerals. "You won’t get a grain of sand out of Ontario."
Critical minerals carry increasing weight for U.S. national defense and industrial manufacturing. The Pentagon has worked to secure reliable supplies of raw materials utilized in military aircraft, missiles, munitions, and advanced electronics as Washington aims to diminish its reliance on China, which controls the mining and refining of several key strategic minerals.
Ford explicitly highlighted high-grade nickel exported to the United States and uranium processed in Ontario.
"What would they do without the high-grade nickel that we ship down to the U.S.?" Ford said.
Ford argued that Canada should weigh increasingly harsh retaliatory measures if Trump continues targeting Canadian industrial sectors, including oil and potash, while Ontario could raise power rates or cease sending electricity across the border.
"We power 1.5 million homes and businesses," Ford said. "Everything’s on the table. I’ll do whatever it takes."
If Trump persists in trying to dismantle Canadian industry, Ford added, "he better have a pack of batteries."
Ford has leveraged electricity in past disputes. During an earlier stage of the trade row, Ontario levied a 25% surcharge on power sent to Michigan, Minnesota, and New York. Trump responded by threatening to double tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum before both sides stepped back.
Auto industry becomes a central battleground
Ford accused Trump of pursuing more than just an improved trade agreement, arguing he intends to dismantle Canadian industrial capacity and transfer manufacturing south.
Ford said Trump wants to turn Canada into a vassal state.
"He wants to bleed out every single sector and bring them down to the U.S.," Ford said.
The automotive industry plays a crucial role in Ontario, serving as the core of Canada’s vehicle manufacturing base. Plants and supply lines across Ontario are deeply integrated with facilities in Michigan and other U.S. states, with components routinely crossing the border multiple times during assembly.
Major automakers including Ford, General Motors, and Stellantis maintain major assembly operations in Ontario, supporting tens of thousands of jobs across the broader supply network. Trump’s warning of a 50% tariff on Canadian-built vehicles and components places the sector directly at the heart of the growing conflict.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer stated on Monday that "the only reason Canada has auto production in the first place" was the 1960s Auto Pact, under which Canada leveraged access to its domestic market to foster northern vehicle assembly.
"If he thinks the Canadian people are going to roll over and just continue buying American-made vehicles, it’s not going to happen," Ford said.
Ford says he opposed preliminary deal
Ford also revealed that he had resisted the tentative draft agreement Carney was reviewing prior to Canada walking away from negotiations.
"I wasn’t supporting the deal," Ford said.
Ford stated he was unwilling to allow American liquor back onto Ontario store shelves as part of a settlement and was prepared to break publicly with the proposed agreement.
"I wasn’t going to put the booze back on the shelves," Ford said. "I was ready to go out there and call a press conference ... and say I’m not buckling over."
Ford noted his understanding that Washington sought provisions late in the talks that would have restricted Canada’s freedom to conclude trade pacts with other nations without U.S. consent. Carney has called that requirement unacceptable and an infringement on Canadian sovereignty.
"Who does he think he is?" Ford said of Trump. "You gotta be kidding."
Reagan fight returns
Ford’s comments regarding Reagan reignited a previous confrontation with Trump. Last year, Ontario funded U.S. television advertisements featuring clips from a 1987 Reagan address cautioning that import tariffs trigger retaliation and trade conflicts.
Trump accused Ontario of misrepresenting Reagan and abruptly halted trade discussions with Canada. Ford subsequently agreed to pause the ad campaign so talks could resume.
"He doesn’t respect anyone," Ford sad.
Despite the sharp rhetoric, Ford maintained that Canada should remain open to dialogue.
"I never believe in walking away from the table," Ford said. "Continue negotiating and see where we go."

While the photo is authentic and shows Trump in Moscow, it is from a visit he took to the Russian capital in 1996, when he was 50. Dubinin was not the nation's ambassador to the U.S. at that time.
Over the years, people have shared an image allegedly showing a 41-year-old Donald Trump during his first visit to Moscow in July 1987. Users' posts claimed Yuri Dubinin, the Soviet Union's ambassador to the U.S., invited Trump to the event. The posts promoted the long-standing claim that the future U.S. president has secret ties with Russia.
The black-and-white picture features Trump standing at a gathering of men in a large room, wearing a tie and overcoat, holding a drink glass and surveying a buffet table.
For example, on Aug. 18, 2026, a Reddit user posted (archived) the image with the caption, "Future reality tv show host, Don Trump, 41 years old, in Moscow at the invitation of Soviet Ambassador to the U.S., Yuri Dubinin. July 1987."
(SteveNtheseagulls accessed via Reddit)
Other users have shared the picture and rumor on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived), LinkedIn (archived) and X (archived). Some posts featured additional claims about Trump's plans for a Moscow hotel and his 1988 purchase of the Plaza Hotel in New York, as well as the claim that officials for the KGB — the former Russian secret police and intelligence agency — recruited him as an asset.
Trump's 1987 book "The Art of the Deal" says a Dubinin invitation did take the 41-year-old future president to Moscow for the first time in July 1987, in part to survey sites for potential Trump hotel properties.
Beyond the claim's age and year inaccuracies, no available evidence has credibly and conclusively confirmed Russia secretly recruited Trump as an asset. We previously reported the facts about a former Soviet and Kazakh security official claiming the KGB recruited Trump in 1987, finding no solid proof for the claims.
The Associated Press credited photographer Igor Tabakov with taking the picture in question on Nov. 5, 1996. The AP's caption read, in part, "In this Nov. 5, 1996, file photo, American real estate mogul Donald Trump, left, visits a reception, as he checks out sites in Moscow, Russia, for luxury residential towers."
The rumors presented alongside the photo follow the trail of other Trump and Russia claims, in particular Russian involvement in the 2016 U.S. presidential election. A Republican-led Senate Intelligence Committee report published in 2020 detailed findings on that matter, telling of a "grave counterintelligence threat" and that Trump associates expected to benefit from the Kremlin's help.
This article documents some of the information known about the other claims that have appeared with the picture on social media.
Trump's first visit to Russia in July 1987
In Trump's "The Art of the Deal," the author describes Trump meeting Dubinin at a luncheon, apparently in 1986. The book describes Dubinin's daughter as being familiar with Trump Tower:
A prominent businessman who does a lot of business with the Soviet Union calls to keep me posted on a construction project I'm interested in undertaking in Moscow. The idea got off the ground after I sat next to the Soviet ambassador, Yuri Dubinin, at a luncheon held by Leonard Lauder, a great businessman who is the son of Estee Lauder. Dubinin's daughter, it turned out, had read about Trump Tower and knew all about it. One thing led to another, and now I'm talking about building a large luxury hotel, across the street from the Kremlin, in partnership with the Soviet government. They have asked me to go to Moscow in July.
Later in the book, the author continues, saying Trump flew with his first wife, Ivana Trump, to Moscow on July 4, 1987:
In January 1987, I got a letter from Yuri Dubinin, the Soviet ambassador to the United States, that began: "It is a pleasure for me to relay some good news from Moscow." It went on to say that the leading Soviet state agency for international tourism, Goscomintourist, had expressed interest in pursuing a joint venture to construct and manage a hotel in Moscow. On July 4, I flew with Ivana, her assistant Lisa Calandra, and Norma to Moscow. It was an extraordinary experience. We toured a half dozen potential sites for a hotel, including several near Red Square. We stayed in Lenin's suite at the National Hotel, and I was impressed with the ambition of the Soviet officials to make a deal.
Later that July, Trump reportedly (archived) told the Press of Atlantic City, a New Jersey-based newspaper, that the Moscow trip did not go well, saying he had given up hopes of building a hotel after Russian officials offered only a joint venture with Trump having a minority control of the property.
A Reddit user posted a photo allegedly showing Donald and Ivana Trump standing in Moscow during the July 1987 visit. That post got the city wrong; the photo was taken at St. Petersburg's Palace Square. A Washington Post article captioned the photo as, "Donald Trump and his then-wife, Ivana Trump, visit St. Petersburg in 1987."
(chennai94, accessed via Reddit)
The Plaza Hotel
Users who shared the black-and-white Trump photo captured in 1996 (not 1987, as they claimed) presented the timing of Trump's Plaza Hotel purchase as suspicious.
For example, one Facebook post (archived) alleged, in part, that during Trump's 1987 visit to Russia he received loans from 16 banks and purchased the Plaza Hotel for $407.5 million.
Research in newspaper archives via Newspapers.com located past reporting on that matter.
In 1988, The Business World, a New York Times Magazine publication, reported Trump received a $425 million loan "provided by a consortium of banks led by Citicorp," as well as that he allocated $407.5 million of the total to his purchase of the hotel and 22 Central Park South.
At the time, Trump spokesperson Howard Rubenstein reportedly credited (archived) Trump's interest in purchasing the Plaza Hotel with Trump admiring the property from his office window. "He keeps looking out and seeing things. That's how he got involved in the [Wollman] skating rink, and now this."
In 1995, The New York Times published news of Trump selling the Plaza Hotel to a Saudi Arabian prince and one of Singapore's leading entrepreneurs. According to the article, banks in the U.S. originally lent money to Trump for his 1988 purchase, with banks in Japan holding a mortgage on the property. The story did not mention Moscow or Russia.
Trump's November 1996 Moscow trip
On Nov. 7, 1996, USA Today reported (archived) Trump as telling The Moscow Times about his trip to Russia, "We're looking at building a super-luxury residential tower, which I think Moscow desperately wants and needs."
The newspaper printed the article two days after Tabakov captured the black-and-white photo of Trump and nearly a decade after his first visit to Moscow.
Voice of America and The Washington Post published further reporting providing more details of Trump's past pursuits to expand his real estate empire in Russia.

Zambia courts sealed off as election petition deadline looms
- Published
Court premises in the Zambian capital, Lusaka, and elsewhere have been shut as the deadline for filing a petition against the outcome of the recent presidential election approaches.
An unusual police presence has been reported at some courts, which have been taped off to prevent access.
Opposition candidate Brian Mundubile said he would challenge the election result, citing irregularities, after coming second with a 38% share of the vote. Incumbent Hakainde Hichilema won a second term with 60%.
Mundubile is in hiding over alleged threats made against him, amid a post-election period marked by controversy, including the shooting dead of an opposition figure and the arrest of others.
Monday is the last day on which petition against the presidential election result can be filed. Such a petition could potentially affect the inauguration of Hichilema, which is scheduled for 1 September.
On Monday, lawyers who arrived at the courts were being asked to depart.
One lawyer told the BBC that three armed men approached his vehicle, identified themselves, and instructed him to leave the area.
The courts that have been sealed off include the High Court in Lusaka, the Supreme Court, which also houses the Constitutional Court, and several local courts.
It is unclear when the premises will reopen. The BBC has contacted the Zambian police and the judiciary for comment.
Local media cite a directive by a judiciary administrative official telling all staff not to report to work following the closure of courts for "security reasons".
The memo, which has also been shared online by some opposition figures, does not give details of the security situation.
Some commentators have raised concerns over the closure while questioning the independence of the judiciary.
A prominent voice for the opposition, Emmanuel Mwamba, alleged the action was aimed at preventing Mundubile from filing his presidential election petition.
Despite the court closure, preparations for Hichilema's inauguration appear to be continuing.
The youth and sport ministry has issued a media invitation for journalists to accompany a cabinet official on an inspection of arrangements at National Heroes Stadium, where the ceremony is expected to take place.
Mundubile last week rejected the presidential election results and said he planned to challenge the outcome through the courts.
He remains in a secure location under the protection of what his campaign describes as an "international human rights body".
He went into hiding after the arrests of opposition figures and the death of former minister Mutotwe Kafwaya during a raid by security officers, in what officials described as an exchange of fire in a security operation in the capital.
The arrests as well as the death of Kafwaya prompted calls from rights groups and the Law Association of Zambia for an independent investigations.
Amnesty International described the Kafwaya's killing as "deeply alarming" and called for prompt, thorough and impartial investigations. The lawyers' association similarly expressed "grave concern" and demanded investigation.
The election day, 13 August, was described by regional and international observers as largely peaceful, but they raised concerns about late electoral reforms, media freedom and access to the media in the run-up to the poll.
The EU observation mission said restrictions on the opposition may have contributed to an "uneven contest".
On vote tallying, the mission described a heavy military presence as intimidating and said it had received reports of attacks on some tallying centres.
It said staff in many centres did not record results on tally sheets as soon as they were announced, and cited weak verification between digital entries and paper records. It added that returning officers frequently paused proceedings while awaiting instructions from headquarters.
The EU mission also called for "maximal transparency" over the poll outcome, noting that the electoral commission did not publish separate polling-station results

Over the last 24 hours, the tiny Spanish territory of Ceuta - home to around 83,000 people - has seen an unprecedented surge in migrant arrivals.

Dozens of people died while trying to make the crossing.

BBC's Sarah Rainsford explains what may have triggered the surge in crossings and what happens next.

Toronto, Aug 25: Canada will announce retaliatory tariffs against the United States on Tuesday, an official familiar with the plans told The Associated Press, escalating a trade fight that has sharply worsened since negotiations with the Trump administration collapsed.
The official spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss the plans publicly.
Prime Minister Mark Carney said Monday that Canada may need to move away from matching US tariffs dollar for dollar and instead use more targeted retaliation aimed at protecting Canadian workers and businesses.
President Donald Trump escalated the dispute again Monday, telling Canadian leaders to “fall in line” or face consequences “far WORSE” than tariffs already imposed and threatening new 50 per cent tariffs on Canadian vehicles, auto parts and steel.
Carney accused Washington of trying to subordinate Canada and said US trade demands had confirmed Canada's fears that the United States was seeking to dismantle major Canadian industries.
“An attitude at the negotiation table that Canada is a subsidiary of the United States” is “not something we're going to accept,” Carney said.
Carney was even more blunt in French.
“We learned during the negotiations that the Americans want to destroy our major industries, including autos, steel and aluminium,” Carney said. “That was one of the main reasons we said no. It was a bad deal.”
The fiery words from both sides show how US-Canada relations have deteriorated since Carney walked away from trade negotiations with the Trump administration late Friday, triggering the president's threatened 50 per cent tariffs the next day on about USD 20 billion worth of Canadian goods.
Carney cast doubt on the US's reliability as a partner, saying Canada was finding reliable partners “everywhere in the world, except in the United States. Except in the United States. And Russia.”
Trump unleashes personal attacks on Canadian leaders
On Monday, Trump came back with further tariffs, warning that he would impose them on Canada's auto industry beginning next year.
“Canada has been ripping off the United States of America for years,” Trump wrote on social media, criticising what he called the country's “ridiculously high tariffs” on American farmers.
Carney said Washington's auto-sector proposals would gradually have the effect of dismantling Canadian production.
“This is the most successful automotive partnership in history,” Carney said, referring to the deeply integrated Canada-US industry.
Meanwhile, Ontario Premier Doug Ford unleashed his own tirade. In an interview with The Associated Press, he said Trump had underestimated Canadians' willingness to endure economic pain rather than give in to US pressure.
“We're all in,” Ford said. “Up here, we're at a fever pitch; everyone's in for an economic war. They know they're going to have to sacrifice.”
Trump responded in a social media post by attacking Ford personally, calling him “the less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive brother of the late, great, Rob Ford,” and once again referring to Canada's prime minister as “Governor Carney.”
Ford dismissed the insults: “If you think an insult from him hurts me? Well, bring it on, buddy, I'm ready.”
Ford is a Progressive Conservative whose party differs from that of Carney, a Liberal, but the two underscore broad political unity in Canada over the trade fight with Trump.
Ford threatens critical minerals and electricity
Ford said “everything is on the table” if the dispute worsens, including cutting off electricity and critical minerals from Ontario.
Critical minerals are increasingly important to US national security and manufacturing. The Pentagon has sought more secure supplies of minerals used in military aircraft, missiles, munitions and electronics as Washington tries to reduce reliance on China, which dominates the mining or processing of several strategically important minerals.
Ford said Canada should also consider increasingly severe retaliation if Trump continues targeting Canadian industries, including oil and potash, while Ontario could raise electricity prices or stop sending power south.
“We power 1.5 million homes and businesses,” Ford said. “Everything's on the table. I'll do whatever it takes.”
Ford has used electricity as leverage before. During an earlier phase of the dispute, Ontario imposed a 25 per cent surcharge on electricity exported to Michigan, Minnesota and New York. Trump responded by threatening to double tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminium before both sides backed away.
Auto industry becomes a central battleground
Ford accused Trump of not simply seeking a better trade deal but aiming to hollow out Canadian industries and move production south.
Ford said Trump wants to make Canada a vassal state.
“He wants to bleed out every single sector and bring them down to the US,” Ford said.
The auto sector is especially important to Ontario, the centre of Canada's vehicle manufacturing industry. Plants and suppliers in Ontario are tightly integrated with factories in Michigan and other US states, with parts routinely crossing the border multiple times during production.
Automakers including Ford, General Motors and Stellantis operate major assembly plants in Ontario, and the wider supply chain supports tens of thousands of jobs. Trump's new threat of a 50 per cent tariff on Canadian vehicles and parts puts that sector directly at the centre of the escalating dispute.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Monday that “the only reason Canada has auto production in the first place” was because of the 1960s Auto Pact, under which Canada used access to its market to encourage vehicle production north of the border.
Ford says he opposed preliminary deal
Ford also disclosed that he had opposed the preliminary agreement Carney was considering before Canada walked away from negotiations, and that he was unwilling to restore American liquor to Ontario store shelves as part of an agreement.
“I wasn't going to put the booze back on the shelves,” Ford said. “I was ready to go out there and call a press conference … and say I'm not buckling over.”
Ford said he understood Washington had sought language late in the negotiations that would have restricted Canada's ability to negotiate trade agreements with other countries without US approval. Carney has called that demand unacceptable and a question of Canadian sovereignty.
Carney said the dispute also exposed a deeper divide over language and culture, saying protections for French and Canadian culture that Washington views as trade irritants are considered fundamental rights in Canada.
“Who does he think he is?” Ford said of Trump. “You gotta be kidding.”

As trade tensions between the US and Canada boil over, Mark Carney pointed out one area where the two countries' interests are closely intertwined: icebreakers.
On Monday, the Canadian Prime Minister said that cooperation on the specialized vessels was a "reminder of one of the many, many, many things that the United States needs from Canada."
Carney was speaking at a news conference in Quebec, where he announced an 11.3 billion Canadian dollar, or $8.2 billion, contract for shipbuilder Chantier Davie to build six new icebreakers for the Canadian Coast Guard.
He also used the occasion to take a jab at the size of the US fleet, which Washington is racing to expand as melting Arctic ice opens new shipping routes and intensifies competition in the region.
"You know, the United States has a handful, and I'm being generous, of icebreakers," Carney said.
The US Coast Guard currently operates three polar icebreakers and has contracts for 11 new Arctic Security Cutters, while working with Canada and Finland to expand icebreaker capacity and expertise.
Davie Defense, which is part of the same industrial group as Canada's Davie Shipbuilding, is contracted to deliver five of the cutters, with two to be built in Finland and three in Texas.
The icebreakers are part of a broader push to strengthen US capabilities in the Arctic, where officials and experts have warned of gaps in surveillance, naval assets, infrastructure, and other tools needed to respond to threats as Russia and China increase their activity in the region.
Carney's remarks on Monday come as relations between Washington and Ottawa have deteriorated sharply over trade.
US-Canada trade negotiations broke down last week, and new 50% US tariffs on about $20 billion of Canadian imports took effect on Saturday. Canada has said it will retaliate dollar-for-dollar beginning September 8.
President Donald Trump said Monday that tariffs on Canadian cars, trucks, auto parts, and steel would be increased to 50% on January 1, 2027.

India is home to more than 1.4 billion people, thousands of communities, hundreds of languages, and five major language families. Many communities have historically practised endogamy and in some regions, consanguineous marriage. This is both a social and a biological fact with medical consequences. India is not one genetic population. Indians carry a layered inheritance shaped by ancient migration, mixing, isolation, ecology, language, culture and marriage patterns.
Our political map shows States and districts. Our genetic map often shows boundaries shaped by communities that lived near each other but did not always marry into each other. This matters, because genes influence inherited diseases, drug response, disease risk prediction, and the success of screening programmes.
Ancient layers
There is no single Indian genome. The oldest layer of Indian ancestry goes back to early modern humans who reached South Asia tens of thousands of years ago. This ancient ancestry forms the deep foundation of the subcontinent’s population history. Later came other ancestry layers linked to populations associated with the Iranian plateau, the Indus Valley world, Steppe pastoralists, and Tibeto-Burman-speaking groups. These movements were not like a single flood covering the whole land evenly. They came through different doors, at different times, and settled into different social worlds. That is why a Punjabi agrarian group, a Tamil caste group, a tribal population in Central India, a North-Eastern community, and an indigenous island community from the Andaman and Nicobar Islands cannot be treated as genetically identical. Some remote island populations preserve deeply distinctive ancestral lineages because of long isolation. But even here, caution is needed. No living community is a fossil.
Genetics can complicate community pride. A community may have a strong language, faith, identity, regional history, or story of origin. These identities matter. They give people belonging. But genes do not always obey the neat boundaries of culture. A group may preserve a language or ritual for centuries while carrying ancestry from multiple ancient sources. Two neighbouring communities may share a landscape but remain genetically distinct because they did not intermarry. Another two groups may speak different languages but share some older ancestry. Cultural continuity does not require genetic purity. It is a story of movement, mixture, separation, adaptation, and memory.
Marriage and disease patterns
After ancient mixing, many Indian communities became socially closed. Endogamy–marriage within a social group, and consanguinity–marriage between biological relatives, became the norm. Both can increase the chance that two parents carry the same rare recessive disease variant. We inherit two copies of most genes, one from the mother and one from the father, and in recessive diseases, a person with one altered copy remains healthy (called a carrier), while persons with two altered copies get the disease. If two carriers of the same disease-causing variant have a child, each pregnancy has a 25% chance of producing an affected child. This is why a child can be born with a serious genetic disease even when both parents are healthy. The family may have no known disease history, but the risk gene may have travelled silently through generations.
When a small community remains genetically closed for centuries, a rare variant present in an ancestor can become more common among descendants. This is called the ‘founder effect’. This is central to India’s public health future. Sickle cell disease is more common among several tribal populations in Central, Western, and Southern India. This pattern reflects old malaria pressure, population structures, and local history. Thalassaemia and other haemoglobin disorders also show region-specific and community-specific patterns. Some metabolic disorders, neuromuscular conditions, inherited hearing disorders, and rare recessive conditions may cluster in particular groups.
The correct message is that specific populations may carry specific risks, and knowing those risks can prevent suffering. Genetics should not be used to label communities; it should be used to guide screening, counselling, diagnosis, and care.
Testing and counselling
Genetic testing without counselling can do harm. A carrier may wrongly think that they are diseased. A family may blame the mother. A marriage proposal may be rejected because a test result is misunderstood. A whole community may feel stigmatised. This is why genetic counselling is not an ornamental part of modern medicine. It is the ethical bridge between a laboratory report and a family decision. Good counselling explains risk without panic. It tells people that being a carrier is common and usually harmless. It helps couples understand reproductive choices. It protects autonomy. It avoids coercion. Carrier screening, when voluntary and confidential, can help couples know their risks before the birth of an affected child. Newborn screening can identify treatable disorders early. Better rare disease diagnosis can end the long and exhausting journey that many families face, moving from one hospital to another without an answer.
Data gap
India does not yet have a large, deeply characterised, health-linked biobank comparable to resources such as the U.K. Biobank. Such a resource would not merely store DNA. It would connect genetic data with health records, laboratory results, imaging, drug response, and long-term outcomes. It would include India’s internal diversity, not only convenient urban samples. It would also require trust, consent, privacy protection, community engagement, and strong ethical governance.
Large population datasets can help identify new disease mechanisms and molecular targets for new medicines. This gap matters. A genetic risk score for diabetes or heart disease developed mainly in European populations may not work accurately in Indian populations. A drug-response marker common in one ancestry group may be uncommon in another. A rare disease variant important in one Indian community may be missed if reference databases are dominated by non-Indian genomes. Precision medicine will remain imprecise if the populations behind it are mismatched.
Mapping medical futures
India’s genetic mosaic is not merely an ancestry story, but a medical map. It can help prevent inherited diseases, improve newborn screening, guide safer prescribing, diagnose rare disorders earlier, and support drug discovery. But the map must be read carefully. Genetics should not be used to make claims of purity, rank communities, or frighten families. Its value lies in the responsibility to turn knowledge into care.
The Indian genome is not a single national portrait. It is a mosaic made of many tiles some ancient, some recent, some widely shared, and some found in small communities and still barely studied. Medicine now has the tools to read this mosaic. Our task is to read it responsibly, without cultural arrogance, without stigma, and without delay.
(Dr. C. Aravinda is an academic and public health physician. aravindaaiimsjr10@hotmail.com; Dr Veera Rajagopal is a physician-scientist and chief scientific officer at Wellytics, a health and wellness solutions company. veera.scientist@gmail.com)

‘You know nothing’: Maharashtra hill tragedy victims' relative refutes iPhone EMI claims
The teen's aunt described the iPhone narrative as a "rumour", claiming that people spreading such tales "know nothing".
An aunt of the 18-year-old boy, who died by suicide in Maharashtra’s Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar on August 21, has refuted the theory that her nephew took the extreme step due to EMIs of an iPhone he had bought.
The teen's parents had also died in a bid to save him. While threatening to jump off a hill, the teen fell into a 250-foot-deep gorge, followed by his father, who was trying to bring him down. His mother, who witnessed the incident, also fell minutes later. However, the iPhone EMI issue may not be the sole trigger, according to the mother's sister.
In a social media video, the aunt described what her family is going through.
“They were none other than... my elder sister, my sister's son, and my brother-in-law. Only we know the state we are in after losing the three of them today," she said, according to a report by NDTV.
She described the iPhone narrative as a "rumour", claiming that people spreading such tales "know nothing". She urged people to "not spread rumours".
"You have expressed your opinions through these videos, but you know nothing. You don't know us, and you are unaware of the truth behind any of this. And yet you continue to spread a false narrative. Do you realise how much pain these videos are causing my parents?" she asked.
She urged people to think of the family left behind before making any video.
"We are not in a state of mind to figure out how to move forward and how to hold ourselves together... we are unable to cope. Before saying anything, remember, my parents are 75 years old, and they would not be able to bear the shock of such words," she pleaded with folded hands.
Not his first attempt
The incident on Friday was reportedly not the teenager's first suicide bid. He had attempted suicide last year from the same cliff, but was persuaded by the police to drop the idea, NDTV reported. The police are now probing whether the dispute over the iPhone EMI was the only trigger behind the teenager's extreme step, Times of India reported.
HT could not independently verify the information.

What do we know?
The 19-year-old allegedly went up the hill at around 10 am after an argument with his parents over his demand for a new mobile phone, news agency PTI reported. The teenager had threatened suicide, prompting his parents, other villagers and police personnel to spend nearly three hours persuading him to give up the bid, according to NDTV.
The boy had allegedly bought an iPhone and had been asking his family for money to pay the EMIs, police said. This led to a heated argument with his father over the latest payment.
Videos of the incident and the prolonged standoff taken by tourists and locals at the site surfaced on social media.

Fire service personnel spread a safety net, father tried to reason with the teen
When the teenager was near the edge, police and fire brigade personnel arrived at the scene and tried to bring him to safety. Fire service personnel also tried to spread a safety net at the base of the hill, but the boy kept moving along the cliff edge, making the rescue effort difficult.
The teenager's father also climbed up the hill after initially trying to reason with his son from below. During the last 15-20 minutes of the ordeal, the father went up the hill. He moved closer to his son at around 1 pm and attempted to grab him as he backed off towards the edge. However, both father and son died during the attempt.
The teenager's mother, who had witnessed the incident, also fell moments later. The bodies were recovered by the police and sent for further formalities.
