When Lil Nas X recently disclosed that he had been diagnosed with bipolar disorder, one part of his story stood out to me more than the diagnosis itself. For years, he had suspected something was wrong. Yet he resisted seeking treatment because he feared medication.
This is a paradox that exists at the intersection of mental health, identity, and achievement. The people who are most capable of recognizing that something is wrong are often the same people most reluctant to accept help. Not because they deny their suffering, but because they have come to view suffering as an inseparable part of their success.
The concern is familiar to anyone who works in behavioral health care. Patients rarely say they want to remain depressed, anxious, manic, or emotionally dysregulated. What they fear is something else entirely. They fear becoming less themselves.
For artists, entrepreneurs, executives, athletes, and high-achieving professionals, that fear often takes a particular form of self-doubt, with thoughts of: What if treatment costs me the very thing that made me successful? What if medication dulls my creativity? What if emotional stability diminishes my ambition? What if managing my illness means losing my edge?
For generations, American culture has maintained a complicated relationship with mental illness. We increasingly accept it as a medical condition, yet we continue to romanticize its symptoms. Nowhere is this more apparent than in the stories we tell about achievement.
The troubled artist. The obsessive founder. The tortured genius.
Popular culture is filled with narratives suggesting that extraordinary accomplishments emerge from extraordinary suffering. That, perhaps, the very qualities that create instability are also responsible for innovation, creativity, and success.
But scientific research tells a different story with evidence that is far less romantic than the mythology. Research examining bipolar disorder consistently finds that delays in diagnosis and treatment are associated with worse outcomes, including higher rates of suicide attempts, anxiety disorders, alcohol use disorders, and long-term functional impairment. A 2025 systematic review published in The British Journal of Psychiatry found that the longer bipolar disorder goes untreated, the greater the burden on a person’s health, relationships, and ability to function in daily life.
Likewise, studies examining the broader impact of mood disorders have found that depression and bipolar disorder are associated with diminished productivity, impaired concentration, lost employment opportunities, increased health care utilization, and substantially reduced quality of life. A 2023 analysis published in the Journal of Patient-Reported Outcomes found that bipolar disorder carries a significant human and economic burden, affecting occupational functioning, social relationships, and overall well-being.
These are not conditions that sharpen performance. More often, they quietly erode it.
Yet the mythology persists because many successful people can point to periods in which symptoms and achievement appeared to coexist. A founder may remember building a company while sleeping four hours a night. An artist may associate periods of intense output with emotional turbulence. A lawyer may credit relentless anxiety for professional success.
What is often forgotten is the cost. Behind the promotion was the panic attack. Behind the creative breakthrough was the insomnia. Behind the extraordinary productivity was a deteriorating marriage, a dependence on alcohol, or a private struggle that few others could see.
As a leader in the behavioral health and recovery field, I have spoken with countless people who arrived at treatment believing that psychiatric care would diminish them. Many had spent years compensating for symptoms through work, achievement, perfectionism, substances, or sheer force of will.
Their greatest fear was not failure; it was becoming ordinary. However, what they discovered was something far different from what they expected.
Effective treatment did not make them less creative. It made sustained creativity possible. It did not weaken ambition; it reduced the chaos that continually threatened to derail it. It did not erase personality; it removed barriers that had prevented them from fully expressing it.
The misconception stems in part from how psychiatric medication is discussed publicly. Medications are often portrayed as either miracle cures or personality-altering chemicals. Neither of these characterizations are accurate.
When properly prescribed and monitored, psychiatric medications are tools. Their purpose is not to flatten emotion or eliminate individuality, but to reduce symptoms that interfere with functioning and quality of life.
For some individuals, medication is essential. For others, therapy, lifestyle interventions, or a combination of approaches may be appropriate. But the broader point remains that treatment is not designed to change who someone is. It is designed to help people access more of who they are beneath the symptoms.
I think this conversation is especially important for men.
Despite growing awareness around mental health, men remain significantly less likely than women to seek treatment. Traditional ideas about masculinity continue to prize self-reliance, emotional control, and endurance. Many men learn early that asking for help is seen as weakness, while suffering silently is seen as strength.
The consequences are visible in rates of suicide, substance use disorders, and untreated mental illness. Too often, treatment becomes the last resort rather than the first intervention.
The irony is difficult to ignore. The same men who would never hesitate to seek treatment for a cardiac condition, a broken bone, or diabetes, frequently resist treatment for illnesses affecting the brain.
We have spent decades working to destigmatize mental health conditions. Yet another form of stigma remains largely untouched, which is the belief that emotional suffering is somehow necessary for exceptional achievement.
It is not.
I believe the most compelling aspect of Lil Nas X’s story is not that he eventually accepted treatment. It is what he described afterward. He spoke about having less fear, about feeling better, and about being able to create freely.
For too long, we have treated mental health treatment as though it requires people to sacrifice part of themselves. In reality, the opposite is often true. Treatment doesn’t diminish human potential, but often liberates it.
Rachel Docekal, MBA, Ed.D., is CEO of the Hanley Foundation, an organization focused on addiction prevention, treatment, and recovery services.

When a company’s software update turns your computer into a useless brick, should fixes be free? Framework, the modular computer startup, apparently thinks so. But it’s not clear that computing giant Lenovo will go that far.
Lenovo confirms Legion Go issues after gamers report bricked devices
I installed Lenovo’s forbidden BIOS and my Legion Go lived. You might be less lucky.
Three weeks after a Redditor presented a nearly $300 repair bill for their handheld gaming PC — among other reports of damage and high repair bills — the company is breaking its silence. It says, in short: try holding down the power button longer, and if that fails, contact customer support.
Here’s the statement Lenovo provided to The Verge, via communications director Jeff Witt:
Lenovo is aware that some Legion Go devices may experience a blank screen during installation of BIOS version V42. BIOS V42 was not distributed through Windows Update or Legion Space, and Lenovo has removed the update from its support website while we continue our validation work. Users who have successfully completed the V42 update should not need to take further action at this time.
If a device encounters a blank screen during V42 installation, users may try pressing and holding the power button for approximately 10 seconds, waiting approximately one minute, and then powering the device on again. If the device does not resume normal operation, customers should contact Lenovo Support for further assistance.
Lenovo continues to evaluate and validate future BIOS updates for Legion Go.
On the official Lenovo forums, it appears another Lenovo employee may have weighed in, too: a “Daniel_Legion” claims the issue “should be repaired free of charge” if you’re under warranty. “In the case of out-of-warranty devices, it should be repaired free of charge, but please check local laws,” they write.
But Daniel_Legion has no other visible posts on the Lenovo forums, and “we’ll repair it if local laws force us to” isn’t a particularly reassuring pitch, so we’re asking Lenovo to confirm his words and their meaning. Will Lenovo extend its warranty to cover bad BIOS bricks?
It’s important to note that not every Legion Go was vulnerable to begin with. You’d need to have the original Legion Go 8APU1, not the Legion Go S or the Legion Go 2, and you would’ve had to download BIOS V42 (N3CN42WW) directly from the company’s website over the two or so months before Lenovo yanked it.
Even then, you might have been safe. The other day, I chose violence and decided to install the forbidden BIOS V42 on my own Legion Go review unit, and… after a long, scary sequence of black screens and progress bars and warnings and more black screens that lasted six whole minutes, it booted up just fine. (Plays games, even lets me log into Windows by typing my PIN with the gamepad controls. I couldn’t do that right before the update.)
Assuming Daniel_Legion is legit, it sounds like the investigation is still ongoing. A team in Europe was able to reproduce the issue with three out of three devices tested, but other teams weren’t able to see it at all, he told the Lenovo forums. “As such the issue is most likely related to specific component used on mainboards in certain batch or batches, or the issue needs to have specific circumstances to manifest,” he wrote.
I strongly feel that a company shouldn’t need to fully investigate before reassuring customers. They should say “if we did it, we will fix it, even outside of warranty.” That’s what Framework did with its device-bricking BIOS update.

Five people have been arrested in Guwahati for allegedly abducting and raping a 15-year-old girl in a homestay, police said on Monday.

The case was initially registered under Section 87 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) for abduction and later Sections 6 (aggravated penetrative sexual assault) and 7 (sexual assault) of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012, were added, officials said.
According to Kamrup SSP Shubhashis Baruah, at around 5:47am on August 24, police received information that the missing girl had been seen in the Panbazar area of Guwahati.
Officials of Dadara Outpost, accompanied by the girl’s family members, reached the area and found her near the Panbazar water tank.

Sliman Mansour, one of the defining figures of contemporary Palestinian visual art, died on August 24, 2026, at the age of 79.
His family announced his death through his official social media accounts. No cause of death was publicly disclosed.
The family wrote, "The final chapter has been written. With hearts heavy beyond words, we share that our beloved father has passed away. To the world, he leaves behind a life filled with beauty, memory, and a legacy that will continue to live through all those he touched. But to us, we lost a father, our source of love, strength and home.”
For more than five decades, Mansour was at the forefront of a Palestinian art movement that sought not simply to depict a homeland, but to preserve and question the idea of one.
His paintings returned, again and again, to the land - capturing the timeless pull of Jerusalem’s ancient stones, the rural villages, and the expanse of fields that once defined home.
Born in 1947 in Birzeit, near Ramallah, Mansour came of age as Palestinian identity was being reshaped by war, occupation and exile. His work, often immediately recognisable, developed a visual language rooted in those experiences.
Perhaps no painting captured that more powerfully than Jamal Al Mahamel, widely known as Camel of Hardship or Camel of Burdens. The iconic work depicts an elderly porter carrying Jerusalem on his back.
The image is simple. Its meaning is not.
For many Palestinians, it came to represent the extraordinary weight of history, loss and attachment to a homeland. Mansour’s art could be direct in that way, but it was rarely uncomplicated. A figure carrying Jerusalem could also be seen as a question: how much can one person carry, and for how long? That question ran through much of his career.
Mansour was also a co-founder of the New Visions collective, formed during the First Intifada. At a time when artists were rethinking the relationship between politics, culture and artistic practice, the group rejected Israeli art materials and turned instead to local elements, including mud and henna. The choice itself became part of the work.
It was a way of making art from the land that had long been central to Palestinian memory.
Over the years, Mansour’s work became closely associated with sumud — the Palestinian concept of steadfastness and resilience. Yet his paintings did not present resilience as something triumphant or effortless. There was often strain in the bodies he painted, weight in the landscapes and a sense that endurance came with a cost.
That may be why his work travelled so far beyond galleries and museums. Mansour was painting particular places and particular histories, but his images carried something more universal: the fear of losing home, and the stubborn refusal to let it disappear.
His death marks the loss of an artist who helped shape how Palestinian identity came to be seen in modern visual culture.
Sliman Mansour leaves behind a vast artistic legacy, including Camel of Hardship, which remains one of the most enduring images of Palestinian steadfastness. His family announced his death on 24 August, 2026, and no further details about the cause of death have been made public.

Shark attack survivor says thinking about daughter gave her strength to fight for life
Sydney schoolteacher Leah Stewart lost an arm after being attacked by a suspected great white shark in June
An Australian woman who lost an arm in a shark attack said thoughts of her young daughter drove her to fight for her life as she faced the "monster".
Leah Stewart, 34, was attacked while swimming near the shoreline at Sydney’s Coogee Beach on 13 June. The schoolteacher suffered life-threatening injuries after being bitten on her arms and legs by what was suspected to be 3.5-metre great white shark.
Ms Stewart underwent several surgeries, was placed in a medically induced coma for nearly two weeks and later had one of her arms amputated.
In her first public remarks since the attack, Ms Stewart said she had made enough progress to regain some independence and was beginning to see a way forward.
"After what has been an incredibly difficult few months, I am so happy that I have progressed enough to build some independence and I can finally see some light after all of this," she wrote in an update posted on her GoFundMe page.
The fundraiser, set up by her brother shortly after the attack, collected nearly A$559,000 (£293,000) to support her rehabilitation, prosthetics, and ongoing medical treatment.
Ms Stewart said the family was closing the fundraiser as the donations had provided enough support for her recovery and future treatment.
"What you have offered has given us enough to recover, to stay in our home, and to give us options for further medical treatment down the road," she said.
She had spent recent weeks concentrating on her recovery and trying to return to "some sort of normal life”. “I still have a long way to go, but my recovery has been remarkable,” Ms Stewart said, “and a huge part of that is because of the absolute army of love, support, prayers and encouragement surrounding my family and I from all over the world."
Ms Stewart said she had been overwhelmed by the support she had received from friends, family and strangers.
"I want you to know that I feel like I’ve been given a second chance at life and I’m not going to waste it," she wrote. "You've inspired me to get better, not bitter."
In an emotional interview with Nine aired this weekend, Ms Stewart recalled coming face to face with the shark and fearing her daughter, August, would grow up without her. "Its face was horrific," she said. “I will never forget. It was a monster.”
“I was holding onto my leg and I just thought of August. And I thought she’s not going to have a mum. I couldn’t handle that. I did not want her to grow up without a mum,” she added. "I just thought, ‘I’ve got to fight it and do everything I can to be here’."
Australia has seen a series of deadly shark attacks this year. Four people were attacked over two days in January, including a 12-year-old boy who later died of his injuries.
A man was killed while spearfishing in Queensland in May, and a father of two died after being attacked by a four-metre shark in Western Australia.

Barely 150 days after Gen Z anger helped propel Balendra "Balen" Shah to Nepal's top job, the same restless street energy that propelled his rise seems to be pinning him down, leaving the former rapper under pressure from public protests, parliament and his own Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP).
Barely two months after he took office, young protesters returned to Kathmandu's Maitighar Mandala demanding his resignation, while opposition MPs attacked his repeated absence from parliament, where he attended only five of the first 39 sittings before speaker Dol Prasad Aryal directed him to appear and answer lawmakers on Aug 26.
The political honeymoon began fraying within weeks of Shah taking office on March 27, after RSP swept 182 of 275 House seats. In April, strict enforcement of customs rules on goods brought across the open India border hit people dependent on Indian markets for groceries, medicines and household essentials, triggering protests in border towns and forcing authorities to relax the move.
Public anger intensified in July after 25-year-old ride-share driver Ganesh Nepali self-immolated outside the passport office in Kathmandu following a dispute over municipal action against his vehicle. 
His death fuelled demonstrations over municipal policing and revived criticism of drives against informal settlements and landless squatters without adequate rehabilitation.
Shah also faced sustained attacks over Nepal's border dispute with India after his statement on Nepal encroaching on India's territory drew the opposition's ire.
Violent communal clashes in southern Nepal along the border with India added another layer of pressure and forced Shah to address the nation after criticism over his delayed response, while in Pokhara former Gorkha servicemen continued demanding a resolution of stalled recruitment of Nepalis into Indian Army under Agnipath.
The strain has spread inside RSP, where lawmakers and senior leaders questioned Shah's distance from party structures and unilateral governing style. RSP MP Jagadish Kharel sharpened the criticism from within while speaking in Parliament, saying, "Govt will not survive if only the dignity of the PM is preserved. Our dignity must also be preserved."

Broken toilets, leaking roofs: Why India's 'cockroach' party wants to fix schools
- Published
The squat one-storey building has recently received a fresh coat of paint and looks respectable from a distance.
But this government-run primary school for girls in Faridabad, a district on the outskirts of the Indian capital Delhi, suffers from a host of problems.
The road outside the school in Khedi Kalan village is dotted with shallow potholes filled with filthy water. Inside, local social worker Satpal Narwat points out the plaster falling from the ceiling.
"It looks new from the outside, but it's crumbling from inside. Four of its eight toilets are unusable and full of trash, while four of the nine classrooms have also been abandoned because they are too unsafe for children," he says, adding that in the rains, "the classrooms get flooded and children have no place to sit".
This is not an isolated case. Many schools, especially in rural India, are starved of funding and in disrepair.
India spends only 4.1% of its GDP on education. While this meets Unesco's lower minimum threshold of 4%, several countries - including France, Germany, Australia, Brazil and the US - spend more than 5% of their GDP on education. Countries like Belgium and Sweden spend even more.
Experts - and the Indian government's own National Education Policy (NEP) - have recommended 6% as the ideal mark for India.
According to official data, 94,000 government schools have closed here between 2014-15 and 2024-25. A report, external by government think-tank Niti Aayog says some were merged as part of efforts to streamline the system, but acknowledges that enrolment has fallen as demand for private schools has risen.
The poor state of government schools is the focus of a new campaign by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP). The online satirical movement made global headlines for its weeks-long protest in Delhi, which culminated in the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan last month.
The protests had erupted in May after NEET, India's biggest medical entrance exam, was cancelled following a question paper leak, forcing nearly two million students to retake the test. More than 20 students died by suicide, with their families blaming the scandal.
Named #SchoolThikKaro (#FixTheSchool), the CJP's latest campaign is aimed at highlighting the crumbling infrastructure in government schools and pressuring authorities into addressing it.
"Government schools, especially in rural India, have been neglected for many many decades now. So, children who grow up in villages don't have equal opportunities and they end up working in farms or as a daily wage labourer or construction workers," CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke told the BBC.
"It's only because they don't get the same facilities and the same opportunities that children in big cities get. And that is what we are trying to change by making schools better."
On Thursday, Dipke said he had visited more than 20 rural schools and had "not found even a single good school".
"There were no benches, no bathrooms, no drinking water, no facilities at all. Even animals would not be kept in such a place," he said.
"What I saw was really heartbreaking. This is very similar to what I used to see when I used to visit my village during school summer vacation. And even after 20 years, nothing have changed there."
In recent days, Dipke and other CJP leaders have shared several videos - of leaking roofs, dirty toilets, children sitting on the floor and angry students - with their 26 million Instagram followers.
"We want to ensure that children get benches to sit on, good washrooms and clean drinking water. They should have smart classrooms with digital boards. That is when they will also feel that they are getting the same quality of education as those living in big cities in the country," Dipke said.
The government of Prime Minister Narendra Modi or his Bharatiya Janata Party have not commented on the campaign.
The BBC has also contacted India's education ministry for a response.
Meanwhile, the CJP's protest in Delhi and the campaign to fix schools appear to have emboldened students across India and opened floodgates of complaints and set off localised mutinies against an administration many accuse of being apathetic.
Armed with mobile phones, school students have been shooting and posting videos on social media - some of which have gone viral and prompted authorities to act.
After one video, external of schoolgirls in Raigad, Maharashtra, mocking the condition of the road leading to their school went viral, the local authorities repaired it
In Uttar Pradesh, another video showed students running into the district magistrate's office demanding a road to their school, while a third , externalshowed schoolgirls asking an official whether he would send his own children to a school in such poor condition.
At Delhi's Jantar Mantar, where the CJP held its earlier protest, the group demanded Pradhan's resignation as well as an overhaul of India's education system with greater accountability.
Journalist and author Nilanjan Mukhopadhyay says "by the end of their protest, it was clear that it wasn't just about one exam or one minister's resignation".
"People there were talking about the state of schools and everything that's wrong with them."
Mukhopadhyay says the #FixTheSchool campaign is an obvious next step and "the way people have contributed with videos, pointing out flaws in school infrastructure, is evidence that the movement is gaining ground".
"It can't be Jantar Mantar 2.0 as it will be much slower and a long-lasting movement. But the CJP will get a lot of support for the campaign because there's plenty to talk about that's wrong with the schools," he adds.
One of the biggest problems government schools face is a lack of teachers and other staff, says Chatar Singh, treasurer of the Primary Teachers' Association in Haryana state where Faridabad is located.
Singh is also the head teacher of the primary school in Atmadpur village. Its new building, funded by a private company's corporate social responsibility programme, and students' trophies make it one of the better-equipped schools in the area.
But as we approach the toilets near the school gate, a stench greets me. Singh says the toilets have not been cleaned properly for the past two days because the part-time cleaner - appointed by the government to come in for a couple of hours every morning - has been sick.
But dirty toilets are not his biggest problem – it is the lack of teachers, he says.
For the school's 910 children, there are 40 teachers. But on Wednesday when BBC visited the institution, 30 had been deployed to help with voters' list revision, four others were off sick, leaving only six teachers to manage the children.
"Teachers are hired to teach, but across India, government deploys them to do a lot of non-teaching assignments. They are used for election duty and to conduct Census. Most of my teachers have been on voters' list revision duty since July. It's affecting the quality of education," he says.
Asked why he thinks the government schools are neglected, Singh says, "Do children of bureaucrats and MPs and politicians study in my school? No. They send their children to private schools because they can afford them."
Most students here are children of migrant factory labourers, he says. "And a majority of them are from underprivileged castes and communities. Anyone who can afford sends their children to private school," he adds.
His claim holds true across India. It is visible in the mushrooming of private schools in small towns and villages.
In Khedi Kalan when he was growing up, Narwat says, there were only government schools near him and he got his education there.
The crumbling girls' primary school which he gave me a tour of upsets him because the 62-year-old studied here from 1968 to 1973.
"In those days, this was the only school in the village for both boys and girls," he says. "The school building was relatively new. There were eight rooms and all were filled with students."
He says flooding became a serious problem after the road outside was raised about 15 years ago, leaving the school below road level.
Narwat, who retired as an officer in the state's electricity office two years back, says he sent his children to the same school, but later moved them to a private school because they have better facilities.
Narwat then takes us to the second primary school in the village - this one for boys, just a couple of hundred metres away. Here, classes are operating out of two rooms and a veranda. A second building with three classrooms was declared "condemned" and demolished about five years ago with assurance that a better one would be rebuilt. The patch is now a parking stand for cycles.
Over the years, Narwat has petitioned chief minister, MPs and district officials, and written to the National Human Rights Commission, seeking improvements to the two Khedi Kalan schools. But he says little has changed.
"I send my grandchildren to a private school," he says. "It's very expensive, but they have all the facilities. In village schools, the teachers are on election duty, and there's no library or laboratory."
The CJP campaign has given him some hope that the schools will finally get attention.
"I think the CJP can be a force for good. They've taught people to fight, to not be afraid. The government has all the power and resources. And now they have to perform."

For the first time, the Tamil Nadu Medical Services Corporation (TNMSC) is procuring various assistive devices and mobility aids, including retrofitted petrol scooters, for the Welfare of Differently Abled Persons Department. Nearly 15 tenders have been floated by the TNMSC after the department asked it to undertake the procurements.
The TNMSC was set up with the main objective of ensuring the availability of essential drugs and medical supplies in all government hospitals across the State through a streamlined procedure for procurement, storage and distribution. According to official documents, including the Health Department’s policy note, apart from supplying medicines for government hospitals, TNMSC also procures and supplies medicines required for various veterinary healthcare institutions functioning under the Department of Animal Husbandry.
Officials confirmed that for the first time, the TNMSC was asked to procure and supply various assistive devices by the Welfare of Differently Abled Persons Department. Following this, it has floated online tenders for fixing of rate contracts for supply of various types of battery-operated wheelchairs, sewing machines, tricycles, hearing aids, reflective folding stick and modular reflective folding sticks, modular reading device and electronic Braille readers, standing frame and corner seat, artificial limbs, metal and plastic calipers, magnifier, goggles and braille watches, axillary crutches, elbow crutches and walking device, augmentative and alternative communication system software with tablet and smartphone, and retrofitted petrol scooters, and specially designed retrofitted petrol scooters for spinal cord injuries.
The TNMSC’s Memorandum of Association and Articles of Association permit it to procure assistive devices, officials said. Earlier, such tenders for procurement of the assistive devices and mobility aids were called for by the Welfare of the Differently Abled Persons Department.
“This was an informed decision taken by the department. TNMSC is well-versed in undertaking such procurements, given the technical nature of assistive devices such as hearing aids. These devices should be procured depending on the condition of individuals such as those with spinal cord injuries. This is based on their request, and the TNMSC has the capability and technical expertise and is allowed to make procurements for all requesting directorates,” an official said. They said the TNMSC’s procurements typically include warranty and maintenance support, which could have been another reason for the department to ask the agency to handle the procurement.
Move criticised
The State government’s decision to entrust the TNMSC with the procurement of one-gram gold rings under the ‘Thaimaman Thanga Mothiram Thittam’ for babies born at government hospitals had already drawn widespread criticism, with concerns that it dilutes the corporation’s core purpose.
A section of government doctors said TNMSC’s mandate was different, and taking on such additional procurement activities could divert the TNMSC from its primary responsibilities. “There are already delays in procuring essential and life-saving equipment due to administrative reasons. Taking on additional responsibilities will only affect its routine work,” a senior doctor said. Another doctor added that this could compromise the TNMSC’s functioning, affecting the quality of service, and, in turn, patient care in the long run.

China probes use of formaldehyde to keep cabbages fresh
- Published
Authorities in China have launched an investigation into reports of formaldehyde being used to preserve the freshness of cabbages for human consumption.
Officials in the northeastern Hebei province confirmed that they had verified footage showing individuals dipping cabbages in a solution before loading them onto trucks for transportation.
An environmental blogger first released the footage last week. Using formaldehyde, a colourless chemical that is known to cause cancer, for preserving the freshness of food in China is strictly prohibited.
China is the world's largest producer of cabbages, most of which are exported to neighbouring countries in Asia.
Police have taken legal action against the individuals involved, according to state media.
Officials are now moving swiftly to prevent panic and restore confidence by carrying out spot checks on markets across the country.
Chinese state media says investigators will also establish how widespread the practice is and take measures to trace affected vegetables.
In a statement issued on Saturday, local authorities in Kangbao county said: "Any illegal or non-compliant practices discovered will be dealt with strictly in accordance with the law to ensure the safety of the vegetable supply."
Xinfadi market in Beijing, one of the major sources of fresh produce in the capital, issued a statement saying that it had investigated the source of its cabbages, adding that none of the affected vegetables had entered its market.
The incident has generated widespread media attention in China.
An editorial in the People's Daily wrote: "The wholesalers focused solely on their immediate economic interests while completely disregarding the lives and health of consumers. [They] crossed a legal red line and breached the moral bottom line."
China produces well over 30 million tons of cabbages each year, nearly half of the world's annual total. Vietnam, South Korea and Russia are among the largest export destinations for the vegetable.
Exposure to relatively high quantities of formaldehyde in some workplaces has been linked to some types of cancer in humans, but the effect of exposure to small amounts is less clear, according to the American Cancer Society.

Four arrested over boxing champion's murder in South Africa
- Published
Four people have been arrested in South Africa in connection with the murder of boxing champion Zolani Tete, who was shot dead outside his home on Friday.
Tete, 38, was gunned down in what has been described as an ambush in Mdantsane, Eastern Cape. A young woman who was with him was also shot and is in hospital.
One of the men being held, a 22-year-old who was arrested on Saturday, will make an initial appearance in court on Monday, and faces murder and attempted murder charges.
Tete held the WBO bantamweight title from 2017 to 2019, as well as the IBF super-flyweight title in 2014. He was later given a four-year ban, which lapsed in July this year.
The remaining suspects, who were arrested on Sunday, are due in court on Tuesday. Two have been charged with unlawful possession of firearms and ammunition. It is unclear whether they will also be charged with murder and attempted murder.
Tete was in his car waiting for the gate to his house to open when two armed suspects in balaclavas emerged from a vehicle and fired "multiple shots" at him and a 27‑year‑old female passenger, according to officials.
The motive behind the attack is unclear.
Tributes have been pouring in for the two-time world champion since his death. South Africa's Sports Minister Gayton McKenzie said: "South Africa has lost one of the finest fighters it has ever produced."
Former Sports Minister Fikile Mbalula also paid tribute to Tete, lamenting the loss of a "a great South African who has made an immense contribution in the sport of boxing".
Tete beat Liverpool's Paul Butler in 2015 in one of the eight times he fought in the United Kingdom.
He also holds a Guinness World Record for the fastest knockout in a title fight, ending his match with Siboniso Gonya inside 11 seconds in 2017.
Tete last fought in July 2022, beating Briton Jason Cunningham by knockout In London, but it was later ruled a no-contest after he failed a drugs test.
He tested positive for anabolic steroid stanozolol and was given a ban by the UK Anti-Doping Agency.
After his death, manager Mla Tengimfene confirmed he had been training for a comeback fight after his ban ended.
Tete had 29 wins in 34 fights, with four losses and one no-contest.
South Africa has one of the highest murder rates in the world.
According to the latest crime statistics, covering the period between January and March this year, around 58 people were killed each day.

Karnataka beggar dies, ₹8.4 lakh savings found as she leaves behind currency notes at home
The cash, accumulated over the years, included ₹10, ₹20 and ₹50 notes. More than 30 sacks containing the money were found inside the house.
A 68-year-old woman in Karnataka, who spent her life begging, died of an age-related illness, leaving behind more than several sacks containing coins and currency notes.
The woman, identified as Hoor, was found dead at her rented home in Mandya, according to a PTI report.
After her death, locals inspected the house and were stunned to find thousands of coins and currency notes stuffed into sacks among her belongings. The cash, accumulated over the years, included notes of ₹10 and ₹20.

₹8.4 lakhs found in Hoor's belongings
A video from the house showed locals going through Hoor's belongings and counting the large collection of coins and currency notes. More than 30 sacks containing the money were found inside the house.
The counting revealed that she had accumulated a total of ₹8.4 lakh, according to a report by NDTV.
Hoor had lived in the rented house with her sister. Both women were unmarried and lived together until Hoor's sister died two years ago. Hoor continued to stay in the house after her sister's death and earned her living by begging, the report added.
After Hoor's death, the money recovered from her home was handed over to her two brothers.

Indore's beggar with cars and property
The discovery comes months after a similar case in Madhya Pradesh, where a government campaign to remove begging from the streets of Indore uncovered the surprising wealth of a man known as a beggar.
In January, the “Beggar-free Indore” campaign led officials to discover that a man named Mangilal owned property and vehicles worth crores of rupees.
The campaign was launched to help people dependent on begging find alternative means of livelihood. During the drive, teams from the Madhya Pradesh Women and Child Development Department identified Mangilal in the Sarafa Bazaar area, where he had reportedly been seen for years receiving money from passers-by, The Times of India reported.
When officials took him in for rehabilitation, they discovered that Mangilal owned three houses in different parts of Indore, including a multi-storey building and a 600-square-foot house, India Today reported. He also owned three auto-rickshaws and a Swift Dzire, which he rented out to generate income.
Mangilal had also received a one-bedroom house under the PMAY scheme, which is intended for people in need, despite already owning property. Officials are now investigating how he became eligible for the benefit.
The investigation further revealed that Mangilal worked as a moneylender, providing loans to small shopkeepers in Sarafa Bazaar and collecting interest. Authorities said charging high interest is illegal and would be examined as part of the investigation.

Trump removes Syria from 'terrorism list'
The Trump administration on Monday formally removed Syria from the State Sponsor of Terrorism (SST) blacklist, in a landmark move that unlocks export restrictions and allows for the US to supply military aid to the country.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement that he also delisted Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham's (HTS) designation as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist.
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, under his nom de guerre Abu Mohammed al-Jolani, was the leader of HTS, an al-Qaeda offshoot.
"These actions represent another historic step by President Trump to give the Syrian people a path to prosperity," Rubio said.
The move follows Israel bombing Syria's Abu al-Duhur airbase last week, which escalated tensions between Washington and Damascus, as well as Syria's main foreign backer, Turkey.

Putin assures India of fuel, fertilisers amid disruptions over West Asia crisis
Jaishankar said PM Modi hopes that President Vladimir Putin would attend the Brics Summit in New Delhi on September 12-13
Russian President Vladimir Putin on Monday assured India of supplies of energy and fertilisers amid disruptions caused by the West Asia conflict, even as external affairs minister S Jaishankar highlighted the need to address the growing imbalance in two-way trade that has soared to $50 billion.
Putin’s expected meetings with Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the margins of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Summit in Kyrgyzstan this month and on the sidelines of the Brics Summit in New Delhi in September figured in a meeting between the Russian leader and Jaishankar in Moscow. Jaishankar is in Russia to co-chair a meeting of the Inter-Governmental Commission on Trade, Economic, Scientific, Technological and Cultural Cooperation (IRIGC-TEC).
Putin pointed out that bilateral trade has increased this year, after declining slightly in 2025, and said Russia is increasing fertiliser supplies to India. He noted that any important issues had figured in the IRIGC-TEC meeting and said: “One of these issues is not only energy – it is, of course, the supply of fertilisers…We are doing everything to resolve this issue for Indian farmers, for agriculture. We are increasing these supplies and are ready to do so further.”
The two sides are also making progress on cooperation in nuclear energy and high-tech, Putin said.
Jaishankar said Modi hopes Putin will attend the Brics Summit in New Delhi on September 12-13. “Prime Minister Modi looks forward to meeting you at the SCO Summit and also hopes that you will have the opportunity to come to the Brics Summit and host this annual summit,” Jaishankar was quoted as saying by state-run TASS news agency.
He also handed over a personal message from Modi to Putin. People familiar with the matter said Putin is expected to attend the Brics Summit, along with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian. The summit is expected to focus on global economic and political challenges, and expanding multilateral cooperation among Brics member states.
While co-chairing the IRIGC-TEC meeting with Russia’s first deputy prime minister Denis Manturov, Jaishankar pointed out that a more than four-fold increase in bilateral trade in goods — from $13 billion in 2021-22 to nearly $60 billion in 2025-26 — had been “accompanied by a significant widening of the trade imbalance” from $6.6 billion to more than $50 billion.
“Addressing this imbalance is today one of our foremost priorities. Progress on market access, removal of tariff and non-tariff barriers, strengthening payment mechanisms and stronger business-to-business engagement will be critical for addressing this imbalance and achieving our shared objective of $100 billion in bilateral trade by 2030,” Jaishankar said at the start of the meeting.
Jaishankar made three proposals for the next phase of the India-Russia economic partnership – focusing on implementation and outcomes to prioritise deliverables and solving problems, strengthening engagement with businesses by aligning institutional mechanisms with industry priorities, identifying bottlenecks and improving policy responses, and exploring new possibilities to address the needs of de-risking and diversifying.
The discussions between Jaishankar and Manturov also encompassed cooperation in trade, investments, energy, fertilisers, nuclear energy, connectivity, technology, space and mobility of professionals. The two sides also reviewed the progress in discussions between India and the Eurasian Economic Union on a free trade agreement.
Manturov said Rosatom’s involvement in building the Kudankulam nuclear power plant in Tamil Nadu could be the basis for expanding cooperation in nuclear energy, including the “creation of new power generation facilities in India, including small-scale ones, as well as the localisation of equipment and nuclear fuel production”.
Russia also sees potential for new joint projects in the extraction and processing of non-ferrous and rare earth metals, Manturov said. Russia and India are also discussing cooperation in space exploration, including manned spaceflight, rocket propulsion and satellite navigation, he said.
The prototype of a high-speed electric train jointly produced by India and Russia will be assembled by the end of the year, after which serial production is expected to begin, Manturov announced at the meeting. “Within this framework, the flagship project in transport engineering — the development and production of the Vande Bharat electric trains — is systematically developing,” he said.
In March 2023, a consortium led by Russia’s Transmashholding won a $6.5-billion tender for the development, production and 35-year service of 1,920 Vande Bharat electric train cars.
Manturov also prioritised cooperation in energy security, including the supply of oil, petroleum products and coal, as well as joint investment projects in hydrocarbon production and processing. Russia is currently among the top two suppliers of energy to India.
Russian energy minister Sergei Tsivilev described India as a key partner for the country’s fuel and energy sector, while deputy prime minister Alexander Novak noted that Moscow is interested in Indian investments in the Russian oil and gas sector, and developing a distribution network involving Russian companies in India.
Manturov also noted that tourist flows between Russia and India had increased by 8% in the first half of 2026, with more than 25,000 Indian tourists visiting Russia. Around 50,000 Russians also visited India, he said. Referring to labour migration, he said Russia and India are focusing on expanding the legal framework to create stable and transparent conditions for attracting workers.
The number of Indian students in Russia has also grown to almost 40,000, Manturov said. Support for talented children and youth can be a new vector of cooperation between the two countries, he added.

- Rebel Wolves has announced that The Blood of Dawnwalker will get a Performance mode targeting 60 FPS on consoles.
- The performance mode will be added to the game when it releases through a launch-day patch.

One of the hotly anticipated games, The Blood of Dawnwalker, is finally getting a 60 FPS Performance Mode at launch. Among the upcoming games of 2026, The Blood of Dawnwalker stands as one of the most promising titles this year, and now Rebel Wolves have heard fan feedback to deliver a 60 FPS mode for PS5 and Xbox consoles on day one, when the game releases on September 3, 2026.
Rebel Wolves Announce 60 FPS Performance Mode for The Blood of Dawnwalker on Day One
In an X post made via the official The Blood of Dawnwalker account, Rebel Wolves wrote, “The Blood of Dawnwalker will receive a Performance Mode targeting 60 FPS on PS5, PS5 Pro, and Xbox Series X on Day 1 through the launch patch.”
The devs further added in the post, “Performance Mode was already in the works, but it was still being tested”. They went on to explain that the only reason why they held off on announcing it was that they didn’t want to make half-baked promises.
In a thread attached to the X post, devs also mentioned that PS5, PS5 Pro, and Xbox Series X will be getting three different graphics modes. Performance mode will target 60 FPS, while balanced and quality mode will aim for 40 FPS and 30 FPS, respectively. The PS5 Pro will also receive overall visual enhancements. Meanwhile, Xbox Series S will only target 30 FPS.

Since the devs previously announced The Blood of Dawnwalker system requirements, revealing that the game could run at 60 FPS on Ultra settings on PC, fans argued why console players are left behind in getting higher framerates.
Ever since the latest announcement of a performance mode, fans have now thanked devs for listening to community feedback and implementing it swiftly with clear communication. The Blood of Dawnwalker releases on September 3, 2026, on PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X|S.

The National Medical Commission (NMC) has proposed a registration system under which a medical practitioner, once registered with a State Medical Council and allotted a Unique Identification (UID) number in the National Medical Register, would be eligible to practise across India without obtaining fresh registration or a licence in another State.
The proposal is part of the draft Registration of Medical Practitioners and Licence to Practice Medicine (Amendment) Regulations, 2026, notified by the NMC on August 11, 2026. The draft seeks to amend the 2023 regulations governing registration and licensing of doctors. The NMC has invited objections and suggestions for 30 days from the date of notification.
Under the proposed system, registration and licensing would be routed through a unified registration portal of the NMC’s Ethics and Medical Registration Board. The State Medical Council would continue to scrutinise applications and grant registration and the licence to practise, but the approval would simultaneously be reflected in both the State Medical Register and the National Medical Register.
The UID assigned in the register would incorporate the State/Union Territory code and the practitioner’s State Medical Register number, the NMC said. Once the State Medical Council grants registration and the Ethics and Medical Registration Board allots the UID, the doctor would not require fresh registration or a separate licence to practise in another State or Union Territory.
The draft also proposes automatic electronic synchronisation between the national and State registers so that a change made in one register is reflected in the other. The National Medical Register would serve as a central repository of registration details as well as disciplinary proceedings, including suspension, removal, and restoration of registration.
The NMR would also carry information on whether a doctor’s license is active or inactive, and details of disciplinary action, if any. The Ethics and Medical Registration Board and the NMC would have powers to seek records and monitor State Medical Councils to promote uniformity and transparency in regulation.
The proposal retains the five-year validity of a license. If a doctor does not apply for license renewal within three months of expiry, the registration will be marked inactive, and the practitioner will not be entitled to practise medicine. The inactive status would automatically be reflected in the NMR.
While seeking to create a nationwide registration framework, the draft leaves disciplinary jurisdiction primarily with the State Medical Council in whose territorial jurisdiction the alleged professional misconduct, unethical conduct or medical negligence occurred.
The concerned State Medical Council would have the power to inquire into and decide the matter, and record the outcome against the practitioner’s credentials in the online register. Where disciplinary action is recommended by a State Council other than the doctor’s primary registering council, the action would be reflected in the NMR and automatically updated in the State register of the council of primary registration.
The draft also provides for an appeal mechanism. If a State Medical Council rejects an application for registration, license or renewal, the applicant can appeal to the Ethics and Medical Registration Board within 30 days. The Board would have 30 days to decide the appeal, and if it allows the appeal, its order directing the State Council to grant registration or a license would be binding on the council.
The proposed amendments also revise provisions relating to foreign medical graduates. Their definition would include Indian citizens and Overseas Citizens of India who obtain a foreign medical qualification in modern/allopathic medicine but do not hold an undergraduate medical degree from an Indian institution. The Foreign Medical Graduate Examination graduates who meet the prescribed conditions would remain eligible for provisional registration for internship and registration in the National Medical Register.
The draft also proposes extending temporary registration for foreign nationals undertaking postgraduate or super-speciality courses from a maximum of 12 months to the duration of the course, subject to a maximum of 24 months, followed by a one-year cooling-off period.
Additionally, existing practitioners who do not have a National Medical Register UID would have to update their details on the Ethics and Medical Registration Board portal within a period to be specified by the Board and obtain the UID as a one-time measure. No fee would be charged for this exercise.
The draft notification has not yet to come into force.

CDPR is aiming to release The Witcher 4 in 2028

CD Projekt Red (CDPR) joint-CEO Michał Nowakowski just revealed that the company is hoping to release The Witcher 4 in 2028. The long-awaited sequel was first announced all the way back in 2022, but didn't get a reveal trailer until The Game Awards in late 2024.
"Simply put, this is our biggest, boldest and most ambitious game to date," he said in a short video posted to social media. "I know it's a bit of a wait and you'd love to play it sooner, but let the team cook."

As we near #gamescom in just a few days, CD PROJEKT RED Joint-CEO Michał Nowakowski would like to personally invite YOU to join us there, and hear about the future of The Witcher franchise!
To that end, Nowakowski confirmed that CDPR will not be showing off the sequel at Gamescom, which starts on August 26. It will, however, be showing a whole lot of the upcoming The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Songs of the Past expansion. A few things are certain in life: death, taxes, LeBron James playing professional basketball — and Americans’ belief that crime is getting worse. Since Gallup began asking about national crime in 1989, a majority of respondents said they thought crime in the US was higher than the year before in every survey year except 2000, 2001, and 2025. Even in that last year, 49 percent still said more crime was happening. It’s perhaps the archetypal example of negativity bias, the mental habit of giving more weight to bad news than good.
America’s murder rate hasn’t been this low in 70 years
The country’s murder drop is still a mystery. Baltimore may help explain one piece of it.
Last week, the FBI put some numbers on just how big that bias is. The American murder rate — which peaked in 1980 at 10.2 per 100,000 — fell to an estimated 4.1 per 100,000 people in 2025, matching the rates recorded in 1955 and 1956 for the lowest ever measured in the country. The violent crime rate (murder, rape, robbery and aggravated assault) fell 9.7 percent, the largest single drop since J. Edgar Hoover was running the bureau in 1936.
That much is known. But what’s not known for sure about the crime drop is almost everything else. Adam Gelb, who runs the Council on Criminal Justice, says that there is no single or easy explanation for the historic lows, while Jeff Asher, the analyst who spotted this decline before nearly everyone else, agrees. For every leading candidate — federal pandemic spending, some normalization after the 2020 social collapse, better violence prevention, even the decline of drinking — there is a corresponding hole.
But there is one American city where researchers can point to a specific program, measure what it did, and put real numbers on it. And it just happens to be the city that spent 50 years — and five award-winning seasons on HBO — as America’s shorthand for murder.
What Baltimore did
Baltimore recorded more than 300 homicides a year for most of the last decade, and more than 200 for most of the past half-century. In one month, July 2015, 45 people were killed — an astounding figure for a city of just around 600,000 people at the time.
But Baltimore finished 2025 with 133 homicides, the fewest since 1977 and about 60 percent fewer than in 2020. Through the first eight months of this year, the city has seen 60 murders, and the police commissioner’s target is to stay under 100.
What caused this? Three things at once.
Baltimore Mayor Brandon Scott’s Group Violence Reduction Strategy identifies the few people most likely to shoot or be shot — two groups that heavily overlap — and sends people to their doors with two messages: you are on our radar, and here is housing and job training. Separately, the longer-running Safe Streets program puts outreach workers with real street credibility between disputes, aiming to interrupt them before they become shootings.
That’s the harm reduction element. There’s also a tough-on-crime component. The state’s attorney office says it has secured 2,129 convictions since 2023 across several gun-related violent-crime categories, with over 1,700 of those defendants incarcerated.
Meanwhile, Baltimore’s homicide clearance rate reached 60 percent by mid-2026. Its nonfatal-shooting clearance rate was 54 percent, up more than 12 percentage points from a year earlier. Criminologists have long held that the certainty of being caught deters criminals more than the severity of the sentence, and more successful shooting investigations are a common thread where violence is falling around the country.
How do you tell whether a program worked, or whether a city just got lucky? Drug trials get a control group; cities don’t. Baltimore got one almost by accident: the strategy launched in the city’s Western District in 2022 and nowhere else, which left the rest of the city as a comparison.
That’s what a team of economists and criminologists used. They measured the Western District against Baltimore neighborhoods that hadn’t started the program yet, and over 18 months the number of people shot there, fatally or not, ran about 30 percent below that stand-in. Killings alone fell by a similar share, but deaths are rare enough that chance couldn’t be ruled out. Police made no more arrests than before. Arrests for serious violent crime rose 81 percent.
A second, looser test set the whole city against a composite of other big American cities and put Baltimore’s murder rate about 25 percent below it. The authors are careful with that one: too much changed in Baltimore at once to say how much it the strategy was responsible for.
Murder is contagious
Baltimore’s success is built on two ideas, and they came from two very different places.
The first came from a doctor named Gary Slutkin, who spent the 1980s and early 1990s fighting tuberculosis in San Francisco, cholera in Somali refugee camps, and AIDS across Africa. He came home to Chicago in 1995, a year the city recorded over 800 homicides.
Key takeaways
- Americans have told Gallup crime is getting worse in nearly every year since 1989. In 2025 the US murder rate fell to 4.1 per 100,000, tying 1955 and 1956 for the lowest ever measured, and violent crime dropped 9.3 percent — the largest single-year fall since the FBI began national estimates in 1936.
- Nobody can say why. Federal pandemic spending, the unwinding of the 2020 collapse, violence prevention programs, Americans drinking less: every leading explanation has a hole in it.
- Baltimore is an exception. Because its Group Violence Reduction Strategy launched in one police district first, researchers could measure it against the rest of the city. Shootings there ran about 30 percent lower — and police made no more arrests than before.
When Slutkin examined the city’s shooting maps, they looked familiar. Clustered in space, clustered in time, and spreading case to case — murder resembled the outbreaks he used to fight. Slutkin reasoned that the way to treat violence was to treat it like cholera: find the people most likely to transmit. Interrupt the transmission. Change the conditions that let it spread. Slutkin built the model into a program called CeaseFire, now Cure Violence Global, and its Baltimore descendant is Safe Streets.
The second idea came from a criminologist. David Kennedy, working in Boston in the 1990s, found that 61 gangs with about 1,300 members — under 1 percent of the city’s young people — were tied to at least 60 percent of its youth homicides. Get those people in a room with police, prosecutors, and community elders, tell them plainly what comes next, and the shooting slows down.
That approach is called focused deterrence. Baltimore’s Group Violence Reduction Strategy is a version of it. To see how it works over a longer period of time, take a trip across the Atlantic to Glasgow in Scotland, which in the early 2000s was considered the murder capital of Europe.
In 2005, in the midst of that wave of violence, Glasgow’s Strathclyde Police established a Violence Reduction Unit that operated with a basic thesis: evidence shows that violence can be prevented. Among other interventions, the unit sent trauma surgeons into schools to describe what a blade does to a face and stationed outreach workers at hospital bedsides to reach victims in the vital hours after an attack, the moment when retaliation can still be stopped.
In 2024-25, Scotland recorded 45 homicide victims, the fewest since comparable records began in 1976 and down from 96 two decades earlier. Every case was solved.
Pull the handle
So we have clues to why crime has dropped so much, but not clear conclusions. As successful as Baltimore’s group violence strategy has proved, a 2023 study of a similar street-outreach effort in Boston found no effect whatsoever. And the latest evaluation of Baltimore’s own Safe Streets — 11 sites, each measured against a stand-in version of the same neighborhood without the program — produced numbers that sound terrific but settle very little: youth homicides down 42 percent and youth shootings down 21 percent, but neither is strong enough to rule out chance. And while some sites saw youth homicide fall by as much as 100 percent, two sites saw it rise by 42 and 89 percent.
Some experts, like the UC Irvine criminologist Emily Owens, argue the crime decline has been so widespread and similar — big cities and small, red and blue governments — that the true cause is some larger social change rather than what any one city is doing. Nor can we be sure the fall will continue. Billions in federal pandemic relief money has supported many of the programs that have worked well in places like Baltimore, and that money is already running out. But we can identify one reason why it happened, and learn from that success.
As it happens, Gary Slutkin was not the first doctor to look at a map of the dead and see a pattern in it. In September 1854, a cholera outbreak was killing hundreds of people in London’s Soho district. A doctor named John Snow had mapped the outbreak and saw the dead were clustered disproportionately close to the district’s Broad Street water pump. Snow had a theory that water was connected to the disease and convinced a Soho parish board to remove the handle of the pump.
Nobody in Soho at that moment could have told you what caused cholera. It would only be 29 years later that someone would definitely identify the responsible pathogen, and in doing so, explain why Snow’s intervention worked. But the explanation could wait. The dying stopped that month in Soho, just as it is stopping in Baltimore and around the US today. And that’s what counts.

The new Shokz OpenFit Air 2 earbuds are nearly 20 percent lighter than the previous generation
They feature an open-ear design that reduces pressure and heat buildup.
Shokz just introduced the OpenFit Air 2 earbuds, a refresh of the original model. These earbuds are around 17 percent lighter than the previous version, clocking in at 7.2g per unit. That's around the same weight as a handful of paperclips.
This is an open-ear design, which delivers a couple of benefits. First of all, there's no ear canal pressure, as the earbuds don't create a seal of any kind. The design also gives users quicker access to their surroundings, making them a decent choice for exercising outside in a busy city. As a matter of fact, the standard Shokz OpenAir 2 earbuds easily made our list of the best headphones for running.
The only potential downside to this form factor is that they connect via an ear-hook. The ergonomic design ensures long-term comfort, with a caveat. These ear-hooks could get in the way of glasses and certain hats. Take a look at photos and decide for yourself.
Otherwise, the company promises "richer bass" and "fuller sound." The earbuds use the company's proprietary Bassphere audio driver and its OpenBass 2.0 algorithm. There's an angled speaker that directs audio toward the ear for a "more natural listening experience" and an app with access to four preset EQ modes and two custom EQ profiles.
The OpenFit Air 2 earbuds last eight hours per charge, with up to 36 hours of use when considering the included charging case. They also offer a 10-minute quick charge that gives three hours of playback. This model integrates with Bluetooth 6.1 and allows for multipoint connections. They will be available to purchase on August 27 for $130.
Shokz also just introduced the OpenRun Air 2 earbuds, which feature a design that wraps around the back of the head. These are also lighter than the previous iteration, with an overall form factor that prioritizes stability and minimizes bounce. After all, these are for runners.
They use a bone conduction driver and also connect to the company's app for EQ adjustments. The battery lasts ten hours on a single charge, with a five-minute quick charge for two hours of playback. The OpenRun Air 2 earbuds are also available on August 27 and, lo and behold, also cost $130.

Woman flagged by ID scanner as nationwide 'public safety concern' after incident in Winnipeg bar
Privacy experts say establishments need to better explain what happens to data
Privacy experts are raising concerns after a Winnipeg bar flagged a woman as a nationwide public safety concern through its ID scanning system, which led to her being denied entry to a Calgary Stampede venue in July.
Alexandra, a Montreal-based lawyer, went to the Riverside bar in St. Vital on June 6, where a person working security scanned her driver's licence at the door using a Patronscan ID scanner.
She said she was not told why they were scanning it and had no idea an incident later that evening would lead to a flag that potentially banned her from bars across Canada.
"This flag had denied me entry at an establishment in a whole other province without my knowledge, without any transparency surrounding how this flag had been established," Alexandra said.
She said she started feeling sick while at the Winnipeg bar and ran to the nearest washroom, thinking she was going to throw up. Someone knocked on the door and told her to leave, and Alexandra asked for more time to pull herself together. She then left without incident, she said.
CBC News is only using Alexandra's first name because she fears professional repercussions by telling her story.
Denied entry to Calgary Stampede venue
On July 9, she went to a venue at the Calgary Stampede that used the same kind of Patronscan scanner and was denied entry. The person using the scanner told Alexandra she had a "criminal record," which she knew was false.
Assuming it was a fluke, Alexandra tried to get into the same venue the next day and was again denied, so she began asking more questions.
The venue worker showed her a flag in their system that was attached to her ID. The flag labelled her a "public safety concern" with a "serious" level of severity because she "went into the men's bathroom and refused to leave," noting the location was the Riverside.
"I quite quickly realized that this was data sharing because how would a flag from a bar in Winnipeg show up at this venue in Alberta?" Alexandra said.
She took a photo of the screen showing this information and shared it with CBC.
"I did find it to be quite outrageous," she said of the specific flag. "There are people who go into bars and assault people and start fights, and do all sorts of horrible things."
Flag network used across North America
Alexandra soon learned the Winnipeg bar is part of Patronscan's flag network, a system the Calgary-based platform uses to alert other venues about problematic people.
This eliminates having to call another bar to warn them of a problem patron or share incident reports with other venues, Patronscan's website says. The system is used across North America and around the world. The idea is that it stops dangerous people from being allowed into venues.
The Riverside's manager said in an emailed statement to CBC News that after Alexandra contacted the bar, it reviewed the matter and determined it was a mistake, saying it should have only been an internal flag. The bar has removed the external flag on her file, the manager wrote.
After her concerns, the bar reviewed its procedures with staff and how flags are entered and "when information should or should not be shared with other establishments," the manager wrote.
The manager added the bar takes privacy concerns seriously but said there is an important distinction between the appropriate use of Patronscan for public safety and this "specific administrative error."
People need to understand how data is used: experts
Experts CBC spoke to said the incident raises multiple concerns related to how people's personal information is used when their ID is scanned at an establishment.
Under federal private-sector privacy laws, an organization must inform individuals in a "meaningful way" of the purpose for collecting, using or disclosing someone's personal information.
The law also states an organization must collect, use or disclose it for a purpose "that a reasonable person would consider are appropriate in the circumstances."
Teresa Scassa, the University of Ottawa's Canada Research Chair in Information Law and Policy, said people need to be asking questions when they are handing over their identification for scanning purposes.
"Is the collection necessary? Is it appropriate in the circumstances? Does it go too far? How is the data being treated? Is it secure? Who's it being shared with? All of these questions come up," she said.
A Patronscan spokesperson said in an emailed statement that when an ID is scanned, they collect the name, date of birth, gender, postal code and expiry date in order to verify someone's age. If nothing happens that night, the record is deleted within 21 days in Manitoba.
If there is an incident, the spokesperson wrote, the venue can record a flag, and the information is held longer. For serious incidents, a network flag can be recorded. Those flags are visible to other Patronscan venues, but only when an ID is scanned.
Public flags keep people safe: BarWatch chair
In Vancouver, the BarWatch program has been running for over a decade, and its 46 bars and clubs all use Patronscan. It gives bars the ability to ban someone who is a gang member, or is deemed to be dangerous or harassing people, across the program.
BarWatch has policies for when someone is given a public flag and works with Vancouver police, said Curtis Robinson, the program's chair and a former police officer.
- Barwatch introduces lifetime bans for weapons infractions at Granville Street bars
- Vancouver bars to dump unattended drinks after VPD warning
A strict code of conduct is posted that patrons must follow or risk getting banned through the system. British Columbia's privacy commissioner gave the program the green light in 2009 on the agreement it would delete the information collected within 24 hours if there were no incidents.
"Individuals that are banned because of bad behaviour, we don't take this lightly. You've basically acted in an unsafe manner, and you're essentially told that, 'Look, because of your behaviour, you can't come in here or … go to any other BarWatch bar,'" Robinson said.
He says people who don't want to have their ID scanned can choose to go to bars that don't use BarWatch.
'Undesirable to whom?'
The entrance to the Riverside has a Patronscan sign, which is below eye level and posted under the machine that scans the identification. Alexandra said she did not see the sign when she was there.
The sign says that if someone is determined to be violent or otherwise "undesirable" from a safety perspective, their name, date of birth, gender, postal code and photo can be kept and shared with other Patronscan establishments.
Scassa said the sign raises several questions about whether this is adequate notice.
For example, she noted, it does not mention that specific incidents will be shared with other venues. In Alexandra's case, the Calgary Stampede venue was able to see the incident involving her in the men's washroom at the Winnipeg bar.
Scassa also said it does not state the data is held by a third party, and it is not clear how many establishments the information can be shared with or their geographic area.
Krystle Shore, an assistant professor at the University of Waterloo, studies the relationship between surveillance technologies to solve social problems. She said these sorts of notifications rely on people stopping, finding the fine print and understanding what it means.
"We get into grey areas when we are looking at a sign that's posted at a bar, below a stand where somebody's maybe not looking directly at it, as they're walking in with 10 friends on a Friday night," Shore said.
She said the Patronscan disclosure sign has a number of red flags — for example, the use of the word undesirable.
"What do we mean by undesirable? Undesirable to whom? And in what context?," Shore said.
It is a system that relies on the subjectivity of one individual and can have real consequences, she said.
"And when we look at the surveillance of undesirables, there's a long history of who in particular is being targeted by that framing," Shore said, adding members of the 2SLGBTQ+ community have historically been labelled as "undesirables."
Bars must display signage: Patronscan
The Patronscan spokesperson said the signage is mandatory for clients and has been updated as needed after various privacy commission reviews.
The company will open an investigation if a person disputes a flag, the spokesperson said.
Alexandra is in the process of making an official complaint to the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada — an agent of Parliament that oversees the compliance of Canada's privacy laws.
Ann Cavoukian, Ontario's former privacy commissioner, described the incident as appalling and said it is something she sees as worthy of a commissioner investigating.
"This individual had no knowledge or awareness that this was taking place and that her information was going to be used in this manner afterwards," she said.
Alexandra said she is telling her story so Canadians understand how their data can be collected and shared by third parties.
"In this world of increasing mass surveillance and use of AI to do these things, I think that someone needs to say something when they notice that their rights are being violated," she said.

Government regulators have spent the last year asking serious questions about Tesla’s electronic, retractable door handles, a cool-looking automotive design flourish that has since been imitated by plenty of competitors.
The handles have been blamed, in the US and in China, for making it difficult for passengers to quickly exit vehicles, and for impeding rescue efforts. A handful of crash victims’ families have even filed lawsuits against Tesla, alleging the door handle designs played roles in their loved ones’ deaths.
Now the door handles have led to Tesla’s largest recall ever—and China’s. The Chinese government is recalling more than 2.9 million Model 3s and Model Ys manufactured in China between 2019 and 2026, the State Administration for Market Regulation announced Friday.
Some of the affected vehicles will be made safer with an over-the-air software update that lowers windows after collisions, making it more difficult for passengers to become trapped inside. But many cars will also need new warning stickers—affixed free of charge—that can help passengers find and operate emergency mechanical door handles. Those handles can currently be hard to identify because they’re similarly colored to the rest of the vehicles’ interiors. The mechanical door handles are especially important when vehicles’ low-voltage batteries fail. (These batteries don’t operate the cars themselves, but power onboard computers, displays, and other accessories, including electronically-powered door handles.)
Tesla didn’t respond to WIRED’s request for comment.
The Chinese government simultaneously recalled more than 1 million vehicles manufactured by eight Chinese automakers, also for safety concerns related to flush door handles. The other automakers are Beijing Automotive, Chery, Dongfeng, First Auto Works, Geely, Leapmotor, Xiaomi, and Xpeng.
Separately, the Chinese government recalled nearly 50,000 imported Tesla Model 3s, Xs, and S’s for insufficiently monitoring drivers using the US automakers' assisted steering technology. The government said the tech increased the risk of collisions. The recall affects some vehicles imported between 2019 and 2026. Some of the vehicles can be fixed with software updates, but some will need new in-cabin cameras that ensure drivers are paying sufficient attention while operating their vehicles.
China has been more aggressive than other countries in regulating new automotive technology. It put in place new rules earlier this year that will soon ban fully retractable door handles in the country. In 2021, a government agency issued regulations more tightly governing the operations of autonomous vehicles, even before that tech had widely hit the road; another agency that same year created specific rules for the data generated by its increasingly software-centric cars.
The US’ top road regulator has started to examine whether it needs new rules governing door handle design, Bloomberg reported last month.
