Mainland China’s ship activity near Taiwan hits record for third month in a row
Beijing has ramped up its law-enforcement and survey operations around island since Tokyo and Manila announced boundary talks
Taiwan’s defence ministry said that in the first 24 days of August it detected mainland coastguard, survey and other official vessels a total of 118 times, surpassing the 117 reported in July and 111 in June.
Those numbers were far higher than in any previous month on record since Taiwan began releasing detection data in July 2024. Before June, the highest count of mainland government ships in a single month was 50 in April 2025, according to a tally by the SCMP.
That record-breaking intensity of activity aligns with findings from an August 19 report by the Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative (AMTI), which noted a “more sustained and assertive presence” by mainland Chinese law-enforcement and survey vessels in waters east of Taiwan.
Using commercial automatic identification system data, AMTI – a programme of the Washington-based Centre for Strategic and International Studies – showed that the ships’ activity around Taiwan between June and August was concentrated in waters where Chinese, Japanese and Philippine maritime claims overlap. Almost no such activity had been observed in that area between January and late May.
Two China Coast Guard vessels accounted for much of the observable activity during that period, while a third had been patrolling the area since August 4, according to AMTI. Within days of the Japan-Philippines announcement, mainland Chinese law-enforcement vessels hailed 198 commercial ships in the area, demanding information about their ports of call and crews, the report noted.

How to cancel your ChatGPT subscription (and why you might want to)
If you want to cancel your subscription, you'll need to go through the same payment system you used to sign up.
Canceling a ChatGPT subscription only takes a few clicks. But if your goal is to quit ChatGPT entirely, stopping the recurring charge may be only one part of it. You might also want to delete your account, keep new chats out of model training or simply stop paying for features you no longer use. Canceling the subscription handles only the billing, so the right next step depends on what you actually want to stop.
Reasons to reconsider a paid ChatGPT plan
A paid plan makes the most sense when you regularly run into the Free tier's limits or rely on tools reserved for higher tiers. If that's no longer true, paying every month gets harder to justify. One option is ChatGPT Go, a lower-cost paid tier that OpenAI now offers in every country where ChatGPT is supported. Spending less doesn't necessarily require giving up a paid plan altogether.
AI subscriptions have another unusual wrinkle: the product can change while you are paying for it. OpenAI retired GPT-4o from ChatGPT on February 13, 2026, after previously restoring it when some Plus and Pro users said they preferred its conversational style. For someone who subscribed partly for access to a particular model, that's a reminder that a paid AI service can change substantially from one month to the next.
Features and price aren't the only reasons someone might reconsider a paid ChatGPT plan. After OpenAI's February 2026 agreement with the US Department of Defense to deploy its models on the department's classified network, Sensor Tower data reported by TechCrunch showed US ChatGPT app uninstalls jumping 295 percent day over day. OpenAI later amended the agreement to explicitly prohibit domestic surveillance of US persons and said its services would not be used by Defense Department intelligence agencies such as the NSA without a new agreement. The Sensor Tower figure measures app uninstalls, though, not paid subscription cancellations.
How to cancel your ChatGPT subscription
For a personal subscription purchased on chatgpt.com, log in, select your profile icon, open Settings, choose Billing and select Cancel under Cancel plan. OpenAI recommends canceling at least 24 hours before the next billing date to avoid another charge.
If you subscribed through Apple, open the iPhone Settings app, tap your name, tap Subscriptions, select ChatGPT and tap Cancel Subscription. On Android, open Google Play, make sure you're signed in with the Google account used for the purchase, then go to Subscriptions > ChatGPT and tap Cancel subscription. Uninstalling the app does not cancel an App Store or Google Play subscription.
If you can't find the cancel option, first check where you originally subscribed. Web, Apple and Google subscriptions are managed separately, and OpenAI warns that it's possible to end up with more than one active subscription across those platforms. If you have lost access to the ChatGPT account or its email address, OpenAI support can also cancel the subscription after locating the account using the email address, the last four digits of the payment card and the date of the most recent payment.
What canceling a ChatGPT subscription does and doesn't change
Canceling the subscription stops future renewals, but it doesn't delete your OpenAI account or erase existing chats. Standard chats remain saved to your account until you delete them, so canceling a paid plan is not the same thing as removing your data.
Whether your chats are used for model training is controlled separately. Under Settings > Data Controls, turning off Improve the model for everyone prevents new conversations from being used to improve OpenAI's models while leaving those conversations in your history. Temporary Chats are another option for individual conversations: they don't appear in history or get used to improve the models, and OpenAI says it may keep a copy for up to 30 days for safety purposes.
Deleting your OpenAI account is separate from canceling the subscription. Account deletion is permanent, prevents access to OpenAI services and triggers deletion of account data within 30 days, apart from limited information OpenAI may retain where required or permitted by law. If Apple or Google is billing you, cancel the subscription through the relevant app store before deleting the account.
What happens after you cancel ChatGPT
Canceling doesn't remove paid features immediately. OpenAI says the cancellation becomes effective the day after the next billing date, so you can keep using the paid plan through the current billing period.
Canceling also doesn't automatically result in a refund. If you subscribed through chatgpt.com or Google Play, you can request one through OpenAI's Help Center. App Store refunds must be requested directly from Apple. For chatgpt.com and Google Play purchases, accidental purchases are generally eligible for a refund if you contact OpenAI within 14 days of the charge.
Customers in the EU, UKand Turkey are also eligible for a prorated refund if they cancel within 14 days of purchase.
Once the paid period ends, your account remains available along with any chats you haven't deleted. Canceling the subscription stops the recurring payment without requiring you to decide whether to keep using ChatGPT.

Iran faces 'greatest financial offensive ever', says US treasury secretary
- Published
The US treasury secretary has threated Iran with "the single greatest financial offensive ever", claiming the US-Israel war with Iran was "entering its endgame".
Scott Bessent said the US would sever all economic ties with the country in "an economic D-Day" and that any nation partnering with Iran financially would also be isolated.
Bessent's threat to the Iranian regime follows several U-turns and extended deadlines from US President Donald Trump's administration on previous threats.
Iran dismissed Bessent's comments and said it would shut down all oil exports from the region "if the war continues", according to news agency Reuters.
The Iranian regime has also issued a new warning to shipping not to pass through the Strait of Hormuz without its permission, the agency reported.
One fifth of the world's oil and gas usually passes through strait, a waterway south of Iran, but the flow has been effectively blocked by the country since the conflict began at the end of February.
Bessent made the comments in an opinion piece for the Financial Times, external. He did not detail what the economic pressure on Iran would involve, but he is expected to do so in a press conference in the US at 13:00 local time (18:00 BST) on Monday.
"The world should understand that our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains the tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone," he wrote in the piece.
The US has made several threats to Iran over the course of its war with the country, including Trump saying in April that "a whole civilisation will die tonight" unless Iran agreed a deal to end the war and unblock the Strait of Hormuz.
The US eventually climbed down from that position after mediator Pakistan intervened and called for more diplomacy.
The Iranian regime already faces tough economic sanctions from the US.
Former US president Barrack Obama and several US allies had agreed a deal with the country in 2015 which lifted many sanctions in return for Iran agreeing to limit its nuclear programme.
However, Trump pulled out of that deal in 2018, calling it "defective at its core, and reimposed all US sanctions on Iran.
During Joe Biden's term as US president, he made some attempts to reinstate the Obama-era deal, but this did not happen.
In April this year, the Trump administration launched a wave of sanctions on foreign banks and firms doing business with Tehran after it became clear its military operations had not caused Iran's regime to surrender.

A new study published in the European Journal of Ophthalmology has found that a smartphone-based AI system demonstrated high accuracy in detecting major eye diseases including diabetic retinopathy (DR), age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and glaucoma, a press release said.
The study, ‘Smartphone-based offline AI for multi-disease retinal screening: Real-world accuracy’, was conducted by doctors from the NIO Super Specialty Hospital, Pune. In this prospective, cross-sectional study, 193 adults (371 eyes) aged 18 years and above with DR, glaucoma, AMD, or normal fundus (healthy back of the eye) were enrolled between May and December 2024.
The study involved the use of a Remidio Fundus on Phone (FoP) platform integrated with Medios AI multi-disease software, an offline AI system. The Medios AI system has received regulatory approval from the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation for clinical use. This platform functions entirely offline.
Dilated fundus imaging was performed using the Remidio Fundus on Phone and Zeiss Clarus 500 cameras. Ungradable images were excluded. The offline MAI algorithm generated disease-specific reports, which were compared to masked grading of the Clarus images by two fellowship-trained ophthalmologists.
The results showed significant diagnostic accuracy: for glaucoma sensitivity was 98.2%, specificity was 99.0%; for AMD, sensitivity was 88.9%, specificity was 97.5% and for DR, sensitivity was 84.6%, specificity was 99.0%.
The study concluded that the results supported scalable, point-of-care retinal screening in resource-limited settings with this system.

Was it meat or glucose that fueled the growth of the human brain? If evolutionary science told us, hitherto, that human brain expansion relied on meat to grow, a new study has an interesting addition to this theory. Published in a recent issue of Science, the study posits a dual fuel strategy - sugar and meat - as having powered brain expansion in humans.
The multi-centre study by Jennie Brand-Miller et al, does not discount the role of meat in brain expansion, but argues that natural sugars and starch found in fruits and honey delivered the required glucose to power a rapidly-expanding human brain. “What foods enabled the evolution of the large human brain? Currently, that diet is usually framed around increasing intake of animal foods: meat, protein, fat, and omega-3 fatty acids,” the authors explain, but go on to model the glucose needs of humans and their ancestors from four million years ago, until recently.
How the brain grew
Over a period of four million years, the size of the human brain is said to have increased from around 300 grams in early hominins (bipeds) to about 1,500 grams in modern humans. As brains grew, so did demand for glucose, which is required by other tissues including red blood cells, kidneys and reproductive organs. “The human brain is unusually large for our body size and requires substantial amounts of energy,” Jennie Brand-Miller, professor of human nutrition at the University of Sydney Charles Perkins Centre and School of Life and Environmental Sciences, said.
The study does not dismiss the importance of hunting or animal protein; rather, it establishes that human brain expansion relied on a balanced, dual-fuel strategy. Meat provided critical amino acids and micronutrients, while natural sugars and starches delivered the essential glucose required to power a metabolically expensive brain.
These findings discover a new glucose pathway to brain development – natural sugars may have supplied the energy needed to support brain metabolism before the advent of cooking which made starch-rich foods easier to digest. The paper is co-authored by archaeologist Karen Hardy, professor of prehistoric archaeology at the School of Humanities, University of Glasgow.
A quarter of dietary energy
Prof. Brand-Miller explained that raw starch will not release glucose, meaning that early humans likely relied on naturally-sweet foods long before cooked grains became a regular part of the diet. The modelling employed by the researchers suggests that sugars provided over 25% of dietary energy, fulfilling the obligatory glucose demand. Pounding and cooking (grains) releases glucose specifically, not merely energy. The evolution of a bigger brain is therefore a story of carbohydrate foods as much as animal foods. “While animal foods were important, the brain’s need for glucose has largely received little attention from anthropologists,” she added.
Explaining the element that the modelling brings to current evolutionary theory, Prof. Hardy, said: “The human evolutionary diet has a strong focus on meat eating and the need for protein. But we also require energy and this is best provided by glucose obtained from plants.”
The earliest hominins such as ‘Lucy’, whose brain was the same size as a chimpanzee, as well as Homo habilis and Homo erectus, were therefore likely highly reliant on carbohydrate-rich foods, particularly fruit, the modelling establishes. It was only later, as the use of fire and cooking became more widespread, that starch from underground food sources such as wild yams, water lily rhizomes and African potato contributed to glucose intake. This might also explain to some extent why humans crave sweet foods.

South African police arrest 4 in the killing of former champion boxer Zolani Tete
South African police have arrested four suspects in the killing of former world champion boxer Zolani Tete
JOHANNESBURG -- Four suspects in the killing of former world champion boxer Zolani Tete were arrested, South African police said Monday.
Tete was in his car outside his home last week when men wearing balaclavas opened fire, police said. A woman who was in the vehicle was injured and has since been hospitalized.
The shooting took place at Mdantsane, Eastern Cape, according to the police. Tete was arriving at his residence and waiting for the gate to open when he was ambushed by two armed suspects.
Police said one of the suspects arrested two days ago was expected to appear in court on Monday, while the other three would appear on a later date.
Tete held the World Boxing Federation flyweight title from 2007 to 2008 and the World Boxing Organization bantamweight title in 2017 and 2019.

Microsoft employees aren't just comparing salaries this year, they're comparing how much AI they use.
An internal spreadsheet viewed by Business Insider shows hundreds of employees voluntarily reporting not only their raises, bonuses, and stock awards, but also the dollar value of the AI tools they used over the past month. Microsoft is offering employees an internal tool to track their AI usage and spending.
The figures offer a rare glimpse into how AI is being used inside Microsoft as the company races rivals, including Meta, Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic, to build AI products.
As the company spends hundreds of billions of dollars on AI infrastructure and pushes employees to weave AI into their daily work, the spreadsheet shows how usage varies dramatically across teams, from just a few dollars a month to tens of thousands. It also suggests that, at least for now, heavier AI use isn't translating into bigger raises, bonuses, or promotions.
Microsoft isn't alone in trying to understand how employees use AI. Across Big Tech, companies are increasingly tracking AI consumption as they spend billions building models and infrastructure.
New to this year's spreadsheet was a column asking employees to self-report their "AI $ Usage Per Month" using the internal tool, which shows the dollar amount of their AI usage over the last 28 days. A Microsoft spokesperson said the AI usage tracking tool is still in early testing.
The document had nearly 600 entries from US employees when Business Insider analyzed the data, showing how much the employees say they received this year in base pay, raises, cash bonuses, and stock awards. About 350 of them had reported their AI usage at the time.
Of those reported, the median AI usage amount was about $300 over 28 days. The highest reported figure was $28,000 from an employee in the Microsoft Customer and Partner Solutions organization.
Business Insider's analysis excluded levels and teams with few entries. The data is self-reported and may contain errors.
Self-reported AI usage among Microsoft employees
| Org | No. of entries | Median AI usage, last 28 days | Range | 
| Azure | 33 | $241 | $1 to $7,500 | 
| Cloud + AI | 107 | $325 | $1 to $15,000 | 
| CoreAI | 14 | $975 | $40 to $16,000 | 
| Experiences and Devices | 69 | $250 | $1 to $3,391 | 
| Microsoft AI | 15 | $490 | $45 to $10,000 | 
| Microsoft Customer and Partner Solutions | 25 | $134 | $1 to $28,000 | 
| Security | 12 | $526 | $58 to $10,000 | 
Microsoft employees typically share this information voluntarily and anonymously to promote pay transparency, but that means the data isn't official or comprehensive. The company had 223,000 employees on June 30, so a spreadsheet with only around 350 figures on AI usage provides a very small snapshot.
Business Insider found no meaningful correlation in the spreadsheet between reported AI usage and rewards. Higher AI usage did not appear to be associated with higher bonus ratings, merit increases, or a greater likelihood of promotion.

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.

UNICEF Executive Director, Catherine Russel, KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing the Global Polio Eradication Initiative funding agreement for US$ 500 million. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reaffirmed its US$ 500 million pledge to the GPEI, initially made in April 2024. Two funding agreements were signed with WHO US$ 300 million and UNICEF US$ 200 million. This contribution will support efforts to vaccinate 370 million children annually, aiming to eradicate polio globally. The commitment highlights Saudi Arabia’s role in combatting polio, particularly in conflict-affected regions such as Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Gaza, where the virus has made a resurgence.

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum 2025 was a significant event that underscored the continued partnership between WHO and KSrelief, as well as with other international partners to address critical humanitarian health crises. The agreements made during the forum are pivotal in combating diseases like malaria, cholera, and polio, and ensuring better healthcare for displaced populations. The forum also highlighted Saudi Arabia’s ongoing commitment to global humanitarian efforts, reaffirming its leadership role in tackling some of the world’s pressing health crises.

Cirque du Soleil acrobat sues circus for $16 million after breaking 11 bones in fall
‘At first, we all thought it was part of the show,’ one spectator said, after the incident in Portland, Oregon
A former Cirque du Soleil acrobat is suing the world-famous circus for $16.75 million after breaking 11 bones in a fall, according to reports.
Russian performer Mariia Konfektova fell 15 feet during one of the traveling circus’s Kooza performances in Portland, Oregon, in August 2024. Now, in a lawsuit filed Thursday and obtained by KGW, she is claiming that Cirque du Soleil failed to install safety mats, nets or fall protection underneath her.
In the lawsuit, which was also seen by The Oregonian, she alleges that she was left with double vision and a concussion, as well as fractures to at least seven bones in her face. Konfektova says she also sustained fractures to her skull, wrist and lower back.
“It just went into silence when she fell,” Benjamin Goldstein, who captured the August 24 fall at the Portland Expo Center on camera, told ABC’S Good Morning America in 2024. “At first, we all thought it was part of the show.”
Brian Goldstein, Benjamin’s father, added: “The Cirque du Soleil response team just showed up on stage, and there was 10 to 12 of them on stage attending to her. So to see something like this is very surprising and very shocking.”
In a statement shared with Fox 12 days after the fall, Cirque du Soleil confirmed that Konfektova had been injured during the 7 p.m. performance.
“In accordance with our emergency procedures, we stopped the show briefly, and the artist was immediately assisted by the tour intervention team and transported to the hospital for examination,” the statement read. “The health and safety of our employees is always our top priority.
“As always, in the case of an accident, the artist will continue to be monitored by the KOOZA medical and coaching team to determine when she can return to the show.”
The Independent has contacted Cirque du Soleil for comment on the lawsuit.
In a GoFundMe campaign launched to raise money for medical costs, Konfektova said she has been left with long-term complications and that she cannot fully return to work while needing surgery.
“Unfortunately, ongoing medical, insurance, legal, and immigration complications have made my situation increasingly difficult,” she wrote. “My access to treatment remains uncertain, and I cannot fully return to my profession while my future surgeries are still ahead of me.”
Konfektova’s fall occurred when she was trying to transition between movements on a hoop, according to a report by Oregon’s Occupational Safety and Health Administration obtained by KOIN.
The acrobat fell to a floor made from a material that the report notes had “some ability to reduce the severity of the impact.”
Cirque du Soleil was fined $8,070 for safety violations by OSHA, the report says. However, the circus appealed at least one of the citations in the OSHA inquiry, with a spokesperson for the agency telling The Oregonian that the appeal was still pending.
Konfektova claims in the lawsuit that she had raised safety concerns to Cirque du Soleil. She says that she raised concerns about the winch in the circus’s rigging system used by her hoop and the weight of the hoop itself.
However, the lawsuit alleges that the acrobat was eventually fired by Cirque du Soleil, with the firm raising concerns over her mental fitness to work.
Konfektova often shares updates about her acrobatic career on Instagram. The artist was entered into the Guinness Book of World Records back in 2021, after she recorded 75 seated aerial hoop rotations in 30 seconds in Zhuhai, China.

“Delhi has registered more than 1,700 cases of swine flu this year,” Health Department officials said on Friday (August 21, 2026), as the national capital sees a surge in seasonal influenza cases during monsoon.
On the day, Delhi Health Minister Pankaj Kumar Singh and representatives of the Health Department are scheduled to meet Union Health Minister J.P. Nadda and senior officials from the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare to review the swine flu situation in the capital.
"A report is being prepared to assess the number of cases and the overall situation. Everything is under control. There is no need for general panic. All government hospitals have been directed to ensure adequate treatment facilities," Mr. Singh told PTI.
The Minister said the government is closely monitoring the situation and has directed all government hospitals to ensure adequate treatment facilities are available.
“Healthcare institutions and officials concerned have been told to keep a close watch on infection patterns, affected areas and potential hotspots,” the Minister said, adding that separate wards are being set up for swine flu patients.
Doctors in Delhi said they are seeing a noticeable surge in number of patients with influenza and influenza-like symptoms, though most cases are mild to moderate.
Dr. Rishikesh Desai, consultant physician in the department of internal medicine at Sir Ganga Ram Hospital, said the hospital is witnessing a rise in seasonal influenza cases. "Most healthy individuals recover well, but influenza can become serious in older adults, pregnant women, young children and people with chronic diseases," he said.
Dr. Neha Rastogi Panda, senior consultant in the department of infectious diseases at Fortis Hospital, Gurugram, also recounted a similar situation. "There has been a sudden increase in patients with influenza and influenza-like illnesses," she said. "Most patients have mild to moderate illness and recover well with appropriate supportive care, so there is no reason to panic." Rastogi further said doctors were seeing more prolonged cough and greater intensity of fever this season, possibly due to reactive inflammation of the lungs due to air pollution, particularly from particulate pollutants.
According to medical practitioners, H1N1 infection — commonly known as swine flu — usually presents fever, cough, sore throat, headache, body aches and fatigue. Those with persistent high fever, breathing difficulty, chest pain, confusion or worsening symptoms are advised to seek medical attention promptly.
"Vaccination, hand hygiene, avoiding close contact while ill and staying home during the infection period are key to limiting transmission," Dr. Desai said.

‘Who started the fire?’ Burnham challenges Putin on first trip to Ukraine as UK-Russia tensions grow
The UK is providing Ukraine with the blueprints to long-range SCALP missiles, the prime minister announced in Kyiv
Prime minister Andy Burnham has hit out at Russian president Vladimir Putin during his first state visit to Kyiv, amid mounting tensions between Moscow and London.
The British leader chaired his first meeting of the so-called “coalition of the willing” to emphasise Britain’s continued support for Ukraine through the provision of long-range SCALP missile blueprints.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said that the move would add “fuel to the fire” and “prevent any progress in the peace process”.
“Who started the fire? That’s the question, isn’t it?” Mr Burnham hit back in an address to Ukraine’s European allies on Monday.
“Putin is now hoping he can win through a campaign of terror using ballistic missiles against Ukrainian civilians.
“This can never be the route to victory, and we need to be clear in sending that message. It means doing everything we can all do, and working with our allies as well, beyond this coalition, to dig into our own stocks of air defence... to protect Ukraine from the missiles that are falling now.”
Mr Zelensky and Mr Burnham both delivered speeches outside Kyiv’s St Sofia cathedral on the anniversary of the country’s 35th year of independence.
“Despite Russia’s outrageous threats to my country, we will continue our support for Ukraine,” he said.
The prime minister compared Ukraine’s battle with Russia to the British fight against Nazi Germany, saying: “My nation kept the flame of European freedom alive in the 20th century; you hold that flame in the 21st.”
It marked his first foray on the international stage, heading the coalition of the willing group of 34 countries set up by his predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, in support of Ukraine.
Tensions between London and Moscow have been mounting for weeks as it emerged over the weekend that Russia had withdrawn its ambassador to the UK, Andrei Kelin, last month after seven years in the diplomatic post.
The lower-ranking charge d’affaires has taken the lead in his absence, according to an embassy spokesperson talking to The Times.
The latest announcement of support by Mr Burnham means that the British government has agreed to allow defence firm MBDA to release classified information and blueprints on UK components for the long-range SCALP missile. The weapons are the equivalent of the French-produced version of the UK’s Storm Shadow.
Last Tuesday, it was reported that British-made drones had been used in Ukraine, prompting Moscow to threaten “consequences” for the support. It warned ominously that the greater the assistance that Britain provided, “the higher price it will pay”.
At the time, Mr Burnham doubled down, saying: “This is the UK doing what it has long said it would do, which is to support Ukraine 100 per cent against this illegal war led by Vladimir Putin.”
The European Commission, meanwhile, has approved a further €6.1bn (£5.2bn) in financial aid for Ukraine, to be spent on buying defence systems, including air defence, missiles, ammunition and radars.
The latest aid package came after €16bn of previously approved procurement plans, of which €8.35bn had already been disbursed, according to the EU.
“As Russia intensifies its attacks, we are stepping up to help Ukraine protect its people and defend its skies. Europe stands with Ukraine and we will deliver what it needs, when it needs it,” EC president Ursula von der Leyen said in a statement.
In other developments in the war, Russian attacks killed three people near Kharkiv overnight on Sunday, according to the region’s governor, while Moscow claimed debris from a Ukrainian drone killed two children in Russia’s Krasnodar.

When the Indian government announced the resignation of its education minister in late July after weeks of protest, there were widespread celebrations. Students from across the country had joined the mass demonstrations led by the Cockroach Janta party amid growing resentment over repeated examination cancellations and question paper leaks.
The pressure of exams in the country has only increased in recent years. The number of student suicides rose from 8,068 in 2014, to 14,488 in 2024 – an increase of roughly 80% – according to the Accidental Deaths and Suicides in India report released by the country’s National Crime Records Bureau. After family problems, failure in examinations has been listed as the leading cause of suicides among students.
For families who say they lost their children to education system mismanagement and examination scandals, watching the protest scenes unfold on television came with mixed feelings. Some were happy that future students may be spared the same fate; others questioned why it had taken so long.
The Guardian spoke to four families about what happened to their children and how they feel today.
Anshika Pandey, 20, Delhi
Anshika Pandey, the eldest of twin sisters and four siblings, was, her father says, the calmest, quietest and most responsible member of the family. Revision books still lie neatly stacked, bags and accreditation cards hang from the nails where they were last placed. Her ambition was to be a doctor in the community where she lived, to be able to help the “poor people in need of medical care” some day.
Pandey studied for more than 12 hours every day, worked part-time at a store for nearly six hours and slept no more than five hours each night.
This year’s national eligibility cum entrance test (Neet) to gain entrance to medical training was her third attempt at becoming a doctor. After sitting the exam on 3 May, she was hopeful. But on 12 May she learned that the exam had been leaked for the second year in a row and there would be a resit.
“Anshika was deeply hurt. She had been hoping to enter college this year and was happy with the exam she had taken. Still, after cancellation, when I tried to console her, all she lamented was how could she hope to give another good exam,” says her father, Indradhar Pandey, a cab driver in Delhi.
Anshika remained calm and performed her household duties and engaged with everyone normally. But two days later, on 14 May, when everyone had left for work and her twin sister and younger brother were napping, she hanged herself.
Anshika’s dream had been to move her family, especially her siblings, from the slum where they lived. Her younger sister, Pragati, hopes to fulfil that dream and reminisces about how the two sisters had talked about it several times.
Anshika’s sketches and positive messages and mantra chants on the walls of their home, which she wrote to motivate herself, are now the memories her family is refusing to let go of.
Sufi Shaheen, 19, Delhi
Before leaving the house on the morning of 25 October 2024, Sufi Shaheen straightened her hair and put on her favourite jeans. As she left, she asked her mother for 10 rupees (8p), unlike other days when she would ask for 100. Then she headed for her joint entrance examination (Jee) lesson.
Her mother, Sultana Khatoon, asked her why she was leaving the house on an empty stomach. Shaheen replied she would be back soon. Twenty minutes later, she jumped from the seventh floor of a tutoring centre, about a mile away from her home.
It has been almost two years since she died, but Khatoon has not recovered from that day. She is being treated for severe depression and bouts of headaches.
“She was my only daughter of the four children and more like a friend. Every time I stepped out of the house, she would help me get ready. Even though she was deeply passionate about studying and becoming an engineer, she also loved dressing up and made everyone in the house do it too,” says Khatoon, as she looks through her daughter’s school photos.
Living with her parents and three brothers on her father’s modest income as a technical engineer, Shaheen had dreamed of becoming a software engineer and “excelling even more than the boys in her community”, says her mother.
A quick learner and highly motivated, Shaheen taught herself to draw and paint, and even learned to speak Japanese and Korean. But she had been stressed for several months and feared not being able to clear her second attempt at the national engineering entrance exam in January 2025.
When India’s National Testing Agency made changes to the Jee exam syllabus, Shaheen couldn’t sleep for days. She remained stressed, cried when talking to her brother and her best friend on the phone, and wrote a note to her parents in which she apologised and asked her younger brother, Masoom, to make their dreams come true.
“Almost two years later, Masoom was ranked 188th in the whole of India in his CUET [common university entrance test]. But we do not have Shaheen to celebrate this with,” says Khatoon.
Pradeep Kumar Mahich, 22, Rajasthan
“Even God will not be able to stop me from becoming a doctor this year,” were 22-year-old Pradeep Mahich’s words to his father right after his Neet exam on 3 May. This was his fourth attempt and, most importantly, he felt confident. But the announcement of the exam paper leak and resit broke his heart.
No one in the family had ever “dreamt so big”, says Pradeep’s father, Rajesh Kumar, a farmer in Rajasthan’s Sikar district. Kumar sold a large part of his farmland and took a loan of 11 lakhs (£8,600) under the farmer’s crop loan schemes.
“Sikar, the main coaching hub for Neet, is only an hour and a half from our village. My eldest daughter, Babita, who was preparing to join the police, and my son were both studying in Sikar, renting an apartment. This was his fourth year of tutoring, and the money from selling the land and the loan was slowly being consumed. I would send monthly expenses of £250 and Pradeep’s annual tutoring fees of £4,000, asking them not to worry about money and focus on his studies,” says Kumar.
“Pradeep had told me, ‘Papa, we will do a big celebration before I go to college. And one day I’ll return to serve the people of the village,’” says Kumar.
On 15 May, as he did every day, Kumar sent milk and curd to his two children on a bus that goes to Sikar; Pradeep came to pick it up at 9.30am then went home and told his sister he would help prepare lunch. But when his sister was showering, he hanged himself. She has taken a break from her studies and returned home.
Seeing students protesting on his television screen, Kumar says he is relieved that the eduction minister has gone but says there should be a proper investigation so that “no family suffers the same fate that we did”.
S Anitha, 17, Tamil Nadu
S Anitha belonged to an underprivileged lower caste, or Dalit, community from Tamil Nadu’s Ariyalur district. Born to a daily wage labourer, her mother died when she was seven, leaving her grandparents to raise her.
As a teenager, she decided she wanted to become a doctor. “At such a tender age, she was so focused that we used to feel proud of her,” says her brother, Manirathinam. “She knew what she wanted and never distracted herself with anything else. She never asked for any clothes, jewellery or food – her focus was clear and she knew the circumstances.”
She scored a perfect 100 in physics and chemistry at school and was offered a place to study aeronautical engineering at the state’s technological institute. But when she could not even meet the cut-off marks in the Neet exam, she realised that she had been studying a different syllabus.
Tamil Nadu had already criticised the national government for imposing an all-India examination – “disrupting the federal structure” – because it had a different education system. As a result, the state was exempted from Neet in 2016, but not in 2017, the year Anitha sat the exam.
When the supreme court ruled on 22 August 2017 that admissions to medical school would be based only on the Neet exam, she lost hope. On 1 September, Anitha hanged herself in her grandparents’ home. Her suicide became the subject of a public debate and led to widespread protests across the state and even in Delhi.
Her brother took part in last month’s protests in the capital and, while happy about the Indian education minister’s resignation in July, argues that all exams should become state-run, rather than by central government, as not everyone can afford the hefty tutoring fees needed to sit the Neet exam.
He now runs a free library and education centre in Anitha’s name.

How to Use AI to Prepare for a Job Interview
Before we get to the applications, which indeed make job interview preparation an easy affair, you must understand the importance of a solid foundation to begin with. Fortunately, this groundwork only requires leveraging existing AI tools you may already be using. After getting to know the details of the job interview, mainstream AI models, such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Claude, and more, can be directed to put you at an advantage from the very initial phase of your preparation. Below is what you must do first.
→ Understand the Role and Generate Role-Specific Interview Questions
Most, if not all, job descriptions are little more than a pile of technical and corporate jargon, often failing to clearly state the requirements. Misaligned interview expectations may already put you in a bad spot during the interview, so you must ensure that you are well-versed with the job description. AI models can help you do so with a few prompts, but you must include a few crucial elements to get the best results. With all this, don’t forget to upload your updated resume for a tailored response.
For starters, you cannot miss out on knowing the core competencies required for the job you’re applying for. AI can help you identify the top non-negotiable technical and soft skills that the recruiter expects of you. Such attributes are often not understood by many applicants, which prevents them from brushing up on existing skills or learning the required ones. Next, your prompt must include identifying the success metrics, or the key performance indicators of the role.
Because every hiring takes place to solve a specific problem of the organization, it’s crucial to have an idea about the performance expectations the recruiter may have from you. For tech roles, it usually revolves around solving existing issues, improving existing processes, and related tasks. In contrast, non-tech roles focus on increasing client retention, establishing business relationships, and related tasks.
Lastly, you must also ask AI to groom you based on your resume. It will help you determine whether your resume aligns well with the role and whether any specific skills need to be spotlighted. AI can not only identify potential loopholes but also help you present your projects to the interviewer in the most convincing way possible. With this initial study of the role’s requirements, you can certainly answer questions and defend yourself with confidence.
→ Study About the Company
While most candidates think they know the company they’re applying to well, the truth is, not many perform a proper deep dive. It is an important part of interview preparation, as knowing the company helps you give more relevant answers instead of generic ones.
AI makes company research much easier, but don’t simply ask it to “tell me about the company.” Start with its current market position, products, competitors, recent announcements, and anything else directly relevant to the role.
Foremost, your prompt should include information about the company’s current market position. You can assist the AI model by attaching the company’s press releases, financial reports, product launch notes, public announcements, and more. Financial reports can also be used to project the company’s future trends, map future goals, and more, which are worth knowing about.
It’s also essential to understand the company’s competitors, as it can help you frame your answers to interview questions in the company’s favor. While you are unlikely to find many, you can ask the AI model to identify and propose viable solutions to the company’s publicly available problems. It can be a significant advantage when handled appropriately and also serves as a good background for obvious questions, such as “What will you bring to the table?” and “Why should we hire you?”
→ Analyze the Interviewer
If you know who will be interviewing you, publicly available professional information can help you prepare better. Their LinkedIn profile, current role, past experience, or area of expertise may give you a fair idea of which parts of your background they are more likely to focus on.
You can provide this information to an AI model and ask it to suggest questions that someone in a similar role may ask. Don’t treat those questions as predictions, though. Use them simply to broaden your preparation and identify areas you may otherwise overlook.
This information is also useful when preparing questions to ask towards the end of the interview. Relevant questions about their team, role, or experience with the company will usually come across better than generic ones.
→ Generate Behavioral, Situational, and Technical Interview Questions
A recommended way to ensure success in an interview is to prepare for the likely questions. The question set should not only include the basic ones, but also challenging ones to put you on the spot. That way, your real-world performance will be sufficient for selection. To begin with, the basics: you can ask AI models to generate common behavioral interview questions, such as “Introduce yourself” and “Why should we hire you?” “What if we don’t select you?” “What makes you fit for this role?” and the like.
The answers to the above questions will be based on your resume and cognitive ability, which is what AI models can help you with. Next, to tackle the technical questions, your prompt must instruct the AI model to fire deep-dive technical, situational, and project-based questions at you. During all this, you can rate your technical skills and promptly improve any weak areas.
Despite the discomfort, ask the AI model to generate questions from the perspective of an interviewer who is not interested in hiring you. Understand the questions, as they can prove to be great at identifying gaps in your resume, incompetencies, and more. You can also ask the AI model to question the relevance of your past experiences, push back aggressively on your answers, and more. This will only improve your chances of getting selected.
→ Practice Mock Interviews With AI Voice Mode
In case you are unaware, most mainstream AI models offer voice modes that are perfect for back-and-forth questioning, making them ideal for interview practice. It’s not surprising that merely reading the questions and thinking you can answer them won’t cut it, which is why you need a simulation of the interview. It may cause you to memorize answers instead of coming up with your own, which may result in you sounding like a teleprompter, or worse, freezing on the spot if you forget the exact answer, leaving a bad impression.
Voice mode is best used on the mobile versions of AI agents. First, you must tell the AI its persona by verbally describing it, uploading the job description, interview details, or any other supporting documents. We also recommend uploading your resume to ensure a curated interaction. Next, you must instruct it to ask all types of questions, including behavioral, technical, and situation-based.
Remember, the purpose of this mock interview is to prepare you for the worst, so take away critical lessons and improve yourself. For this, you can ask the AI model to rate your answers and provide you with detailed assessments to help you identify your weak points. Not only will it cure the interview phobia that you may have, but it will also improve your speaking skills, conversational awareness, and your ability to answer curveballs.

Exponent Practice
Best for: Tech candidates who want peer mock interviews
The biggest hurdle in job interview preparation is the gap between practice and the actual interview, which many people fail to bridge. Fortunately, Exponent Practice (formerly Pramp) can help if you struggle in this regard, as it’s unlike other tools that put AI front and center. Exponent Practice’s unique selling point is its peer interview feature, which is incredibly helpful, to say the least. The tool serves only those looking for an IT-based role, so it’s perfect for practicing interviews in product management, data structures and algorithms, system design, data science and ML, SQL, and more. Exponent also offers practice questions, coaching, job referrals, and more.
Exponent Practice’s standout peer-interviewing feature works by scheduling an interview first, then matching with a peer who shares similar goals. The one-hour session includes 30 minutes of you getting interviewed by your peer, after which you must also interview the other person in the second half, followed by grading each other’s performance. This way, both parties benefit, as they not only get a dual perspective but also structured, actionable feedback. The platform includes a real-time collaborative code editor, so you need not worry about it. There’s an AI mock interview feature as well, a 10-20 minute session where AI evaluates your transcript, grades you, and provides overall feedback.
Pros:
- The peer interview feature is the best way to practice with a human
- The free version includes 5 free peer interviews per month, which should suffice for most
- Highly praised for its effectiveness because it enables a hybrid (peer+AI) interview approach
Cons:
- Its AI mock interview and advanced AI features require a paid membership, which currently works out to $12 per month when billed annually.
- Scheduling isn’t as frictionless, and the quality of the peer interview depends on the other person

Useful AI Prompts for Job Interview Preparation
Mainstream AI models like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude can be surprisingly effective for interview preparation if you give them enough context. A common approach among job seekers is to provide the actual job description and resume, then have the AI conduct the interview one question at a time instead of generating a generic list of questions. Here are a few prompts worth trying.
1. Analyze the Job Description and My Resume
I am preparing for an interview for the job below. Act as an experienced hiring manager and analyze both the job description and my resume.
Identify:
The five most important skills or requirements for this role
The parts of my resume that match them best
Important requirements where my experience looks weak or unclear
Questions an interviewer is likely to ask about those gaps
Technical or industry topics I should revise
Five achievements from my resume that I should make sure to highlight
Don’t invent experience or skills that aren’t present in my resume.
Job description: [paste]
Resume: [paste/upload]
2. Conduct a Realistic Mock Interview
Act as the hiring manager interviewing me for the role below. Use my resume and the job description as your primary context.
Conduct this like a real interview. Ask only one question at a time and wait for my complete answer before asking the next one. Ask natural follow-up questions based on what I actually say instead of following a fixed list.
Include a mix of behavioral, situational, resume-based, role-specific, and technical questions where relevant.
Do not give me hints or feedback while the interview is taking place. Once the interview is finished, score my performance on answer quality, relevance, clarity, confidence, and completeness. Then identify my five biggest weaknesses and tell me how to improve each one.
Job description: [paste]
Resume: [paste/upload]
3. Give Me a Difficult Mock Interview
Act as a skeptical interviewer who isn’t yet convinced that I am the right person for this role.
Use my resume and the job description to identify weak points, career gaps, vague achievements, missing skills, questionable claims, or areas where another candidate may be stronger.
Ask me one difficult question at a time. If my answer is vague, generic, evasive, or unsupported, push back and ask a follow-up question. Don’t compliment every answer or make the interview artificially easy.
At the end, tell me which answers could hurt my chances in the real interview and show me how I could make them stronger without exaggerating my experience.
4. Build My STAR Interview Stories
Help me prepare 5 reusable stories from my career for behavioral interview questions.
Use my resume and the experiences I provide to identify strong examples involving leadership, conflict, failure, problem-solving, teamwork, initiative, and working under pressure.
For each story, organize the answer using STAR:
Situation: What was happening?
Task: What was I responsible for?
Action: What specifically did I do?
Result: What changed because of my actions?
Keep Situation and Task brief and spend more time on Action and Result. Ask me for missing details rather than inventing them. Where possible, help me quantify the result.
Finally, tell me which common behavioral interview questions each story could answer.
Excel in Interviews With These AI Tools
AI has made preparing for job interviews a lot less daunting than it used to be. For most people, mainstream AI models such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude are already good enough for understanding a job description, researching a company, preparing likely questions, and improving answers.
Dedicated AI interview tools become useful when you want something closer to the real thing. Exponent Practice and Interviewing.io make more sense for technical candidates, Yoodli is particularly good for communication and behavioral practice, while MyInterviewAI works well for resume-based preparation. Big Interview helps with overall delivery, Huru AI makes quick job-specific practice easy, and Ophy AI covers the widest range of interview-preparation needs.
Whichever tool you choose, don’t stop after one mock interview. Upload your latest resume and the actual job description, complete a practice session, review where you struggled, and repeat it after fixing those areas. Two or three focused mock interviews will be far more useful than memorizing dozens of AI-generated answers.
Critique My Interview Answer
I will give you an interview question followed by my answer.
Evaluate the answer as a demanding hiring manager. First, tell me:
Whether I actually answered the question
What was convincing
What sounded vague or generic
Whether I gave enough evidence
Whether I spent too much time on irrelevant context
What follow-up question an interviewer would probably ask
If it is a behavioral question, also evaluate it using the STAR method.
Only after giving me this critique, provide a stronger version that retains my real experience and sounds natural when spoken aloud. Don’t turn it into a polished corporate script that nobody would actually say in an interview.
FAQs about AI Interview Tools
Can ChatGPT help me prepare for a job interview?
Yes. You can give ChatGPT your resume and job description and ask it to identify likely interview questions, evaluate your answers, conduct mock interviews, research the role, and point out gaps in your preparation. Voice mode makes the mock interview experience significantly more natural.
Are AI mock interviews actually useful?
They can be, especially when the AI asks follow-up questions and gives detailed feedback instead of simply generating a list of questions. They are particularly useful for repeated practice, although they shouldn't completely replace practice with another person when that is available.
Which AI interview tools are free?
Exponent Practice offers a limited number of free peer mock interviews, while Yoodli has a free tier. Huru AI provides free access to try its mock interviews, and Ophy AI offers free starting credits. The exact limits can change, so check each service before signing up.
What is the best AI interview tool for software engineers?
Interviewing.io and Exponent Practice are the strongest options on this list for software engineers. They focus much more heavily on coding, system design, algorithms, and other technical interview formats than general-purpose interview coaching tools.
Can I use AI during an actual job interview?
That depends entirely on the employer and interview rules. Some companies prohibit outside assistance during interviews and assessments. Unless the interviewer explicitly allows it, the safer approach is to use AI extensively during preparation and answer the actual interview questions yourself.
How many AI mock interviews should I practice?
There is no fixed number. Instead of repeating mock interviews endlessly, complete one, review the feedback, fix the weak areas, and try again. A few focused sessions with clear improvement between them are more useful than doing many interviews without reviewing your mistakes.

The Swift space observatory has been in operation since 2004. It specializes in gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), the most energetic electromagnetic explosions known in the universe. Its original mission was supposed to last just two years. More than two decades later, it continues to explore some of the most violent phenomena in the cosmos. Now it is nearing the end of its life.
Swift doesn’t have a propulsion system capable of significantly raising its orbit. Although it is hundreds of kilometers above the Earth’s surface, there are still atmospheric particles at that altitude that exert a small but constant drag on the satellite. With each orbit around Earth, it loses a tiny amount of energy and, little by little, altitude as well. If this process continues without intervention it will eventually reenter the atmosphere.
NASA knew that Swift had limited time left. Some models had indicated that the observatory could remain in orbit until the 2030s, but increased solar activity during 2024 changed those projections. Energy from the sun heated and expanded the upper layers of Earth’s atmosphere, increasing the drag on the satellite and accelerating its descent. Estimates eventually placed its likely reentry before the end of 2026.
Faced with the rapid deterioration of Swift’s orbit, NASA decided to attempt a rescue maneuver straight out of a movie. The plan was simple in concept but astonishingly complex to execute. A robotic mission would catch up to Swift, capture it with mechanical arms, and use its own thrusters to raise the observatory to a safer orbit, where it could continue operating. To do this, NASA turned to the company Katalyst Space Technologies and its LINK spacecraft.
LINK was launched into space on July 3, 2026. However, problems arose soon after. The spacecraft suffered failures in its attitude control system, which is responsible for keeping it properly oriented and stable in space. For weeks, engineers worked to regain control.
On Wednesday, NASA canceled the rescue mission. In a statement, agency administrator Jared Isaacman explained that the decision was due to problems with the spacecraft’s control system. LINK will no longer capture Swift or raise its orbit. The spacecraft will continue to approach the observatory to conduct demonstrations of rendezvous, navigation, and close-proximity operations. The agency hopes to use this attempt to gather information that can be applied to future missions aimed at repairing, relocating, or extending the lifespan of satellites in orbit.
“This is not the outcome we were working toward, but it does not change why this mission was worth attempting. The team moved with extraordinary speed to give Swift a chance to carry out more science while advancing capabilities America will need for satellite servicing in the future. We are going to learn everything we can from LINK’s rendezvous attempt and put those lessons to work on the missions that follow,” Isaacman said in a press release.
The agency had warned from the outset that this was a high-risk mission. Swift was not built to be captured or repaired in orbit, while LINK was developed and launched against the clock in response to the observatory’s rapid descent.
“NASA should be willing to move quickly and take smart risks when the potential return is worth it, and that is exactly what we did with this mission,” Isaacman noted.
Without an intervention to raise its orbit, Swift will continue to lose altitude until it reaches the denser layers of the atmosphere. During reentry, much of the observatory will be destroyed by intense heating and aerodynamic forces. It is still too early to determine exactly when and where this will occur.
For now, NASA estimates that Swift will likely reenter the atmosphere before the end of the year.

Two dead and others missing after Tunisian migrant boat travelling to Europe capsized
A boat carrying migrants has capsized off southern Tunisia, leaving at least two people dead
At least two people have died and 12 remain missing after a boat carrying migrants overturned off the southern coast of Tunisia, the national guard confirmed on Saturday. A single survivor was rescued.
Guard spokesperson Houssem Eddine Jebabli informed state news agency TAP that two retrieved bodies were taken to a hospital on the nearby island of Djerba. Speaking to national radio station Mosaique FM, he added that approximately 15 people were thought to be aboard when the boat launched between Zarzis and Ben Guerdane.
The boat set off early on Thursday morning. A commercial vessel discovered the lone survivor wearing a life jacket on Saturday, according to details reported by Mosaique based on the survivor’s account.
A helicopter and coast guard boats were deployed to the location to search for additional survivors, an Associated Press photo journalist at the scene said. The migrants were believed to be travelling towards Italy.
Zarzis has long served as a key departure point for Tunisians and individuals from across Africa and beyond seeking to make the Mediterranean crossing to Europe.
The city experienced a similar tragedy in 2022 when a vessel carrying 18 people disappeared. That event triggered weeks of demonstrations, with relatives accusing officials of failing to conduct adequate searches and burying several recovered bodies without establishing their identities or contacting their families.
Migrant departures from Tunisia have fallen sharply since the European Union and Tunisia signed a comprehensive pact in 2023. The agreement included EU financial assistance and technical support for border control and coast guard training to curb irregular migration and deter human traffickers in the Mediterranean basin. The EU allocated 105 million euros ($121 million) in migration support to Tunisia in 2023 alone.
The drop in numbers has not stopped dangerous crossings from Tunisia’s southern coastline, where families in Zarzis have spent years searching for relatives missing at sea.
Human rights organisations have raised concerns over the treatment of migrants and asylum seekers in Tunisia since the EU deal, pointing to reports of collective expulsions, racial violence, arbitrary detention and abuses against Black migrants.
In July, Amnesty International stated that EU support for border security in Tunisia was continuing to fuel grave rights violations, adding that refugees and asylum seekers were being "deliberately trapped in a system that offers neither protection nor a safe way out."

Donald Trump is presiding over an unexpected clean energy boom, as rising electricity demand spurs investment in new capacity despite the US administration’s efforts to thwart a solar and wind rollout.
Clean energy additions will rise by a record 45 gigawatts this year, according to S&P Global Energy—equivalent to the average electricity demand of Turkey. The increase is roughly 25 percent higher than the record set in 2024.
The US president’s war in Iran, which has driven up global energy prices, along with surging power demand from AI data centers and developers’ rush to capitalize on expiring tax credits, are driving the cleantech boom, said analysts. Trump’s administration has also been pragmatic in the face of its energy needs.
“There was a campaign promise to go against renewables, but at the same time they’re realizing that you can’t do without it,” said Izzet Bensusan, chief executive of Captona, an energy infrastructure investment group. “I don’t see a world where power demand is flattening out.”
S&P said new solar and wind capacity will jump in 2026 by nearly a third and almost 50 percent respectively. Solar will set another record in 2027, while wind falls back before recovering.
White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers, however, touted “record-high oil and gas production” under Trump.
“The president has delivered on his promise to unleash American energy,” Rogers said. “At the same time, the administration has ended subsidies for costly and unreliable energy sources that American taxpayers were unfairly forced to fund.”
The solar and wind additions come despite Trump’s early efforts to kill an energy transition pushed by his predecessor, Joe Biden.
The Trump administration broke up Esmeralda 7 in Nevada. It would have been the largest single solar project in the US.
The president’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act also slashed tax credits for solar and wind, and his administration has interfered with routine project approvals, including for more than 150 onshore wind projects. But under the terms of the OBBBA, solar and wind developers had until July 4 to begin work on projects and until 2030 to finish them.
The deadline “prompted developers to hurry and begin construction,” said S&P Global renewables analyst John Murray.

Tamil Nadu will launch the ‘Chief Minister’s Elderly Health Insurance Scheme’, covering nearly 38 lakh senior citizens aged 70 and above. The scheme will provide free medical treatment, including cancer care packages, advanced cardiac surgeries, organ transplants, and high-end diagnostic services, at empanelled government and private hospitals, with no ceiling on income, Health Minister K.G. Arunraj announced in the Assembly on Monday (August 17, 2026).
The Minister made 115 announcements for the Health Department at a total estimated outlay of ₹2,997 crore. It covered areas including policy reforms, universal free health services, new posts creation, infrastructure projects, equipment and procurement, direct beneficiary programmes and digital health initiatives.
The 87-year-old Tamil Nadu Public Health Act, 1939, will be replaced with a modern, comprehensive Act to address contemporary and future health challenges. Dr. Arunraj said a new provision would make unsupervised home births outside hospitals a punishable offence. Noting that Tamil Nadu was known as the country’s health capital, he said that ‘TN Medicity’, a world class integrated medical hub comprising clinical services, research, medical tourism, and AYUSH, would be established. The government will allocate ₹10 crore for the preparation of a Detailed Project Report in the first phase.
‘Nalam 360-Annual Free Health Check-up for All’ scheme will be rolled out. Under this, everyone aged 30 and above will receive 14 basic tests annually, free of cost, across 1,257 government health facilities in the State.
This will include blood pressure, ECG, haemoglobin, complete haemogram, random blood sugar, urea, creatinine, total cholesterol, serum bilirubin, urine albumin, and VIA screening. For the first time in the State, the Health Department will introduce Home Based Diagnostic Services — sample collection and testing services — in metropolitan areas on a public-private partnership model, he said.
Policy reforms
The department will come up with a ‘Positive Health Policy’ to promote holistic health and wellbeing at the community, family, and individual levels, accompanied by the “Nalam 360” mobile application. A new legislation ‘TN Institutions of State Importance in Health Care Act’ will come up to create institutions of State importance to provide world-class medical services.
Addressing a long-standing demand, Dr. Arunraj said 2,500 permanent posts of staff nurses would be created. Existing contract nurses on consolidated pay will be absorbed into regular time-scale pay. A total of 1,695 nursing posts on consolidated pay will be created at a cost of ₹42.72 crore.
A total of 3,594 medical staff across 24 categories, including pharmacists, nursing assistants, village health nurses, and ophthalmic assistants, will be recruited through the Medical Services Recruitment Board. Additionally, the department will create 284 temporary super speciality posts across 25 specialities such as neurology, cardiology and nephrology on time-scale pay to take advanced medical care to the district-level.
These posts will be created to accommodate doctors who complete their post-graduation every year and are posted in government hospitals on bond conditions. A number of announcements for infrastructural development such as new hospital buildings and medical equipment were also made.

The federal government is expanding a safety investigation into a number of vehicles manufactured by General Motors after receiving hundreds of reports of brake failure. The problem affects more than 1.1 million cars, including many of GM’s electric vehicles, as well as ones it has built for Honda and Acura. The problem is with the brake-by-wire system (which GM calls eBoost), which can suffer a spindle fracture while driving.
GM says that in the event of that happening, the car should still retain a number of critical safety features—antilock brakes, traction control, and stability control—at least until it comes to a complete stop, at which point they become inoperable. But NHTSA’s ODI says that it has received many reports that contradict this behavior and allege that eBoost failures are followed by an immediate loss of braking, which obviously poses a safety risk.
Indeed, NHTSA has received 227 incident reports, a number that grows to 745 once you include the hundreds of occurrences reported to GM. Twenty-two cases resulted in crashes, and while six people have been injured in five crashes, thankfully there have been no fatal incidents.
NHTSA says that the following vehicles are equipped with eBoost: “2023-2026 MY Cadillac Lyriq, Chevrolet Colorado, and GMC Canyon; 2024-2026 MY Buick Enclave, Envision; Chevrolet Blazer EV, Equinox EV, Traverse; Cruise Origin; and GMC Acadia; 2025-2026 MY Cadillac Celestiq and Optiq. ODI is also aware of 2024-2026 MY Acura ZDX and 2024-2026 MY Honda Prologue vehicles that were built with this system.”

Fab Four and Fleming on the phone - England's first-Test takeaways
- Published
England's crushing victory over Pakistan was the ideal start to Joe Root's second reign as Test captain.
The home side could not have wished for a more straightforward beginning to a new era as they look to move on from the chaos of the past year.
England's innings win comes with the context of a desperate performance from Pakistan, so any judgements on progress should be reserved for now.
Still, Headingley taught us some things. Here are the takeaways.
Fab Four keep England in the fast lane
England are rebuilding their bowling attack for two reasons.
First, the retirement of Ben Stokes has robbed them not only of inspiration, but of balance.
Secondly, Stokes has followed Stuart Broad, James Anderson, Chris Woakes and, most likely, Mark Wood out of the door. That is 1,871 Test wickets lost in less than three years.
The first stab at a post-Stokes team included four frontline seamers – Jofra Archer, Ollie Robinson, Josh Tongue and Gus Atkinson – supported by the part-time off-breaks of Dan Lawrence.
In helpful conditions, it could not have gone better for England. Robinson and Tongue took eight wickets apiece, while Archer and Atkinson improved after a rusty first innings when they struggled to adapt following a month playing in The Hundred. Lawrence bowled only one over in the match.
Clearly, there will be times when England need a frontline spinner, but there is no consistently Test-class spinner in the country right now.
There is an argument to be made that England should continue to stack their attack with seamers because they are the best bowlers – Root said they "don't know how good they could be".
The likes of Sam Cook and Brydon Carse wait in the wings to step in or provide different skills if necessary, meaning England have a large squad of pacemen to choose from.
A trip to Bangladesh in February will mean England have to find some spin. For now, they should stay in the fast lane.
- 'Plug him in as attack leader' - England-Pakistan player ratings 
  - Published15 hours ago
- It would be 'nice to have choice' over Ashes venues - Root 
  - Published13 hours ago
Cox rocks
Jordan Cox has waited a long time for a proper opportunity in Test cricket. Now that it has finally arrived, the Essex batter looks at home at the highest level.
Deputising for the injured Jacob Bethell at number three, Cox impressed with an assured 73. He showed patience and sound judgement, though still had the range of strokes to push the scoring along at a healthy rate without taking risks.
Admittedly, the Pakistan attack Cox faced was far from the most fearsome in Test cricket. None of their seamers had the pace to test his ticker against the short ball.
But, occasionally, players come along and appear instantly suited to Test cricket. Cox seems to fit into that bracket.
His blemish was missing out on the really big score that would have made it impossible for the selectors to leave him out when Bethell returns. Cox potentially has four more innings in this series to make himself undroppable.
If the 25-year-old does demand a place in the XI for the December tour of South Africa and beyond, it leaves England with a dilemma.
Is opener Emilio Gay vulnerable? Bethell is now England's opener in one-day cricket, while Cox opened for Kent at the beginning of his first-class career.
Cox can also keep wicket. Might he put pressure on Jamie Smith? Speaking of whom…
Smith behind the sticks
Smith was one of the players who most noticeably wilted under the pressure and scrutiny of the Ashes tour.
He was not helped by a lack of attention to his wicketkeeping in training. Whether it was because a threadbare backroom team was overworked, or England's overall attitude was not good enough, Smith was rarely seen doing the hard yards with the gloves on.
There has been a change this summer. Since joining the coaching staff, former England women's wicketkeeper Sarah Taylor has worked closely with Smith, who has also been able to do more wicketkeeping training with his county Surrey since recovering from a finger injury.
Another circumstance was an injury to Surrey's regular keeper Ben Foakes, one of the best glovemen in the world. It gave Smith three consecutive games behind the stumps in the County Championship in the early part of the season.
The result has been a definite improvement in Smith's keeping for England. It's not as if the 26-year-old ever looked out of place behind the stumps in Test cricket, but he has shown off a greater range of skills this summer, particularly standing up to the fast-medium of Robinson.
At one point, in the third Test against New Zealand at Trent Bridge, Smith even stood up to the pacey Archer.
Not all progress is linear. Smith's Test batting average has dipped below 40 and he needs to avoid developing a habit for maddening modes of dismissal.
The man who somehow got out to a Marnus Labuschagne bouncer in Sydney tamely holed out for 25 on Friday morning when there was an opportunity for a much bigger contribution.
If Cox or Lawrence fill their batting boots this summer, then England's top-order will become congested. Smith must ensure he does not become vulnerable.
Flem on the phone
Stephen Fleming, England's new Test coach, is not here. Brendon McCullum's replacement is not due to arrive in the UK until September, by which time the Pakistan series could be over.
Fleming was appointed last month, yet will not take charge of England in a Test until South Africa at Christmas.
The delay has not fully been explained, apart from perhaps a desire to give Fleming a break after almost two decades with Chennai Super Kings.
You will have your own opinions on that one. Being in charge of an Indian Premier League team is intense, but CSK's last match was on 21 May, seven months before England's first Test against the Proteas. Could Fleming, now with one of the biggest jobs in coaching, not have been part of a month-long series against Pakistan?
Either way, Root revealed the New Zealander had been in daily contact during the Headingley Test. "It's been great to have him on the end of the phone," said the captain.
Fleming's influence is not immediately obvious, simply because England were not tested in Leeds.
Should things get more difficult in the remaining two Tests, or if a crucial selection decision needs to be made, perhaps vital input will come from the Flemphone.
- 'I fear for them' - pundits lament 'desperate times' for Pakistan 
  - Published13 hours ago
Pakistan problems
A win is a win for England, much needed after only two in their previous 10. However, they should have been better than two wins in 10, and the dismal nature of Pakistan's performance means Root's men can only take limited encouragement from their week in Leeds.
Nothing went right for Pakistan, from the moment captain Babar Azam was ruled out with a thumb injury. Their batting was brittle, their bowling scattergun and their fielding shoddy.
Babar's team beat West Indies in Trinidad earlier this month to earn a 1-1 series draw, yet that was Pakistan's first Test win away from home in more than three years.
They are heavily reliant on winning Tests on spinning pitches, which is why they switched to worn tracks on England's last visit to Pakistan in 2024. When pace bowling becomes the dominant weapon, Pakistan have neither the bowlers nor batters to thrive in the conditions.
Now they head to Lord's, where not one over of spin was bowled in England's shootout win over New Zealand in June.
The surface at the home of cricket could be much different this time around, or a sporty pitch could act as a leveller between the two teams.
Still, the smart money is on another England victory to complete their first series win against anyone in almost two years.
