Hot vs cold: What's the ideal temperature for solar panel efficiency?
There is a correct answer, but ambient temperature is just one of several variables.
Sunlight is a solar panel's best friend. But heat, not so much.
The most common number you will see is 77 degrees Fahrenheit. That is 25 degrees Celsius, which is the temperature of the cell when manufacturers rate panels under standard test conditions, alongside irradiance of 1,000 watts per square meter. It's a good indicator, but it's not a magic outdoor temperature at which your roof achieves peak output.
So yeah, cold wins, technically. The efficiency of solar cells is typically higher at lower temperatures because the voltage decreases more than the current increases with temperature. The problem is that efficiency and total electricity production are not the same. A cold panel might generate more power from the same amount of sunlight, but a hot summer day might generate more power because there might be more sunlight.
Why solar panels lose efficiency as they get hotter
The first wrinkle is that the temperature on your weather app isn't necessarily the temperature of the panel. A module in direct sunlight can be much hotter than the ambient air temperature, and Sandia National Laboratories, a US Department of Energy lab, models module temperature based on ambient temperature, solar irradiance, wind speed and mounting configuration.
As soon as the cells get hotter than their rated reference temperature, output begins to drop according to the panel's temperature coefficient. There isn't one universal 0.5 percent penalty. REC Group, a leading solar panel manufacturer, has a maximum-power temperature coefficient of -0.24 percent per degree Celsius for its current Alpha Pure-RX, while solar manufacturer Qcells lists -0.29 percent per degree Celsius for its residential Q.TRON BLK M-G2+ series. If you live in a place that's really hot, that's something to consider.
Nor is 77 degrees Fahrenheit "too hot" in the sense that the panel is in danger. The Q.TRON model has a continuous operating range of up to 158 degrees Fahrenheit, according to Qcells. REC lists a T98 module operating temperature of 176 degrees Fahrenheit for the Alpha Pure-RX. The Department of Energy says extreme heat can still damage cells and other module materials and shorten their operating lifetimes.
The best weather for efficiency isn't always the best for production
This is where the simple hot vs cold answer gets complicated. While a bright, cold day can be great for solar efficiency, clouds, snow, roof orientation, sun angle and daylight hours may be more important to the amount of electricity your system can generate.
So the best time is not necessarily 10AM to 4PM. Output generally rises as more direct sunlight reaches the panels, then falls later in the day, but an east-facing array will be different from a west-facing array. Although panels can run hotter in the summer, the longer days and often stronger solar resources can result in more total electricity being produced.
That's also why some homeowners size a solar system above their typical electricity needs. The 20 percent rule for solar panels is based on giving a solar system some breathing room when conditions aren't ideal.
The National Laboratory of the Rockies' PVWatts calculator (the lab's free online estimator) allows you to input location and system information to estimate monthly and annual production, which gives you a more specific answer than "summer" or "midday." NLR does not specify a single best month or time of day, and it cautions that PVWatts cannot account for all site-specific variations or differentiate between higher- and lower-performing PV technologies.
Its expected production range is based on 30 years of actual weather data.

It was a normal July morning in the Indian state of Assam. After finishing her chores and eating breakfast, Gitali Phukon, a resident of the town of Gaurisagar, left her home to buy groceries. After two days of rainfall that had made the unpaved roads muddy and slippery, the sun was shining.
But less than an hour later, she returned home to a nightmare: the Mitong River, which runs through the town, was overflowing and water was gushing through the streets.
“I could not believe my eyes. The water came with great force. It quickly rose to waist level,” she says. She had seen the surrounding paddy fields flood in the past, but never before on this scale.
As evening approached, flood waters entered most of the homes in her neighbourhood. The rain resumed, and darkness descended. Standing on her veranda with a candlestick in her hand, Phukon watched as her neighbours moved to their rooftops or the elevated highway to escape the rising water.
They waved at each other, signalling they had survived. No one slept that night. “We feared we would all be drowned,” she says. Along with mosquito bites, they had endured a foul smell emanating from the flood waters.
The next morning, the situation worsened. Most villages in Assam depend on wells. “People were thirsty; they were crying for water. But there was no water to drink as the groundwater was contaminated,” says Phukon.
“Thankfully, I had some stored water, and I shared that with my neighbours,” says Phukon. People ate biscuits and puffed rice for at least three days until the water started to recede.
People in the Sivasagar district of Assam, as well the neighbouring districts of Charaideo and Jorhat on the southern bank of the mighty Brahmaputra River, reported similar experiences.
The Sivasagar village of Nepalikhuti, about 60 miles west of Gaurisagar, lies in ruins. As far as the eye can see, there is thick mud and silt. Drowned cars, dead cows and the broken walls of a house demonstrate the scale of the calamity. There is no sign of any cattle, goats or other livestock, the main means of support for the residents.
At least 10 people from the village of 3,000 people have died, and many remain missing. Villagers say they have seen several unidentified dead bodies floating on the Dikhou River.
Assam, in the far northeastern corner of India, is one of the most flood-prone regions in the country. About 40% of its land is vulnerable to inundation from the Brahmaputra and Barak rivers and other smaller rivers, and it sees at least two or three major floods annually.
According to official figures, about 2,690 villages in 25 districts have been flooded this year, affecting more than 1 million people. As of 11 August, 101 people have lost their lives. The death toll is likely to rise, officials fear.
In 2025, the death toll due to floods and landslides was 36. The year before, when all 35 districts of the state were affected by floods, at least 110 people died.
According to Partha Jyoti Das, a specialist in water and climate hazards with the environmental organisation Aaranyak, the current disaster was inevitable. The climate crisis has led to heavier rainfall, and changes to the landscape made flooding more likely.
“It’s a much-abused landscape, turning into a burial ground,” he says. Had it been just flood waters, the damage would have been less, but the rain brought with it debris, mud, silt and soil from the hills of Nagaland.
“These areas have seen mining and quarrying, both legal and illegal, for several years. From coal, sand or boulder mining, everything happens in these places. The whole landscape has been changed by large-scale deforestation, encroachment and excavation,” he says.
By 11 August, flood waters had receded in several villages, leaving behind heavy layers of mud and silt. However, low-lying areas of Sivasagar, Jorhat and Charaideo districts are still flooded, including the well-known Jokaichuk paddy field, a vast stretch of agricultural land shaped like a jokai, or bamboo fishing tool, near Gaurisagar.
“The floods have ruined 95% of the farmland across Sivasagar,” says Himadrijyoti Dutta, who works with farmers in the district through his non-profit organisation, Krishak Nyas, and has been visiting different villages to provide relief materials.
“The flood waters have washed away all the hard work and financial investments of the farmers. They have all been left poorer and desperate.”
Kalyan Das, a geography professor at Guwahati’s Cotton University, says the latest disaster will trigger a wave of migration. “Assam is already witnessing a serious crisis of out-migration of people from every block. There are many factors – primarily land degradation – making farming unsustainable,” he says.
Employment-driven migration from Assam rose from 16.3% in 1991 to 24.4% by 2011, according to a 2022 study. In rural areas, floods and soil erosion were the primary causes, the study said. “The latest floods have destroyed homes and agricultural fields. The villagers will be forced to migrate in search of livelihood opportunities,” Das says.
Eight years ago, Mintu Hazarika, 30, left Kosumari village in Sivasagar district for the IT hub of Bengaluru (formerly known as Bangalore). He earns 25,000 rupees (£195) a month by working double shifts as a security guard in Bengaluru’s Marathahalli suburb and sends half his earnings home.
“My father is a farmer, so is my elder brother,” says Hazarika. “They tend paddy fields, but it is not financially viable. So they also work as daily wage earners in nearby urban areas to supplement the household income.
On 22 July, Hazarika received a call from his father. He was told that the floods had destroyed their family’s two-hectare paddy field. “I don’t know how my family is going to survive. My elder brother is planning to come to Bengaluru to find work. There are already so many men from Sivasagar and other parts of Assam working in Bengaluru,” he says.
Bitupan Raidongia, district president of Sivasagar for the Bharatiya Janata party, the ruling party in Assam, says the authorities are providing support for affected communities. “Our government is doing its best to rescue marooned people. We are also reaching out to affected families by providing them with food items, clothes and other essentials.”
Sivasagar’s district commissioner, Mridul Yadav, adds that the local administration was making a coordinated effort to address the flood situation. “Various departments are working together on rescue, relief distribution, and damage assessment. Health camps, essential medicines, drinking water, livestock fodder and relief kits are being provided. Several relief camps remain operational to support affected families and restore essential services,” he adds.
But the authorities’ response has been criticised as too little, too late. In a video that went viral, the Assam-based singer Nilotpal Bora said thousands more people would have died were it not for the intervention of local charities and individuals.
“You people [the government] had a delayed response in reaching out to the affected people. If common people had not distributed relief, at least 3,000 people from flooded areas would have died because of hunger and thirst,” he said in response to a comment from Assam’s chief minister, Himanta Biswa Sarma, that “the situation was under control”, and the public should not raise money to help flood victims.
Meanwhile, local groups and people are doing what they can to help. About 40 bikers from One Northeast Motorcycle Club are travelling to affected areas to distribute food, clothing, sanitary items, candles, matchboxes and other essentials. “It’s a heartbreaking sight,” says the club’s founder, Chow Sureng Rajkonwar.
“Hundreds of people across villages have become homeless. Their homes were destroyed and flattened to the ground. Those that remain are filled with polokh [alluvial silt or sediment left behind by flood waters]. All their belongings were destroyed or washed away with the water. It will take months to rebuild those houses,” he says, adding that people are living in tents made of plastic sheets and tarpaulins on roads or higher ground near their villages.
Phukon was one of the luckier ones. Although the water level was more than 1.5 metres (5ft) high in her courtyard, it did not enter her house, which is built on higher ground.
For almost a week now, she has been providing relief aid to flood victims after getting distress calls from family, friends and acquaintances. “I decided to leave my home and reach out to people who need food, clothing, and other essentials. Everyone I know has been affected by floods.”
Maitreyee Boruah is a contributor to the Migration Story, where this story was first published

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to unveil new economic sanctions on Iran
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is expected to unveil a new round of economic sanctions on Iran on Monday, in what he has described as the "single greatest financial offensive ever."
President Trump has called it an "economic D-Day" and pledged to go after other countries who extend an economic lifeline to Tehran.
In anticipation, the Iranian currency, the Rial, has plunged to a record low.
What are these new sanctions and how much more pressure can they pile on?
The U.S. already has extensive sanctions on Iran, some stretching back almost 50 years, and as recently as June had imposed further penalties for entities that helped Iran evade existing financial restrictions. There has also been a months-long U.S. naval blockade of Iran, which has cut off most goods to Iran from the outside world.
This latest suggestion from President Trump and Secretary Bessent appears to be focused on putting more pressure on the countries and governments — not just the businesses — that host the entities providing cashflow for Iran.
In an editorial for the Financial Times published overnight, Bessent wrote, "our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains the tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone." He appeared to reference countries that still trade with Iran, saying they should "consider the consequences of doing so."
That includes China, Iran's biggest oil customer, which Bessent criticized last week for historically buying about 90 percent of Iran's oil.
But some analysts question the actual utility of fresh economic sanctions.
Alan Eyre, a former American diplomat who was part of the U.S. negotiating team over Iran's nuclear program until 2015, told NPR's Emily Feng that the U.S. has already targeted "the low-hanging fruit, the mid-hanging fruit, the high-hanging fruit, the tree," and that "there are no new sanctions that are effective."
Iran vows a "seismic" retaliation to any sanctions
Iran's new security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, said in an interview on state TV over the weekend that Iran would retaliate in a "seismic manner" to Trump's latest attempt at economic warfare. Rezaei, a hardliner who used to lead Iran's Revolutionary Guards, is now a military adviser to Iran's Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei.
Rezaei warned Gulf states that any countries partnering in these new economic restrictions would be considered an enemy of — and a target for — Iran.
Since the U.S. and Israel launched their war on Iran nearly six months ago, Iran has attacked U.S. bases in Jordan and Gulf countries including the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait and Saudi Arabia. Several have led to serious injuries and fatalities.
Rezaei said Iran would retaliate by further targeting oil tankers that are transiting the Persian Gulf on the Omani side of the Strait of Hormuz, warning that "not even a single drop of oil will leave the region."
Iran is not currently interfering in these routes, so such actions could further hamper oil supplies. Energy exports from the Gulf region have already suffered the biggest disruption in their history because of the war and Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
Gulf countries that invested billions on pipelines that can help avoid the Strait of Hormuz, have not yet commented on the U.S. plans for fresh sanctions.
New sanctions will make a dire economic situation worse for ordinary Iranians
Iran has weathered some U.S. sanctions for almost half a century, since the Islamic Revolution of 1979, with ordinary Iranians bearing the brunt of the subsequent economic pain.
The Iranian economy was already struggling when the U.S. and Israel launched this war against Iran in February, with double-digit inflation and currency devaluation. According to the Iranian government agency, the Statistical Centre of Iran, inflation is now at almost 90 percent.
NPR spoke to one 30-year-old Iranian woman, who said most ordinary Iranians are now buying food using a credit system because they do not have enough cash.
"Since I am in debt to the grocery store, I couldn't even buy tomato paste to cook pasta," she told NPR's Hadeel Al-Shalchi. She did not want to be named for fear of retaliation from the Iranian government.
She said lifesaving medicines like insulin have become too expensive for many, and that daily life is becoming increasingly difficult, with frequent power cuts and unemployment rising.
Economic pain and the high cost of living were among the factors driving Iranians to protest on the streets earlier this year, in demonstrations that were met with a deadly government crackdown.

Hello, and welcome back to This Is India.
For this week’s newsletter, I’m looking at India’s evolving relationship with Israel, and how it has deepened as conflict swept across the Middle East. Why is it that India has formed an even closer bond with a country that has faced mounting international isolation and backlash over a military campaign in Gaza that has left the territory in ruins and killed more than 70,000 Palestinians, – many of whom were children?
Under Narendra Modi, India’s ties with Israel have taken on a different character, for a country that once championed the Palestinian cause and led the Non-Aligned Movement. To better understand it, I turned to Stanly Johny, Indian foreign policy expert and the international affairs editor at the Hindu. He told me it isn’t just a political or diplomatic shift, “it’s also at the strategic and defence level”.
The evolution of India’s role was revealed in a recent Amnesty International investigation, which showed that India was now a key part of Israel’s weapons supply chain. This represents a fundamental change. For years, New Delhi had primarily been a major customer of Israeli weapons. But, through joint ventures and manufacturing partnerships, it is now a “significant contributor” to Israel’s weapons production, according to Amnesty, which offers the most extensive account so far of the scale of India’s involvement since the war in Gaza began.
Indian companies, including state-owned enterprises, have delivered drone warheads, artillery shell casings, small arms parts and military vehicle components to Israeli military suppliers despite the substantial risk these could end up in weapons deployed in Gaza, it added.
By examining publicly available shipment-level trade data, Amnesty said it traced hundreds of thousands of weapons components shipped from Indian factories to Israeli military suppliers between 7 October 2023 and 30 November 2025, including:
 390,516 small arms parts for military grade weapons
  564,970 parts of explosive ordnance
  298 components of military vehicles
Many western nations, including Britain, have restricted or banned arms supply to Israel over its conduct in the war, citing risks that the weapons could be used to commit or facilitate violations of international humanitarian law. (The United States accounts for the overwhelming share of major arms transfers to Israel.)
An independent United Nations commission of inquiry concluded in September that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza, and earlier this year another commission found that Israel is continuing to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children. Separately, the international criminal court has issued an arrest warrant for the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, accusing him of committing war crimes.
Yet, the Amnesty report hasn’t resulted in any large-scale public debate or political backlash in India, despite some scattered media coverage. Johny believes this is a result of the support for Israel by Modi’s voter base. “There is a clear ideological confluence between Hindutva and Zionism,” he said. In rightwing circles in India and elsewhere, he argues, Israel is increasingly seen as a bulwark against the expansion of Islam.
Hindu nationalists have long admired Israel, viewing it as a model of a nationalist state that can assert itself in a volatile neighbourhood. Author Pankaj Mishra chronicled this affinity in a 2017 essay, writing that his grandfather was among high-caste Hindus who saw Israel as an example of how to deal with Muslims “in the only language they understood: that of force and more force”.
The war on Gaza doesn’t appear to have significantly shifted views. A Pew Research survey published in June found that more Indians view Israel favourably (32%) than unfavourably (28%). This is in contrast to the decline of support for Israel in many western countries, including the United States, since the war.
Modi, for his part, has cultivated a personal rapport with Netanyahu. In 2017, he became the first Indian prime minister to visit Israel, and Modi’s visit to Israel earlier this year came just 48 hours before Israel and the United States launched their attacks on Iran. The optics of Modi hugging Netanyahu on the tarmac, coupled with New Delhi’s noticeably muted response at the outbreak of war, were a clear sign of where India’s political establishment stands. It has not gone unnoticed. In July, after the US vice-president, JD Vance, rebuked Netanyahu by calling the US Israel’s “only powerful ally” left in the world, Netanyahu shot back: “We have some other friends, like a small country called India. It has 1.4bn people, and boy, do we have tremendous support there.”
The government has previously declined to give a direct answer about weapons supplies to Israel. When asked in parliament in 2024, external affairs minister S Jaishankar said that information is not in public domain and that exports of military products are guided by “national interest”. Amnesty identified three state-owned Indian companies – Munitions India Limited, India Optel Limited and Advanced Weapons and Equipment India Limited – supplying Israel with weapons, which it said, could expose India to the hazard of “complicity in ongoing genocide in Gaza”. Foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal responded that India’s exports are governed by national laws and international obligations.
The pushback has largely come from human rights activists, student bodies, trade unions, India’s left-leaning parties and the Congress party. The courts have offered no recourse, either. In 2024, a group of civil servants, activists and academics petitioned the supreme court, demanding India suspend its military exports to Israel. The court dismissed the case, ruling that the matter fell within the discretion of the executive.
“In India, you don’t see any anger towards the government for its relationship with Israel, despite the allegations the Israeli government is facing,” Johny said. This, he believes, is a sign that foreign policy debates in India are being stripped of moral concern.
Weapons aren’t the only thing India has sent to Israel during this period. Thousands of Indian workers have also gone to Israel, in many instances to replace Palestinians barred from entering the country after 7 October 2023. Last year, the government told parliament that more than 20,000 Indian workers, in construction work and caregiving, had moved to Israel after an agreement signed in November 2023.
India, meanwhile, has shored up its own arms supplies from Israel. Between 2021 and 2025, New Delhi was Israel’s largest defence customer, accounting for 29% of total arms sales, according to Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.
But for Johny, India’s growing closeness to Israel is beginning to come at a cost. The war in Iran threatens India’s energy security and could have wider economic repercussions across the Gulf, home to a large Indian diaspora. “India has to continue to stay engaged with Israel, but it is important to restore balance to its approach to west Asia,” he said, adding that it needs to forcefully defend its own interests.

Hong Kong's Tiananmen activists convicted in national security trial
- Published
Two Hong Kong activists who organised annual vigils to commemorate the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown have been found guilty of inciting others to subvert state power under the city's controversial national security law.
Lee Cheuk-yan, 69, and Chow Hang-tung, 41, face a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison after being convicted under the China-introduced law. Sentencing is expected at a later date.
A third defendant, Albert Ho, 74, pleaded guilty in January.
Lee and Chow "incited other persons to organise, plan, commit or participate in acts by unlawful means with a view to subverting the state power", according to a summary on Friday. Chow told the court in May the law itself was on trial.
Hong Kong used to be one of the only places in Chinese territory where people could gather to mark the deadly 1989 crackdown against pro-democracy protesters.
Authorities banned these gatherings in 2020, citing Covid-19 policies, but they have never resumed. This was also the year the national security law, which makes illegal a wider range of dissenting acts, officially came into force.
In mainland China, authorities have banned even oblique references to the 1989 crackdown.
In the courtroom, Chow smiled as the verdict was read out, while Lee showed little emotion as he made a heart gesture and folded his hands to show his gratitude to those in the gallery.
Lee, a lawmaker, and Chow, a lawyer, were also leaders of the now-defunct Hong Kong Alliance (HKA), which has been described as a "toxic tumour" by Chinese authorities.
The HKA was founded in May 1989 to support students holding pro-democracy rallies. Weeks later, the Communist Party crushed pro-democracy protests in Beijing's Tiananmen Square with troops and tanks. Estimates of the death toll range from a few hundred to many thousands.
Over the next three decades, HKA called on authorities to accept responsibility for the crackdown, free dissidents and introduce democratic reform.
The Alliance's leaders were charged in 2021 and have been behind bars since.
Rights group Amnesty International has said the case "relies on vague, overly broad and arbitrary definitions of 'subversion'".
Sarah Brooks, Amnesty International's deputy regional director, said Chow and Lee had "not committed any recognisable crime".
"Chow Hang-tung and Lee Cheuk-yan are prisoners of conscience who should never have been prosecuted in the first place. They must be released immediately and unconditionally," she added.
Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch, said the convictions showed "how public displays of mourning have become a crime in Hong Kong".
In a separate case, Chow was arrested in June 2021 for "inciting" the public to take part in that year's vigil and later found guilty.
However, Hong Kong's top court overturned that conviction in 2022, with a judge ruling the police hadn't properly justified the vigil's ban.
Chow Hang-tung spoke to the BBC in 2021, weeks before her arrest on 4 June 2022.
"I am prepared to be arrested. That is how Hong Kong is now," she had said.
"I am willing to pay the price for fighting for democracy."
Critics say the national security law has eroded Hong Kong's autonomy and created a climate of fear. Authorities insist it is needed to maintain stability.
Among other things, the law criminalises anything considered as secession - or breaking away from China - as well as subversion, terrorism and collusion with foreign or external forces.

Australia coach Kiss wants Suaalii in Wallabies midfield
MELBOURNE, Aug 25 : Australia coach Les Kiss has no plans to shift Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii to the outside backs despite the growing competition for places in the Wallabies midfield ahead of the two-test series against Argentina.
Dual code international Suaalii missed the last test against Japan with a hamstring strain but is expected to be available for the opener in San Salvador on Saturday.
In his absence, Isaac Henry performed well in the number 13 jersey in Townsville in a midfield pairing with Hunter Paisami, while centre Len Ikitau's return to fitness has also given Kiss options.
Suaalii has experience as a test winger and as a fullback for the New South Wales Waratahs in Super Rugby Pacific but Kiss poured cold water on the prospect of redeploying the versatile 23-year-old.
"No. The intention from the start has been to keep him at outside centre, and that remains the preferred position for now," he told reporters in San Salvador.
"However, the back five need flexibility. Players are being asked what other positions they can productively fill, allowing the team to broaden its selection options and deal with different situations.
"Suaalii has already moved to the wing, while the team's No. 10s can also play fullback. That positional flexibility is important, but for the moment the preference is to persist with Suaalii at 13."
Since taking over the Wallabies for the Japan series, Kiss has shown a willingness to try new things and had two poachers operating in his back row in the second half in Townsville when Fraser McReight joined Carlo Tizzano on the field.
The ploy proved effective and revived memories of Michael Cheika's "Pooper" combination of David Pocock and Michael Hooper which helped Australia reach the 2015 World Cup final.
Kiss said it was "certainly enticing" to put McReight and Tizzano to work again but did not see it as a fixture going forward.
"There are also other combinations involving the team's power in the back row that the coaches want to explore," he said.
Kiss praised his players for buying into new mechanisms and ideas brought by the new Wallabies staff, and said their work on defence under Scott McLeod, a former All Blacks assistant coach at the last two World Cups, had already paid dividends.
The tests against Argentina would be a good measure of their progress, he added, as the Wallabies build toward next year's home World Cup.
"Once the (Argentina) crowd gets going, it can become a very difficult environment, so Australia will need to be good enough to quell that and withstand it," he said.

Fans suffer firework burns and eye injuries in Eredivisie
- Published
Dutch club SC Cambuur said fans have suffered "burns, hearing damage and eye injuries" after Feyenoord supporters threw fireworks during Sunday's league match.
Play was suspended for around 10 minutes in the first half after visiting fans in the away end at the Kooi Stadion lit a large number of red flares and threw fireworks.
Some of the fireworks were aimed towards sections containing home fans and SC Cambuur said in a statement that five supporters were confirmed to have been injured.
Feyenoord said it "firmly distances itself from the unacceptable events" and that head coach Giovanni van Bronckhorst - an assistant to Arne Slot at Liverpool last season - apologised on behalf of the club to SC Cambuur after the match.
"It should be clear that setting off and firing fireworks is completely unacceptable and has no place in a football stadium whatsoever," SC Cambuur said.
The club, who were promoted to the Eredivisie last season after three seasons in the Dutch second tier, said it would work with the authorities to make sure those responsible were punished, while Feyenoord said they would request camera footage.
Last season, an Eredivisie match between Ajax and Groningen was abandoned after fireworks and flares were ignited behind one of the goals at Johan Cruyff Arena.
Feyenoord's general manager Robert Eenhoorn said he "cannot be happy" with their 5-2 victory in Leeuwarden, adding "frustration prevails too much for that".
"This problem obviously does not only affect Feyenoord and is unfortunately something we have been unable to put a stop to for decades," Eenhoorn said.
"We will therefore have to sit down again with all stakeholders, clubs, the KNVB [Dutch football association], and the authorities to look for a solution together."
Leeuwarden mayor Foort van Oosten also condemned the incident and promised an investigation, while the Dutch football association said it would revisit its protocols for incidents of disorder.
The game resumed despite the injuries to the fans, but it would have been abandoned had a player or match official been hit.
"That doesn't feel right," Jan Bluyssen, the KNVB's manager of professional football competition affairs, told Dutch news agency ANP.
"We need to examine whether the protocol is still appropriate and how we might want to adjust it."

'Missing' Baptiste serving prison sentence in Morocco
- Published
An English athletics coach and former gold medallist said by media reports to be missing is serving a prison sentence in Morocco, BBC Sport can reveal.
Leon Baptiste, who was coaching a clutch of top British track athletes in the run-up to this summer's Commonwealth Games and European Championships, suddenly went off the grid more than three months ago.
Neither UK Athletics, for whom he worked as a consultant sprinting coach, nor the sprinters he coached knew why he was out of contact.
In May, Baptiste sent the group of athletes he coached a short message saying he would be absent from training "for a while". They have been given no further explanation.
Over the weekend, he was reported in the media as being "missing" and was said to have disappeared in Morocco.
On Tuesday, a brief email was sent to the people coached by Baptiste - the 200m gold medallist at the 2010 Commonwealth Games - in which he resigned from the position, citing unspecified ill health.
A source at the Moroccan Ministry of Justice confirmed to BBC Sport that Baptiste was arrested in Marrakech in May, has subsequently been convicted and is now serving a custodial sentence in Al-Oudaya prison.
"In relation to the reports concerning the alleged 'disappearance of Leon Baptiste' - an English athletics coach reportedly missing in Morocco for more than two months under questionable circumstances - please note that the information published in this regard is inaccurate and does not reflect the facts of the case," said the source.
"The foreign national concerned had not lost contact with his surroundings and was not subject to any disappearance or unexplained absence.
"He is currently being held at the local prison in Marrakech, where he is serving a custodial sentence following his conviction by the competent judicial authorities in connection with a misdemeanour case."
They added Baptiste, 41, was "in good health".
No details of what he was convicted of, or the length of his sentence, were provided.
The MMJ source said that was not uncommon in the Moroccan judicial system.
A spokesperson for the Morocco Public Prosecution Office confirmed: "The British national is currently being held at the local prison in Marrakech, where he is serving a custodial sentence following a court judgment against him in connection with his involvement in a criminal case."
Asked directly about Baptiste, a UK Foreign Office spokesperson said: "We are supporting a British national who is detained in Morocco and are in contact with the authorities."
Sources told BBC Sport that Baptiste travelled to Marrakech with three other British former athletes, who have all since returned to the UK.
BBC Sport has made attempts to contact the athletes but had no reply.
Baptiste's family are understood to be aware of his imprisonment.
Baptiste's absence left some British sprinters - including Olympic bronze medallist Charlie Dobson, Paralympic gold medallist Sophie Hahn and Paralympic silver medallist Zac Shaw - without a designated coach before the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow and European Championships in Birmingham.
Four-time European gold medallist Adam Gemili and relay coach Martyn Rooney stepped in to provide extra assistance to the athletes affected by Baptiste's abrupt departure.
But BBC Sport has been told the sprinters' training was heavily disrupted during a crucial period of their careers, leaving them ill-prepared and frustrated.
Those close to Baptiste who BBC Sport has spoken to describe him as a highly professional and dedicated coach with a reserved personality who keeps his private life to himself.
BBC Sport has approached UK Athletics for comment.
How did 'missing' reports turn into news of a prison sentence?
Once Baptiste's disappearance was reported in the media last weekend, BBC Sport began investigating his whereabouts.
We contacted a variety of figures in the British athletics community, people who know Baptiste, the UK Foreign Office, and authorities in Morocco in order to piece together the timeline of events.
It quickly became clear that Baptiste's whereabouts were known but his status was being withheld.
But Moroccan authorities confirmed details of Baptiste's case to BBC Sport when asked to do so.

Colombia’s far-right president, Abelardo de la Espriella, has announced a crackdown on immigrants, ordering authorities to detain and deport people who are in the country irregularly or have committed crimes.
In office for just over two weeks, the millionaire former lawyer made the announcement on Sunday as the country continued to grapple with the aftermath of a 7.4-magnitude earthquake on 10 August that killed more than 300 people and destroyed more than 30,000 homes.
De la Espriella said the first joint operations involving the police and the migration authority should begin “this very week”.
“Let the coordinated operations begin to track down illegal immigrants: first, those committing crimes; second, those who have not regularised their status and who will have to be deported immediately,” de la Espriella said during a cabinet meeting held on Sunday in Barranquilla, the Caribbean city that has in effect been turned into an alternative capital.
He echoed the “Americans first” rhetoric of his ally, US president Donald Trump, saying that from now on it would be “Colombians first, Colombians second and Colombians third”.
The Colombian president has joined other Trump-aligned leaders in the region who have also tightened migration rules, including Argentina’s Javier Milei and Chile’s José Antonio Kast.
De la Espriella’s order is facing criticism from the opposition and human rights activists, who say it will end a migration policy that endured for more than a decade under both rightwing and leftwing governments and benefited above all migrants fleeing the humanitarian crisis in neighbouring Venezuela.
Although he used the anti-immigration rhetoric characteristic of other far-right candidates during his campaign, his platform focused chiefly on his promise to pursue an iron-fist policy against criminal groups.
In the same announcement, he also declared that all gangs involved in drug trafficking, illegal mining, extortion and smuggling were “terrorists and we will treat them as such. Whatever happens, we will defeat them, by reason or by force.”
The president did not directly mention Venezuelans when discussing immigration, but they account for roughly 90% of all migrants in the country. Of the 2.8 million Venezuelans living in Colombia, about 848,000 are in an irregular situation, including 193,000 children and adolescents.
The leftwing senator María José Pizarro Rodríguez reposted the president’s announcement and asked whether he was “proposing a Colombian ICE against fellow Latin Americans”, in reference to the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). She added that the “order to deport irregular migrants is pure xenophobia and aporophobia”.
“Instead of persecuting people fleeing poverty and violence, regularise their status. There are thousands of migrants who work hard and contribute to the economies of the countries that receive them,” she wrote.
The Colombian newspaper El Tiempo reported that sources within the migration department believe the agency does not have enough staff to carry out the operations De la Espriella has promised.
Analysts have also noted that under Colombian law there is no such category as an “illegal” immigrant, as De la Espriella said, but rather migrants in an “irregular” situation, since being in the country without the proper documentation is not a crime.

Why do US elections cost so much money?
In the United States, elections are big business.
No other country spends as much on them, and few political capitals are as heavily shaped by money and lobbyists as Washington, DC.
But the vast amounts of money poured into state and federal races aren't there to cover operational costs so Americans can access the ballot box.
They're designed to influence the narrative.
According to the OpenSecrets project which tracks campaign financing, nearly $5 billion was spent on the 2024 presidential and congressional election cycle by individuals, groups, and outside spenders combined.

Before 2010, that figure was below $1 billion.
Why are we examining this now?
Abdul El-Sayed staged a stunning upset in Michigan earlier this month, when he beat Congresswoman Haley Stevens to clinch the Democratic party's nomination for the Senate.
Stevens, a centrist, was backed by the Democratic establishment as well as the state's governor. Sayed, a progressive who has never held political office, could now become the first ever Muslim senator if he wins in November.
But his win is being framed as an upset due to the record-setting influx of cash in the campaign to defeat him.
More than $50 million from corporate and single-issue organisations was thrown behind Stevens in the race. The pro-Israeli lobby alone spent $30m to ensure her win.
Sayed benefitted from a little over $5m in outside spending, mostly from a progressive values group.
This is separate from what each of their campaigns raised via donations - and all of it just for a primary, not even a general election.
That's because in the US, the sky's the limit for groups who want to support a candidate without having to route their money through the candidate's campaign.
And typically, the more money you can spend on things like television adverts to attack your opponent, or social media videos to boost your public image, the more likely it is you will emerge victorious.
"Money usually wins. So when it comes to campaigns, whoever spends more money usually wins by a 95 percent chance," Craig Holman, a government affairs lobbyist with Public Citizen, a consumer advocacy non-profit, told Middle East Eye.
But as we saw with Sayed's campaign, sometimes there are exceptions.
What is the legal basis for all this spending?
In the 2010 Citizens United case, the Supreme Court struck down limits on how much corporations and special interest groups could spend to influence elections. The justices ruled that such limits infringe on free speech - and that the spending itself is considered political expression, which should not be stifled.
"The Government may not suppress political speech based on the speaker's corporate identity," the ruling read. "No sufficient governmental interest justifies limits on the political speech of nonprofit or for-profit corporations."
That ruling set the stage for the rise of Super Pacs. More on that later.
For now, it's important to know that there is still a cap on direct individual donations to candidates, limited to $3,500 for federal races such as the presidency and the legislature, according to the Federal Election Commission (FEC). The cap can vary at state level.
Individuals may also donate to the national party overseer, such as the Democratic National Committee or the Republican National Committee, up to a limit of $44,300. These institutions vet candidates and develop their party's election strategy.
Earlier this year, the Supreme Court further de-regulated campaign financing by allowing candidates to gain control over the funds their party committee allocates for their race.
President Donald Trump hailed the decision as a victory.
What is a Pac?
Groups that have long-term interests and want to target specific candidates can get around the $3,500 limit by forming a Political Action Committee.
Pacs are rife within the US political system. All candidates across the political spectrum use them.
They must be registered with the FEC, have at least $1,000, and usually, they plan to outlast one or two election cycles given they are playing the long game in politics.
They can be single-issue dominated, or aligned with a party's general platform.
Anyone can start a Pac, campaign finance expert Anna Massoglia told MEE, but Pacs can only accept money from individuals and not organisations.
There is still a contribution limit when an individual gives money to a Pac on behalf of a cause or attached to a candidate. This is typically $5,000 at the federal level per election cycle, but those limits can again vary at the state level.
This means an American citizen is permitted to donate once as an individual, and a second time as a contribution to a Pac, but at no more than $7,000 in total.
The candidate, with whom the Pac works closely, can then use the funds however they choose.
Super Pacs, however, are another story.
What are Super Pacs?
These have unlimited spending power, and can collect as much money as they want from wealthy individuals and corporations.
"They are legally prohibited from coordinating with candidates in most ways, but they can spend in support of them," Massoglia said.
"They're what's called 'independence expenditures', and so basically they can take over $100m if they wanted to from a single individual, and spend all that money in support of a candidate," she added. "And as long as they disclose the spending, and whoever the donor is - at least the immediate donor - then that is perfectly legal."
The United Democracy Project (UDP) is an example of a Super Pac that is one of the highest spenders on US elections. It is a single-issue group, driven by pro-Israeli interests at the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac).
UDP spent more than $60m trying to shape the 2024 election cycle.
"What we all know is, if I'm spending a million dollars on behalf of a candidate, the candidate probably knows that I'm doing that, right? And so they'll have the same sort of sense of indebtedness to me as the spender," Michael S Kang, a law professor who teaches a course on regulating money in politics at Northwestern University, told MEE.
Super Pacs employ the kind of outside spending that is limitless, and can tip election results one way or another.
Aipac, as a Pac, is limited to the $5,000 cap per candidate, per election cycle.
And it's important to keep in mind that primaries and general elections are counted as separate cycles.
What is 'dark money'?
Not all donors who influence US election outcomes are known - even if they legally should be.
Since the Citizens United ruling in 2010, these so-called "dark money" actors have spent well over $4b on federal elections alone, Massoglia found.
"Oftentimes, they'll be spending on ads that mention a candidate in favourable or disfavourable ways, but [they] do not explicitly call for voting for or voting against that candidate," she explained. "They avoid those terms or any other related 'magic words' [so] they don't have to disclose their spending to the Federal Election Commission."
In essence, they make the argument that they are not really campaign finance actors at all, Kang said.
"They spend millions of dollars often on campaign spending that's indistinguishable from the campaign spending by political committees and by Super Pacs [and] over the last 15 years, 20 years, that type of entity has been able to get away with that," he said.
In some cases an anonymous donor would contribute funds to a non-profit group, and that non-profit group would make the contribution to the Super Pac, ultimately shielding the donor from financial disclosures, Massoglia said.
Others use shell companies to make political contributions, making tracing difficult.
Who are the biggest spenders?
In the 2024 election cycle, Republican interest groups far outspent those supporting Democrats, at 65 percent to to 29 percent, respectively.
The Make America Great Again Super Pac was the top fundraiser, with $410m collected to exclusively back Trump's third bid for the White House, and spread his agenda.
Nearly 91 percent of all outside spending was ideological or single-issue, broken down into categories such as gun rights, anti-abortion, defence policy, and oil and gas, among others.
But often ranked at the top, over multiple election cycles, are the US Chamber of Commerce, lobbying on behalf of businesses; the National Association of Realtors, influencing property laws; and the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America, shaping health policy.
Tech giants like Meta and Amazon are also climbing fast.
As a Pac, Aipac was the third biggest spender in the 2024 election. Its Super Pac arm, UDP, ranks among the top 15 spenders across all industries.
No other group laser-focused on the interests of a foreign country has this much influence.
For the 2026 races, a report by Americans for Tax Fairness found that, as of 1 March, nearly 80 percent of all the billionaire contributions to Super Pacs were for Republican candidates and causes.
The funds mostly came from Tesla and SpaceX boss Elon Musk, Wall Street money manager Jeffrey Yass, and tech mogul Greg Brockman.
How does this system impact democracy?
The House of Representatives runs on two-year terms. The presidency runs on four. The Senate runs on six.
In a system where money creates the brand, candidates are continuously fundraising and worrying about the next election even in the early weeks and months of their term.
"It undermines the democratic process," Holman told MEE.
"It allows wealthy individuals, wealthy groups, corporations, and even foreign interests to invest heavily into who is elected to our government. If [candidates] want to remain in office, they know where the money is coming from."
Kang noted that the ability to raise large sums of money can be critical at the grassroots level, when, for example, a relative unknown is trying to run for local office for the very first time, and needs to be able to pay campaign staff.
"There are people who say that fundraising is kind of a proxy for popularity, but that's not really true, because we come from different communities and different communities have different amounts of wealth, and so the way that the role and the importance that money plays in politics has a way of favouring the wealthy [gives them] outsized influence," he said.
A 2016 paper by the conservative think tank The Manhattan Institute insisted that money did not buy election outcomes.
"Political scientists have had great difficulty determining the level of influence - if any - that contributions have in the legislative process," the paper read.
"Donations to campaigns are rarely given for the sake of changing politicians' minds. Rather, donors generally give money to people with whom they already agree - and who have a shot at winning."
Are there efforts to reform campaign financing?
Yes - and many begin at the state level.
Mop Up Michigan is one group gaining traction after Sayed's primary victory, building on his messaging on getting money out of politics.
It's calling for a ban on utility companies and corporations from donating to political campaigns, and urging transparency so the public can understand who is funding political ads for or against candidates.
"I know Arizona is one state that's really worked hard to tackle this to try to at least shine some light on 'dark money', requiring additional disclosure around the ultimate source of funds," Massoglia told MEE.
"I would say those efforts have been somewhat successful but limited, because oftentimes 'dark money' groups and the operatives running them will continue to come up with new methods and tactics in order to hide their spending."
In recent Congresses, both major parties have proposed campaign finance bills, but no major amendments have become law.
The Brennan Center for Justice at the New York University Law School has advocated for what is describes as "the most effective and promising solution" to the problem of big money in politics: small donor public financing, whereby public funds match or multiply each contribution.
This incentivises candidates to seek out many supporters, not just a few big donors, the think tank argued.
But that also requires more legwork, and greater outreach, when it can be easier to fall back on the millions of dollars in favourable ads that a Super Pac will run.
Current campaign finance regulation "is useless at this point", Holman told MEE.
"Even though the courts have not yet struck down contribution limits to actual candidates and political committees, they decided to open up a huge loophole of no limits and no source restrictions on contributions to nonprofit electioneering groups," he said.
"The biggest effort is to reform the court system, because it's the courts that have destroyed our campaign finance laws."

More than anything, ChatGPT has saved me time and drama by being a study partner for my kids.
What spurred this were the progress reports that my daughters, ages 8 and 6, got from school last year. I found out that one struggles with math, and one  struggles with reading. Not that they're doing poorly, but maybe below where the district thought that they should be.
I knew we could try to spend more time on these areas. But at the end of the day, I thought I might not be the best person to explain a concept like TouchMath, a multi-sensory math curriculum, which I'd never heard of until I had to help the girls with homework.
I decided to take a picture of their homework and have AI explain some concepts to them. Using voice mode, ChatGPT now quizzes them, varies the questions, revisits what they missed, and explains the same concept several different ways without becoming impatient.
At first, I wasn't sure if the time it took to set this up was worth it. Five minutes in, they were talking to ChatGPT about "KPop Demon Hunters." I needed to revise it a little.
Through trial and error, it became something that really saved time and I think improved their grades. I'm not sure how it's going to look as things get more and more complicated with their schoolwork, but at least for now, it works well.
I programmed an AI tutor to make sure they truly understand the material
Both my daughters have weekly math and spelling tests at school.
In general, I tell ChatGPT what kind of test my daughters are preparing for, take a picture of the study sheet, and instruct it to stay focused — despite the inevitable interruptions by my daughters.
I prompt ChatGPT by saying something like: "You're a tutor helping grade schoolers study for math and spelling tests. You'll be given images of the study guides, and you'll work with the students until they can confidently and accurately answer all questions."
I also add some guardrails: "You will not be distracted if other topics come up. Express interest in those topics, make them relevant to what you're discussing, but keep it on the task at hand."
Many of the instructions are for ChatGPT to politely and firmly make sure my daughters are comfortable and confident in the material, not engaging just for the sake of engaging. If they're able to quickly say what 9+3 is, they're able to write that on a test.
I also make sure I'm present to hear both what they're saying and what ChatGPT is saying. If I hear that something is very clearly wrong, I can jump in and steer things back to the task at hand.
Overall, AI has been pretty efficient at maintaining their attention, adapting to how they are thinking in that moment, and repeating something for the sixth time without making it feel like punishment. It's surprisingly useful at absorbing some of that friction.
Since last year, their progress reports went from being a little "below satisfactory" to being "above satisfactory." Both of their grades have improved, but the more valuable result may be that studying has become more interactive and less adversarial. I am still involved, but I can spend more time observing where they are struggling instead of simply reading questions from a worksheet.
I also use AI to digitize their school handouts into a calendar
AI also helps me manage the constant stream of information that comes with having two grade-school children.
Every Monday, I open their take-home folders and take pictures of school flyers, calendars, permission slips, and classroom notices, then use ChatGPT to extract dates, deadlines, supplies, and action items. It turns paperwork that would otherwise require another round of mental sorting into something much easier to track.
The prompt I use is: "You'll be given images of take-home folders. Please review this for key dates and things that require action or follow-up on behalf of anyone. Add relevant tasks to my calendar." ChatGPT then exports the scanned events as .ics files that I then import into a school calendar in Outlook.
At this point, ChatGPT hasn't really dropped the ball. It is really nice not to discover at 8 p.m. that there is a project due the next morning — and then spend the rest of the evening scrambling to figure out what we need.
AI frees me up to have more fun with my kids
We also do quite a bit of generative art, asking ChatGPT to provide an image for my daughters to draw on their own.
Originally, we'd ask for something like Disney's Ariel and Elsa dancing underwater in a sandcastle. ChatGPT declined the request, citing copyright restrictions. I asked it to provide an open-source alternative, such as a generic red-headed mermaid and blonde ice princess. Everyone was happy.
Now, a few times a week, my daughters can draw or paint whatever character crossover they want.
AI does not so much create new free time as help us get much more out of the time we already have. We spend less time looking for things, figuring out instructions, or trying to understand a new concept from scratch, and more time actually doing projects, making art, playing games, or just having fun together.

Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay on Wednesday (August 19, 2026) made a slew of announcements in the health sector, including an increase in the coverage under the Chief Minister’s Comprehensive Health Insurance Scheme from ₹5 lakh to ₹25 lakh. Construction of a 400-bed multi-super-speciality hospital at a cost of ₹300 crore in Perambur, the constituency he represents, and allocation of ₹673.44 crore for the Cancer Mission also formed part of his announcements.
“The value of life should not be determined by a person’s income. The TVK government is firm that there should be no discrimination in providing treatment based on a person’s economic status. Medical care is a basic right of every human being, and not a concession,” he said.
Gender-affirming surgeries
Making a suo motu statement in the Assembly, Mr. Vijay said medical services and surgeries for transgender women would also be offered at Stanley Medical College and hospitals attached to medical colleges in Tirunelveli, Thoothukudi, Chengalpattu, Tiruvarur, Dharmapuri, and Kanniyakumari under the Chief Minister’s Comprehensive Health Insurance Scheme.
Cancer care
Mr. Vijay said as Tamil Nadu was witnessing an increase in cancer cases, the Chief Minister’s Cancer Care Mission would be upgraded at a cost of ₹673.44 crore. A cancer treatment section would be created at the Rajiv Gandhi Government General Hospital at a cost of ₹471.98 crore. The building for the cancer treatment section would have a ground floor and 14 upper floors.
Besides, Regional Cancer Centres would be created at medical colleges in Thanjavur, Coimbatore, Madurai, Tirunelveli, and Villupuram districts. In the first phase, a Regional Cancer Centre would come up at Madurai Rajaji Medical College at a cost of ₹84 crore. The centre would be housed in a ground-plus-eight-floor building.
The Chief Minister said ₹106.17 crore would be sanctioned to government medical college hospitals for robotic surgery, Linear Accelerators (LINACs), modern equipment, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy.
HPV screening
Mr. Vijay said the government would spend ₹2.77 crore on providing training to doctors and nutritional supplements to patients. Moreover, HPV DNA screening tests would be conducted for 1.22 lakh women in Dharmapuri, Villupuram, Tiruvannamalai, Perambalur, and Ariyalur at a cost of ₹8.70 crore.
The Chief Minister said as no nursing colleges had been started in Tamil Nadu after 2014, the government would create additional seats for nursing, pharmacy, and paramedical courses at a cost of ₹351 crore.
The government would launch seven nursing colleges and create 660 B.Sc. Nursing seats. Besides, 1,925 seats would be created in existing nursing colleges, along with 2,778 additional seats for physiotherapy and 735 seats for pharmacy courses.

It's tariff time in America and Canada — again.
On Saturday, after trade talks between Canada and the US collapsed, the Trump administration imposed 50% tariffs on a slew of Canadian items, including alcohol and hockey equipment. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has already announced a dollar-for-dollar counter-tariff, marking yet another bumpy moment in tensions between the two formerly friendly neighbors.
The specificity of the tariffs means that different sectors of the economy — and your everyday purchases — will get hit unevenly. The tariffs affect alcohol, milk, plywood, and more. For consumers craving Canadian whisky or finally getting around to home renovations, that might mean a bigger bite out of their wallets.
Census Bureau data showed that paper and paper products alone accounted for $3.3 billion of the roughly $382 billion in goods imported from Canada to the US last year. On top of Saturday's announcement, President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social on Monday that tariffs on cars, trucks, automotive parts, and steel from Canada will rise to 50% in January 2027. Passenger cars accounted for about $25 billion of imported goods last year.
Debbie Safran, the owner of Houndstooth Pet Boutique in Burlington, Vermont — which is situated about 45 miles away from the Canadian border — said she's worried about a shipment of her favorite winter coats for dogs.
"We've spent years building up and getting a client base for it because we love it so much. They're made by a woman-owned business in Canada," Safran said. "I've already placed my order for this season, and they haven't arrived yet. So when they arrive, I'm going to get stuck with a massive tax bill, and I'm not happy."
What it means for the American economy
Saturday's tariffs are likely to fall heavily on the sectors directly named, and on states like Michigan that rely heavily on cross-border trade. However, their limited scope makes them unlikely to significantly affect broader American employment. Any upward pressure on inflation from the tariffs might also contribute to ongoing interest rate discussions.
"While it won't be a big macro employment impact, it will have big, big impacts in these sectors that are hit particularly hard," said Erica York, a senior economist at the Tax Foundation.
Inflation rates are already stubbornly high due to recent supply shocks — geopolitical tensions, the pandemic, and the last rounds of Trump's tariffs. The newest tariffs could present yet another shock. Inflation cooled to 3.4% in July, still above the Fed's 2% target. The trend has contributed to higher interest rates, and the Federal Reserve is likely to hike rates at least once in 2026, per the central bank's most recent economic projections. Kevin Warsh, the Fed's new chair, has a reputation for being hawkish on inflation.
While a single rate decision doesn't directly impact consumers, Americans may feel a ripple effect. A pattern of hikes would drive up mortgage rates, making it more expensive to both buy and rent a home.
Canada is also a major supplier of lumber, a key material in homebuilding. A tariff impacting lumber prices would increase construction costs for new homes, just as cities like New York, Austin, and Raleigh, North Carolina, double down on policies to boost housing supply.
Home prices are already out of reach for many lower- and middle-income households, with expensive houses sitting empty while buyers scramble for a limited number of affordable listings. And because the US has far less publicly owned forest land than Canada, it will be difficult to fill the gaps with domestic supply.
Border states could also feel the heat of new tariffs in their beacon industries, including in Michigan's large auto industry.
"Tariffs may have hit Michigan harder than almost any other state. Building a car means moving parts across the U.S.-Canada border multiple times," an Instagram post from Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer said. "Now, Michiganders are paying the price, with higher costs for everything from cars and gas to groceries."
Olu Sonola, head of US Economics at Fitch Ratings, said the higher autos and parts tariffs could mean an "additional tariff burden" of up to $5 billion.
"January is still several months away, leaving room for negotiation, but the uncertainty alone will strain the highly integrated North American auto supply chain," Sonola said.
Across the border, the situation might be more grim. Trevor Tombe, an economics professor at the University of Calgary, found that nearly 90,000 Canadian jobs, including in various manufacturing sectors, could be affected.
"Those losses go beyond where the tariffs directly land. Alberta is a good example: its exports are barely affected by the new tariffs, yet I estimate roughly 9,000 jobs there are at risk," Tombe wrote.
Of course, tariffs landing now don't mean they'll stick around. Trump's persistent efforts to raise levies — or threaten them — have been walked back or struck down before, and that might end up being the case for this latest round. But if these stay in effect, they might continue to erode the once-friendly, neighborly relationship.
"Naturally, the way the trade kind of flows, it's easier for Canada to trade with us and us to trade with Canada just because we're so close to each other," said Bob Schwartz, the sales and marketing director at the Vermont-based von Trapp Family Lodge and Resort, which sits around 45 miles away from the Canadian border. "It's very difficult when these things happen because it kind of throws a wrench in everybody's business plans."

Moses Itauma fights could soon become must-see events across the world. The 21-year-old, undefeated KO artist is that talented. On Saturday, Itauma gets the biggest test of his career and his first opportunity to become a world champion. Itauma faces Filip Hrgovic for the vacant IBF heavyweight title at the O2 Arena in London. You need to watch. Let's talk boxing.
Itauma Vs. Hrgovic: Key Facts
| Detail | Info | 
|---|---|
| Date | Saturday, August 29, 2026 | 
| Venue | The O2 Arena, London | 
| Title | Vacant IBF heavyweight | 
| First bell | 5 p.m. BST | 
| Main event ring walk | Around 10 p.m. BST | 
| How to watch | DAZN pay-per-view, UK and US | 
| Promoters | Queensberry, Most Valuable Promotions | 
| Itauma | 14-0, 12 KOs, 21 years old | 
| Hrgovic | 20-1, 15 KOs, 34 years old | 
| Why vacant | Oleksandr Usyk gave up the belt in June 2026 | 
| Mandatory next | Frank Sanchez, 26-1, 19 KOs | 
Why Itauma Is Worth Your Saturday
What makes Itauma such an elite prospect? It's tough to know where to start. He has hand speed that is most often attached to a smaller man. He has good feet, explosive power and while he's not a towering heavyweight like Tyson Fury or Deontay Wilder, his 6-foot-4 height is plently when coupled with his gifts.
Hrgovic is no slouch. While some may have preferred to see Itauma win the belt from Oleksandr Usyk, the man who vacated the IBF strap, this win — if Moses can get it — is not a walkover victory. Hrgovic is big, skilled and he has proven to be rugged. He's 34, which is prime for most heavyweights, 20-1 with his only defeat coming by way of stoppage against current WBO champion, Daniel Dubois in June 2024.
To put it plainly, this is a legitimate heavyweight championship fight that fight fans should be excited to watch. The sport needs heavyweights with star power and Itauma is that guy.
The IBF belt has been vacant since Usyk gave it up in June. Itauma is 14-0 with 12 knockouts, Hrgovic 20-1 with 15.
Whoever wins is already boxed in. Frank Warren paid Frank Sanchez a step-aside fee, and Sanchez, ranked first by the IBF, gets the first defense.

Bitdefender VPN was reliable in my time using it, as well. I didn’t experience any connection drop-outs or periods of unusually slow performance.
These are solid results, though not the best. For example, I saw slightly better speeds (up to 540 Mbps, the same as when not connected to the VPN) while using IVPN with the WireGuard protocol enabled, for example.
Still, Bitdefender is plenty fast, very reliable, and I can’t say I found the gap in performance noticeable outside of in particular testing. I expect that most people will find the data rates provided by Bitdefender VPN to be more than adequate.
Privacy Promises and Compromises
Unlike Mullvad, a privacy-pilled alternative that positions itself as a tool against mass surveillance, Bitdefender VPN focuses more on avoiding geo-restrictions, ads, cookies, tracking, and Wi-Fi sniffing. There’s nothing wrong with that approach, but if you want a service that puts the P in VPN, you should look elsewhere.
Bitdefender’s VPN is provided through a partnership with IPVanish. IPVanish provides the infrastructure, while Bitdefender provides the client software, branding, customer service, and so on. It's worth mentioning, as IPVanish took a reputation hit back in 2018 when it handed user logs to the US Department of Homeland Security. This occurred in 2016 and happened despite having a no-logs policy.
However, IPVanish ownership has exchanged hands several times since then, and it’s now owned by media company Ziff Davis. IPVanish has undergone a number of successful independent, no-log audits, the most recent of which occurred in 2025. IPVanish also publishes a transparency report showing the volume of requests it has received from law enforcement and the data it has provided in response.
That’s good news, but wrinkles remain. IPVanish is a US company, and US law is pretty strict when it comes to law enforcement demands for data. IPVanish can’t provide what it doesn’t log, but privacy nerds often prefer VPN companies in less draconian jurisdictions.
It’s also unclear how Bitdefender’s service interact with IPVanish’s no-logs policy. Bitdefender obviously retains at least some information about the user, because a Bitdefender account is required to use the VPN, and users have to pay with a credit card. Bitdefender has some customer service information about its no-log policy, but the specific wording means this could be referring to the IPVanish audit.
Whether any of this matters depends on what privacy means to you. If you want an extra layer of network security to ward against trackers and prevent issues on compromised Wi-Fi connections, then Bitdefender VPN will do the job. However, Bitdefender VPN isn’t going to meet your needs if you’re worried about nation-state tracking or want to move across the web in near secrecy.
Conclusion
Bitdefender’s VPN is an easy-to-use service that works best for people with basic expectations for what a VPN should offer. It provides typical features and delivers solid network performance at a competitive price. It’s not the ultimate VPN for privacy and it’s lacking a few features some people will want, like Linux support and a static IP option.
Pricing might push you toward Bitdefender VPN—at least for the first year. The introductory offer of $35 for a year of service is an outstanding value. Just remember to check pricing again before it’s time to renew, as Bitdefender’s pricing after the first year is less enticing.

Shein aims for almost $27bn valuation in stock market debut
- Published
Fast-fashion giant Shein could see its stock market valuation reach almost $27bn (£19.8bn) when its makes its debut in Hong Kong on 1 September.
The long-awaited move comes after failed attempts to list in the US and London due to regulatory challenges amid scrutiny of the firm, which has its headquarters in Singapore but was founded in China.
Since it was founded in 2008, Shein has risen to become one of the world's biggest fast-fashion retailers, with customers in more than 150 countries.
The e-commerce giant is known for selling ultra-cheap clothes, backed by a vast network of factories in China that are able to quickly manufacture new products based on the latest trends.
Shein said in a filing on Monday, external that it will offer nearly 280 million shares for between HK$47.60 ($6.07; £4.45) and HK$49.50 each.
At the top of the range, the share sale would raise $1.77bn (£1.3bn) for the company and give it a market valuation of $26.8bn.
But that is much lower than the $100bn it was worth in 2022, reflecting weaker sales growth and higher costs.
The initial public offering (IPO) is being backed by Wall Street investment giants Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley and JP Morgan.
The company will make its highly anticipated debut on the Hong Kong stock exchange after efforts to go public since 2023.
Hong Kong has been revived as "one of the largest IPO markets" after attracting more firms from mainland China, said economics associate professor Feng Qu from the Nanyang Technological University.
Shein is likely to command a higher valuation in Hong Kong than it would in London, where regulatory scrutiny derailed its plans to sell shares there, Feng said.
Chinese companies may also be wary of selling shares in the US as tensions between the world's two largest economies could result in firms being de-listed, he added.
Competition and roadblocks
Shein's listing will test investor confidence in the fast-fashion industry and its position in an increasingly competitive market.
In July, Shein said it had swung to a quarterly loss as its sales slowed after US President Donald Trump removed an import duty waiver on small packages called the de minimis exemption.
The company said it lost $99m in the first three months of the year, compared with a net income of $395m a year earlier.
It also came as uncertainty remains over the tit-for-tat US-China tariffs wars, which is currently paused.
"In response to the increased duties and taxes, we are pursuing a wide range of options, including increasing our prices in the US market to offset a portion of the increased costs," Shein said at the time.

The company also said the Iran war had hit demand, increased costs and caused delays of deliveries in some markets.
The first-quarter figures also partly reflected a paper loss of $328m due to an accounting change for special investor shares. The shares can be turned into ordinary stock later, and their value can change before a listing.
Some investors are questioning whether higher costs and regulatory challenges will affect Shein's ability to get goods swiftly and cheaply to market.
Marguerite LeRolland from market research company Euromonitor International told the BBC that the firm's sales have slowed in the US partly due to the end of the de minimis exemption.
The exemption helped retailers like Shein and its fierce rival Temu grow quickly in the US as they were able to deliver goods without incurring import taxes.
These factors could "narrow the price gap" between Shein and competitors like Primark and H&M, she added.
Jane Foley, Rabobank's head of FX strategy, told the BBC's Today programme that the ending of the de minimis exemption "really did undermine the core business model of Shein", adding that the EU has done something similar.
Richard Lim of research firm Retail Economics said Chinese retail giants such as Shein have caused "a huge wave of destruction" in markets like the UK, with more established companies struggling to compete.
The British retail industry believes Shein is "not playing on a level playing field", he told the BBC.
It is expected that the UK will impose similar restrictions as the US and EU on small packages from Chinese retailers in 2028.
As of the end of March 2026, Shein had 281 million active customers - a rise of more than 16% on a year earlier - who placed a total of more than one billion orders.
But its fast-fashion business has faced concerns over its environmental impact, and allegations of forced labour in supply chains. The company has previously told the BBC it has a "zero tolerance for forced labour".
Its attempt to go public on the London Stock Exchange collapsed after the company came under scrutiny over its refusal to answer questions about its supply chain practices.
