The DJ dropped the beat and 70 women started throwing punches. By the time the first kickboxing combination was called out, Moon Bar, a Visakhapatnam club had shed its weekend persona to turn into a makeshift fitness floor, with women punching, kicking, squatting and burpee-ing their way through an hour of high-energy cardio.
There were no opponents, no rings and no gloves to take a hit. Instead, four trainers led the women through combinations designed to raise the heart rate and work the whole body, while the music kept the tempo going. It was a part workout, part social gathering and a glimpse of how women are increasingly choosing to exercise with more intensity, more variety and with strength in mind.
Hosted by The Social Wave, a women-centric community in the city, Club Cardio brought kickboxing into a club setting, combining martial arts-inspired movements with high-intensity cardio drills. The one-hour session was conducted in collaboration with Altcrew and led by four trainers.
For Komal Bagrodia Saraf, who founded The Social Wave with Preksha Dugar, the format was designed to make exercise feel less like a scheduled obligation and more like something women would actively seek out. “The idea was to turn a bar into a fitness bar,” she says. “There is a trend of Gen Z turning a bar into a Pilates bar. We wanted to bring something more intense than Zumba.”
The response also reinforced the value of a shared workout, she says. “There was some initial reluctance among a few participants, but once we made a circle and started, the music and community spirit helped. It became a community workout.”
The format was deliberately social. The 65-minute session at Moon Bar was structured to keep the pace building. After a 10-minute warm-up, the women spent the next 40 minutes learning kickboxing combinations and working dance moves into the routines. Participants worked through combinations of punches and kicks before the final 15 minutes turned into what Komal calls the “monster challenge”, featuring squats, bicep curls and burpees.
According to Komal, a sense of community may be as important to the emerging fitness format as the workout itself. The growing interest among women in strength training, boxing, running and other high-intensity forms of exercise points to a broader change in how fitness is being understood.
Fitness coach Martina Fernandes, who attended the session, sees that change in her own experience. “I have never really believed exercise has to feel like punishment,” she says. Having played sport for much of her life, Martina associates movement with “fun, competition, music, adrenaline and people”.
She usually trains alone and considers herself self-motivated, but says community workouts offer something different. “When you are laughing, sweating, listening to good music and pushing yourself alongside other people, it stops feeling like ‘I have to work out’ and starts feeling like ‘I want to be here’.”
For Martina, physical strength has little to do with a number on the weighing scale. “It means being capable,” she says. “It is being able to pick up something heavy, run, jump, play sport, carry my kids, travel, climb stairs and generally trust my body to do what I ask it to do.”
That focus on capability becomes particularly significant as women age, she adds. “I do not want to just look strong. I want to actually be strong. I am all about longevity.”
Kickboxing, she believes, also brings a psychological dimension. Learning combinations requires concentration and coordination, leaving little room for distraction. “There is something incredibly empowering about learning that your body can hit, move, react and defend itself,” she says. “You feel more confident, more alert and more connected to your body.”
For women in their 30s and 40s, she says, preserving muscle, supporting bone health, maintaining metabolic health and remaining independent become increasingly relevant. “The scale is one very small piece of the picture. Your strength, energy, performance and capability tell you much more about your fitness.”
Participant Tanya Dhawan, who had never tried kickboxing apart from some martial arts as a child, signed up because she was looking for something new to do in Vizag. The addition of a DJ was an added attraction. “Music is always part of my workouts, so combining it with a high-energy workout sounded like a lot of fun,” she says.
She had expected a conventional kickboxing class centred on technique. Instead, she found a high-intensity cardio workout driven by music and group energy. “The music, the energy of the girls and the entire crew kept the momentum going, especially when the workout got tough.”
The appeal of women-only fitness spaces, Martina says, lies partly in removing the apprehension that can accompany entering a gym or combat-sports environment. “A lot of women walk into a gym or a boxing environment worrying that everyone is watching them or judging how much they can lift,” she says. An all-women setting can make it easier to be a beginner and gradually take on greater challenges.
Community can also make consistency easier. “Motivation gets you started, but community is often what keeps you going,” Fernandes says. For women balancing careers, children and family responsibilities, she believes the expectation of seeing familiar faces can make fitness less likely to be the first commitment sacrificed.
Komal, too, sees wellness as a larger focus for The Social Wave. The group is looking at more experiences that combine activity and social interaction, including an upcoming pickleball coaching session.

Amazon is developing a new generation of highly automated warehouses that use AI and robotics to process packages at the final stop before delivery.
The initiative, internally called Project Tetromino, is intended to build "fully automated" delivery stations, according to an internal planning document from last month that Business Insider reviewed. Delivery stations are the final facility in the shipping process, receiving packaged items from fulfillment centers before sorting and staging them for drivers to deliver to customers.
According to the document, Amazon planned to invest $103 million in an initial Tetromino pilot in 2028, followed by five sites in 2029 and 10 more in 2030. Each 2029 site could cost about $85 million, bringing the total Tetromino investment to more than $530 million by 2029, the document said. It also said Tetromino could process packages at roughly 2.5 times the rate of its existing delivery station design.
An Amazon spokesperson told Business Insider that this is an "early-stage concept" and the specific financial figures and road map in the document are "inaccurate and don't reflect our current plans."
"We're always exploring and testing new technologies across our operations to improve safety and the delivery experience for customers," the spokesperson said. "Like any early-stage concept, this is one of many initiatives we regularly evaluate, and plans evolve significantly as we learn."
Tetromino offers a glimpse of how Amazon is trying to automate one of the most stubbornly manual parts of its logistics network. Industry analysts say tasks such as organizing and loading packages into vehicles at delivery stations remain difficult and expensive to automate.
The project comes as Amazon accelerates a broader warehouse automation push. On its latest earnings call in July, the company said it expects to more than double its fleet of robotic arms in 2026. Business Insider previously reported that Amazon is also deploying software that automatically recommends where warehouse workers should be assigned as workloads change.
Amazon's Tetris-like challenge
One of Tetromino's key technologies could come from Boxbot, an AI and robotics supply chain startup, according to the planning document. Boxbot's system moves packages from conveyors onto trays for storage, then uses AI to retrieve and sequence them for delivery. Boxbot's website says the system can make the vehicle-loading process up to 10 times faster. Boxbot did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider.
The Tetromino name itself may be a nod to the game Tetris, reflecting the puzzle-like challenge of efficiently organizing packages for delivery vehicles.
Amazon isn't alone in trying to automate these tasks. FedEx is expanding its use of AI-powered Dexterity robots that autonomously load packages into trailers, while UPS and DHL use robots for unloading. The Amazon spokesperson also pointed to delivery station pilots announced last year as part of a €700 million investment in European facilities, including machines that unload, sort, and scan packages.
The push toward more automated facilities raises questions about what Amazon's warehouses will ultimately need humans to do.
Amazon robotics chief Tye Brady previously told Business Insider that robots are intended to make frontline work safer and more efficient, not replace employees. Nevertheless, Amazon has internally projected that some warehouse robots will "flatten" its hiring curve over the next decade, Business Insider previously reported.
The Amazon spokesperson told Business Insider the company's delivery-station initiatives are "designed to complement and empower our workforce and employees remain central to how we operate."

Washington, Aug 25: President Donald Trump is moving toward levying a new tariff on China that would penalise the world's second-largest economy for flooding the global market with underpriced goods, according to three people familiar with the matter.
Two of the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal deliberations still being finalised, said Trump is considering setting the new tariff at 7.5 per cent. It's a level administration officials believe would not endanger the one-year trade truce between Washington and Beijing or a planned White House meeting between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping expected to take place in late September.
The move, if finalised, appears to be a calibrated effort by the White House to work around a Supreme Court decision earlier this year that struck down Trump's plan to implement a sweeping, high-tariff scheme not seen since the 1930s.
After that decision, the Trump administration announced in March it was launching formal investigations targeting excess industrial capacity and forced-labour regulations in China and other nations.
It isn't clear if the US administration is also nearing its decision in its probes of the other economies that it announced it was investigating for unfair trade practices, including the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Norway, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, South Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Mexico, Japan and India.
The White House and the US Trade Representative's office did not respond to requests for comment on the tariff deliberations, which Bloomberg News reported earlier Monday. The Chinese embassy in Washington also did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The excess industrial capacity probe of China was initiated under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows the president to levy tariffs against nations that discriminate against US companies or commerce.
The new tariff would come on top of existing tariffs on China
The people familiar with the deliberations stressed that Trump could still change his mind on the new tariff on China.
It would come on top of tariffs of 10 per cent to 12.5 per cent announced last month for 60 economies around the globe that the Trump administration accused of failing to effectively enforce a ban on goods produced with forced labour.
Many countries, including China, protested that move, which took effect just as the clock ran out on temporary tariffs Trump had turned to after the Supreme Court in February struck down sweeping “reciprocal” tariffs he levied on nearly every US trade partner.
China last month pushed back against claims of overcapacity, anticipating that the US would soon release results of its probe and impose new tariffs.
Massive capacity in a slew of Chinese industries, from autos to solar panels, cement and steel manufacturing, has drawn increased attention from Beijing's trading partners in recent years.
Although China's own leaders have prioritised rebalancing the economy, slowing domestic demand has prompted companies to expand into overseas markets. Surging exports pushed China's trade surplus to a record of nearly USD 1.2 trillion last year.
China has never sought a large trade surplus, the Ministry of Commerce said in a recently published report titled “China's Position on the So-called Excess Capacity Issue.”
The deliberations come as the Treasury Department on Monday warned countries doing trade with Iran that new secondary sanctions are in the pipeline aimed at ostracising nations that continue to do business with Tehran. China is Iran's biggest trade partner.
Washington has promised the new sanctions would put even more pressure on an Iranian economy already battered by previous sanctions and a US naval blockade as the US and Israeli war against Iran nears the six-month mark.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's announcement Monday provided little detail and did not name which countries could face secondary sanctions.

Topline
Ontario Premier Doug Ford blasted President Donald Trump in a searing press conference Monday, calling him a “bully” and “dictator” as the U.S. and Canada exchange increasingly stark blows amid a trade war that has resulted in tit-for-tat tariffs.
Key Facts
Ford told reporters Monday that Trump is a “bully” and “dictator” who he would not “take any advice off,” referring to the president as the “king of bankruptcies,” a jab at the six business bankruptcies Trump’s casinos and hotels filed for in the 1990s and 2000s.
When asked about a comment he made on the radio Monday morning in which he told Trump, “Kiss my a–,” Ford doubled down during the press conference, adding, “I have a lot of real estate on my a–, so he has a lot of room to kiss my a–.”
Ford said Trump is underestimating Canada, which is “all in” on an “economic war,” and said, “We need to throw everything and the kitchen sink at them.
Ford’s comments came after a Truth Social post in which Trump said the U.S. “has been carrying Canada for decades,” with the president later calling Ford a “Flunky.”
Trump threatened Monday to slap 50% tariffs on all cars, trucks and parts from Canada starting next year.
Ford also said red states in the U.S. would be “hit hard” by Canada’s retaliatory tariffs.
What To Watch For
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Saturday Canada will enact dollar-for-dollar tariffs against the U.S. starting Sept. 8. Sectors targeted by those tariffs include steel, agriculture, dairy and electronics, according to Carney.
Key Background
The broader trade war between the U.S. and Canada is rooted in Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs announced last year, when a 25% universal tariff was placed against Canada and Mexico. However, Trump briefly exempted the majority of trade by delaying penalties for goods compliant with the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement. The Trump administration declined to renew the deal during a joint review in July, opting against a 16-year extension over concerns it would not rebalance trade deficits or improve manufacturing jobs in the U.S. The trade war reached a fever pitch this month as U.S.-Canada trade talks failed last Friday. Following the collapse of negotiations, the Trump administration imposed 50% tariffs on some Canadian products and impacted roughly $20 billion in Canadian exports, according to CNBC. Carney then announced Canada’s dollar-for-dollar tariffs, telling reporters Saturday, “You're at war when you get attacked. We got attacked.”

Ecuador intelligence chief and five Americans killed in Kenya helicopter crash
- Published
Ecuador's intelligence chief and his wife have been killed in a helicopter that crashed at Mount Ololokwe in central Kenya.
Michele Sensi-Contugi, 44, and his wife, fashion designer Stephany Hollihan, 42, were among the group of seven people - six tourists and the pilot - killed in Samburu county at approximately 09:13 (06:13 GMT) on Wednesday.
Five of victims were Americans, a US State Department spokesperson said. The Reuters news agency reports that Hollihan also held US citizenship.
The Kenya Civil Aviation Authority (KCAA) said the helicopter was on a scenic flight from a wildlife conservancy in Loisaba to Ewaso Nyiro, a river that flows along several national reserves.
Samburu county is a popular tourist destination with many private wildlife conservancies and is renowned for its stunning landscape.
Images from the scene show smoke at the wooded crash site on Mount Ololokwe, as members of the Kenya Red Cross approach the still-burning wreckage.
Ecuador's President Daniel Noboa named Sensi-Contugo director of the country's Centre of Strategic Intelligence (CIES) in January 2024.
The office of the president and Ecuador's National Assembly expressed their condolences over his death and that of Hollihan.
The Italian-Ecuadorean businessman had had close links to Noboa even before he was chosen to lead the intelligence service and was considered a close ally of the president.
Shortly before being named head of the CIES, he had served for four months as a minister in his cabinet.
Noboa has declared three days of national mourning starting on Thursday.
Newspapers in Ecuador have also run obituaries of Hollihan. The Guayaquil-based designer founded Sensi Studio, a brand praised for incorporating traditional Ecuadorean elements and materials in its designs.
Lady Lori Helicopters, which operated the Eurocopter EC130 B4 aircraft, said it was "deeply saddened" by the accident.
"Our deepest sympathies are with the guests, crew, their families and loved ones, and all those affected by this tragic accident," a statement read.
According to a memo seen by the BBC's US partner CBS News, external one of the Americans killed in the crash was NBCUniversal journalist José Alberto Suárez.
In the memo, NBCUniversal called Suárez "a deeply respected leader and beloved friend and colleague.
"José was an exceptional colleague and mentor to many," the memo read.
Miami restaurateur Roger Duarte was among the Americans killed in the crash, according to local and US media.
Commenting on his death on X, US Rep Carlos Antonio Gimenez wrote: "Our prayers are with their loved ones during this incredibly difficult time. May their memories be a blessing."
The other victims have not yet been identified.
Helicopter crashes are not uncommon in Kenya.
In February, a helicopter crash in the Rift Valley county of Nandi killed six people, including a member of parliament.
In 2024, the military chief, Gen Francis Omondi Ogolla, died after an army helicopter that was carrying 11 people crashed in the west of the country, with only two survivors.
In June 2021 at least 10 soldiers were killed when their helicopter crashed while landing near the capital, Nairobi.

Tehran has vowed to retaliate against any country that cooperates with the US attempt to impose fresh sanctions against Iran in what the Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, has billed as “the single greatest financial offensive ever marshalled against an adversary”.
In advance of the US announcement, the United Arab Emirates, Iran’s single biggest trading partner in the Middle East, announced it was ending all trade with Iran, a move Tehran believes was coordinated between Washington and the UAE.
The US has said it will impose sanctions on any country or entity trading with Iran – what is known as secondary sanctions.
The test of the US rhetoric is likely to rest on whether countries such as India, China and Russia believe continued trade with Iran would lead to credible US reprisals against their economies. China has for decades been the main importer of Iranian oil.
In May, the US threatened sanctions against Chinese refiners and the banks funding them, but the Chinese commerce department directed Chinese firms to ignore US warnings over Iranian oil imports, saying the threats were illegitimate and deploying for the first time a government statute designed to render US sanctions ineffective in Chinese jurisdictions.
The US had imposed sanctions on Hengli Petrochemical (Dalian) Refinery Co in April but Washington largely backed off as Donald Trump realised he was risking a wider trade and tariff war with China that the US was likely to lose.
This time the Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson, Lin Jian, again said China opposed unilateral sanctions that lacked basis in international law and China believed that military means, sanctions and pressure tactics were not the solution.
However, unlike in May, Iran’s oil shipments to Asia have already all but ended due to the effectiveness of a US naval blockade of Iranian ports, driving the cost of those cargoes to the highest levels in years. Last week, Iran’s central bank governor, Abdolnaser Hemmati, admitted his country’s crude exports had “virtually stopped” due to the US blockade.
The White House believes the Iranian economy is as a result once again on the brink of collapse due to hyperinflation and lack of foreign exchange income caused by the US blockade of oil exports. The rial was trading at 1.992 million per dollar on the unregulated market on Monday, down 4.5% since the US president announced a “crushing economic operation” against Tehran last week.
But Iran has been under some kind of US economic maximum pressure campaign for more than 20 years and so far survived.
Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, said Tehran would respond with an “earthquake-like” retaliation if Washington proceeded with the proposed measures. He also warned Iran’s Gulf neighbours against joining the US sanctions campaign.
“If the countries surrounding Iran join the Americans in their economic war, not a drop of oil will leave the Persian Gulf and the strait of Hormuz,” Rezaei said, adding that Iran would also target other oil export routes from the Gulf.
Shipping through the strait remained severely disrupted over the weekend, putting further pressure on global energy markets.
Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, dismissed the expected sanctions as a sign of US desperation, arguing that the measures would fail to defeat Tehran. He said the US had shifted from military operations to what he described as “the same old plans”.
Reza Nasri, an international lawyer with links to the Iranian foreign ministry, said: “The announcement is not a measure against Iran. It is a claim of jurisdiction over the world, and every sovereign state on Earth is its real addressee. Iran is merely the occasion. The demand that no country allow its own banks, businesses, airports or ship registries to engage in lawful trade with another country is aimed at everyone else. Sovereignty itself is the target.”
Esmail Baghaei, the Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson, said: “Repeating methods that have previously proven to fail will not produce any different results, except that it shows the extent to which America is hostile and spiteful towards each and every Iranian, because it knows very well that the effects of these sanctions will affect ordinary Iranian citizens.”
He added: “Obliging or intimidating other countries to stop or limit their trade relations with another country means violating the most important foundation of international relations and the most fundamental pillar of the United Nations charter, which is respect for the national sovereignty of countries.”
Hassan Ahmadian, a professor of west Asian studies at the University of Tehran, said: “There isn’t a single new sanction. Everything in Iran has been under primary and secondary sanctions since 2018. Since these sanctions failed to achieve the goals the US and Israel wanted, both sides turned to military action. The big fanfare about an ‘economic war’ is really just a public admission of a major step backward. After failing militarily, Washington is clearly stepping back to square one – the economy.”
He said Iran had been signalling in recent weeks that US economic warfare was no longer an acceptable option for Tehran and it would prefer going to war rather than standing idly by in the face of the US implementing the blockade. He said this involved “Iranian calculations related to military capabilities, the American domestic situation, and the Iranian domestic situation”.
Last Thursday Bessent claimed in an interview with CNBC that “the US will lead the Islamic Republic of Iran to collapse with the toughest sanctions in history”.
The Treasury secretary claimed “the US government is asking its allies and the rest of the world to stop trading with Iran”. He added that the US “will use all its power against anyone who does not comply with this demand”.
“Either the countries are with us or against us,” Bessent said. “It is time for our allies and the rest of the world to decide, and we will destroy the economy of this regime.” Writing in the Financial Times on Sunday, he said: “Total financial isolation can obviate the need for American force while enlarging the sphere of freedom for our allies. Those who sever Iran’s remaining financial and commercial connectivity will reinvigorate their own. They will deepen their access to global capital, reinforce confidence in their markets and attain the standing they seek in the world economy.”
But China and Russia have so far shown no interest in succumbing to US pressure.
By coincidence, Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir, flew to Tehran on Monday where he will explore the opportunity to revive talks on the stalled memorandum of understanding signed in June, but not implemented either by Iran or the US largely due to a dispute about whether the memorandum granted Iran interim control over shipping in the strait of Hormuz.

Great camera. Strong battery life. Solid performance. Qi2 25W support. Slick contextual AI features.
TIRED
Not much is new. eSIM only in the US. Secure face unlock still doesn’t work in the dark.
The hot pink Hibiscus color is dazzling, but is Google’s 11th-generation Pixel just another iterative upgrade, or does it dial things up to 11? Diving beneath the surface, we find a slightly better chipset and camera, faster wireless charging, a fresh batch of AI features, and not much else. Don’t get me wrong: This is a slick smartphone, perhaps the best Android phone for folks who are comfortable with Google and Gemini AI, but it’s only a very slight improvement over last year’s Pixel 10.
Although it lands alongside the Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL, the Pixel 11 shares more in common with the new Pro Fold (review coming soon). The Pro models' more powerful camera system, with the gimmicky, glowing HiLight LED, is what sets them apart. The base model storage has finally jumped up to a more practical 256 GB, but that means the starting price of the Pixel 11 is $100 more than the 10 at $899 (not technically a price bump since the 256 GB model of the Pixel 10 was the same price).
Refinement has been the pattern in smartphones for the last few years, and the Pixel 11 does nothing to buck that trend. If you’ve got a 3-year-old handset and you’re in the market for a new phone, the Pixel 11 should be in the conversation, but if you’re looking for a justification to upgrade from last year’s Pixel 10, you won’t find it here.
Minor Makeover
Photograph: Simon Hill
The instantly recognizable design has been slightly refined; most notably, the pill-shaped camera bump is thinner and all-glass. Stick a case on the Pixel 11, and it will lie flat on a desk. It sports the same satin finish on the recycled aluminum frame and gloss finish on the glass back as last year’s phone, but with some fun new colors.
I was delighted to get Hibiscus (otherwise known as hot pink), but there’s also a more subtle Pistachio (warm green), and the usual Frost (white) and Obsidian (black). I’m sad they cut Indigo (surely everyone’s favorite from last year). Like Apple, Google seems to save the fun colors for the regular Pixel, and the Pros look more muted.
Despite a 6.3-inch screen, this is what passes for a small phone nowadays. Switching from last year's Pixel 10 Pro XL, I really appreciated how easy it was to handle the Pixel 11 one-handed. It’s a little thick, but it feels good in hand and has almost the same profile as the Pro, so you can use cases interchangeably. And I do recommend snagging a Pixel 11 case; I already scuffed the paintwork when I dropped it on the beach.
The screen is the same as last year’s: an excellent 6.3-inch OLED display with a 1080 x 2424-pixel resolution and refresh rates of 60 or 120 Hz. It’s a shame Google didn’t upgrade to a variable refresh rate (1 to 120 Hz) since it can save battery life. It also defaults to 60 Hz, and you have to dip into the Display settings to toggle on the smoother 120 Hz. The display is plenty bright with a 3,000-nit peak brightness; I never found myself squinting. Side by side with the Pro, it’s not quite as bright or sharp, and it has larger bezels, but you have to look closely to see the difference.
The fingerprint unlock is as good as any, but Google’s Face Unlock still doesn't work in the dark, which will annoy any iPhone defectors. US buyers will also have to do without a SIM slot, as the Pixel 11 is eSIM-only stateside. Physical SIM cards make switching between phones more straightforward, but phone makers and carriers have made that process smoother with eSIMs than in the past. Sure, it’s much easier to pop a card in than to go through your carrier when traveling abroad, but setting up an international eSIM isn't that complex. Both have benefits, but with US phones and carriers embracing eSIM over the past couple of years, it's become a nonissue.
Power Up
The new chip, Google’s Tensor G6, is supposed to deliver 20 percent gains in power efficiency, 25 percent faster browsing, and 15 percent faster app loading. The Pixel 11 has 12 GB of RAM and 256 or 512 GB of storage. For everyday use, it feels fast and responsive. I had no issues with loading apps or scrolling web pages, and the camera app feels a bit faster. Compared with my Pixel 10 Pro XL, I also noticed the Pixel 11 notified and loaded video from my Nest video doorbell a second or two faster.
I put it through its paces with the challenging mobile game Wuthering Waves. It was playable, but the action stuttered, and even on the Balanced (graphics and performance) setting, there were dropped frames aplenty during combat. After an hour, the Pixel 11 was warm, and the battery went from 40 to 26 percent. Less demanding games, like Mini Metro and Alto’s Odyssey, were fine, but dedicated gamers should still look elsewhere.
The 4,985-mAh battery is a disappointing 15-mAh jump over the Pixel 10, but Google claims battery life has improved 25 percent from 24 hours to 30 hours. I’m not sure it’s quite that much based on my first week of testing, but the Pixel 11 has seen me through very busy days without hitting empty, though I still think daily charging will be the norm for most folks.
The Pixel 11 charges at 30 watts wired (cable but no charger included), but support for Qi2 25W enables faster wireless charging. I recommend buying a Qi2 wireless charger. The magnetic Pixelsnap (Google's version of Apple's MagSafe on iPhones) feels a touch stronger than the one in the 10-series, and it’s such a handy feature that saves you from fumbling with cables. Google has also expanded the screensaver so you can have a multiple swipe function on the nightstand, including clock, weather, photos, charging status, and smart home controls.
Google has also switched to a MediaTek modem in the Pixel 11. I wouldn’t normally mention a modem, but the Samsung variant Google used in last year’s 10 series was prone to draining the battery and not holding a signal terribly well. Anecdotally, the Pixel 11 does better in a few spots where I’ve traditionally had trouble with my Pixel 10 Pro XL, which is great news for when you want to use your phone for calls. Your mileage may vary.
AI Everywhere
Photograph: Simon Hill
Google’s phones have always been about software over hardware, but the real-world value of AI features comes down to context. If I have to go digging or remember that a feature exists, I probably won’t get much value from it. This is why Google weaves its AI into everything, rather than applying it as a layer on top. The latest Gemini Intelligence features extend Google’s lead in this space.
Rambler improves the Pixel’s voice-to-text, cutting ums and ahs and letting you draft messages conversationally. I didn’t like it as much as my colleague, but I’m not really a speech-to-text guy, and I have a Scottish accent that it sometimes picks up wrong. I use the Pixel’s Recorder app a lot and love it for instantly transcribing my interviews, but Rambler doesn’t show the text as you talk like Recorder does; everything pops up after you’re done, which I don’t like as much.
AI overviews pop up right there in the Messages app when someone texts with a meet-up request, and you can add it to your calendar, or if they have a restaurant suggestion, you can tap to open it directly in Maps. Gemini can also dig details like flight numbers out of your Gmail to share via Messages if you let it. This is quite handy.
Fans of Circle to Search will be glad to know you don’t even have to snap a photo anymore; you can open the camera app, hold down the nav bar, and circle anything in the viewfinder to get info on it. You can also get location-based suggestions on the lock and home screen, such as a shortcut to your loyalty card in Google Wallet when you’re in a relevant store or recommendations for what to order at a restaurant from Maps.
There’s nothing groundbreaking here, but features like Call Screen for screening spam calls and Now Playing for surfacing the name of the song you can hear are still there, and those are the kinds of things that I miss when I switch away from a Pixel phone.
AI is firmly embedded in Google’s apps, and there’s no switch to turn it off completely, but you can choose to turn off Gemini, cut its access to apps like Photos and Messages, and turn off features like Circle to Search. Most of the camera app AI options are exactly that: options. But if this all sounds gimmicky and the idea of an AI-infused phone gives you the creeps, the Pixel line is not for you.
Camera Magician
The triple-lens rear camera is one of the top reasons to buy the Pixel 11. The camera feels faster, with less processing delay than the Pixel 10, and you can snap a shot and instantly load it into the gallery. Spec-wise, it’s almost identical, with a 48-megapixel main camera, 13-megapixel ultrawide, and 10.8-megapixel telephoto for 5x optical zoom. The main camera sensor is larger, enabling slightly better low-light performance, and the digital zoom capability is up from 20x to 30x. The 10.5-megapixel front-facing camera is the same.
Screenshot: Simon Hill
Everything works beautifully. Most people probably only ever use the main camera and the selfie camera, and reviewers can get too far into the weeds, but the bottom line is that you don’t need a particularly skilled hand or eye to snap great photos with the Pixel 11. I really appreciate the telephoto lens. I rarely have a use for the ultrawide, but the telephoto is great for zooming in from a distance, and though the 30x zoom is digitally enhanced by combining multiple images, there’s no generative AI at work, so you get a real image.
The camera app is feature-packed if you want to dive in. The most notable new features are the Camera Looks, which are like filters you select before you snap a shot. Phone cameras are typically tuned a certain way—Google’s phones tend to be punchy and high-contrast with realistic colors, while Samsung saturates colors and Apple prefers brighter images—but Camera Looks lets you tweak that to opt for warmer colors or dial up the shadows.
Photograph: Simon Hill
Google Pixel 11, main camera
Magic Capture is a clever new feature that lets you hold your phone up at a party or event and record video and select still shots simultaneously, without having to watch through the viewfinder. It’s a nice way to be more in the moment, and a safer way to hand your phone off to Mum and maybe get decent photos back.
No one really needs to upgrade their phone every year or two. It’s only by skipping a few releases that you’ll feel a real difference, and this is especially true for Google's phones because so much of what makes them special is on the software side, and many of those features will make it onto older phones too, though they might take a while.
For slick software features and a camera that’s easy to get great results from, the Pixel 11 is tough to beat in this bracket. If you want performance, both the Samsung Galaxy S26 and the Apple iPhone 17 are superior. Unless you’re a keen photographer, I don’t see a compelling case for paying more to get a Pro model. The Pixel 11 is the value sweet spot in Google’s new lineup, at least until the A-series next year.
Simon Hill is a senior writer for WIRED and has been testing and writing about technology for around 20 years. You can find his previous work at Business Insider, Reviewed, TechRadar, Android Authority, USA Today, Digital Trends, and many other places. Apple’s four-pack of second-generation AirTags is down to $79 (originally $99) at Amazon and at Target, which is the bundle’s lowest price yet. You can get an AirTag for $24 right now piecemeal, but getting four together as a set is a way to save even more. Why pay $96 for four when you can save $17? It felt like we had to wait longer for the cost to fall this much for first-gen AirTags, so it’s a little surprising to see the newer, better model available for less.
Apple’s four-pack of second-gen AirTags is $20 off
Big savings on the latest. We also found deals on Elgato’s biggest Stream Deck, a handy Switch 2 accessory, and more.
Apple AirTag (second-gen)
Apple’s latest AirTags features an upgraded ultra-wideband chip for more precise location tracking, a noticeably louder speaker, and an expanded Bluetooth range.
The second-generation AirTag looks identical to the first-generation AirTag. All of its upgrades are inside, and primarily include spec improvements to let you more easily find it. It includes boosted speaker volume, longer range, and overall better tracking capabilities. My colleague Victoria Song had a much easier time tracking the latest AirTag on different floors compared to the older model. Read our review.
Some other great Verge-approved deals
- The biggest Stream Deck that Elgato makes is down to its lowest price since Amazon’s Prime Day in late June. Originally $249.99 for the gadget with 32 programmable keys, it’s $50 off at Amazon and Best Buy, totaling $199.99. Each key can be customized within Elgato’s desktop software for Windows or macOS, letting you set not just the command that executes when you press it, but also the imagery that displays on the key. You can assign simple functions to keys, like muting a mic or turning off a webcam. The integrations run deep, though, letting you create multi-button macros that run with a single button press.
- If you own a Switch 2 but still need a way to keep your original Switch’s Joy-Con recharged, there’s a great accessory that can charge Joy-Con for both systems and is half off at Amazon. Fastsnail’s charging dock that includes a USB-C-to-A cable and four Joy-Con charging sections is $6.99 (was already a great deal at $13.99) when you use the code NMSV9HX3, which the community at Slickdeals surfaced.
- Backbone’s One controller is one of the best ways to play games on your phone. It offers a comfortable, complete set of controls, whether you’re playing native phone games, or streaming console or PC games. Normally about $100, the Backbone One PlayStation Edition that works seamlessly on iOS with Sony’s Remote Play app is just $27 in used condition at eBay. The seller VIPOUTLET claims that the product is in “fair/good condition” and may have some blemishes, and it includes a 60-day warranty. WildBrain, the Canadian animation studio that owns and manages a huge library of family entertainment including Teletubbies, Strawberry Shortcake, Yo Gabba Gabba! and Inspector Gadget, has acquired 100% of Personality AI, a generative AI startup focused on bringing character experiences to life.
The immediate purchase price was USD $11 million in cash plus 1 million WildBrain shares. The company didn’t disclose the value of the shares, which closed on the Toronto Stock Exchange Monday at CAD $1.47. Personality stakeholders will receive another $2 million on the first anniversary of closing, payable in up to 1 million WildBrain shares with any balance in cash.
The deal terms also call for additional performance-based cash consideration up to U.S. $56 million in aggregate tied to Personality AI’s business hitting certain revenue targets in 2027, 2028 and 2029 — a move to align the interests of Personality AI’s management, led by founded and CEO John Goscha, with WildBrain shareholders and incentivize continued growth.
Watch on Deadline
Goscha will join WildBrain’s executive leadership team as EVP, Personality AI, reporting to WildBrain president and chief executive Josh Scherba. WildBrain is bringing in Personality’s team of experts in app and product creation under Goscha.
The deal adds a new core capability and category to WildBrain’s global licensing, franchise management and content production, introducing scalable character experiences that can be built once and deployed anywhere. The goal is to enable deeper consumer engagement with entertainment IP beyond traditional licensing and content.
“Our strategy at WildBrain is centred on building long-term value by activating IP on a global scale. As fan engagement continues to evolve, we believe interactive AI experiences represent an important new opportunity for brands to connect with audiences in meaningful ways,” Scherba said. “Personality AI enables more continuous interaction between fans and brands, strengthening our ability to deliver end-to-end franchise solutions to partners” and IP owners.
Personality AI shares “WildBrain’s commitment to children’s wellbeing, which is why we employ rigorous safety standards to ensure appropriate, authentic and trustworthy content and experiences for kids, parents and IP owners alike. I look forward to working with Josh and the WildBrain management team to bring our capabilities to more brands, platforms and audiences around the world,” said Goscha, who launched the AI platform in 2025.
An example of Personality AI’s work includes a generative platform for Amazon Kids+ last year. Projects include Hey Peppa Pig, an interactive voice experience developed with Hasbro that lets kids talk with Peppa Pig through games and activities inspired by the brand’s official series.
WildBrain’s licensing division will handle Personality AI deals with third parties.

Diego Maradona’s ‘Hand of God’ football sells for US$3.35 million at US auction
The ball used by the Argentinian to score his infamous 1986 World Cup goal against England had been estimated to fetch US$10 million
The football with which Diego Maradona scored his “Hand of God” goal against England at the 1986 World Cup has sold at auction for US$3.35 million.
The Dallas-based auction house had placed a US$2.5 million starting price on the Adidas Azteca ball.
Maradona scored twice in Argentina’s quarter-final victory over England on June 22, 1986 at Estadio Azteca in Mexico City.
He controversially punched the opener beyond England goalkeeper Peter Shilton before scoring a superb individual effort, later voted “Goal of the Century”.
The Argentina playmaker, who died aged 60 in November 2020, claimed his contentious first goal was scored “a little with the head of Maradona and a little with the hand of God”.

Mark Zuckerberg has amassed a real estate portfolio that has easily exceeded $100 million, but, until recently, he kept it within the confines of the US.
A spokesperson for Zuckerberg confirmed to Business Insider that he and his wife, Priscilla Chan, purchased a 200-year-old castle in Waterford County, Ireland.
"Mark and his family are excited to continue caring for this historic home and look forward to spending time in Ireland, where Meta maintains its international headquarters," Zuckerberg's spokesperson, Brian Baker, said in an email statement to Business Insider.
The purchase price is unknown; however, The Irish Times, which first reported on the sale, estimates Zuckerberg paid between 20 and 30 million euros — or between $23 million and $35 million. A drop in the bucket for the Meta CEO, who has an estimated net worth of $192.4 billion, according to Forbes.
The castle is just the latest addition to Zuckerberg's portfolio, which includes a doomsday bunker in Hawaii and a waterfront mansion in Miami.
See what other Zuckerberg properties are in his portfolio.
Zuckerberg owns a residential compound in Palo Alto.
It's no surprise that a tech titan has more than one property in Silicon Valley. The Meta CEO owns five homes in the Crescent Park neighborhood of Palo Alto.
He gave viewers a rare peek inside one of them in 2016; the house is even tricked out with a "custom-made artificially intelligent assistant," according to CNBC. The home is only a 10-minute drive from the Meta HQ in Menlo Park.
He bought the first Crescent Park property in May 2011 for $7 million.
Architectural Digest described it as a "'no frills abode" that chooses function over extravagance. Zuckerberg then spent over $43 million on the four homes surrounding his original residence in Crescent Park, The Wall Street Journal reported.
He sold his San Francisco townhouse in 2022 for a reported $31 million.
The four-bedroom, four-bathroom home is located near San Francisco's Dolores Park. He and his wife, Priscilla Chan, reportedly spent $10 million to purchase the townhouse in 2010.
At the time of the sale in 2022, it was the largest residential real estate deal in the city.
He bought two adjacent estates on the shore of Lake Tahoe around 2019.
Lake Tahoe is a popular vacation destination for wealthy Californians in both summer and winter, and Zuckerberg and his family are no exception.
The tax records of the two properties — known as Carousel Estate and Brushwood Estate — display the same address as tax records of other properties linked to Zuckerberg, according to documents viewed by BI.
Zuckerberg reportedly paid $59 million for both properties.
At 5,322 square feet, the Brushwood Estate features six bedrooms, five baths, and two half baths, according to SF Gate. Inside are high-beamed ceilings and picture windows; outside are lush trees, a private dock, and a hot tub. There's also a 2,293-square-foot guesthouse.
The Meta exec owns over 1,200 acres of land in Hawaii.
It's unclear exactly how many acres of land Zuckerberg currently owns on Kauai, but he began buying up a region of the island back in 2014.
Business Insider tracked down at least 1,200 acres between 17 parcels of land that have the same tax address as other properties mentioned above, but are owned by LLCs including Kahu'aina Holdings LLC and Pila'a International LLC.
The 1,200 acres include about 750 acres he reportedly paid $100 million in 2014 for. That encompasses a more than 350-acre span of land on Pila'a Beach.
His plans for Koolau Ranch seem to be in preparation for the worst case scenario.
Another part of Zuckerberg's Hawaii holdings is the nearly 600 acres of land on Kauai's North Shore that reportedly cost him around $53 million in 2021.
On one of his Hawaiian parcels, Zuckerberg is reportedly building a huge compound that's said to include a 5,000-square-foot underground bunker with an escape hatch. It's been dubbed Koolau Ranch, and Wired reported that buying the land and creating the compound cost the executive an estimated $270 million.
In March 2025, he purchased a 15,000-square-foot mansion in Washington, DC.
As Silicon Valley continues to infiltrate Washington, DC, Zuckerberg established a residence in the US capital, Politico said. The home that's reportedly his new pad is situated in Massachusetts Avenue Heights, not far from the Naval Observatory and the Washington National Cathedral, according to Builder magazine.
Zuckerberg kept the purchase private, Politico said. The mansion in question was sold for $23 million in cash. It was designed by local firm Robert Gurney Architect and sits on about one acre of property.
Business Insider was unable to independently confirm that Zuckerberg purchased the property.
Zuckerberg is also moving down the street from Jeff Bezos after reportedly buying property in Miami.
Mark Zuckerberg is reportedly adding a second East Coast property to his portfolio after buying a home in Miami, according to The Wall Street Journal.
Zuckerberg is said to be purchasing a waterfront mansion on Indian Creek, an exclusive island in South Florida that's home to Jeff Bezos, Carl Icahn, and Jared Kushner.
It's unclear how much this off-market deal was worth, but an empty lot next door to Bezos sold for $105 million in 2025.
Zuckerberg went international and bought a 200-year-old castle in Ireland.
In his first reported international buy, Zuckerberg purchased a three-story Gothic castle on 440 acres.
The castle, named Strancally Castle in Waterford County, Ireland, is about 140 miles south of Meta's international headquarters in Dublin. It was built between 1825 and 1835.
Zuckerberg bought the castle from the cofounder of the London-based private investment firm RAB Capital for an undisclosed amount. The Irish Times estimates the castle sold for between $23 million and $35 million.
Hillary Hoffower contributed to an earlier version of this story.
Correction: February 26, 2026 — An earlier version of this story incorrectly stated the previous owners of Zuckerberg's Miami home.

A surprise inspection at a prison hospital in Mandya, Karnataka, revealed special treatment provided to an undertrial prisoner. The prisoner was found staying in a special ward with a girlfriend, despite not requiring hospitalization according to visiting medical staff guidelines. The inspection was conducted by visiting judges, exposing security breaches within the facility. Officials from the prison department stated that responsibility for guarding undertrial prisoners undergoing medical treatment lies with the local police department rather than the prison administration.
A political confrontation has intensified at Jadavpur University in Kolkata following reports of anti-national wall graffiti and poster displays inside the Arts Division boys' hostel premises. Concerning photographic representations and videos were submitted through official grievance channels, highlighting controversial artwork, including slogans supporting Palestine and hailing a fallen Naxal leader. The ongoing friction involves opposing student organizations operating both within and outside the university campus. University authorities and education officials have been directed to investigate these activities, while concerns have been raised regarding the absence of CCTV cameras, national symbols, and security protocols on the campus.
The Allahabad High Court has rejected a petition filed by a class 11 Muslim student from Tagore Public School in Prayagraj seeking permission to wear a hijab with her prescribed school uniform. A division bench comprising Justice JJ Munir and Justice Indrajeet Shukla observed that wearing a hijab cannot be established as an essential religious practice of Islam. The court upheld the school management's authority to enforce a uniform dress code, emphasizing that personal choices cannot alter prescribed uniforms and that school policies must remain unbiased. The court noted that the petitioner failed to provide proof establishing hijab as an essential practice of the faith. Referring to similar past rulings, including from Karnataka, the court reaffirmed that school administrations hold total independence to determine dress code regulations to maintain uniformity among students unless religious sentiments are unjustifiably harmed.
A bizarre scene unfolded in Kanpur, Uttar Pradesh, as a crowd rushed to collect discarded chocolates dumped in the garbage by a factory. Visuals show people filling their bags with the chocolates, which had expired in 2024. The incident has raised major food safety concerns over the potential health risks associated with collecting and consuming expired discarded food items.
A fresh food safety controversy has erupted after a maggot was found inside a cake dessert from a Paul Bakery outlet in Pune. The customer shared a video of the incident on social media, prompting calls for an inspection by the Food and Drugs Administration. This comes shortly after a similar incident at the chain's Gurugram outlet, where a live worm was discovered inside a sandwich. While the bakery had issued an apology and launched an internal probe following the Gurugram incident, no official statement has been released regarding the Pune case. The Maharashtra Food and Drugs Administration has stated that suo moto cognizance will be taken to investigate the matter.

Normal deliveries are declining and C-section deliveries remain high at the Government Hospital for Women and Children at Kottaparamba in Kozhikode City, Keralam.
According to the Health department, there were a total of 5,201 deliveries (2,729 normal and 2,472 C-section) in 2020-21. This number came down to 2,238 (1,387 normal and 851 C-section) in 2025-26. A large number of people from the urban areas of Kozhikode are dependant on this hospital.
The data also reveal that between 2020-21 and 2022-23, a high number of deliveries were in the C-section category. In 2020-21, of the 5,201 deliveries, 2,472 were C-section; in 2021-22, of the 3,552 deliveries, 1,841 were C-section; and in 2022-23, of the 2,205 deliveries, 1,148 were C-section.
Though there were fewer C-section deliveries between 2023-24 and 2025-26, the percentage remained higher than the ideal population-level rate, between 10% and 15%, as suggested by the World Health Organisation. It is even higher than the national average of 21.5%, claims Satheesh Parannur, chairman of the Kozhikode-based rights organisation, Pouravakasha Samrakshana Samithi, who gathered the data through a Right to Information Act (RTI) query.
Mr. Parannur says that between 2020-21 and 2023-24, the number of total deliveries came down by 61% from 5,201 to 2,019. Though this number slightly went up to 2,238 in 2025-26, it was fewer than what was reported in 2020.
The RTI data show that in-patient admission dropped from 8,315 to 4,683 between 2020-21 and 2023-24. The next year, 5,089 people were admitted. The number again dropped to 4,838 in 2025-26. Meanwhile, a high number of people are seeking outpatient (OP) treatment. In 2020-21, a total of 81,329 people sought OP treatment and in 2024-25, this went up to 1,55,257 and slightly declined to 1,50,305 in 2025-26.
Inquiry sought
Mr. Parannur claims that though a large number of people could be approaching the hospital for medical check-up and medicines, at least some are not willing to get admitted there for deliveries.
He says the Health department should conduct a detailed inquiry into the decline in the number of deliveries and IP admission.

Manga-inspired theme park to be built near Paris
- Published
Three theme parks will be built near Paris as part of a €6bn (£5.13bn) deal agreed between France and Saudi Arabia.
The new development is expected to include a manga-themed park, inspired by the popular Japanese franchise Dragon Ball Z.
French President Emmanuel Macron hailed the move as on a scale not seen "since Disneyland Paris", and added "you know my interest for manga".
An opening date for the parks - which will be built near Cergy-Pontoise - has not set by the Élysée Palace, but they will open in stages and construction is expected to take years.
The project was given the green light during a two-day state visit to France by Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
It stemmed from a previous discussion between Macron and bin Salman about their shared passion for Japanese comics, "in particular Dragon Ball Z," advisers to the president told reporters on Monday.
Macron is known to be a manga fan and earlier this year ended a press briefing with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi by doing a hand gesture from the Dragon Ball series.
The project will be led by Qiddiya Investment Company (QIC) - part of Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund - which previously revealed plans in 2024 to build a Dragon Ball theme park near the country's capital, Riyadh.
According to local reports, the theme parks could be built on the site of the former Mirapolis park in Val-d'Oise, which closed 35 years ago.
But the deal, which the Élysée said would create about 2,000 jobs, also signals deeper ties between France and Saudi Arabia.
The leaders are expected to sign several agreements on health, transport and energy during bin Salman's visit, which will include talks on the US and Iran conflict.
In a post on X on Sunday, Macron said bin Salman's two-day state visit marked an "important milestone".
He added that in the face of challenges in the Middle East, "France and Saudi Arabia have always worked together to promote peace and stability".
Saudi Arabia is aiming to diversify its economy away from its dependence on oil revenues, including via investment in the leisure and entertainment industry.
On Sunday, Macron hosted bin Salman at the closing of the Esports World Cup, which was due to be held in Riyadh but was moved to Paris due to safety concerns over the conflict in the Middle East.

Ask a sixteen-year-old about a social media ban, and you get an answer sharper than most adults arguing about bans. She says, “It doesn’t prepare us for the real world when we will have to deal with these distractions in our life”. The teenager’s response strikes at the core of the ban vs. no ban debate: the necessity to teach and develop self-regulation.
The argument for and against bans
Lawmakers banning social media are working from the angle that if we remove the option altogether, the posting, compulsive scrolling, and ensuing anxiety will go away with it. The opposing argument is that bans prevent self-regulation, built through practice with social media access readily available.
Behavioral science has a fairly precise answer for which of these arguments holds up.
The bans themselves are moving fast and in earnest around the world. Australia was the first country to impose a sweeping ban on social media outright for children under-16 in 2025. Multiple countries in the EU are attempting to follow suit. These decisions to ban social media rest on neuroscientific insights showing that the human brain’s reward circuitry matures years before the prefrontal cortex that reins it in, leaving adolescents genuinely more vulnerable to engineered design working actively to grab their attention. Lawmakers are right to take this seriously.
But are social media bans for teenagers the panacea that they are made out to be?
How social media functions
Social media platforms function like a Skinner box for the modern human: our engagement on them runs on the same reinforcement-based learning as B. F. Skinner’s animal experiments. People on social media post faster exactly when their recent rate of reward, meaning engagement, has been higher. A pattern known as the law of effect, more ‘likes’ leads to more posting. Engagement on every platform runs on an unpredictable schedule; we never know which posts are going to land. Rewards are also hyper-personalised: an unending carousel of perfectly-matched content delivered based on every prior click and scroll.
What makes matters worse is that social media’s unpredictable and personalised rewards are exactly the training that will make children persist on these platforms through the interruption that comes from a ban. When there are multiple ways to get on social media, our behavior distributes itself across those options in proportion to the corresponding rewards. Think of a building with many entrances: remove one entrance without touching the others and people will continue to be able to get in. Underlying behavior does not vanish; It simply reallocates to a different mode. If a regular account stops working, we create a bustling market for fake accounts and new platforms not covered by the bans, effectively pushing teenagers to unregulated corners of the internet.
Perhaps predictably so, Australia’s ban, sweeping on paper, is showing that an estimated 85% of children under-16 are still finding their way onto restricted platforms, through borrowed logins and fake accounts, in a recent study. Bans are leaky. Short of closing every door at once, children will simply find the ones still open. But setting up strict age verification measures can be seen as an infringement upon teenagers’ rights to a private life, one of the reasons France’s newly-enacted social media ban was recently struck down by their Constitution Council.
In any case, let’s assume we manage to pull off the most stringent enforcement of a ban. Children with support systems in place will now have time to learn skills, build hobbies, and form real relationships. What happens to the vulnerable teenagers without a supportive home environment? A ban restricts access, but it does not fix the environment around the child. For teenagers building their sense of autonomy, that restriction in itself can cause harm.
In April, a commentary drawing on a year-long international working group on digital safety noted that bans are “unlikely to be effective” because they overlook how social platforms can be redesigned to build resilience, and instead place all the onus on teenagers. A nuanced solution is one that addresses the problem from both sides.
What, then, can work?
Nobel Prize winner Richard Thaler coined the term ‘nudge’ to describe choices that reshape the environment. When workers avoided retirement plans, a nudge that automatically enrolled them in superannuation funds profoundly impacted their savings. On social media, forcing platforms to batch-deliver notifications into fixed windows instead of letting them arrive at all times, and adding friction to sharing sensitive content, and disabling autoplay and infinite-scroll by default are nudges. We mandate structural corrections on the platform side. A boost, on the other hand, gives young people the skills to manage their own actions instead of complete restriction. The option to use social media stays available. Decision rules around time on social media, and encouraging goal-setting for healthier digital habits are examples of boosts.
Which brings us back to that 16-year-old. She was right: a ban will not teach her self-regulation. But unfettered access to social media where she is left to fend for herself will not work either. What she actually needs is a nuanced alternative, one that is, unfortunately, not on offer in her school’s policy.
(Maithri Sivaraman is an assistant professor at Teachers College, Columbia University. maithri.sivaraman@tc.columbia.edu)

Jimmy Kimmel has opened up about potentially moving on from his ABC late-night show, again.
Kimmel and his wife Molly McNearney, who is also an exec producer of Jimmy Kimmel Live!, appeared on Dax Shepard’s Armchair Expert podcast and the pair were asked about retirement, particularly whether he would regret it once he leaves.
“I know people who’ve been in that situation. It’s funny. People make a big show of like ‘I’m done and I’m tired doing this’, and then they make a lesser comeback trying to do the same thing. That’s always a bummer. I always look at that and go, Oh, is that going to be me?,” he said.
“Do you ever think to yourself, ‘How would I explain this to me at 25 years old, just giving up, just letting it go?’ I know that 25-year-old me will be like, ‘Are you crazy?’ I would have just been so excited to work at a place that had a snack table that was free,” he added.
Watch on Deadline
But Kimmel also said that “it depends on what you mean by retirement”. “I’m never going to stop doing things. It’s just a different scenario,” he said.
McNearney admitted that Kimmel gets asked this question a lot but “I feel like it changes”.
In December, Kimmel signed a one-year extension with Disney – a couple of months after he was pulled off the air over a joke about Charlie Kirk. Insiders at the time briefed that this would likely be his last deal with the company.
But the comedian has debated the topic over recent years. In 2021, he told Howard Stern that he was “vacillating” over whether to sign a new deal and then signed a three-year deal in 2022.
His current deal runs through May 2027.
“Our show has been renewed until May of 2027. Or until the world ends – whichever comes first,” he said on the show after signing the contract. “I was giving a lot of thought and decided I would like to spend less time with my family, and so to our audience here and at home – I’m honored and humbled to be a part of your routine. Whether it’s in bed at night, or during your morning toilet time.”
McNearney said she was “good either way”.
“I would be happy to be done with the show and end it in a great way and do my own next thing. But I do care deeply about that show and the people who work there, and I think the voice is really important right now,” she said. “It definitely appeals to me, for the nervous system of the household, but I also feel Jimmy has like a fly rod in one hand and like a torch in the other right now. It’s like he deserves to go out there and just be on the river and relax, but I also want him to keep fighting, and I feel this sense of desire to not quit because I think what he’s doing is incredibly important right now.”

Nvidia shares set for $280 billion price swing after earnings, options show
NEW YORK, Aug 25 : Options traders are pricing in a $280 billion swing in Nvidia's market value after the company reports second-quarter earnings on Wednesday afternoon, as investors seek fresh insight into the demand driving the technology sector.
The chipmaker's options are pricing in a 5.4 per cent move in either direction on Thursday, a day after the company reports results, which is below the 6.5 per cent move implied ahead of its May earnings report.
The implied move translates to about $280 billion in market capitalization — more than the individual market value of about 90 per cent of S&P 500 constituents. The expected move also remains well below Nvidia's historical average price swing of 7.4 per cent over the last 12 quarters, according to analytics firm Option Research & Technology Services (ORATS).
"That shows some complacency for Nvidia, and it means it's getting more predictable," said Matt Amberson, founder of ORATS.
The relatively modest moves reflect a pattern over the past two years in which actual post-earnings stock swings have frequently fallen short of what options markets had priced in, said Chris Murphy, co-head of derivatives strategy at Susquehanna, a market maker.
"I think the beginning of the AI era when Nvidia was surprising everybody with the huge earnings beats and 10, 15, 20 per cent moves, that's kind of over," said Murphy. "There's just not a huge view that they're going to catch everybody off-guard with some giant beat and the stock's going to really rally."
Nvidia shares on Monday posted a decline for the seventh consecutive trading day, but they have risen 11.7 per cent this year. The S&P 500 is up 11.8 per cent year-to-date and the Philadelphia SE Semiconductor index has risen 61 per cent.
BROADER MARKET PRESSURES
Nvidia's pullback has come at a time of broad market unease. Concerns over rising energy prices and mounting U.S. government debt have pushed Treasury yields higher, with 30-year yields last week hitting a 19-year high and prompting the Treasury to unveil measures aimed at easing market strains.
Reports that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent could draw on the government's nearly $1 trillion Treasury General Account to help fund bond buybacks rather than increase issuance sent the 30-year yield a tad lower on Monday, though it still hovered above 5 per cent.
The recent yield surge has hit growth and technology stocks, pushing Wall Street's major stock indexes lower and heightening focus on Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh's planned speech in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, later this week. It may provide clues on how policymakers view the economic outlook, particularly for interest rates.
Against this backdrop, investors will be watching Nvidia's revenue guidance, chip demand, profit margin and whether major cloud providers continue to increase AI-related capital spending. As the dominant supplier of AI chips, Nvidia is viewed as a bellwether for the broader AI trade.
Nvidia recently partnered with six major financial institutions on financing platforms targeting more than $500 billion for AI infrastructure, highlighting the massive capital required as companies and governments race to build data centers for AI workloads.
Nvidia probably has "a pretty good pulse on the hyperscaler capex trajectory. Return on investment from the hyperscalers is really important," said Will Sterling, chief investment officer at TritonPoint Wealth. "That will dictate whether or not they continue to invest with their capex. If that happens, then I think that'll be beneficial from a risk-on perspective in the entire ecosystem."

The Criterion Collection 4K, Blu-ray and DVD release of Netflix’s KPop Demon Hunters officially has cover art and its release date is nearly two months earlier than first reported.
Released on Netflix on June 20, 2025, KPop Demon Hunters went on to become the most-streamed film in the platform’s history in its three months of release, with 325.1 million views. Directed by Maggie Kang and Chris Applehans, the animated movie musical went on to dominate movie awards season, winning Oscars for Best Animated Feature and Best Original Song (for “Golden”) and won the honors in the same categories at the Golden Globes and the Critics’ Choice Awards.
KPop Demon Hunters’ award-winning ways weren’t done after the 2026 Academy Awards, however. On May 25, KPop Demon Hunters won four American Music Awards, including Song of the Year for “Golden,” which honored The Singing Voices of HUNTR/X: EJAE (Rumi), Audrey Nuna (Mira) and Rei Ami (Zoey). Arden Cho, May Hong and Ji-young Yoo provided the speaking voices of Rumi, Mira and Zoey for the film.
Two days after the film’s big wins at the AMAs, Amazon listed pre-order information for the Criterion Collection version of KPop Demon Hunters for a Dec. 31 release, reported various outlets including Animation Magazine and KTLA.
Recently, however, the Criterion Collection’s retail page listed a new release date for its release of KPop Demon Hunters on physical media, and the disc set is coming a lot sooner than originally reported. As such, three different offerings are available for pre-order on the site for release on Tuesday, Nov. 3.
The 4K + Blu-ray version of KPop Demon Hunters retails for $39.96, while the Blu-ray version retails for $31.96. The Criterion Collection is also offering KPop Demon Hunters on DVD as well, for $23.96.
The Criterion Collection 4K + Blu-Ray Release Of ‘KPop Demon Hunters’ Comes With Bonus Extras
According to the Criterion Collection retail site, the new 4K digital master with a Dolby Atmos soundtrack was approved by directors Maggie Kang and Chris Applehans.
The set includes a 4K UHD disc of KPop Demon Hunters presented in Dolby Vision HDR, plus two Blu-ray discs with the film and special features. The features include a full feature-length animatic with a new introduction by Kang and Appelhans, a new making-of documentary and two video essays by film Taylor Ramos and Tony Zhou (Every Frame a Painting).
The 4K + Blu-ray Criterion Collection release of KPop Demon Hunters also includes lyric videos, an essay by critic Karen Han and collectible postcards of original illustrations by some of the artists who worked on the movie.
KPop Demon Hunters is the second of two high-profile Netflix films to be released as a Criterion Collection title this fall. A director’s cut of Guillermo del Toro’s Frankenstein — retitled Frankenstein: The Reborn Cut will be released.
Several KPop Demon Hunters items have hit store shelves in the past few months, including fashion dolls, role-playing items and other collectible toys, with action figures soon on the way.
Rated PG, KPop Demon Hunters is streaming exclusively on Netflix.

'101-year-old great-grandmother' arrested for selling cannabis in Nigeria
- Published
An elderly woman, who the authorities say is 101, has been arrested in Nigeria for allegedly selling cannabis, in a case that has drawn widespread attention.
Esther Ogunmabo, described as a great-grandmother, was apprehended on Saturday in Ogun state, in the south-west of the country, the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) announced.
Femi Babafemi, the agency's media director, said the centenarian was found with "retail sachets of skunk, a strain of cannabis weighing 90 grams, which she claims she sells to locals".
The NDLEA said the suspect told investigators that she turned to the illicit drug trade after her provisions shop was destroyed by fire. She has been released on bail.
According to the Ndlea, one of her daughters, who lives in Lagos, allegedly arranged for the supply of the substance to her every four days. Ogunmabo is accused of then selling it on in smaller quantities to customers in her community.
Ndlea chief executive Mohamed Marwa directed that the suspect be granted bail and given counselling because of her advanced age.
Ogunmabo’s bail status means she could still be charged for criminal activity.
Her daughter has also been arrested.
Ogunmabo’s arrest came as the Ndlea also reported significant drug seizures along Nigeria's maritime routes.
In Akwa Ibom state, operatives acting on credible intelligence intercepted a wooden boat on the high seas last Friday, which was heading to Cameroon, and arrested three people on board.
More than 42kg of narcotics were recovered from the suspects.
In what the agency described as a milestone, the Ndlea also recorded its first-ever seizure of illicit drugs shipped from Thailand.

Suwadi can barely see five metres in front of him when he steps outside his home in Indonesian Borneo.
Each breath, he says, feels “like smoking a cigarette”.
It has been like this for weeks in Kalimantan, the Indonesian side of Borneo island, where fires have raged across tens of thousands of acres of land, including ancient rainforest, triggering a trans-boundary haze now threatening Malaysia and Singapore.
In West Kalimantan there has been a spike in emergency room visits, with about 5,000 people arriving with respiratory symptoms each week since July, compared with 500 per week in the first half of the year, health ministry data shows.
Children continue to go to school and adults to work, but many are suffering from the unhealthy effects of breathing in thick smoke, constantly. “What about babies, the elderly, and pregnant women who are exposed to this?” asks Suwadi.
Some classes have been suspended, with parents urging schools to switch to online learning.
Fires each year in Kalimantan are often blamed on “slash and burn” techniques used to clear land for plantations that produce palm oil, of which Indonesia is the world’s largest producer.
Authorities say this year’s “super” El Niño may be intensifying the blazes, with the weather phenomenon expected to peak in September.
Experts have warned the worst could be yet to come as the dry season continues into October, and the rains that could extinguish the fires look unlikely before November.
The haze is fast becoming a regional issue, with Malaysia and Brunei agreeing to raise it at Asean as thick smoke from forest and peatland fires drifts across the border.
On Tuesday, the Malaysian capital, Kuala Lumpur, was the most polluted city on earth, followed by Jakarta, according to air quality monitoring company IQAir. Almost 600 schools in the Malaysian state of Sarawak on Borneo island closed due to hot and dry conditions. Singapore went on alert.
On social media, Indonesians have tried to draw attention to the issue – highlighting the huge blazes in Kalimantan, and also in Sumatra, West Papua, and in Lombok where a fire destroyed a traditional Sade village over the weekend.
Forestry ministry data shows that nearly 94,000 hectares (232,000 acres) have burned nationwide this July alone.
On Monday, the Indonesian president, Prabowo Subianto, ordered authorities to revoke the business permits of corporations suspected of directing the land clearing, state news agency Antara reported. Indonesian police arrested 72 people suspected of starting fires in Borneo and Sumatra, with most accused of deliberately burning land to clear areas for plantations.
The response comes as regional experts fear this could be another devastating fire year, with many of Indonesia’s most severe blazes occurring during El Niño cycles. In 2015, another El Niño year, more than 6m acres were burned, with trans-boundary haze again plaguing neighbouring Malaysia and Singapore.
During a recent visit to the region, Prabowo promised government resources to contain the fires, including helicopters and water pumps.
But some Indonesians have expressed frustration at what they see as government inaction against the companies allegedly involved.
Indonesia’s unique rainforests are home to peatland ecosystems, which should be naturally resilient to fire when water tables remain high.
However, drainage networks built to clear land for pulp and oil palm plantations have robbed the soil of its natural capacity to retain water, experts say.
Fires on degraded peatlands are more difficult to control because they burn deep underground, says Justin Sentian, a professor in climate change at Universiti Malaysia Sabahand. And they produce thick, acrid smoke.
“If authorities only act after hotspots appear, they will forever be playing catch-up,” says Sentian. “True prevention must address the soil itself by halting the conversion of peatlands and actively restoring degraded areas.”
On Monday another fire broke out near the factory where Suwadi works in Kalimantan. With houses burning and smoke everywhere, Suwadi says he is afraid for the future of the region.
“The fire is getting dangerously close to homes,” he says, “People are [in] panic now.”
With Agence France-Presse and Associated Press

KEA UGCET 2026 2nd Round Seat Allotment Result: The Karnataka Examinations Authority (KEA) has announced the final second-round seat allotment results for UGCET 2026 on August 24. Second-round final seat allotment result: August 24
