In March 2023, Jason Arday, a rising star in British academia, became a professor of sociology of education at the University of Cambridge. At 37, he was the youngest Black person ever appointed to a professorship in the university’s history.
The tragedy of Jason Arday
What we should — but probably won’t — learn from the frenzy around racism and DEI in academia.
Arday’s personal story also attracted widespread attention. He claimed that autism left him unable to speak until he was 11 and unable to read or write until he was 18. Nonetheless, Arday eventually received a PhD from Liverpool John Moores University and continued to rise through the ranks of British higher education.
Soon after starting his position at Cambridge, Arday was accused of plagiarizing portions of his 2015 doctoral thesis. And that was just the beginning. The British press began to comb through his personal story and discovered there were more questionable claims.
This all reached a fever pitch earlier this month, when Arday announced that he would be resigning his position, writing that the intense scrutiny and personal attacks had taken a profound toll on him and his family. Nine days later, Arday was found dead in his home.
To understand what to make of a story of alleged academic plagiarism turned media frenzy turned tragedy, Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram spoke with Atlantic staff writer Tyler Austin Harper, whose recent essay, “The Truths That Failed Jason Arday,” examines what we can learn from Arday’s story.
Below is an excerpt of the conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
You wrote that everyone following this story would do well to engage in some reflection. I don’t think everyone following this story necessarily feels like they should be engaging in some reflection. So I wanted to ask you why you wanted to convey that thought.
I would say blame is not a finite resource and I think there’s plenty of it to go around in this case in particular. I think blame that belongs to conservatives and that belongs to Republicans and that belongs to various kinds of institutions. And that of course belongs to Jason Arday, the man.
I think this is a person who is clearly a serial fabulist, and I think one could fairly say a con artist, who was able to, through an increasingly implausible array of stories about his background — that he was mute until age 11, that he was illiterate till age 18, that he ran 600 miles in six days, a feat which is just 50 miles shy of a world record — flatter the vanities of people at Cambridge University who were very desperate to get a magical minority in the door. And they were so hell bent on their desire to engage in diversity politics that they overlooked what should have been very obvious flaws.
I think it’s also true simultaneously though, that you cannot just blame Arday or liberal institutions for this, and particularly for how this ended. This was, it’s worth noting, an academic scandal that — on the order of academic scandals — is not one that perhaps should be international news, but that’s very much what it became, in no small part because the British press turbocharged it.
If you look at any major British outlet, there were many, many, many, many articles written, each one chronicling every minute of this entire affair. And I think it’s worth noting that it’s hard to imagine that this degree of scrutiny would be applied to an academic scandal if Jason Arday had been white. It’s also hard to imagine that Jason Arday would’ve been hired if he was white. I think people would’ve asked more questions about his implausible claims if they weren’t so predisposed to just try to get him in the door.
What compelled Jason Arday to make up so much of his backstory?
It’s hard to know what’s inside his mind, but one imagines that he correctly understood that a certain kind of elite liberal would be very willing to overlook quite a lot and that [they] would be willing to swallow a whole lot of implausibilities to get him in the door. And I think he understood how the system works.
One of my frustrations with the way discourse of this story has unfolded, particularly after his tragic death, is he is being treated as somebody with no agency. And I think Arday, if you look at what he did, was clearly relatively savvy. He understood that there was a market, that he was being branded as the youngest Black professor in the 800-year history of Cambridge. And he fabricated a story that told people what they wanted to hear.
Not only was he Black coming from rough circumstances, but he was disabled, he was severely autistic, he had this miraculous recovery, also all sorts of medical ailments. He survived a brain tumor, testicular cancer, epilepsy, et cetera. He clearly knew how the game was played. He knew that he could leverage these various identity claims in service of advancement, which is what happened.
The story was not nearly as big in the United States as it was in the UK, understandably. But a lot of people want to place blame for Arday’s death on the British press. American Ibram X. Kendi said [Arday] was “lynched by the media.” Do you think that’s going too far?
I think that’s going way too far. First of all, there are few things I find more grotesque, at least in terms of everyday discourse, than treating lynching as a metaphor, which is something I think you see quite a lot. I think anyone who has seen a hanging tree knows that throwing the term around — “lynching” — for mere journalistic scrutiny is vile beyond measure.
Was the British press scrutiny far too intense? Yes. Do I think it was racist in the sense that I have a hard time imagining there would be this much scrutiny on a white academic who did the same thing? Yes, I think you can absolutely say that. To me, there is a question about, “Okay, what is the line between appropriate journalistic scrutiny and obsession?”
But I also think it’s worth noting, to be fair to the British press, that they’re responding to the way in which he was marketed to them nationally. He was marketed by Cambridge as the youngest Black professor in the 800-year history of this very venerable institution. To some extent, when you brand someone that way, when you film BBC specials with a closeup on his Black hands nestled in the white ones of the head of the Faculty of Education, I think some degree of scrutiny is warranted.
I think it was excessive. But at the same time, Jason Arday was a public figure. I think that is fair to say. His memoir is poised to make a splash. And he took this position that made him a minor academic celebrity. And again, I think it’s very fair to ask whether the degree of attention on what is ultimately an academic scandal in which no one was hurt was far too much. But the idea that we would place the blame on the media rather than on Simon and Schuster, who clearly overlooked obvious inconsistencies in his story, and on Cambridge — I find that absurd.
I think we need to blame the people who put him on the mountaintop rather than the people who ripped him down, even as I think some of those people putting attention on him were unscrupulous.
In your piece at the Atlantic, I thought you bravely related your own experience to that of Jason Arday. Did that come naturally to you or did you have to hold your breath?
Look, I am a Black guy who has been the beneficiary of various kinds of DEI and affirmative action initiatives. And I certainly have encountered a certain kind of white liberal who is very eager to metaphorically grasp my Black hands in their white ones and stare lovingly into my eyes like the Cambridge Faculty of Education person did. So I had some degree of sympathy with him.
I find those kinds of encounters revolting. But I also can understand from Arday’s point of view, coming from a relatively disadvantaged background, he’s the children of immigrants. Then you have all of these people paying attention to you, showering you in accolades — and I think fetishizing you, but it probably didn’t seem that way to him. And you tell a small lie, and maybe that small lie then becomes a bigger lie and then a bigger lie and a bigger lie and a bigger lie.
What he did was wrong, but I can imagine the kind of incentive structure he saw laid out before him. And it’s not hard to see that he made a decision that could in some sense be understood as yes, self-serving, but also giving people what they wanted.
Do you think we’ll learn anything from it?
No. I think people have retreated into their camps. I think progressives are blaming the media for doing what I’ve seen thrown around as a digital lynching. I think conservatives are blaming academic institutions or Jason Arday or just gleefully basking in the glow of having torn this guy down a peg. I haven’t seen a single lesson really learned.
I’ve seen a lot of blame being apportioned. I don’t think there’s much reflection about whether or not these policies are good or bad — the kind of policies or the kinds of extremist versions of affirmative action that go well beyond the spirit of what most people understand as affirmative action.
Whether those kinds of initiatives are good, whether the press scrutiny was fair. I don’t see a lot of self-reflection. I see a lot of blame. And even as I’m wanting to say that there’s lots of people to blame, I also think we should be a little more self-critical.
My first impulse on learning of the Jason Arday affair was to find it somewhat amusing, I will be honest. Here was this guy who managed to tell all of these obvious lies and these very, very smart people believed them hook, line, and sinker. It was objectively funny, but it became unfunny very quickly. And so I think, like I said in the piece, we could all stand to do some reflection about how we ended up in this situation, how Jason Arday ended up in this situation. But will that reflection happen? I highly doubt it.

How to watch the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope's launch
NASA is broadcasting the event live on August 30.
The Nancy Grace Roman telescope is heading to space in a few days. It's set for launch on August 30, no earlier than 7:26AM Eastern time, with NASA's live coverage to begin at 6:20AM. The agency's engineers completed the final inspection of the telescope's primary mirror in late May to make sure it hadn't been damaged during testing. In early June, NASA announced that the telescope will launch earlier than the September schedule it had previously planned.
Nancy Grace Roman was NASA's first Chief of Astronomy and was known as the "Mother of Hubble" for being instrumental in the observatory's planning and development. This telescope named after her has a field of view at least 100 times larger than Hubble's and will be able to observe a wider swath of the universe at any single time. It was designed to use different techniques to study dark energy and help us answer questions about the mysterious force. The telescope also has the capacity to block starlight in order to better see exoplanets, so it can provide more data for scientists to figure out what determines habitability and how common solar systems like ours are.
The infrared telescope is already encapsulated inside a SpaceX Falcon Heavy fairing at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida. It will fly on top of a Falcon Heavy rocket from Launch Complex 39A. If the launch doesn't go through on August 30, NASA and SpaceX will try again on August 31 at 7:22 AM Eastern time. You can watch the rocket launch live on NASA's website or on SpaceX's X account. In addition to the launch itself, NASA will also broadcast a mission science briefing on August 29 at 9AM ET with the Roman telescope team, followed by a prelaunch news conference.

Did a goat herder's lucky $200 nugget spark a gold rush in western Kenya?
- Published
A goat herder from a remote area of western Kenya has told the BBC his discovery of a golden nugget has sparked a gold rush, overwhelming his small village over the last few weeks.
When people found out that 33-year-old Manasse Lomachar had sold his three grams of gold for 36,000 Kenyan shillings ($280; £205) several weeks ago, he believes this led to thousands of prospectors arrived in Cheporor.
And it is true that what last month was just bushland and rough grazing ground near the village is now scarred by pits, mounds of earth and makeshift mining camps.
It is not clear if was Lomachar's lucky find or other recent discoveries that sparked the excitement. But local authorities estimate that about 10,000 people arrived at the height of the rush.
Even a small amount of the precious metal can transform the futures of these men and women - from Kenya and neighbouring Uganda - many of whose precarious lives rest on an unreliable farming income.
People do sometimes pan for gold in these parts - but rarely find anything significant.
Lomachar's says his discovery came about purely by chance. While he was searching for a missing goat he encountered a group of women panning along a riverbed.
"I joined them, and that's how [the village] realised there was gold in this area," he says.
Farmer and herder Patrick Lokolia, from neighbouring Napawoi village, joined the gold rush hoping to earn some extra money to support his family.
"I have children in school, and paying school fees has been a big problem for me," he tells the BBC wearing an old Chelsea football top and standing amid the mining activity.
Eighteen-year-old Abigael Chelengat says she had never mined before coming to Cheporor from a nearby district, but arrived hoping to find enough gold to pay her school fees and help keep her younger siblings in school.
Behind her hundreds of people work side by side, hacking into the rocky ground with hoes and shovels.
Others carry the earth to a nearby seasonal river, where mostly women crouch in the murky water, washing and sifting mud and sand hoping to detect a tiny trace of the element.
Some of the more experienced miners are deep in holes excavating the earth and drilling at rocks with the same goal.
Hope is kept alive by stories of those for whom the effort has paid off - like Lomachar.
Samuel Kiarie, the deputy commissioner of West Pokot county, says he thinks the rush began after two notable discoveries.
"Young men found what appeared to be a substantial amount of gold. The following day, women made another significant find in the same area," he tells the BBC.
Kiarie explains that women have been finding small quantities of alluvial gold along the same seasonal riverbed for years, typically earning $8-$23 a week.
But the uncovering of larger quantities at the beginning of August is what caught the attention of many people.
Kiarie reckons as rumours spread, the number and size of the discoveries were exaggerated - drawing in ever larger groups of people with little or no mining experience who hoped to replicate the reported early successes.
Since the initial rush, the number of prospectors has gone down to around 2,500 as some have given up the search.
While there is little doubt that some gold has been found in the area, questions remain about the size of the deposit in the earth and its commercial potential.
"I can confirm that small-scale gold traders told us they received an average of about 100 people every day," the deputy commissioner says - though whether the finds were actually gold is not known.
Individual discoveries reportedly range from amounts worth a few hundred Kenyan shillings to one find valued at approximately 78,000 shillings ($600).
West Pokot county borders Uganda, and communities on both sides have long-standing social and family ties.
Mugisha Godfrey, an artisanal miner from Busia in eastern Uganda, travelled to Cheporor after hearing about the discovery from a friend.
He immediately set out for the village spending about 100,000 Ugandan shillings ($27) to get there.
However, the living conditions in Cheporor are not favourable, he says.
"We sleep under the trees, and when morning comes, we continue working. Sometimes we work both day and night," Godfrey tells the BBC.
So far, he has found nothing. But he is not discouraged.
"We can't return unless we find something. Only when we have found what we need can we go back home," he says.
For others, the gold rush has created opportunities without requiring them to dig.
More than 200 businesses have emerged around the site, according to local officials, selling food, water and other essentials to the village's new population.
Irene Ameja travelled from neighbouring Baringo county to cater to the crowds. She sells bottled water, soft drinks, bread, milk and other foodstuffs.
"I am hoping that when I leave, I will have made enough money to continue with my business and expand it," she says.
But the rapid growth of the settlement has also exposed the area's lack of basic services.
"This is a forest and we are in the middle of the mountains," she says. "We don't have clean water to drink or even to bathe."
For women, she adds, the challenges become greater after dark: "You have to find somewhere safe to stay because most of the people sleeping here are men."
Local officials admit the influx has placed enormous pressure on an area with little infrastructure, no piped water and limited sanitation.
Public health officials have been deployed to monitor conditions and help prevent disease outbreaks.
The authorities say they have also increased security patrols amid concerns over sexual violence and the vulnerability of women and girls at the site.
Officials are also worried that children could be drawn into mining activities as schools prepare to reopen in September.
Measures are being put in place to discourage young people from remaining at the site once the new school term begins.
Those still searching are increasingly turning to deeper excavation.
Several truckloads of material have already been transported to nearby Ortum town for processing, with the authorities awaiting the results.
Until then, the size and commercial viability of any mining remain uncertain.
For Lomachar, the answer is not to stop the mining, but to make it more organised.
He wants the government to help local miners establish safer and more effective ways of finding and extracting the gold.
"We would ask the government to help us with things like metal detectors, which could help us find out whether there are other minerals here, so that our community can develop," he says.
He points to the homes nearby as evidence of the area's poverty.
"If you look around, there are hardly any houses with iron-sheet roofs; most are just thatched houses."

The story so far
The National Dope Testing Laboratory got approval from the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) to manage the Athlete Biological Passport (ABP) on December 6, 2024. ABP is an advanced anti-doping tool that enables longitudinal monitoring of biological markers to detect potential doping practices. ABP routinely collects samples (blood and urine) and monitors and analyses the athlete’s haematological, endocrine, and steroidal profiles in specified time intervals. This profiling could act as corroborative evidence of doping during anti-doping violation cases. The ABP is not a substitute, but complements traditional testing by providing indirect evidence of doping and enhancing detection accuracy. While doping is usually read as reducing from the spirit of sportsmanship, it is necessary to understand it from the health perspective of the athlete.
What is doping?
Doping, as described by the National Anti-Doping Agency Rules 2021, consists of violations such as the use of prohibited substances and the presence of the substance or their metabolites in the body sample, evasion or refusal of testing of banned substances, whereabouts failures during testing, possession or trafficking of prohibited substances without proper justification, administering these substances to others, complicity in violations, association with ineligible individuals, and acts or retaliating against whistleblowers.
Nick Kyrgios provisionally suspended after testing positive for cocaine, admits ‘huge mistake’
Doping is banned to uphold the integrity of sports by ensuring fair play and creating a level playing field for athletes. While these reasons are rooted in ethical concerns, the physical health of the athlete consuming these substances is a direct and often overlooked issue. Performance-enhancing drugs can cause several short-term and long-term health consequences for the athletes.
The practice of doping dates back to ancient Greece, when athletes consumed herbal stimulants to win competitions. By the late 19th century, the development of modern pharmacology led to the introduction of substances such as cocaine and strychnine. The mid-20th century saw the emergence of anabolic steroids, which were initially developed for medical purposes. The WADA Prohibited List categorizes substances into two types: banned at all times and banned during competition. Substances banned at all times are prohibited both in and out of competition due to their performance-enhancing or masking effects. The substances banned during competition are restricted only when athletes actively participate in events.
Substances for doping
What are these substances then? Firstly, anabolic agents (e.g. testosterone). These substances mimic the effects of testosterone, enhancing protein synthesis and promoting rapid muscle growth and recovery. They allow athletes to train harder and recover faster, increasing strength, endurance, and muscle mass. The unfair advantage lies in the unnatural enhancement of physical capabilities, enabling athletes to outperform competitors who rely solely on training and natural ability. However, their use carries serious health risks, including cardiovascular diseases such as heart attacks and strokes, liver damage, hormonal imbalances leading to infertility, psychiatric disorders like aggression and depression, and weakened tendons that are prone to injury.
Peptide Hormones (e.g., Erythropoietin) are used too. Erythropoietin increases red blood cell production, boosting oxygen delivery to muscles and significantly improving endurance in sports like cycling and long-distance running. Growth hormone stimulates tissue repair, muscle growth, and fat metabolism, aiding recovery and physical performance. The health risks include thickened blood, leading to blood clots, strokes, and heart attacks, insulin resistance, acromegaly (abnormal growth of bones and tissues), and an increased risk of cancers, particularly colorectal cancer.
Then there are Beta-2 Agonists, drugs which enhance respiratory efficiency by relaxing airway muscles and improving oxygen intake during intense activities. They may also have mild anabolic effects in higher doses, promoting muscle growth. Health risks include tremors, headaches, palpitations, and potential heart rhythm disorders over prolonged use. Hormone and Metabolic Modulators (e.g., Tamoxifen). These substances modulate hormonal levels, boosting testosterone production and aiding muscle growth and recovery. The risks involve blood clots, pulmonary embolism, liver damage, and an increased likelihood of endometrial cancer. Diuretics are used to rapidly reduce body weight, aid athletes in weight-class sports, and mask the presence of other banned substances. This allows athletes to manipulate their weight or evade doping tests. Diuretics cause severe dehydration, electrolyte imbalances, kidney damage, and an increased risk of sudden death due to cardiac arrest.
The following substances are banned during competitions: Stimulants (e.g., amphetamines) that stimulate the central nervous system by enhancing alertness, reaction times, and energy levels. It helps athletes stay focused and perform longer under intense conditions. The health risks are significant, including addiction, high blood pressure, cardiovascular problems, and severe mental health disorders like psychosis. Narcotics (like morphine) reduce pain perception, allowing athletes to push through injuries and physical discomfort. But, it leads to respiratory depression, addiction, and organ damage, particularly with long-term use. Cannabinoids may reduce anxiety and enhance focus, potentially aiding performance in high-stress situations.
The risks include cognitive impairment, respiratory problems, and a higher likelihood of dependency. Glucocorticoids -Drugs like prednisolone reduce inflammation and pain, enabling athletes to compete despite injuries or overtraining. Health risks include suppressed immune function, osteoporosis, and long-term hormonal imbalances. Beta Blockers are banned in precision sports, because they lower heart rates and reduce anxiety, improving precision and steadiness in sports like shooting and archery. However, they can cause fatigue, dizziness, depression, and chronic low blood pressure.
Therapeutic use exemptions
Therapeutic Use Exemptions (TUEs) allow athletes to use prohibited substances for legitimate medical reasons. To qualify, athletes must provide comprehensive medical documentation and demonstrate that the drug is necessary for their health. A panel of experts evaluates these applications, ensuring transparency and fairness.
Doping in sports compromises fairness and poses significant health risks to athletes, ranging from dehydration and tremors to long-term consequences such as cardiovascular disease, organ damage, and psychological disorders. Doping fuels a global illicit drug trade, as acknowledged by Interpol, which classifies it as a low-risk, high-profit activity for criminal networks.

'This star is for Africa' - Angélique Kidjo on making Hollywood Walk of Fame history
- Published
Five-time Grammy award winner Angélique Kidjo, who made history on Tuesday to become the first African musician to get a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, has told the BBC she wants to dedicate the accolade to the continent of her birth.
"This star is for all the continent of Africa. Because if I was not African, would I be here?" said the 66-year-old musical icon from Benin.
She reiterated her message, made at the ceremony in Los Angeles to mark her four-decade career, about the importance of Africans to the world of music.
"Without the blues brought by the slaves in America, there's no R&B, there's no rock and roll, there's no soul music, there's no jazz. All of it comes from Africa."
- Angélique Kidjo's secret to success: Being hangry 
  - Published17 November 2023
Kidjo told BBC Focus on Africa TV that Africans themselves needed to appreciate what they had given the world, and nurture talent at home.
"Let's celebrate our artists in their own right on the continent. Let's give them visibility, strength, because music creates economy," she said.
Most African artists - besides mega stars who have a global fanbase - struggle to make a living as they rarely get paid the royalties they are owed.
"We need to recognise our artists and create a system for them to make money on their continent and to participate also in creating jobs."
As her illustrious career was immortalised in Los Angeles, Kidjo became emotional - wiping away tears.
"At that moment, I'm like, dad, mum, I wish you were here with me to see [this]" the songstress explained to the BBC.
"I couldn't take the emotion. They were not here to taste the fruit of what they've created. How they have nurtured my curiosity, my love for music."
Kidjo - who has taken African sounds to global audiences, blending influences from home with funk, jazz and pop - grew up in Benin and then went to Paris aged 23, citing oppression from the country's then-communist government.
At her Walk of Fame ceremony, she was joined by other family, friends and stars such as Hollywood actors Willem Dafoe and Djimon Hounsou, who is also from Benin, and Nigerian musician Adekunle Gold.
The gathering was filled with singing and dancing in celebration of her career, which has included collaborations with big names such as Burna Boy, John Legend, Bono and Alicia Keys.
Her latest album, HOPE!!, was released earlier this year with tracks produced by Pharrell Williams, and collaborations with Ayra Starr, Quavo, Nile Rogers and Diane Warren.
Kidjo has released 18 albums in total and has been nominated for 17 Grammy awards, which she has won five times.
She also won the 2023 Polar Music Prize, and two years earlier was named as one of Time's 100 Most Influential People.
"She is without a doubt the hardest working woman in showbusiness," Dafoe said at the ceremony.
"The first time I saw Angélique perform live, I thought her music, her dancing, her commitment were incredible."
The Spider-Man star likened her energy to that of soul singer James Brown, who he called the "hardest working man in showbusiness".
"She's not only an incredible performer... songwriter and musician, but also an incredibly kind and giving person and a real deal activist."
Kidjo is a Unicef and Oxfam goodwill ambassador, and is the co-founder of the Batonga Foundation, which helps vulnerable young girls and women in Benin.
At the Los Angeles gathering she was also praised by Harvey Mason Jr, the CEO of Recording Academy - the organisation that also oversees the Grammy awards.
"She's connected cultures, she's crossed borders, she's reminded audiences everywhere that while we may come from different backgrounds, her music unites in a way that few other things can," he said.
During her interview with the BBC, the musician's phone kept ringing with those wanting to congratulate her.
"Yesterday I received the call of the president of Benin," she said.
"Today I received the call of Chris Blackwell, the founder of Island Records, the producer of Bob Marley, the maker of U2 and so on and so forth."
Kidjo explained how fundamental Blackwell, who signed her in the 1990s, had been to her success - launching her breakthrough album Logozo.
"I said to him at that moment… 'Can I do the music I want to do and keep my cultural identity without anyone imposing any other music on my shoulder?' He said… 'It's no brainer.'"
Kidjo joins Charlize Theron, a white South African actress, in representing Africa on the Walk of Fame, which comprises more than 2,800 stars.
She said she was amazed to hear a year ago that she had been nominated for a Hollywood star, telling Focus on Africa she did not believe the news given to her by her husband until she said she had seen it on the BBC.
And when asked about the significance of becoming the first African musician with a star, she replied: "Changes that last take time."

A Freedom 250 Event That Actually Worked
Other patriotic spectacles this summer felt like Trump rallies. This was a car race.
An interest in the thrills of car racing is not what drove me to spend my Sunday afternoon at the Freedom 250 Grand Prix, the latest of the spectacles that Donald Trump has presided over during the United States’ big birthday celebrations all summer. I was there yesterday because I was worried about art. The event involved 25 cars zipping around a number of D.C.’s museums and historic buildings at worryingly high speeds—147 times. Preservationists and conservators had raised concerns ahead of the contest, leading me to imagine creaking sculptures and rattling ceramics, all because the president wanted a race around the National Mall. Seeing the National Gallery of Art’s huge black Alexander Calder sculpture outside, surrounded by wood boards as if the poor thing were hunkering down for war, didn’t help.
But it turns out that playing art patrol is rather difficult at an IndyCar race, especially when you find yourself crammed into a sweaty crowd as blurs of color whiz by. This proximity to the action means you are a participant in a much more visceral way than at many other sporting events: You can feel the vibrations in your toes. Somewhere among the vrooms, I realized that this was not like the other Freedom 250 productions I had attended, like the Great American State Fair with its drab triumphal arch and the Freedom Trucks with their selective history. Instead, in some moments, the Grand Prix was … fun?
The good vibes began when I spotted the driver Sting Ray Robb’s maintenance truck, decorated with the ridiculously wholesome image of seven puppies climbing on his race car. He immediately gained a fan in me, though he crashed early on. The course, with its many bumps, was tricky for drivers, and just more than half of them even finished. Kyle Kirkwood, another American, won.
Many might be tempted to slot the IndyCar race next to other Trumpian events that have disrupted life in the nation’s capital. More than that, the race could easily serve as another example of how little an administration that has pressured museums and diluted historic-preservation laws cares for the nation’s cultural heritage. These interpretations aren’t overblown.
Earlier this year, the Grand Prix unveiled (and later walked back) a disturbing T-shirt that featured a white-clad figure and read: One Nation One Race. In and around the city yesterday, the traffic was a pain for locals, the nearest airport had to stop flights for three hours, and the noise—including multiple deafening flyovers—was nothing short of a public nuisance. For those without tickets, access to the Mall was closed off. Madhan Subramanian, who lives by the course, told me he was “just a little annoyed by everything.” He thought it was a cool event, but “it was harder to get groceries and just do our normal thing.”
The worries about vibrations and damage to artifacts were legitimate, too. In the middle of the race, I put my hand on the boarded-up geometric I. M. Pei skylights outside the National Gallery and found them shaking like a cellphone on vibrate. (Not great!) A man yelled to me over the thunderous cars, “Are we okay?” I replied, in earnest, “I’m not sure.” (So far, there have been no reports of damaged art.)
Reckless is one word for what unfolded in the capital yesterday. But one person’s reckless is another’s exciting. And the Freedom 250 Grand Prix certainly had oomph to it. Trump did a lap of the track at the beginning of the race to the sound of mixed cheers and boos, and although I noticed Trump gear—Trump 2028 hats, for example—for sale outside the race perimeter, inside many fans had opted for checkers and race jerseys.
In other words, this didn’t feel like another Freedom 250 event that was more about Trump than about America. Race-car driving occupies its own indomitable universe of fandom, kitsch, design, and hype. Ultimately, a race is a race, and many in the crowd appeared to be there simply for the sport.
Keith Cole, a former amateur racer and F1 fan, was among them. A car race in downtown Washington seemed like a once-in-a-lifetime thing, so he came to D.C. with a friend despite some low-grade partisan energy they didn’t care for. “We don’t see a lot of people like us here,” Cole, who is Black, told me, noting some MAGA-hat sightings, too. “I understand how they want to use it to politicize it, but this is sports. You gotta, kind of, take it out of it.”
Most of the time, the National Mall is a reflective space flanked by quiet, regal buildings that command a certain respect. Yesterday, though, America’s “front yard” felt more like a backyard. IndyCar fans played cornhole and giant Connect Four on the grass, which was dotted with lemonade stands and picnic tables. In one moment, I was surrounded by beer-drinking racing fanatics; in the next, I was engulfed in the smell of gasoline and the sound of revving engines; minutes later, after a short stroll, I was standing in the National Gallery in front of a Georgia O’Keeffe.
Inside one of the galleries, I found Carol Madden—a native of Indianapolis, IndyCar’s namesake and the site of its premier event, the 500—seeking a break from the heat near some Renaissance-era earthenware. “The Indy 500 is Christmas for my family. We don’t come home for Christmas and Easter—we all come home for the race,” she told me. This was her 55th race, which she attended with her whole family, she said, getting teary-eyed.
Nearby, Diana Vinson, as much a race-car fan as a museum lover, was immersed in a photograph on the wall. She didn’t see her appreciation for the two things as entirely separate. Both art and racing are all about precision; they’re about tiny decisions—in brushstrokes or tire pressure—that add up. “You have to understand your mediums,” she told me.
The museum was making the most of any connection it could find with the event, which forced it to partially close for the race; the portion of it that remained open was accessible only to IndyCar ticket holders. (The National Gallery has been notably savvy about garnering attention of late, as evidenced by its viral videos of a Gen Z–whispering senior curator who called that Renaissance earthenware “bussin’.”) Outside, signs promised “iconic art (and air-conditioning).” Staff members had set up a tent where they sold T-shirts featuring a portrait of George Souders, who won the Indy 500 in 1927, from the museum’s collection.
Earlier, out on the Mall, I had spoken with Bill Sherman, a fan of “anything that makes noise and goes fast,” who told me he thinks people are drawn to car racing because they can see themselves in it. “I’ve driven these roads hundreds of times,” he said. “It’s one of the few sports that you can look at and say, I can go out and do that every day on the Beltway.”
Though that would certainly spice up your commute, you shouldn’t. Just like you shouldn’t send thousands of pounds of metal flying around historic sites. But watching cars hurtling past the National Archives, barreling toward the Air and Space Museum, with the U.S. Capitol looming in the distance, you might just convince yourself otherwise.

The only GameCube that could play CDs and DVDs is rarely found below $1,000 today
This is one strange console.
One reason GameCube games hold their value so well today is that, compared to other Nintendo consoles, it wasn't exactly a hot seller. Why was that? Well, it's partly because the PS2 had what the GameCube didn't: a built-in DVD player. Out of that market pressure was born the Panasonic Q. While this oddball GameCube/DVD player hybrid barely got off the ground, its scarcity has led to a second life as a niche collector's item.
The Japan-only Panasonic SL-GC 10, widely known as the Panasonic Q, arrived in December 2001, three months after the Nintendo GameCube debuted in Japan. Looking less like a Nintendo console and more like a home-theater appliance, the Q had a reflective front panel, a backlit LCD and ports with a blue glow. If you want quintessential 2001 consumer electronics design, look no further.
The oddball pairing of Panasonic branding with Nintendo gaming stemmed from an existing relationship between the two companies. It turns out Panasonic's then-parent company, Matsushita (which is essentially Panasonic today), helped design the GameCube's optical miniDVD format. It seems likely Nintendo saw the gaping DVD hole in its console strategy and decided to roll the dice.
A GameCube for the DVD era
The Panasonic Q was a bizarre mashup. Its motorized disc tray accepted GameCube discs, DVDs and audio CDs. The company took the home theater part seriously. The Q had a Cinema mode for picture processing, along with audio features like Dolby Digital, DTS (Digital Theater Systems) for surround sound, Dialogue Enhancer and Bass Plus.
Those home theater features sure must have been nice for games like Super Mario Sunshine or Metroid Prime, right? Unfortunately, no. That's because the Q's home theater features were split off from the game console. Game audio was limited to the GameCube's standard analog connections. There was even a hardware button to manually switch between the two modes because it wouldn't change automatically based on the disc type. When it was time to switch, the system effectively powered down one side and restarted the other.
The Q also came with Panasonic-branded accessories reflecting the product's duality. There's a gray GameCube controller with Panasonic branding for games and a matching gray remote control for the DVD player. This wasn't so much a hybrid device as it was two distinct machines from two companies sharing the same chassis. Oh, early oughts, how we miss you.
Setting aside the exterior, the gaming half of the Q was no different from a standard GameCube. You could pop in Super Smash Bros. Melee or Mario Kart: Double Dash!! and have an identical experience to your friend with the regular version. It had the same controller ports, memory card slots and full compatibility with the GameCube library (although unmodified models were region-locked to Japan).
The weird industrial design did lead to one tradeoff: the GameCube's Game Boy Player didn't fit. The optional accessory, which let you play Game Boy, Game Boy Color and Game Boy Advance games, lodged underneath Nintendo's system. But because the Q's base was different, Panasonic had to release a modified version of the Game Boy Player designed for its shiny, weird console.
Despite all of that effort, the Panasonic Q struggled to find an audience — mostly because it was damn expensive. It launched in Japan at ¥39,800 (roughly $313 at the time) — a lot of money for such an oddball product. Although that matches the PS2's Japanese launch price, Sony's console arrived nearly two years earlier, had already built a huge audience and made the DVD player a central selling point. Not to mention, you didn't have to reboot your console to switch between the two modes. Plenty of modded imported units made it overseas, but the Q never launched outside of Japan.
A rare piece of gaming history
And that brings us back to its collectible status today. Because of all that, there just aren't that many Panasonic Qs in the wild today. So when they do turn up on places like eBay, they can fetch a pretty penny. Loose consoles generally sell in the $1,200 to $1,300 range. Models with the original packaging and paperwork can surpass $2,000. It wasn't a legendary product, but for those who held on to one, it ended up being a good investment.
It's only fitting that one of the weirdest game consoles ever made also has one of the strangest stories: being more successful as a 2020s collector's item than it ever was as a consumer product.

You probably heard about the Trump administration’s rapid take down in 2025 of the U.S. Agency for International Development after it had been around for 63 years. Well, in 2026, the Trump administration been doing a much quieter take down of another long-standing federal agency—the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality. The repercussions of this takedown of AHRQ, though, will likely be heard and felt by many, many patients for years and even decades to come.
On July 15 AHRQ Halted At Least 104 Grants
That’s because for 27 years, the AHRQ has been the only federal agency focused on supporting work and research into improving the safety and quality of healthcare—hence the name of the agency. That’s pretty darn important stuff if you happen to have a human head and body and thus require healthcare at some point in your life or at least care about someone who does. An analysis conducted by the agency had estimated that in the 2014 to 2017 period alone, AHRQ-funded studies had saved around 20,500 deaths and $7.7 billion in healthcare costs.
Such studies have included research on preventing and controlling healthcare-associated infections, reducing of medical errors, safely dispensing medications, measuring hospital quality and developing technology that can help improve the safety and experience of patients. An estimated 250,000 to 400,000 people in the U.S. die each year from preventable medical errors. And an estimated 75,000 to 99,000 die each year from healthcare-associated infections.
However, without AHRQ, those interested in researching such areas may struggle to find funding, especially with what the Trump administration along with Elon Musk’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency have done to National Institutes of Health and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention funding. Therefore, a July 15 letter from the AHRQ must have made a lot of healthcare quality and safety researchers around the country go “Argh”—telling them that AHRQ was halting at least 104 of their grants.
AHRQ Had Gone A Year Without Issuing New Grants
That’s after the AHRQ had gone over a year without issuing any new grants and spending less than $15 million of the $345 million allocated by Congress to the agency for the current fiscal year. So unless AHRQ somehow ends up issuing, oh, $330 million in grants from now to September 30, the Trump administration will have basically ignored what Congress had wanted and indicated, which wouldn’t be the first time that’s happened.
Last August, the Society for General Internal Medicine did initiate a lawsuit against AHRQ Director Roger Klein, MD, JD, and U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., JD over AHRQ’s not issuing new grants. The lawsuit alleges that such actions—or rather inaction—violates a 1974 law that emphasizes that Congress and not the U.S. President and his Executive Brach ultimately determines what federal agencies can spend on what. Of note, the July 15 grant-halting letter from AHRQ did not mention the T-word—meaning “termination”—and instead used the phrase "not awarded continued funding," which may have ramifications when it comes to what happens to lawsuits like the one initiated by SGIM.
HHS spokesperson Emily Hilliard has indicated that AHRQ has been aiming to establish a new "framework" for grants. However, it’s not been clarified what this framework might be and when it might be revealed. I will continue to reach out to contacts at HHS for more clarification.
AHRQ Has Shed And Lost Three-Quarters Of Its Personnel
In the meantime, if you do try to call or otherwise reach out to AHRQ to ask questions about what’s happening, good luck getting a response. The agency has lost about three-quarters of its personnel since Donald Trump ascended to the U.S. Presidency in January 2025. Those personnel losses have come through a range of different firings, layoffs resignations and other so-called RIFs or reductions in forces. Those who have been at AHRQ told me that by late 2025, the number of empty chairs already far outnumbered the number of people at AHRQ meetings.
Trump Had Already Wanted To Eliminate AHRQ During His First Presidential Term
What’s happening right now with AHRQ should not be a surprise. Back in 2017, I wrote in Forbes about how the proposed budget being put forth by then first term U.S. President Donald Trump and his administration had already tried to effectively eliminate AHRQ. Congress at the time, though, essentially treated this budget proposal like a pair of parachute pants and ignored it, leaving AHRQ with a budget.
The Trump-appointed Director Of AHRQ Has Not Been Spending The Funds That Congress Allocated
However, during Trump’s second term, his administration seems to have more trump cards up its sleeve when it comes to ignoring Congress when Congress ignores the Trump administration’s budget proposals. In 2025, the second coming of the Trump administration once again kept AHRQ out of its proposed budget, as I covered in Forbes. Congress once again ignored such a proposal and budgeted money for AHRQ. This time, though, the Trump administration has apparently circumvented Congress by just keeping AHRQ from spending its Congressional allocated funds.
It remains to be seen whether the Trump administration will even keep AHRQ as a separate agency or dissolve it entirely. Kennedy did announce in March 2025 plans to roll AHRQ and other HHS agencies into a new Office of Strategy. And Klein hasn’t really made public statements to help everyone clearly understand the direction of AHRQ since the Trump administration appointed him in July 2025 to be the new AHRQ director. Klein’s AHRQ website bio does lists him as “a board-certified molecular pathologist and attorney who was formerly Chief Medical Officer of OmniSeq, Inc., a tumor profiling company that was acquired by LabCorp” but doesn’t mention much about his vision for healthcare quality and safety.
Historically, federal agencies have incorporated various advisory committees of external scientific experts to help provide more transparency and oversight of its activities—especially its funding ones. But actions like Trump’s executive orders and the new White House Office of Management and Budget rule that I’ve covered in Forbes have progressively lessened the role of scientific peer review and other such external oversight in guiding federal agency operations such as grantsmaking. That’s concurrently increased the power of the President and his political appointees over what the federal agencies do and where the agencies’ funding goes.
The trouble is healthcare quality and safety work may seem like something you can cut without immediately clear ramifications—sort of like cutting the White House pandemic preparedness and response capabilities in 2017 and the food-borne illness prevention and control programs in 2025. But eventually the ramifications of such cuts will be seen, which is what happened in 2020 with the COVID-19 pandemic and this year with the 12 active food-borne illness outbreaks now occurring. And it’s safe to say that cutting work on healthcare safety and quality will have its ramifications down the road.

Kazakhstan's pro-government party wins parliamentary election
Officials say Kazakhstan’s pro-government Adilet Oarty won a landslide victory in the Central Asian country’s parliamentary elections
Kazakhstan’s pro-government Adilet Party won a landslide victory in a parliamentary election, officials announced Monday, a result expected to further strengthen President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s grip on power in Central Asia's largest nation.
Adilet, which is led by the former head of Tokayev’s presidential administration, won 71% of Sunday's vote, Kazakhstan’s central electoral commission said, according to preliminary results.
The second-place Auyl Party won 6.26% of the vote, with three other parties – the Nationwide Social Democratic Party, Respublica and Aq Jol – reaching the 5% threshold needed to win a place in parliament.
Election monitors for the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe said the vote was marred by a lack of distinct political opposition, with “all contesting parties supporting the incumbent president’s policies.”
Some 74% of the country’s 12.6 million eligible voters took part in the election, the central electoral commission said, which was the first vote to Kazakhstan’s new single-chamber parliament.
Known as the Kurultai, the new body is the culmination of a constitutional overhaul initiated by Tokayev in March, when 87% of voters supported a referendum to merge the two chambers of parliament.
The vote also gave the president authority to appoint key officials, subject to lawmakers' approval.
Last month, Kazakhstan’s Constitutional Court ruled that the amendments effectively reset the clock on Tokayev’s previous terms in office, clearing the way for him to seek another seven-year term when his mandate expires in 2029.
The decision echoes those seen in several former Soviet republics, including Russia, Belarus, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, where leaders have used new or amended constitutions to revise statutory term limits.
The 73-year-old Tokayev, a former Soviet official and Kazakh diplomat who previously worked at the United Nations, has been in office since 2019.
He has sought to maintain a balance between Moscow and the West since sanctions were imposed on Russia over the war in Ukraine. Tokayev has justified the constitutional changes by citing the need for rapid decision-making in a fast-changing world.
The election comes at a difficult economic moment for Kazakhstan, where inflation hit 10.2% in February and tax increases have fueled public discontent.
Analysts say the economic strain has made authorities wary of a repeat of the unrest of January 2022, when fuel price protests spiraled into violence that left dozens of protesters and police officers dead — a scenario Tokayev is seeking to guard against by concentrating power in his own hands.
The vote also took place against a backdrop of intensifying crackdowns on press freedom. Media organizations have urged Tokayev to drop criminal charges against several journalists under house arrest and to revise legislation to ensure freedom of speech. Authorities have opened roughly 10 criminal cases against independent journalists and popular bloggers.

The brains may come from the US, but the body could very well be Made In China.
At Physical Intelligence, a San Francisco-based startup, cofounder and researcher Sergey Levine is building the models, or brains, designed to provide intelligence for a range of robots — be they warehouse robots or humanoid machines. Physical Intelligence is one of many startups in Silicon Valley working on robotics software.
In an episode of The Peterman Pod published Monday, Levine said the US robotics industry has its own advantages against competition abroad, but the one area that could significantly advance America's progress is building the hardware supply chain.
"Availability of reliable low-cost hardware is a big deal. And right now, hardware used for robotics research — a lot of that does come from China," Levine said. "It's good. It's relatively inexpensive. It's of high quality and meets the standards that people generally need. But it'd be awfully nice to be able to source all of that domestically as well. I don't think there's anything impossible about that."
Building an AI capable of making robots smart enough to handle a wide range of tasks is only part of the industry's challenge.
In the US in particular, robotics leaders have said sourcing the physical components for robots — the motors, chassis, batteries, sensors, and other materials — will be a major bottleneck for scaling, and that companies often rely on China to fill the gaps.
"The United States is no longer competitive in manufacturing, and we're falling further behind every day. Any company that builds hardware can tell you that if you source from China instead of making it here, it's generally 5 to 10 times cheaper," Evan Beard, CEO of Standard Bots, said during a congressional hearing in April.
A June analysis from McKinsey found that China holds a "significant share of capacity" for robotics parts, including 90% of permanent-magnet processing. China's progress, according to the report, is due in part to its electric vehicle ecosystem, which shares some of the components needed in robots.
US robotics executives and policymakers say China's rapid progress in robotics and AI — combined with a strong manufacturing base — could hamper America's ability to effectively compete in what they view as a critical emerging industry.
The concern is heightened as Washington sees China as a strategic adversary. In July, the Federal Communications Commission effectively blocked new foreign-made humanoids and other advanced robots from entering the US market, citing national security concerns.
While US manufacturers welcomed the move, some researchers and startups told Business Insider's robotics reporter, Rya Jetha, that the ban locks out access to affordable hardware.
Levine said in the podcast that "different industries that contribute to robotics need to individually be very healthy."
"I think that it's important to sort of fully embrace that this is a holistic thing and not something where we can do just one piece of it and outsource everything else," he said.

Ipswich sign Strasbourg duo Enciso & Ouattara

Ipswich Town have signed winger Julio Enciso and midfielder Abdoul Ouattara from French club Strasbourg.
Paraguay international Enciso, 22, and Ivorian Ouattara, 20, have both penned five-year contracts with the Tractor Boys.

"I am still young but have had some good experiences already and I can't wait to meet the fans and my team-mates and get started," Ouattara said.
Since securing promotion from the Championship last season, Ipswich have spent £150m with the acquisitions of Ouattara and Enciso taking them up to 12 major signings.
Ipswich begin their Premier League campaign at home to Sunderland on 22 August.

The Ebola outbreak in Congo has reached 5,000 cases, government data showed on Wednesday (August 19, 2026), as responders warn it is spreading at an unprecedented speed outpacing efforts to slow it in one of the country’s remotest regions.
Data from Congo’s Ministry of Health showed the outbreak had so far recorded 5,021 cases, including 2,378 deaths as of Sunday (August 16, 2026), as it rages in some of the most challenging conditions imaginable fuelled by insecurity, displacement and intense population movements.
The outbreak has infected and killed more people at a greater speed than any other outbreak in history.
Starting from the first detected case, it has spread about three times faster than an outbreak from 2014 to 2016 across West Africa, which was the deadliest Ebola outbreak on record with more than 11,000 deaths.
The outbreak “has spread rapidly and the risk of further national and international spread remains high,” World Health Organization Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said on Tuesday (August 18, 2026) at a meeting convened by the agency.
“We must be frank: the epidemic is far from being under control,” he said.
Safety concerns have limited the response as health workers are targeted, particularly in Ituri, the province that has been hit the worst by the outbreak.
Residents on Monday (August 17, 2026) attacked a health team in the territory of Aru after a suspected case was reported there. A mob set fire to an ambulance and damaged two other vehicles, according to Michael Wani, president of the Union of Cultural Associations for the Development of Ituri.

The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which has put state government schools at the centre of its ongoing campaign, wrote to all state governments on Monday (August 24, 2026), seeking data on school infrastructure, teacher vacancies, and funding over the last five years.
In identical letters addressed to Education Ministers, CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke said visuals from government schools circulating on social media showed that many children still lacked basic facilities such as safe drinking water, functional toilets, proper classrooms, and even benches.
"It has been 80 years since India gained Independence...No child in this country should be forced to study in such conditions. They are being treated worse than animals," Mr. Dipke wrote.
The letters are the latest step in CJP's campaign regarding the condition of government schools. The youth-led outfit has been highlighting dilapidated school buildings and inadequate facilities on social media while demanding greater public spending on education.
The campaign has also seen confrontations on the ground. A CJP team, including co-convenor Ashutosh Ranka, was allegedly assaulted during a recent visit to a government school in Rajasthan.
The CJP accused BJP workers of carrying out the attack, a charge the party disputed, and cross FIRs were subsequently filed over the incident.
In its letters to the states, the CJP has now sought details of the number of government schools renovated over the past five years and those still requiring repairs or complete renovation.
It has also asked state governments to disclose the number of sanctioned, filled and vacant teaching posts and provide figures on funds allocated to government schools over the past five years against the amount actually spent.
The party also sought estimates of how many additional government schools are needed to ensure reasonable access to quality education and details of non-teaching duties assigned to government school teachers.
It has also sought data on how many schools have adequate computers and digital-learning facilities, clean and functional toilets, and proper sports facilities and equipment.
"This is not about politics or any one government. This is about the future of our children," Mr. Dipke said.
"Every child, irrespective of where they are born or how much their parents earn, deserves a safe classroom, clean drinking water, a functional washroom, a bench to sit on, and a teacher to teach them," he added.
The party has urged the Education Ministries to make the information public and take "urgent steps" to address deficiencies in government schools, calling for improvements to public education infrastructure on a "war footing".

A purported statement by Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke is circulating on social media. In the viral post, Dipke is quoted as saying, “We are demanding responsibility, not resignation from the chief minister (of Jharkhand), so that problems don’t arise regarding papers in the future.”
The apparent statement was shared by a verified Instagram handle named ‘indians’ on August 14. The post received has over 74,600 reactions till date. The page has around 9 million followers. (Archive)
The caption of the post reads:
“… Dipke said he does not want Soren to resign, but wants accountability to ensure such incidents do not happen again. His stand has sparked questions among citizens over why accountability is being sought instead of resignation in this case, while Dharmendra Pradhan faced demands to resign.”
After Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned following CJP’s Delhi protests, a similar protest erupted in Ranchi over alleged paper leaks and irregularities in Jharkhand’s government recruitment exams. Protesters, including students and activists, demanded chief minister Hemant Soren’s resignation.
It was against this backdrop that the quote attributed to CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke went viral. The viral posts reinforce the key BJP charge that CJP was comparatively restrained when allegations of exam irregularities emerged in Opposition-ruled states, particularly Jharkhand. BJP leaders have used this argument to accuse the group of selective outrage. In comments to the above Instagram post, many users replied saying Dipke’s stance showed his ‘hypocrisy’ or ‘double standard’.
The same quotation was also shared by Facebook pages named The Youth – India and Saale Dost Ko Thanks Bolta hai. The follower counts of the two pages are 141,000 and 4.9 million, respectively.
Fact Check
To find more on the purported statement by Dipke, we first went through his X timeline, since the CJP founder regularly posts about his media interactions and public statements on his X account. We could not find any post corroborating the viral claim.
We, however, found a post from August 2 where Dipke is speaking to the protesting students in Jharkhand on a video call. “The CJP stands with all the students in Jharkhand and support their demands,” he wrote. He makes the same point in the video as well.
Spoke to the students who are protesting in Jharkhand over irregularities in JPSC and JSSC recruitment exams.
The CJP stands with all the students in Jharkhand and support their demands. pic.twitter.com/lLSRhFVpv1
— Abhijeet Dipke (@abhijeet_dipke) August 2, 2026
Next, we performed a keyword search on Google, looking for news reports on the said statement. We used the keyword combination: “Abhijeet Dipke Jharkhand Hemant Soren resignation”.
We could not find a single report which mentioned that Dipke had said they were only seeking accountability and responsibility, and not the Jharkhand chief minister’s resignation. Instead, we found several reports on the CJP and its founder supporting the Jharkhand students’ stir. For instance, this report in The Hindu states that Abhijeet Dipke “was in touch with the protesters and supported their demands, and they will go to Ranchi to express solidarity.” Similar reports were carried by outlets like The Print and The Times of India.
None of the articles mentioned anything similar to what the purported quote claims.
We also found an ANI post containing Dipke’s detailed response to the Jharkhand situation. He says, “… We offer our full support. Our delegation has visited the area, and our people are distributing food there. We stand firmly with them and support all their demands… I, too, intend to go… Although, I am currently dealing with some health issues…”
#WATCH | Chhatrapati Sambhaji Nagar, Maharashtra | On students’ protest in Jharkhand, Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) Founder Abhijeet Dipke says, “We offer our full support. Our delegation has visited the area, and our people are distributing food there. We stand firmly with them… pic.twitter.com/R3XbAv5jaT
— ANI (@ANI) August 7, 2026
In another interview with PTI, Dipke said CJP would support demands for educational reforms, irrespective of which state was in question and which party was in power.
Alt News then reached out to Abhijeet Dipke and asked him whether he had made the statement shown in the viral posts. Dipke replied: “Never said this. These people (the social media pages) are running anything they want.”
To sum up, the viral post quoting Abhijeet Dipke as saying that they were seeking accountability but not Jharkhand CM Hemant Soren’s resignation is baseless. There is no credible evidence of the CJP founder having made such a statement. Dipke himself refuted the claim.

For many watching Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial, the primary takeaway has been how the deaths of her three small children—Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and Callen, eight months—were tragically preventable.
Lawyers for the Massachusetts nurse are arguing that she’s not criminally responsible for strangling her children, because she suffered from severe postpartum psychosis, a rare mental health condition that causes new mothers to experience delusions and intrusive thoughts. Defense attorney Kevin Reddington has put Lindsay’s health care providers on the stand, in an attempt to demonstrate how his client repeatedly sought help for her terrifying thoughts, only for her to be minimized, dismissed, and overmedicated at every turn.
For others, including a thriving community of TikTok armchair detectives and conspiracy theorists, the Clancy trial has resulted in a much different takeaway: Lindsay’s husband, Patrick Clancy, was responsible, either literally or by virtue of being a neglectful husband. Many TikTokkers are convinced that he actually committed the murders and framed his mentally ill wife so she would take the fall.
To be clear, there is no evidence whatsoever to suggest this is true. Patrick is not on trial for the deaths of his children, and there has been no indication that he ever will be, or that he is anything other than a deeply grieving father. (Clancy did not respond to a request for comment.) But it’s hard to overstate just how popular this conspiracy theory is, and how rapidly it has overtaken discussion of the trial. The tabloid media has obsessively focused on Patrick, constantly publishing headlines about his life with his new wife Rachel Danis in New York (Patrick remarried earlier this year), and there are countless Reddit threads parsing their social media posts and analyzing his testimony.
Much of the TikTok commentariat’s focus has been on Patrick’s behavior prior to the murders, especially as it pertained to his wife’s postpartum mental health struggles. Per his own testimony, he was not always present at home, even at the height of her suffering. He went to brunch with his friends amidst her struggles with suicidal ideation, and took his daughter on a skiing trip. A month prior to the killings, Lindsay had disclosed to him that she had thoughts of harming the children, but according to his own testimony he had waved them off after she’d assuaged his concerns.
Some experts following the case say that while they understand the impulse to cast suspicion on Patrick, they caution against speculation or cruelly attacking the grieving father of three brutally slain children.
“It’s very easy to try to vilify the husband,” says Leslie Dobson, a forensic psychologist who covers the case on her social media platforms. “But the idea that he actually set her up, or drugged her, or actually killed the children—that’s very extreme.”
But a major driving force behind the antipathy toward Patrick appears to be that women recognize the broad contours of his alleged behavior toward his wife—and they are pissed as hell about it. This is evident when you look at the social media comments on the TikToks accusing Patrick, which are filled with harrowing stories from women whose husbands treated them insensitively while they were struggling with postpartum anxiety or depression, left them for another woman while they were at their lowest, or even emotionally or physically abused them.
(As many TikTokkers have pointed out, Rusty Yates, the husband of Andrea Yates, the woman suffering from severe postpartum psychosis who drowned her children in 2001, reportedly urged her to get pregnant again while she was in recovery from postpartum depression after her fourth pregnancy, against her psychiatrist’s advisement.)
Many right-wing (male) pundits have been inclined to dismiss these comments as the ramblings of female hysterics, who are somehow using their own terrible experiences with new motherhood as an excuse to demonize men or exonerate Lindsay. In an X post from last week, far-right pundit Matt Walsh referred to Lindsay’s defenders as “psychotic women on the internet … outright exalting or celebrating” her, attributing this sentiment to “a deep sickness in our culture.” Others have criticized those casting suspicion on Patrick as frivolous misandrists, who are too obsessed with true-crime podcasts and millennial feminism to maintain a logical perspective on the case. (An astrology meme suggesting that Patrick killed his kids because he was a Gemini is often cited as evidence of this perspective.)
Walsh’s reading is an extremely shallow one. The fact that women are empathizing with Lindsay does not suggest they are “celebrating” or “exalting” her, let alone excusing her crimes. But what it does suggest, pretty damningly, is deep structural perversity—not just with the institution of maternal health care in this country, as so many commenters have pointed out, but with the state of motherhood in the United States. Lindsay’s suffering ran so deep that ultimately she thought the only way to end it was to end her own life, and take the lives of her children. Nobody seems to be asking why so many women empathize with that.
The statistics tossed out every time someone proffers an analysis on why American mothers are so damn unhappy offer some insight. Mothers who work full-time in the US do 1.6 times as many childcare duties and household labor as full-time working fathers. Mothers are more likely than fathers to report feeling stressed or exhausted by parenting, and also more likely than fathers to report feeling like their parenting is being judged. Mothers are more likely to report higher levels of depression and anxiety than fathers; and a study published in 2021 found that suicidality rates among moms have nearly tripled within a decade through the mid 2010s. One study found that anxiety levels in some new mothers were equivalent to that of combat soldiers; similar findings were found among mothers of older children with special needs.
Many of the women commenting on the trial online speak directly to these feelings of immense stress and overwhelm, and clearly, Patrick serves as the ultimate stand-in for that frustration. “So many women have husbands that weren't present or husbands that just didn't know what the fuck to do for their wives after they gave birth,” says Dobson. “Patrick comes off as very tech-savvy but also very aloof, very not present. So we can easily project those feelings onto Patrick.”
Anne Emerson, the host of the true-crime podcast Criminally Obsessed, posits that the antipathy toward Patrick stems from women feeling as if the case “has opened up a new platform to talk about how hard it is” to get through the postpartum stage with so little support. “I definitely think that anyone who may feel they have a partner who isn’t supportive, this is a chance to rail against the system to some degree,” she says of the conspiracy theorists.
There’s no real reason to believe Patrick is guilty of killing his kids, but there is reason to believe he is guilty of failing his wife on some level, as many, many other husbands have. The outpouring of sympathy for Lindsay, as well as the calls for his head, indicates that women would like to see a lot more men held accountable for this specific behavior.
“I think the case could open up more opportunities for women to get help after they have their babies, as opposed to being villainized if they go through a medical emergency,” Emerson says. “Look at the lengths Lindsay went to to get herself help—and it failed catastrophically. Why did it fail? It wasn’t just the number of prescriptions she was on—it was a whole bunch of things. We have to take a cold, hard look at that.”
Ultimately, the obsessive focus on Patrick has nothing to do with Patrick at all. It has to do with a culture that makes it extremely easy for women to believe that someone like Patrick would frame his mentally ill wife for the murders of their children when her sickness became too much of an inconvenience. The fact that this scenario is more plausible to the majority of TikTok than the alternative—that Lindsay was struggling, and Patrick was simply tragically unable to support her—is a lot more damning than anything that Lindsay’s attorney could present on the witness stand.

England drop Carse after nightclub incident
- Published
Pace bowler Brydon Carse has been removed from England's squad for the second Test against Pakistan amid an ongoing investigation into an incident that led to him being handcuffed by police.
Images that appeared on social media on Sunday showed Carse, 31, in handcuffs outside a bar in Derby on Saturday night.
It is understood he was not arrested, though the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) has referred the incident to the Cricket Regulator.
The Regulator will investigate and, as a result, Carse has been removed from the squad and replaced by Sonny Baker.
It is the latest of a string of off-field incidents involving the England team - Carse has become the third player to this summer to miss a Test because of a disciplinary issue.
"Following a referral from the ECB, the Cricket Regulator have confirmed that they will investigate events on Saturday night in Derby," said an ECB statement.
"Brydon Carse will no longer be available for selection for the second men's Test while this investigation is ongoing and the full facts are obtained."
Carse was part of the England squad for the first Test against Pakistan, which the hosts won by an innings inside three days at Headingley.
When he was not named in the starting XI, Carse was released to play for Durham away at Derbyshire, a game the Division Two leaders won on Saturday evening.
Following that win, Carse was filmed in handcuffs outside a bar in Derby. It has not been confirmed why he was detained, though he was released without charge.
The incident occurred less than 48 hours before Carse was scheduled to arrive in London to join up with the rest of the England squad for the second Test at Lord's.
Also in the footage was Carse's Durham team-mate Matthew Potts, while former England captain could be seen in the background. Though Stokes has retired from international cricket, he is still under a central contract with the ECB, as are Potts and Carse.
In June, Stokes and Gus Atkinson were present in a London nightclub when a member of England's security staff was struck by a Saracens rugby player.
Both men missed the second Test against New Zealand while the incident was investigated, and the pair were eventually given a written warning as to their conduct.
Stokes and Atkinson breached an England team curfew that was introduced following late-night incidents during the winter.
Harry Brook was punched by a bouncer outside a nightclub in Wellington and Ben Duckett was filmed, apparently drunk, on England's Ashes holiday in Noosa.
On replacing Stokes as England captain, Joe Root began his second spell in charge by removing the curfew. Guidelines issued to players on the consumption of alcohol around matches and in public were also relaxed.
On the day before the first Test against Pakistan, Root acknowledged called on his players to be "really good role models and good human beings".
"You always want to represent your country in the best possible light," Root told BBC Sport.
"We might have fallen short of that on a few occasions in the recent past. The only thing we can do to rectify that is be really good role models, good human beings and put in really strong performances on the field."
In the summer of 2024, Carse was given a three-month ban for historical betting offences.
He has subsequently rebuilt his career to become an England regular across formats. Since Carse made his Test debut in October 2024, no England bowler has taken more than his 58 wickets.
It is unlikely Carse would have played at Lord's - instead he would probably have been a back-up to England's four frontline seamers from Headingley.
His omission means another opportunity for 23-year-old Baker, who won his only Test cap in the second match of the series against New Zealand in June.
