The Unibook looks unassuming at first glance, somewhere in the neighborhood of an Asus Zenbook. It feels like a cop-out to describe something as “nondescript,” but this is a pretty down-the-middle clamshell PC design.
To begin with the good, the Unibook far outstrips the port offerings of the MacBook Neo or the new XPS 13. It offers a pair of USB-C ports, a full-size HDMI port, two 5Gbps USB 3 ports, one USB 2.0 port, a micro-SD card slot, a headphone jack, and even an Ethernet port. I’ve never loved the little folding-out design for Ethernet ports that some laptops use to save a little space—if and when the little hinge breaks, it will start flopping around and looking bad—but so many laptops use thin-and-lightness as an excuse to ship a bare-minimum allotment of ports that it’s nice to see a budget-minded laptop ship with a ton of connectivity options.
The Unibook’s M.2 2280 drive is also pretty easy to replace. Remove the 11 Philips-head screws on the bottom of the laptop, and its bottom pries up with a bit of pressure. If you want a larger drive or just one from a better-known company, it’s easy to put one in (the built-in SSD is made by “HOGE,” a name that means about as much to most North Americans as “Chuwi”). The Wi-Fi/Bluetooth module is also easily accessible; the battery is, too, if you can manage to find a replacement somehow.
Also in the “good” column is the laptop’s perfectly not-bad keyboard. The keys aren’t as firm or satisfying as those on the keyboards in the MacBook lineup or in Framework’s Laptop 12 or Laptop 13, but the typing feel is decent, and the backlight is nice and even. The computer is missing a fingerprint reader (there’s also no face-scanning camera, which means the Unibook has no biometric login option at all), but this is a corner that the MacBook Neo’s base model also cuts.
Judged by the standards of the category, the Unibook’s screen isn’t awful. It’s a 13-inch IPS display panel with a decent 1920 x 1200 resolution and 16:10 aspect ratio, a step up from the 16:9 1080p displays you’ll still find in some ultra-budget systems. But it’s also not very nice by the MacBook Neo’s standards: only 300-ish nits of maximum brightness, pretty noticeable backlight bleeding around the edges (at least on our unit), and around 59 percent coverage of the sRGB color gamut, according to my colorimeter. At that level, colors appear visibly faded or washed-out to the naked eye; I find it particularly noticeable with shades of red and purple.
MacBook Neo on top, Chuwi Unibook on bottom.
Credit:
Andrew Cunningham
MacBook Neo on top, Chuwi Unibook on bottom.
Credit:
Andrew Cunningham
The mediocre screen was an unpleasant surprise given that this thing advertised 100 percent sRGB gamut coverage when it was announced and on its product page for many weeks (the Internet Archive captures it here). But since then, the company has said that only a higher-specced Unibook 315 actually has a screen with 100 percent sRGB gamut coverage, in addition to an extra P-core on the CPU, 12GB of RAM instead of 8GB, and a 512GB SSD. You still can’t buy this version of the Unibook, though Chuwi says it “may” be available this month and it “may” cost $599.
I run out of nice things to say about the Unibook after the screen. The webcam is usable, insofar as it functions, but the image quality is fuzzy, and it has trouble with white balance. The speakers produce sound under some circumstances (more on that later).
The trackpad is probably the worst of the Unibook’s core features. The actual finger tracking is OK, one gift of the precision trackpad era that endures despite the hardware’s shortcomings. Aside from that, it’s awful—it’s stiff. It’s hard to click. It’s so, so loud. It’s a trackpad that makes you glad for tap-to-click. It’s almost bad enough to ruin the laptop all by itself, though it does have some other help.
Weird software
When you buy a no-name PC, part of what you have to assume is that you are essentially out in the cold with respect to aftermarket software support. Maybe you’ll get some driver and/or BIOS updates directly from the manufacturer, and maybe you won’t! But you should assume that you won’t, and you should assume that whatever driver support page exists might be busted or deleted at pretty much any time. The driver page for the Unibook has not worked even once at any point during the weeks I’ve been using it.
Sadly, Chuwi’s support database was “Working Un-normal” for the entire time I was using the Unibook.
Credit:
Andrew Cunningham
Sadly, Chuwi’s support database was “Working Un-normal” for the entire time I was using the Unibook.
Credit:
Andrew Cunningham
Usually this means putting up with things that feel just a little off or downright weird, like a BIOS that seems to expose every possible setting whether it’s necessary or not, a shortcut to a Windows 7-era Control Panel applet sitting on the desktop by default for some reason, or the system’s pre-installed Microsoft Office 2024 suite.
If you think it’s odd that a $449 computer would come with Microsoft Office pre-installed or that it’s even more odd that Chuwi doesn’t advertise pre-installed Microsoft Office, you’re right. The copy installed on our review unit was definitely activated using a common activation script, something I verified by running the script and checking Office’s activation status.
Security-wise, the Windows install seems to check out, insofar as it meets Windows 11’s Security dashboard’s “enhanced security” baseline (at least, it did after a round of updates and a reboot). Chinese PC makers will occasionally ship a driver, inadvertently or otherwise, that comes with malware on board, so it’s something you need to watch for.
What the Unibook does ship with is all kinds of weird little Microsoft bits and bobs that don’t come with a clean-from-USB Windows 11 install, including a “mobile plans” app (the laptop has no modem, and the app opens to a blank window that does nothing), and the obscure “Microsoft PC Manager” app. The only page I can find for it on what is apparently Microsoft’s actual website is full of bizarre, possibly auto-translated sentence fragments like “Cleanup your system and free up spaces” and “Enhance the efficiency of computer use”). Some Chinese language packs are also preinstalled.
Windows re-installers beware
Normally, I’d treat this sort of PC the same as I’d treat most computers from most OEMs: Blow away the stock Windows installation and control my own destiny. Sure, a “clean” install of Windows 11 isn’t the cruft-removal magic wand that it used to be, but it’s still a good way to make sure you’re dealing mainly with Microsoft’s nonsense and not additional manufacturer-added nonsense on top of that.
For the Unibook, this wasn’t smooth sailing.
As you saw earlier in this review, Chuwi’s support site is currently suffering from an acute case of “Database Working Un-normal.” This made downloading drivers pretty difficult, partly because Wildcat Lake is new enough that Windows Update doesn’t seem to have drivers ready to go.
As a precaution, I replaced the Unibook’s drive with a spare 256GB SSD I had pulled from some other laptop at some point. When I ran into problems getting some of the hardware to work, I switched back to the old SSD and used Windows’ built-in DISM servicing tool to export every single third-party driver installed on the system.
If you need to reinstall drivers onto the Unibook without the benefit of a backup from the existing system, this patchwork also seemed to clear all the exclamation points from the Device Manager:
Generic GPU and NPU drivers from Intel (Wildcat Lake uses the same drivers as Meteor Lake and other Core Ultra/Arc models)
Various Intel chipset drivers (Management Engine, Software Integrated Package, etc.) from Dell’s support page for the XPS 13 DX13260, which is Dell’s similarly specced Wildcat Lake laptop.
A Realtek 8852BE Wi-Fi driver from Windows Update.
If you want a Bluetooth driver other than the generic built-in Windows one, I’ll offer my archived version that I extracted from the laptop—I couldn’t find a serviceable replacement.
But even with a nice, clean Device Manager, sound still wasn’t coming out of the Unibook’s speakers—it didn’t even see that an audio output was installed. By diving into the “System devices” section and selecting a generic audio controller driver, I was able to install an “Intel Smart Sound Technology Bus” device that finally seemed to make Windows recognize the remainder of the not-installed audio drivers, which got everything working again.
For your convenience, I am also including the pile of audio drivers I extracted from the Unibook’s default Windows install here.
The audio problem was also present in Linux, when I tried Kubuntu 26.04 LTS on the system. In addition, the laptop wouldn’t go to sleep when its lid was closed, which put a pretty good dent in the battery life. Some others have had some success getting this stuff working, but it wasn’t something I spent much time on for this review.
Good enough performance, outstanding battery life
Wildcat Lake is Intel’s first genuinely compelling low-end laptop processor in quite a while.
It used to be standard for lower-end laptop CPUs to be cut-down versions of high-end ones, based on the same architecture and manufacturing process. But as manufacturing improvements have gotten harder to do, Intel (and others) have turned to rebranded previous-generation chips to serve more budget-minded systems. Intel’s 12th- and 13th-generation Core processors weren’t especially impressive laptop chips in the first place (mediocre battery life; same GPU as 11th-generation), and getting warmed over and returned to market as the Core Series 1 and Core Series 2 families didn’t make them any better.
Wildcat Lake only has one or two P-cores (one for this version of the Unibook), four E-cores, and one or two GPU execution units. But they at least benefit from being built on the same architectures as the Panther Lake Core Ultra Series 3 processors, including the Intel 18A process for the main CPU die.
Objectively, performance is not impressive. But even a single P-core means a much faster and snappier-feeling computer than you’d get if you used one of Intel’s all-E-cores budget processors, and the Core 3 304 chip is perfectly serviceable for browsing, communicating, or streaming video. The comparison to Apple’s A18 Pro, the MacBook Neo’s chip, isn’t especially flattering for Intel—the Core 3 304 has one fewer P-core and higher power consumption, which means its performance-per-Watt for heavy tasks is pretty bad (it doesn’t use a ton of power, but it takes a very long time, so overall efficiency for these tasks isn’t great.) The Core 3 304’s single-core GPU also looks pretty bad next to the A18 Pro’s.
If you were hoping to play games or edit photos or video, the other blocker is the 8GB allotment of RAM, which was little enough that it kept benchmarks like Cinebench 2024, Cinebench 2026, or many GPU benchmarks from running entirely.
But its saving grace is its battery life—because it uses newer manufacturing tech, Wildcat Lake enables the Unibook’s 53 WHr battery to last for nearly 15 hours while running the PCMark Modern Office benchmark with the screen brightness set to 200 nits. That’s more than enough to make it through a full day away from an outlet.
I’m sorry, but no
The Core Series 3 chip is generally decent, but too many other things about the laptop don’t clear that bar.
Credit:
Andrew Cunningham
The Core Series 3 chip is generally decent, but too many other things about the laptop don’t clear that bar.
Credit:
Andrew Cunningham
If a computer’s price in 2026 seems too good to be true, it probably is—Chuwi’s Unibook is interesting, but I’d hesitate to recommend it as a primary laptop to pretty much anybody. Some of that comes down to the hardware—mainly the awful trackpad, but also the worse-than-expected screen—and some of it is that you’ll be mostly on your own for hardware and software support after you buy it. A MacBook Neo or even the new Dell XPS might be more expensive, but at least you’ll have someone to call if something goes wrong.
And that’s before you get to the actual specs. The Unibook is a decent showcase for Intel’s Core Series 3 processors, which offer pretty stellar battery life, along with performance that’s more than good enough for basic computing. But 8GB of RAM will severely limit the kinds of apps that run well (or run at all) on a PC, and trying to play anything other than basic 2D games on a laptop like this won’t go well.
The good
Intel Core Series 3 chips (codenamed Wildcat Lake) offer good-enough performance and very good battery life.
Lots of ports.
Good screen size and resolution.
A decent keyboard with a nice backlight.
The bad
Screen is worse than originally promised, with way less than 100 percent sRGB color gamut coverage. 300 nits of peak brightness also isn’t great.
No fingerprint reader or other biometric authentication options.
Poor speakers and webcam quality.
8GB of RAM will slow the laptop down once you open too many apps or browser tabs, and some kinds of apps and games don’t want to run at all.
Broken driver support page (and weird audio setup) makes a clean Windows (or Linux) install more difficult than it should be.
The ugly
Awful, stiff, loud trackpad is a genuine displeasure to use.
Andrew is a Senior Technology Reporter at Ars Technica, with a focus on consumer tech including computer hardware and in-depth reviews of operating systems like Windows and macOS. Andrew lives in Philadelphia and co-hosts a weekly book podcast called Overdue.

For 26 days, India watched as Sonam Wangchuk wasted away. His hunger strike, held in solidarity with India’s “Cockroach” youth protest movement, would prove to be one of the most politically consequential fasts held in the country’s modern history.
Many in the country view the gruelling fast, which began on 28 June, as the crucial spark that helped propel the Cockroach movement into one of the most formidable challenges to the government of prime minister, Narendra Modi, in more than a decade.
Abhijit Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach movement, said Wangchuk had “awakened the conscience of an entire nation” through his sacrifice.
The Cockroach movement was launched in May, following the cancellation of a key nationwide exam to enter medical college after a paper was leaked. The cancellation was devastating for the 2 million students who had already sat the exam, a dozen of whom reportedly took their lives.
The movement took its name from comments made by India’s chief justice, Surya Kant, who had compared some unemployed young people to cockroaches and parasites in a court hearing.
Dipke’s demand for education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, to show accountability for the leak by resigning struck a nerve, and anger that had been seething below the surface surged out on to the streets.
The protest ballooned into a nationwide movement. For weeks, deadlock prevailed between the government and Dipke, backed by thousands who flocked to his sit-in protest in Delhi. Eventually, after an unprecedented police crackdown which further influenced public opinion in its favour, the protesters triumphed and Pradhan resigned on 25 July.
The victory was not a foregone conclusion and Dipke has acknowledged the importance of Wangchuck’s fast in determining the outcome. Unlike the students, Wangchuck was a well known and respected figure, recognised for his decades-long efforts to secure educational reforms and environmental protection. Last year, he was arrested in Ladakh on charges of inciting anti-government protests.
The timing was also key: crowds at the Delhi protest site had been thinning before he started his fast on a stage there on 28 June, injecting new energy and momentum into the movement.
Wangchuk had declared he would not end his strike until the government had listened to the demands of India’s protesting youth. He lay outdoors at the Cockroach protest site in the heart of Delhi, day and night, enduring rain, torturous heat and mosquitoes. Already a lean and slight figure, he lost 11kg over the 26 days.
“I felt confined, trapped … like a prison,” he told the Guardian. “The heat and humidity were awful.”
In the aftermath, Wangchuk, a softly-spoken engineer, environmentalist and educationist, remains humble about his role. “I was a known entity and that helped,” he said. His reverence is reserved for the hundreds of thousands of young people in the Cockroach movement, which he says has changed Indian politics for good.
Wangchuk is adamant that the Cockroach movement’s success is far bigger than a single resignation. In an era where dissent is routinely criminalised, young people, he said, had seized back the power of political protest.
“They have stripped away the curtain of fear that existed,” he said. “They are now engaged. They have tasted success in getting results and I expect them to continue.”
The 60-year-old admits the hunger strike took a gruelling toll. By the time he broke his fast on 24 July, he had pushed his body to the limit and was perilously close to organ failure. But as thousands of young people and politicians flocked to his side, his spirit remained unbroken throughout.
The greatest test, he says, came when he was forcibly removed by police from the protest site and taken to hospital against his will. Videos of his frail body being dragged away by burly police went viral and Wangchuk was hailed by young people online as a national hero. When mass protests erupted the following day, Wangchuk’s name was chanted and held aloft on placards.
Wangchuk was not always an obvious figure of anti-government resistance. Born in Ladakh, he rose to international prominence as an engineer and environmentalist, best known for inventing the ice stupor, a unique technique for water storage in human-made glaciers. He became a prominent champion of the rights of Ladakhis and set up his own school and cultural and environmental institution.
He had been a vocal supporter of several prominent policies of Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) but it soon turned to resistance as he accused the BJP of failing the people of Ladakh. Last year, as protests in Ladakh escalated, he was imprisoned by the government for almost six months under draconian anti-terrorist laws.
While his focus has been on rebuilding his body in recent weeks, regaining about 60% of his previous weight, Wangchuk has also continued his call for political reform, albeit without any overt criticism of the Modi government.
In a video message posted before India’s independence day in August, Wangchuk called for a “second independence movement” and urged Indians to choose men and women of “character and substance” to lead the country.
He has urged people to share the names of individuals of integrity who can be trusted and once he has a list, he plans to meet them in Mumbai and Delhi to discuss how elections can be cleansed of those with a criminal background.
“Indians have to trust those at the top,” he said. “At the moment, there is no trust in anything, not in elections, not in exams, not in civil servants. Clean and honest leaders are the first step to a better future.”
He expressed his support for the decision by the Cockroach movement to resist calls to become a political party and instead focus on being a pressure group, championing issues of education. “When we used to talk during the long days of the fast, I used to advise them that being a pressure group is the best way to keep clean and neutral,” he said.
For now, he is back living quietly in Ladakh, finally able to enjoy the one food that lingered on his mind during his hunger strike. “I did dream of apricots,” he said, “but that was just because I was wondering if mine back home had ripened.”

After nearly 40 years in clinical medicine, I retired in 2022. While I expected to feel a sense of freedom, quitting medicine brought me an unexpected sense of loss over the thought of decades of accumulated knowledge, experience, and judgment suddenly going to waste.
Volunteering at a nonprofit community clinic gave me the chance to continue using my knowledge and skills. But it also taught me firsthand what I had not learned in private practice: For millions who must pay out of pocket for their health care, the options are very limited. Both community clinics and retired doctors are underutilized resources.
The community clinic serves the “working poor” — those who are employed but cannot afford high insurance premiums or deductibles, those who are ineligible for federal aid, and the unemployed. Most clinic patients do not speak English, and caring for them via translation is challenging and inefficient. Scribes assist by entering patient data into the electronic health record. Our scribes are pre-medical students who volunteer part time at the clinic to gain clinical experience, a requisite for admission to medical school. I enjoy mentoring these future doctors by explaining key clinical findings of patients we had seen, having them listen to a heart murmur through my stethoscope, or answering their many questions about life in medicine.
At the clinic, I learned that many modern imaging techniques are difficult to access or too expensive for the self-paying patient. An EKG machine is readily available, but advanced imaging such as echocardiography requires referral to an outside site and some diagnostic tests are prohibitively expensive despite “discounted prices.” For years, the National Institutes of Health had offered advanced cardiac imaging at no cost to uninsured patients who volunteered for clinical trials. However, in January 2025, the NIH enacted a stricter registration mandate requiring documentation of citizenship for all NIH campus visitors, which deterred many patients from this option. So, in evaluating patients, I must rely more on my eyes, my stethoscope, and my hands, using skills learned in medical school — skills that have been fading as clinicians increasingly rely on high-tech imaging.
I learned that for the self-paying patient, just filling a prescription can be daunting, because drug prices vary widely between pharmacies even for older generic drugs. On the GoodRx website, a one-month supply of lisinopril 10 mg, a commonly prescribed generic antihypertensive medication, costs $5.90 (“without coupon”) at one pharmacy and $29.21 at another. The cost of a one-month supply of generic sacubitril/valsartan used to treat heart failure varies between $39.33 and $700.75. Brand-name drugs are even more expensive. Medical therapy based on affordability makes it difficult to achieve optimal outcomes and often requires using combinations of several older, less effective drugs. Our clinic pharmacists spend countless hours price-hunting to help patients find the most affordable way to fill their prescriptions.
The stakes are higher when an uninsured patient requires urgent but non-emergency surgery. I evaluated a patient with a severely narrowed aortic valve who, in my former practice, would have been referred promptly for valve replacement. I was unable to find a private cardiologist who would accept an uninsured patient. Although the emergency room remains a safety net, my patient was reluctant to go, knowing he might be discharged with a bill if not deemed sick enough for admission. The clinic doctor is left walking a tightrope, managing patients conservatively until they are sick enough to be admitted, worrying that they will suddenly decompensate in the interim. It is both frightening and frustrating when former referral pathways are no longer available and established lifesaving treatment is difficult to access due to cost. I took the chance to “cold call” an ER physician at a nearby tertiary hospital, and fortunately, after I conveyed the seriousness of the patient’s condition, she agreed to admit the patient, who subsequently underwent successful lifesaving valve replacement surgery.
For the uninsured, limited access to care can be a matter of life and death. According to KFF, an estimated 26.7 million people in this country are uninsured. Increasing layoffs, stricter Medicaid work requirements, and reduced subsidies will only add to the number of the “working poor.” In addition to providing basic care, community clinics can lower overall health care expenditure by reducing preventable ER visits and hospitalizations. A published analysis of a California clinic found that every $1 invested yielded $13.18 in savings.
While millions lack access to basic care, thousands of physicians retire each year. This growing “retirement cliff” and “brain drain” represents a loss of valuable medical expertise. Community clinics like ours provide an ecosystem that could benefit multiple participants if hurdles are removed. Offering low-cost national licensure and expanding good Samaritan protections could encourage more retired physicians to volunteer. More hospital systems could partner with community clinics to coordinate essential post-discharge follow-up care. Nonprofit hospitals, in exchange for their tax-exempt status, could allocate a fair share of imaging and hospital care to uninsured patients at little or no cost.
It was only after retiring from mainstream medicine when I fully comprehended the callous limitations of our health care system and how it impacts the most vulnerable among us. In volunteering, I’ve learned how community nonprofit clinics can serve multiple needs: providing essential cost-effective care for safety net patients, clinical experience for future physicians, and renewed purpose for retired doctors who wish to continue practicing at a different pace. Volunteering at the clinic extends the value of my medical education and enables me to contribute a small amount of care to those our health care system has forsaken.
Benjamin I. Lee is a retired cardiologist who volunteers at a community-based clinic in Maryland.

The internet kind of sucks right now. And it’s been getting harder and harder to use over the past several years.
Is Reddit still for humans?
AI comes for the last real place on the internet.
Imagine you’re training for a marathon, or just trying to get in better shape, and you want to buy a new pair of shoes. Well, good luck! You’re going to have to wade through sponsored links, affiliate marketing, AI summaries, and websites seemingly engineered for search engines instead of human shoppers.
Maybe you just want to connect with friends on Instagram or discover recipes on TikTok. But even there, everyone is selling something. “Get Ready With Me” videos are sponsored by CeraVe, movie reviews are actually ads for the movies being reviewed, and the guy who posts your favorite mobility routines really wants you to try his protein powder.
So people have developed a workaround: Simply add “Reddit” to the search.
Looking for a shoe with high energy return? Reddit. Want to know if an Airbnb you’ve been eyeing has a sketchy listing? Reddit. Trying to figure out the fastest way to the international terminal in Atlanta’s humongous airport? Chances are someone on Reddit has shared very specific thoughts and instructions.
It’s a strange situation. Reddit is filled with pseudonymous strangers, and yet these people can somehow feel more trustworthy recommending a skincare product than an influencer hawking cleansers to millions of followers. Why? Because the random person on Reddit doesn’t seem to have anything to sell you.
That’s why, for many people, Reddit feels like one of the last “real” places on the internet. The site has become so integral to navigating the internet that Google took notice; in recent years, it’s begun surfacing Reddit threads more prominently in search results.
Then came artificial intelligence. Chatbots need massive amounts of human language to learn how we communicate. AI-powered search also needs somewhere to turn when we ask the kinds of hyper-specific questions that newspapers, Wikipedia, and government websites haven’t answered. Reddit has plenty of both.
Unfortunately, whenever something online becomes valuable, people and companies figure out how to exploit it.
The stakes go far beyond a brand tricking someone into buying a lousy face cream. Reddit works because people trust that there’s a real person on the other side of the screen. It doesn’t have to become totally overrun by bots or marketers for that trust to disappear. We just have to start questioning who — or what — we’re talking to.
To break down how Reddit is changing, what the platform and its moderators are doing to push back, and what it could mean for the increasingly blurry line between human conversation, marketing, search, and AI, Today, Explained co-host Noel King spoke with the Verge’s Mia Sato, who recently wrote about the new wave of AI spam beleaguering the platform.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
Are you a big Reddit user?
Yeah, I think so.
What do you mainly use it for?
I think it’s become a big part of finding information on the internet. I usually use Google as the sort of doorway into Reddit, but if I search something on Google, really, it’s a high likelihood that I will end up on Reddit in the end.
That’s a trend that you write about in your piece, which I thought was very interesting because it was something that has also been happening to me and it happened without me realizing how often it was happening.
You start this piece in the Verge with an example from a post on a skincare-focused subreddit, a place you write that you visit often. Can you take us through what happened?
The skincare subreddits that I mentioned in my story are actually subreddits that I often read because I want unfiltered or true opinions about products before I buy them. And I go to Reddit for skincare recommendations quite a bit.
I suspected that if you are a skincare brand and you want people to be talking about your product, you will go to these subreddits because some of these subreddits get like one and a half million viewers a week. They’re doing crazy numbers and they have a very committed and active community. So I was like, if I were a brand and I wanted to market myself, I would probably post on Reddit.
I was curious how the moderators of these skincare subreddits were handling that, because also marketing firms had told me, “Yeah, all our clients, they really want to know how to crack Reddit. It’s really hard. They want to figure out Reddit.”
And so I talked to a subreddit moderator who does one of the skincare subreddits, and she gave me a ton of detail about the amount of spam that they were getting. She sent me one example, which was a thread of someone asking about a certain spray that people use for acne treatment.
The person who posted it asked, like: “Magic Molecule Hypochlorous Acid Spray - is it really that good? Recently I have seen a lot of good reviews about this product. Any of you tried? Do you recommend? What is your take on this?”
And, you know, it got like dozens of answers. Some people said, “Yeah, it’s great.” Others said, “They all work the same.” But one of the answers was from just a random account that said, “I’m sorry, I don’t have any experience with that product, but I have tried this other one that I was skeptical of, but I really like it actually.”
If you’re reading that comment, you probably would think nothing of it. But what you don’t see unless you click over to the profile and do some digging is that this random account had actually — over the course of several days, maybe even months, and across different skincare subreddits — been recommending the same product over and over and over, and using very specific terminology, saying, “It has all these recommendations from certified dermatologists, which made me feel a bit more confident trying it on sensitive skin.”
It was very controlled messaging. Of course, the moderators were like, “What normal person is going to go across different subreddits and keep pushing this product? For no reason?”
So that is one of the ways that this new type of spam on Reddit takes shape, which is brands pretending to be normal users on Reddit.
For Reddit moderators, I’m thinking they can’t individually suss it out immediately or it wouldn’t be happening. Are they doing the search themselves to try to figure out, like, is everything on here real? How are they dealing with this?
They have a bunch of tools. Some of them are auto-moderator tools, where basically a bot will look at every submission that comes through and move some things to a filtered folder where moderators can look at [it].
One of the funniest things that several moderators actually told me was they keep shit lists of companies that they think have spammed them in the past. The skincare subreddit told me about this. A weight-loss subreddit moderator whom I interviewed also said this. They have a running list in the background where if they think you’ve spammed or astroturfed their community in the past, they keep all those brands’ names. And now if you mention that brand name, your post will automatically get filtered out.
Wow. Okay.
The moderators are trying to send a message: “If you spam us, all of the posts that are not even your spam will get filtered out and we will take a closer look at them.” They’re pretty strict with it. Some moderators that I spoke to said that they’ve really seen an increase over the last six to eight months, maybe.
I can give you a couple of the numbers that Reddit has released publicly because Reddit has said also that they know that this is a growing problem. The company said that it removes 25,000 spammy posts and comments a day. They block something like 23 million spam views. And they also tackle spam upvotes — a way on Reddit to sort of signal agreement.
But Reddit knows that it is kind of a new era of spam, and they’ve said that they’re using LLMs and other AI-powered moderation tools to try to catch this stuff better.
Let me ask you something. Maybe it comes down to what Reddit is and always has been, but I will go on Instagram, I will go on TikTok, and my sense is like half of it is just crap that’s trying to sell me something. It might not be real. It just all feels pretty garbagey to me.
I feel like when you wrote this piece, you were saying there are stakes here to Reddit being the thing that must kind of stay pure, must stay away from this. What is it about Reddit that makes it important?
One part is that the concept of influencers doesn’t really exist on Reddit in the same way that it exists elsewhere.
And if you are an influencer, there are very few places that you can post without getting in trouble. Many, many subreddits have explicit rules saying, “You may not self-promote here, and we will ban you if you do.” That is a totally different environment than Instagram, where sort of the expectation is that someone is selling you something.
The other part that makes Reddit unique, I think, is that for better or for worse, and deserve it or not, Reddit, in the minds of people using the internet, has come to sort of be associated with real opinions or real people. Which is funny because the platform is anonymous, you know? Most people are using just a random username, not their full name. So it’s kind of stumbled into this reputation of being filled with real, helpful opinions and perspectives.
Reddit has deals with certain AI companies where they allow LLMs to be trained on troves of Reddit data, of real people having conversations. And so I think over the last few years as Google search feels like it’s gotten worse and people have gone to places like Reddit to answer their questions, Reddit’s stock literally has skyrocketed as a place where you can find information where people aren’t trying to sell you something all the time. Or are they? That’s kind of the part that I wanted to untangle.
Does Reddit actually have to become overrun with marketing, fake posts, people saying, “Oh, you should definitely buy this skincare,” because they’re getting paid to say that for this to be a big problem? Or does it just have to get to the point where I am suspicious that I’m not talking to an actual person on Reddit and I start doubting a platform itself?
For me personally, in the course of reporting this story, I was like, “Hmm, maybe I shouldn’t buy things based on a recommendation from Reddit.”
It’s a new type of problem and a new way of looking at a platform. As it relates to AI search, if these chatbots love to cite Reddit so much for their answers, can the AI systems detect when something is spam? Can they detect when a comment is coming from a brand or when the person who left that comment, if you go to their account, they’re always promoting that product?
I am not convinced that Google’s Gemini or ChatGPT can suss out when something is promotional and when it isn’t. Because I’ve written about this before and I know that they can’t.
Hmm!
It’s a strange thing where I think the deception on one platform ends up trickling through other places as well, as the Reddit thread gets cited by search features and LLMs.
Have you changed your buying habits based on what you’re seeing now on Reddit?
I feel like I’m just way slower to buy things. I’m just like, let me keep this in my head. Let me put it on my wishlist and do some research to see what other people, what real people think, and also make sure that they have a good return policy.

Enough new coalmining projects were proposed last year to increase global supplies by 2.5bn tonnes a year, an increase of 11% from the year before, even as demand for coal plateaus, according to a new report.
Global Energy Monitor, an NGO, found that India ignited a rise in new coalmine proposals in 2025 despite a global slowdown in the number of mine openings because of falling demand for the fossil fuel.
The increase was driven almost entirely by the states of Jharkhand and Odisha, which doubled their proposals for new coalmines in line with an ambitious plan from India’s ministry of coal to increase the country’s output.
India plans to increase its coal production by nearly 100m tonnes to 1.15bn tonnes in the 2025-26 fiscal year to help meet the country’s rising demand for electricity to support economic growth and contend with heatwaves, which have become more severe and more frequent because of the climate crisis.
The planned increases come despite signs that the world is beginning to turn its back on coal in favour of renewable electricity, Global Energy Monitor said.
Coalmine proposals slowed in the years after the Covid-19 pandemic but have begun to climb again, raising concerns that mining could increase in the future despite a slowdown in the number of new facilities.
The startup of new coalmining projects has fallen steadily in recent years, according to the Global Energy Monitor’s latest report.
It found that enough new coalmines to produce about 113m tonnes each year began operations last year, down by 40% from 2024, which was already the lowest annual total in a decade.
This was largely owing to a slowdown in new mines in China and Australia, which fell by 44% and 96% respectively.
Global Energy Monitor warned that India’s rise in new mine proposals was at odds with the slowdown in global coal demand predicted by the International Energy Agency for the end of the decade.
Wind and solar power surpassed coal generation in the global electricity mix for the first time last year, according to a separate report from energy thinktank Ember, in a “milestone moment” for climate action.
China and India were largely responsible for the rise in renewables, according to the Ember report, while the US and Europe continued to rely more heavily on fossil fuels.
Tiffany Means, a senior researcher at Global Energy Monitor and co-author of the report said: “The economic rationale for expanding coalmining becomes progressively weaker as low-cost clean energy continues to displace coal.
“Rather than locking in decades of additional coal production, governments have an opportunity to cancel projects that remain in the development pipeline before they advance to construction.”

Doctors from a private health facility in West Bengal have successfully treated a seven- year-old boy suffering from thalassaemia using an advanced Haplo Cord transplant process.
The parents of the 7-year-old child diagnosed with HbE Beta thalassemia, who needs monthly blood transfusions, were counseled to register under the “Save the Sibling” programme. They underwent IVF (in vitro fertilization) and pre-implantation genetic testing to produce a matched thalassemia-free sibling with compatible HLA (human leukocyte antigen), which is critical for bone marrow transplantation.
A haplo-cord transplant was performed using the cord blood from the patient’s sibling and some stem cells from his father. The transplant was conducted by Narayana Health. During the transplant period, the child developed complications such as infections, mucositis, liver derangement, and persistent low blood counts, which were effectively managed. The patient has recovered well and is now transfusion-free, the doctors said.
In another feat, the team treated a 62-year-old male patient from Myanmar with brain cancer after a successful CAR T-cell therapy (an advanced type of immunotherapy). The patient was initially found to be having gait disturbance (an unusual change in the way a person walks). He was then diagnosed to have primary CNS lymphoma, a rare, aggressive type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma where cancer cells form in the brain, spinal cord, cerebrospinal fluid, or eyes.
After receiving four cycles of high-dose chemotherapy yielding unsatisfactory results, the doctors decided to have him undergo CAR T-cell therapy. He underwent lymphocyte collection, bridging with radiation and other medications, before receiving a dual CAR targeting CD19 and CD22 on the cancer cells.
Speaking about these two rare recoveries, Joydeep Chakrabartty, Senior Consultant, Hemato Oncology & Clinical Lead - BMT Programme (East), Narayana Health, said that the recoveries are landmark achievements with both facing potential fatalities.
“Using the Haplo-cord technology for the child and the CAR T-cell therapy for the aged patient, the expert team of doctors attending them have been able to turn their lives around for the better. Narayana Health has always been at the forefront in breaking new grounds in medical science, and these two cases clearly reflect that,” Dr. Chakrabartty said.
Also read: Evidence of CAR T-cell therapy against cancers presented at US conference
Prasanta Chowdhury, Laboratory Director, Cord Life Sciences India Pvt. Limited, said that cord blood banking is a complex issue involving medical, financial, ethical, and scientific debates. “The core dilemma centres on choosing between private storage for family use and public donation for general use, weighed against high costs and low statistical odds of personal use. In these two cases, we have successfully addressed every single concern with absolute compassion and clarity,” Dr. Chowdhury said.

Harvard University’s International Office is advising F-1 and J-1 international students and J-1 scholars enrolled in on-campus programs this fall to consider being in the United States before a new Department of Homeland Security rule takes effect on September 15, 2026.
The guidance comes amid uncertainty over how the new rule will affect students who travel outside the US after the effective date, as well as ongoing legal challenges seeking to block the changes.
Harvard’s International Office said students and scholars who are already in the US when the rule takes effect will be treated differently from those who leave and subsequently return.
Those who are in the country on September 15 will generally be allowed to remain without filing an extension until the later of their program end date or the expiration of their post-completion work authorization, subject to a maximum four-year period.
However, students and scholars who leave the US and return after September 15 will become subject to the new rule upon reentry.
Harvard acknowledged that the situation remains uncertain.
“We understand that the rule change, and the lack of clarity surrounding it, has been confusing and unsettling for all of us across higher education,” the HIO said.
The new rule would also change the grace period available to international students after completing their authorised period of study.
Students already in the US when the rule takes effect would retain the existing 60-day grace period for F-1 visa holders, while J-1 holders would retain their 30-day grace period.
For F-1 students entering or reentering under the new system, however, the grace period would be reduced to 30 days.
Harvard said students returning to the US after September 15 could also see changes to the “Admit Until Date” listed on their I-94 arrival record.
Under the new system, the date could correspond to the student’s program end date. Harvard warned that this could affect how future extensions of status are handled.
The change could therefore have practical consequences for students whose academic programmes extend beyond their initial authorised period.
One of the major changes under the rule is how international students seek to remain in the US beyond their authorised admission period.
Students would be required to file an extension application with US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS).
Under the existing system, students can generally extend their programme dates through their universities without separately applying to USCIS for an extension of stay.
The rule would also place new limits on students’ ability to transfer institutions or change their plans of study.
The university said it has been working with national higher education associations to understand how the rule will operate but acknowledged that some questions may remain unanswered even after the September 15 effective date.
“It is possible we may not have clarity around some of those questions by the effective date of September 15, 2026,” the HIO guidance said.
Harvard said it would continue monitoring developments and provide additional information as more details become available.
The guidance comes shortly after a coalition of higher education organisations and labour unions filed a lawsuit seeking to prevent the DHS rule from taking effect.
The plaintiffs have also asked a federal judge for a preliminary injunction that would temporarily block implementation while the case proceeds.

Trump administration expands U.S. sanctions on Iran targeting countries with business ties to Tehran
Treasury says it has mapped the networks Iran uses to smuggle oil and evade sanctions
U.S. President Donald Trump's administration on Monday announced an expansion of secondary sanctions it can impose on entities and countries that maintain business ties with Iran, significantly ratcheting up economic pressure on Tehran as the war nears its six-month mark.
At a press conference, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent unveiled what he described as an "economic D-Day" aimed at giving countries a final warning to sever business ties with Iran or risk having key companies and entities cut off from the dollar-based financial system.
"We are launching an economic onslaught against Iran’s financial connections around the globe. Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone," Bessent said.
The U.S. Treasury Department said it has mapped the networks, facilitators and financial channels Iran uses to smuggle oil and evade sanctions, and that Washington would work with U.S. partners to target any source of Iran's "illicit revenue."
The department said it has issued determinations against five sectors — digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping — that the Iranian government uses to prop up its economy. The Treasury has also imposed sanctions on nearly 60 entities, individuals and vessels.
China has for several years been the biggest buyer of Iranian oil. Washington has intensified efforts to clamp down on Chinese purchases but has so far stopped short of designating larger Chinese banks that may be facilitating the trade.
The war with Iran is nearing its six-month mark and has pushed energy prices higher worldwide. While heavy fighting has subsided, diplomatic efforts to end the conflict have stalled, and oil and raw-material shipments through the Strait of Hormuz remain blocked, keeping energy prices elevated.
Trump's approval rating has fallen to a low point, with just 33 per cent of Americans in the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll approving of his performance. He says the economic costs are necessary to ensure Iran does not obtain a nuclear weapon.
The U.S. has maintained sanctions against Iran for decades. Most have been aimed at curtailing the country's oil revenues, targeting its aviation sector and cryptocurrency activity, restricting its procurement of weapons components and other military hardware, and cutting off funding for business enterprises controlled by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, a dominant force in the Iranian economy.
The sanctions bar designated entities from the dollar-based financial system, but Iran has been successful in quickly standing up new front companies, entities and vessel registrations to evade them.

Divorce, smartphones and control - BBC sees how Taliban run Afghanistan
- Published
Governor Abdullah Sarhadi gives money to treat a boy's broken arm and hands out funds for a local mosque - then, in his office in northern Afghanistan, an astonishing exchange unfolds.
A young woman tells the grey-bearded former Taliban commander that she wants to divorce her husband, who she accuses of months of abuse and beatings.
She will not take no for an answer.
In a country where girls are banned from secondary education, the 18-year-old argues her case calmly and confidently, her face completely hidden behind a full-face veil and sunglasses.
"If there was any chance to live together, I wouldn't be here… I have taken my decision," she says.
After trying to persuade her to avoid divorce, the governor later comments that women are "mindless" and "deficient in intellect", to laughter from the male officials, bodyguards and elders around him.
The moment gives a rare glimpse into the day-to-day realities of the Taliban's rule, five years after they swept aside the US-backed government in 2021.
In that time, women have been excluded from most workplaces, banned from universities and may not travel alone or visit parks and leisure centres.
In encounters spread over two years, the BBC gained unusual access to influential figures in the extreme Islamist movement, spending time with men who once planned suicide attacks or spent years in underground hideouts, but are now officials and soldiers.
The Taliban came into power saying they had changed, but many of their policies are similar to the hard-line interpretation of Sharia - Islamic religious law - they imposed in the 1990s.
The men we met seemed to want to present themselves as reasonable, yet were not keen to discuss their past violence. And we saw moments of unease between the rulers and those they rule.
Governor Sarhadi says Tuba – not her real name – should stay in the marriage.
"Ask yourself: 'Who would marry me after I get my divorce?'" says Sarhadi. "You'll have to compromise a lot or you'll lose your dignity and honour."
"Mr Governor, my honour and dignity have already been ruined," she responds.
Her husband listens, awaiting his turn to speak.
Under Sharia, a woman requesting that her husband agrees to a divorce may have to return some or all of the money given to her by him when they married. A financial settlement is often agreed. But this woman's husband says he wants four times the amount, which her family refuses to pay.
The governor says the woman should be given her own room. He adds that officials will warn him not to beat her - "otherwise he'd be jailed".
Unsatisfied, Tuba's father later tells the BBC the family will pursue divorce through the courts, even though, under the Taliban's court system, it is very difficult for a woman to get a divorce without the husband's consent.
Sarhadi was a military commander during the Taliban's first stint in power in the 1990s. He was among thousands of insurgents who surrendered in late 2001 as a US-led coalition ousted the group.
He was held for several years in US detention in Guantanamo Bay, but eventually released.
When the Taliban regained power, he became a governor - first in the province of Bamiyan, then when we met him in late June, in Sheberghan city in Jawzjan province. He has recently become deputy commander of a military corps in the northern province of Kunduz.
Tapping on an old-style mobile with a tiny screen, he says a recent ban on smartphones for officials has slowed things down. "Before, you could send a quick message… sending documents and getting an answer fast." If he says any more about the ban, "it will cause trouble", he adds.
But in other ways his worldview seems largely unchanged from the Taliban's position 25 years ago. Then, he was a military commander in Bamiyan, where the Taliban blew up ancient giant Buddha statues, triggering international shock and condemnation.
He initially tries to avoid our questions about the archaeological site, but eventually, he says: "I destroyed it with my own hands.
"Whatever we did and we do is in accordance with the guidance and God's law… We smash idols rather than sell them. Why should I regret? It was God's will."
In the capital Kabul, we meet another senior Taliban figure who swapped a violent past for a role with the ruling administration.
Habibullah Badr drives us through the streets in an armoured car.
He says he was previously "responsible for the operations of suicide attackers" in Kabul.
"I know all the roads and streets very well… we had all the information we needed about Kabul and its alleys," he says. "There were areas that needed a long time to plan."
Taliban suicide attacks killed thousands of people in Afghanistan, including many civilians.
Badr is cautious about discussing his past though, fearing it will "make people upset" and could "reopen wounds".
Asked about civilian deaths, he says the Taliban targeted US convoys and that civilians were urged to stay away from foreign bases.
Whenever I try to ask him about specific attacks that took place in civilian areas, he evades the question.
He is currently taking time out from official roles for medical treatment, but was previously deputy head of prisons for the whole country – and ran the very jail where he was held on death row under the previous government.
Badr invites us to join him at a tribal gathering, where the head of a charitable foundation is to honour him with a medal. But things take an unexpected turn.
"Mr Badr is a pride for Afghanistan and a great fighter," says Sultan Mohammad Talaee. "But I also have a complaint. If the schools and education were open to all it would be a great work for Afghanistan. I hope this doesn't offend you."
An awkward silence follows, his audience unsure how to react. Talaee's microphone is swiftly removed.
Afterwards, he tells the BBC: "I requested for the girls' schools to reopen… seeking knowledge is an obligation for both men and women in Islam."
He adds: "There were other things I wanted to say but they didn't let me talk more."
Often those who speak out face much more severe consequences.
Women told us of the deep despair they felt over dreams thwarted by restrictions on education, and of friends jailed for protesting.
Most journalists we spoke to said they had been summoned or questioned by the Taliban's intelligence organisation, Estikhbaraat.
The BBC put some of these concerns to the Taliban government's spokesman, known as Zabihullah Mujahid.
He has been a public face for the Taliban government since 2021. He still uses the pseudonym he went by for years during the insurgency, but he told us his real name is Tahir Shah Seddiqi - revealing it publicly for the first time.
In a lavish press centre funded by the Americans for the previous government, we ask him about the first press conference he gave there, two days after the Taliban took control of the country.
Then, he told the world the Taliban government would allow women to work and study "within our frameworks" and they would "be very active" in society. Why did they fail to keep their word?
"We are committed to women's rights, freedom of speech and other things within Sharia," he replies. "We should see everything through the Sharia lens."
Allowing women to work in offices such as his own "would lead to immoralities" and "their dignity would be undermined", he adds.
He says the issue of education for women is "under discussions… we need a Sharia-based solution for it".
When questioned about the Taliban's crackdown on media freedom, he says: "In a society like Afghanistan we have our restrictions. We can't let media do whatever propaganda they want… they can't broadcast against Islamic laws and rites."
The Taliban government sits in Kabul, but Mujahid spends a lot of time in the southern city of Kandahar, the Taliban's heartland, which some now consider the de facto capital.
We ask to meet the Taliban's supreme leader, Hibatullah Akhundzada, who is based there. He rarely appears in public and has never given a media interview - we are told it will not be possible at the moment.
Restrictions have been tightened in Kandahar since I last visited two years ago. Now men must have beards. Radio stations are not allowed to play music or broadcast women's voices, and we were not allowed to film in the city.
Two hours' drive away, along dusty roads, some of the group's most devoted former fighters showed the BBC the insurgents' old secret cave network.
Abid Lalai, a former fighter who now mans a checkpoint as part of a security force under the interior ministry, shows us the holes he fired from and the places he used to put his Quran and hang AK-47s.
His superior, Abdul Samad, shows us an unmarked graveyard, saying his father is buried here, killed fighting for the Taliban.
The area is one of the most deprived in a country where the UN says three in four people cannot provide for their basic needs. Samad says the local population desperately need water, roads and clinics.
"Emirate [Taliban] officials have not forgotten us," says Samad. He says the leaders may be busy with other priorities. "We are hopeful, they will look after us sometime."
Five years since the Taliban began their second stint in power, poverty, unemployment and economic instability remain pressing concerns.
Taliban figures we spoke to said they were working to tackle them, but we met other people who believe the group itself is the country's main problem.
"I'm speechless about how a group that has no understanding about life is suddenly in power," says Hoda - not her real name - a woman who protested on the streets when the Taliban first returned to power.
"Women can't accept this situation," she tells the BBC. "They might advance restrictions but it won't stay like this forever."
"I think the Taliban are scared of educated women," she adds. "That's why they restrict women. They want uneducated women so they can't raise wise men. Because that would end the Taliban."
Additional reporting by Hafizullah Maroof

Soon after his appointment as the BJP’s national social media co-convenor, Arun Yadav made his X account private and then deleted more than 60,000 posts before making it public again. When the account was locked, it showed around 65,500 posts. By August 22, only 2,794 remained — a deletion exercise that wiped out virtually his entire publicly visible posting history.
At present, the oldest post that can be traced on Yadav’s timeline dates to August 19, 2026. All posts preceding it have been deleted. Many of those posts included abusive and racist remarks, attacks on women’s character, and content directly targeting Muslims in communally provocative terms.
On August 17, the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) announced a new social media cell where Deepak Mhaskey replaced Amit Malviya a the party’s IT cell chief. One of the newly inducted members of the social media cell was Yadav, who had previously been removed from his position as head of the Haryana BJP IT Cell.
When attention turned to Yadav’s old social media record following his new appointment, he locked his X account, @BeingArun28. Yadav has now made his account public again, but not before deleting the posts on a massive scale. The sequence of events indicates that making the account private might have given him the opportunity to remove his old controversial posts and wipe his social media record clean.
A review of Arun Yadav’s social media activity over the past several years reveals a clear pattern: abusive and racist remarks against opposition leaders, attacks on women’s character, and several explicit instances of directly targeting Muslim minorities and making communally provocative statements.
The Post that Led to his Ouster in 2022
Arun Yadav’s history of controversial remarks goes back several years. In 2017, he shared an image of the Kaaba in Mecca alongside a glass of whisky and wrote in an objectionable post that he could see “the Prophet in a peg of alcohol”. Questions continued to be raised over the remark for years. Finally, amid mounting pressure, Haryana BJP removed Arun Yadav from his post as state IT Cell chief on July 8, 2022.
The timing of the action taken against him was particularly significant. It came just a month after then BJP spokesperson Nupur Sharma’s derogatory remarks about prophet Muhammad of Islam had sparked a massive controversy in India and abroad. During a television debate, the BJP spokesperson had made offensive remarks about the prophet, triggering an international backlash.
Amid intense international pressure, the BJP had termed its spokesperson a “fringe element” and expelled her from the party. The following month, a screenshot of Arun Yadav’s old objectionable post went viral on social media. In this sensitive environment, Yadav’s removal was, in a sense, a tacit acknowledgement that his post had crossed a line the party was not prepared to publicly defend at the time.
The significant new responsibility handed to Arun Yadav within the party sends a serious political message: the conduct for which his own party had once sacked him has not stood in the way of his appointment to a higher position with greater responsibility.
“The Digging will Continue until God leaves India, Keep Digging”
In May 2022, Arun Yadav made another objectionable remark about Islam, writing: “The digging will continue until God leaves India, keep digging.”
The post was made at a time when the Gyanvapi Mosque dispute was before the Supreme Court. The Hindu side had claimed that a “Shivling” was present within the mosque complex. Given the sensitivity of the case, the Supreme Court transferred the suit filed by the Hindu side from the trial court to a more senior and experienced district judge.
In this tense legal and social environment, Yadav’s statement was not merely an inflammatory post or an insult directed at a particular religion. It also sought to frame the “digging” of sites containing mosques across the country as a coordinated campaign.
Attack on Rahul Gandhi
Political opponents have also been among Arun Yadav’s targets. In a post from January 2023, he shared a video of Congress leader Rahul Gandhi’s speech and used the phrase “the harvest of the brown aunty” for him.
The remark was not merely a deeply insulting personal attack but also reflected a clearly racist mindset. It was a direct reference to Rahul Gandhi’s mother, Sonia Gandhi, and her Italian origins. However, this is not an exception among BJP leaders. They have often been seen using such derogatory language targeting Sonia Gandhi’s foreign origins in the name of political opposition.
“…They Aren’t as Afraid Even when Their Wives Undergo Halala with other Men”
In a May 2022 post, Arun Yadav targeted Muslim women who were opposing surveys and excavations of mosques, making an obscene remark about them. Referring to the sensitive subject of “halala”, Yadav wrote: “As afraid as they are of the excavation of mosques, their wives aren’t even when they undergo halala with other men.”
In India, “halala” has long been the subject of an intense public debate. In Yadav’s post, the term was not merely used as part of a comment, but as a weapon to demean Muslim women.
More Islamophobia
In May 2022, Arun Yadav made another highly provocative post directly targeting Islam and the Muslim community. He wrote: “What kind of an ignorant community must those be whose Allah lives in temples stolen and looted from others?”
This was not simply a comment on the temple-mosque dispute. It was a direct attack on the Muslim community as a whole, using the dispute as a pretext. Yadav’s post was widely circulated.
“Who Got a Nine-month Recharge for Rs 500?”
One of the most shameful instances of Arun Yadav’s repeated targeting of Muslim women and making demeaning remarks about them emerged in May 2020. The case involved Jamia Millia Islamia student and activist Safoora Zargar.
Safoora was pregnant at the time and was imprisoned under the UAPA in connection with the 2020 Delhi riots case. While the detention of a pregnant woman was drawing criticism in India and abroad, Arun Yadav mocked Safoora’s pregnancy by comparing it to a mobile recharge plan.
Making a direct insinuation about her character, Yadav posted: “Who got a nine-month recharge for Rs 500?”
The matter did not end with the derogatory post. Yadav also actively endorsed other obscene and abusive comments posted under it. Arun Yadav was not the only BJP leader to make such remarks about Safoora’s pregnancy; several BJP leaders had also made demeaning comments about it.
The BJP’s IT Cell has long faced criticism over the spread of misinformation, targeting of minorities, promotion of regressive attitudes, circulation of controversial content and trolling. Its significance goes beyond the party’s own messaging: As one of the country’s most powerful political social media operations, it plays a significant role in shaping the information ecosystem — what millions of users see, discuss and believe online. Against that backdrop, Arun Yadav’s elevation is striking. A party that once disciplined him over communal posts has now entrusted him with a larger role in its national social media machinery. What was once grounds for his sacking has, years later, not come in the way of promotion.

The Indiana Pacers schedule typically comes with some built-in advantages. Their proximity to their Central Division foes keeps them low in the miles travelled department most years – last year, they had the fewest.
This year, that division is weaker in quality, adding another edge for the blue and gold. They’ll play both the Chicago Bulls and Milwaukee Bucks four times each, and they are two of the seven teams that have a projected win total below 30, per FanDuel Odds.
Yet their typical travel advantage is muted (it’s still the lowest number of miles travelled in the league) ever so slightly by one of their home games being played in Mexico City. And the rest of the Eastern Conference? It’s pretty good, making life more difficult for the Pacers as they try to bounce back to contention after a 19-63 season.
And they have one built-in disadvantage: Their NBA Cup group is hellish. The random drawing for the groups is based on records from last season, and the Pacers ended up in a five-team pod with the New York Knicks, Philadelphia 76ers, Cleveland Cavaliers, and Miami Heat.
The Heat acquired Giannis Antetokounmpo this summer. Tyrese Haliburton is back for the Pacers. Both LeBron James and Jaylen Brown are in Philly now, and the Cavs return a conference finals core while adding Peyton Watson. It’s a stacked group, only adding to Indiana’s challenging slate of games.
It all begins in New Orleans on Wednesday, October 21. “When I saw the schedule I was like, ‘oh wow’,” Haliburton said of the Pacers kicking off their season on the road, reacting to his return from injury not being in Indiana. “I was shocked to see that.”
Instead, the Pacers home opener will be two days later against the Dallas Mavericks. Their first nine games are fairly manageable in terms of perceived opponent quality, but things ramp up in difficulty from November 9 through the end of 2026.
What else is hard about the Pacers schedule?
InTheNo published a schedule breakdown for all 30 teams, and it reveals some of the other challenges baked into the Pacers 80-game slate (with two more to be added based on NBA Cup Group Stage results).
- The Pacers have 15 back-to-backs (two games in consecutive days) this season, tied for the second most in the league. Only five teams have more (16 each).
- Indiana has just nine games with a rest advantage (more days between games than their opponent) this season, the fourth-fewest in the league. Some teams have as many as 15.
- On the flip side, the Pacers have 12 games with a rest disadvantage, tied for the third most. Three teams have just seven. The Pacers have three more games with a rest disadvantage compared to an advantage, one of just five teams with a figure that low. The Pelicans rank last at negative five in this stat.
On the upside for the Pacers:
- The Pacers grade out slightly below average in how often they cross timezones this season. Shorter trips are good for any team.
- Only nine teams have fewer instances of three games in four nights. The Pacers have 20 of those.
The Pacers are well aware that they could be in for a slower start to the season as Haliburton gets back up to speed and Ivica Zubac gets fully integrated with his new teammates. “We’re also patient about this as well… Once he steps back on the floor, it’s not going to be instantly back to [the old] Tyrese,” Pacers general manager Chad Buchanan said in late June. “I think we all have to have some grace with him. He knows that’s going to be part of his recovery.”
Yet the demanding nature of the team’s schedule, both in terms of November and December opponents combined with their back-to-back count, makes a fast start important. Haliburton and Zubac won’t have much time to build chemistry that they very much need.
On the bright side for the Pacers, several of their back-to-backs feature one opponent that currently doesn’t project to win many games. They’ll need to pick up wins whenever they can in a stacked Eastern Conference – one that the Pacers hope they can win once again.

A video of Prime Minister Narendra Modi moving around a stage greeting people while the national anthem plays in the background is viral on social media, with users claiming that the Prime Minister was being disrespectful to the anthem.
An user on Facebook, Kumar Raj, shared the purported video on August 15, Independance Day, with Modi circled out. The post has garnered 2.3 million views. It was shared around 14,000 times and has received 30,500 reactions.
Activist Piyush Manush shared the same video on Facebook, which was viewed over 76,000 times.
Several X users also amplified the viral video, amplifying the same claim.
Fact Check
A keyframe in the viral video showed a screen placed on the podium which mentioned the location of the event as Jasauli Kharag, located in Bihar’s Siwan city. The date mentioned was June 20, 2025.
A relevant keyword search led us to the original video uploaded from the Prime Minister’s official YouTube channel. In this video dated June 21, 2025, Modi, seen in the same attire as the viral video, walked onto a stage while he was being introduced by the speaker. Amid cheers from the audience, he waved to them and shook hands with other dignitaries present on the stage. At no point can the national anthem be heard playing in the clip.
Thus, the claim that Prime Minister Narendra Modi disrespected the national anthem by walking around the stage while it played is misleading. The original video shows Modi being introduced by the speaker and waving to a cheering audience, with no national anthem playing in the clip. The anthem heard in the viral version was added later to the original video, altering the context of the footage to amplify a false claim.

A non-profit organisation based in New York City, representing a number of small supermarkets, grocery stores, as well as bodegas is suing the city and its mayor, Zohran Mamdani, in order to stop his planned opening of five grocery stores owned by the government.
The organisation, the Multicultural Business Coalition, has filed a class-action lawsuit in the New York County Supreme Court on Monday. The lawsuit alleges that the plan to open up these government-run stores violates the rights of small store owners and people belonging to minority communities who operate grocery stores since they would not be able to provide as much discount as the government store would.
Mark Jaffe, who is the general counsel of the group as well as the president of the Greater New York Chamber of Commerce, told CNN regarding the lawsuit, “You cannot expect hard-working small business owners to compete with a supermarket that isn’t going to pay rent, won’t have to pay an electric bill and won’t have to buy their products at full price,” adding, “They cannot possibly compete because no one will be subsidizing them.”
Mamdani was asked about the lawsuit in a press conference on Monday, where he said that he is confident his administration's plans regarding these stores are legal.
“We’re talking about delivering five city-run grocery stores in a city of eight and a half million people that has more than 1,000 grocery stores,” the NYC mayor said, as per CNN.
He also pointed out that two markets have opened up in Brooklyn and Manhattan using a similar model, but there has been no adverse effects on bodegas near them.
The markets Mamdani referred to are managed by NYC's Economic Development Corporation. This body rents out properties owned by the city at rates below the market to private vendors while also covering operational costs.
This is the third time that an affordability measure taken by Mayor Mamdani has faced legal resistance. Earlier this month, a collective of homeowners of NYC sued the administration as well the finance director of the city over the pied-à-terre taxes that were rolled out earlier this month.
The taxes have been blocked by a Staten Island judge.
The grocery stores will likely offer food staples at a 30% reduced rate so that those struggling with inflation can afford healthy food that is cheap. The mayor's office, when announcing details of this plan last month, said that these stores are being opened up in order to cut down on the average grocery bill of a New York family by around 15% or $90 per month.

The Tamil Nadu Assembly witnessed intense political debate following the release of the postmortem report regarding the deaths of three Tamil men in Karnataka. The report revealed that the deceased suffered severe injuries, broken ribs, and close-range gunshot wounds, contradicting claims of defensive firing by forest officials. The opposition questioned the government's response to the incident, demanding a thorough investigation, justice for the victims' families, and adequate compensation. While Karnataka authorities alleged the men were involved in illegal deer hunting, several parties have called for a detailed CBI inquiry to uncover the truth behind the firing in the forest region.
India Today accessed the autopsy reports of two individuals from Tamil Nadu killed in a jungle in Karnataka. The post-mortem report revealed shotgun injuries in the abdominal wall, pellet fragments, and multiple injuries on the left chest and right thigh, along with a rib fracture and air pockets in the carotid artery. The findings indicate that the firearms were discharged from close range, raising serious questions regarding the circumstances of the deaths. The incident has triggered a political row between Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, with demands for a detailed investigation and justice for the victims' families.
